The empirical prior is weak, and that is why it wins.
It comes out at a mean rate of 0.045 per epoch, resting on 0.8 of an event, since the scenarios’ fresh pages drain at rates from 0.002 to 0.5: each page’s own losses soon decide.
It gains most on the page whose start is wrong, 0.5 % against 1.2 % with whole chunks, and costs nothing on the pages whose start is right, although it ignores that start.
The moment-matched prior gains a little on pages mixed from sources that drain differently, a few tenths of a point on the two mixed pages, since it starts them unsure, but loses on the page whose source is sure of the wrong rate, 3.8 % against 1.2 % with whole chunks.
Moved content, being colder than its source, is that case more often than not, as the open questions note, so this draft starts moved content from the empirical prior too, until the sources’ rates are corrected for what their content’s survival says.

What would change
In either draft, the estimate becomes a posterior, the index is computed from it by (a), and every constant the estimate had becomes a parameter of the prior.

“Estimating how fast a page still drains” would keep a posterior: with one rate per page, the Gamma posterior’s two parameters in place of rho; with a static share, the discounted loss events and exposure, the touched and untouched chunks’ counts, and the class counts in place of the fit’s sums, and the mixture in place of the fit and its test.
The page table would keep a Drain of 12 bytes with one rate per page, against the single-rate draft’s 8, or 22 with a static share, against the static-share draft’s 18; with a static share, each statement’s record would also give a bit to mark its first loss.
The fold would keep two running averages per page kind, of the sizes of the ranges it supersedes and of their squares, for the dispersion \sigma, and five running sums over the pages it has watched through their first epochs, for the empirical prior.
A new page would start from the file’s empirical prior, where the drafts start it from a byte-weighted mean rate with a fixed weight; its moved content would start from its sources’ posteriors, moment-matched, only once those are corrected for moved content being colder than its source.
Ranking would compute a page’s index by (a) at each of its losses, from a table of \Phi computed once, and age it between losses as the drafts do; (b) needs no table, and cost a few points more in simulation only on pages of a few large chunks that die whole.
Bytes that consolidation moves out of a page would lower its live bytes without counting as losses; the posterior’s evidence on the rate stays, and with a static share, a chunk moved out leaves the page’s touched or untouched counts, whichever held it.
The constants would all become the prior’s:


























the drafts’ constantbecomesthe forgetting rate \betathe drift of the prior over the rate’s path, \delta = e^{-\beta}the starting estimate, and its weight of 1/\beta epochs or n_0learned: for fresh content, the file’s empirical prior; for moved content, its sources’ posteriorsthe static-share test’s cthe weight \nu_\pi of the prior on the draining fraction, in chunksthe floor R_\text{min}a background rate that the model asserts for all content
Open questions

Moved content is colder than its source.
The survivors of a cleaned page outlived what died around them, so they drain slower than the page they came from, whose posterior they bring; the moment-matched prior overstates their rate, if by less as the source’s own evidence is weaker.
Discounting a source’s rate by what its survival says about it would correct that.
A starting prior’s weight is exposure, fixed in byte-epochs.
On a page that drains fast, and shrinks, a strong start outweighs the page’s own losses for longer than the drafts’ averages of fractions let it; a learned prior is strong only where the file’s pages, or a page’s sources, agree.
Chunks of unequal size.
The mixture takes the untouched chunks at their mean size; the exact posterior weighs each subset of them by its own sizes, which a page of a few large chunks and many small ones would notice.
What a loss event is.
The dispersion treats every superseded range as one event, but one write that supersedes ranges on several pages, or several ranges of one page, is arguably one event; which grouping calibrates the posterior best is a question for measurement.
Pooling evidence across pages, beyond the start.
The empirical prior pools the file’s pages once, at a page’s start; the pages one flush wrote hold content the application wrote together, and a hierarchical prior, with the rates of one flush’s pages drawn around a rate shared by them, would go on lending each page the others’ losses.
A drift that fits the file.
A page’s next loss can make a ripe page unripe, so cleaning at the first ripe epoch cleans early; (c), which guards against every loss the page could still suffer, waits too long, and (c′), which weighs each by its predictive probability, does nothing, since the predictive trusts the posterior’s dip.
The dip comes from the prior’s drift, which forgets a page’s losses at \beta whether its rate changes or not.
The drift could be learned from the file as the prior’s other parameters are, for instance by how well each page’s posterior predicts its next losses, and a slower drift for pages whose losses stay steady would dip less.
Moved content’s classes.
Chunks moved from a source where they had been touched could arrive known to drain, and the draining fraction’s prior could come from the sources’ mixtures as the rate’s does, rather than from their shares with a fixed weight.
Epochs, not time.
The model counts rates per epoch, as the drafts do, and so shares their open question about the clock.

drafts/consolidation-from-statements.title: Sparse leaves, and consolidation from the statements up
drafts/consolidation-from-statements.content:
Status: a finding, resolved, and a direction for a redesign.
The consolidation policy of Consolidation, as kladde-rs implemented it, kept address-table leaves far emptier than data pages, so that 4 to 33 % of a file’s live pages were leaves it would not have needed had they been as full as its data pages.
Three causes did it, and each is gone.
The newest size rule let the statements that kept nearly empty leaves alive die, and removed the reason the cut refused them; that left leaves half empty, so that fuller ones would have saved 2 to 15 % of the live pages.
A fill floor on retiring leaves kept them so, and the budget loop no longer holds leaves to it, since retiring a leaf opens no page; leaves as full as the data pages would then have saved 0.4 to 6 % of the live pages.
Since kladde-rs also prices a leaf at its coverage, where it priced it at 1.25 times, the leaves come out about as full as the data pages under main’s churn floor, and fuller ones would save at most 2.8 %.
The three causes had one root, which is not a tuning constant but the way the policy interleaves three decisions, which page to retire, which statements to write, and where to put them, so that each constrains the others.
The second half of this draft starts over from the logical level of the address table and keeps the three apart.
The finding
Leaves now come out nearly as full as data pages: on every run but the small tiger, 62 to 69 % full against 72 to 82 %, and at most 38 % of them under half full.
On kladde-svg’s drawings, with svg-bench’s edits keeping to one part of the drawing at a time, a journal of 4 pages, and main’s consolidation at its default churn floor, at kladde-rs 714c602 on its branch defrag-shifts:



















































































































drawinglayouttable pagespages neededfillleaves under half fullunder a tenth fulldata pages under half fullshare of live pagestigerbase10.87.166 %23 %0 %4.7 %29 %tigerpacked5.43.769 %20 %1 %6.8 %27 %tigersmall0.50.234 %88 %6 %6.3 %3 %coat of armsbase25.716.062 %29 %0 %1.6 %28 %coat of armspacked14.79.363 %28 %0 %3.0 %29 %coat of armssmall2.41.667 %38 %1 %2.4 %5 %world mapbase131.381.462 %28 %0 %0.3 %27 %world mappacked80.050.563 %25 %0 %0.4 %23 %world mapsmall13.38.866 %29 %0 %0.3 %4 %
“Table pages” is their mean count, “pages needed” what their live statements would fill, “fill” the ratio of the two, and the last column the table pages’ share of the live pages.
The means are over the rows svg-bench records every 1000 edits, and the shares over histograms of every live page’s fill taken at the same flushes, by scratch instrumentation that did not change what was written.
Were the table pages as full as each run’s own data pages, the files would carry 0.4 to 6 % fewer live pages, the most on the world map in its base and packed layouts.
The small tiger is the exception to the ranges above: its statements need a fifth of a page, which the header mostly holds, and it has one leaf at a time, or none.
What kept leaves a few points emptier than data pages was their price, not a rule that kept them out.
A leaf’s restatements were estimated at 1.25 times its coverage, since restated statements were thought to lose their neighbours’ delta encoding, so at the default churn floor a leaf was a victim only up to 40 % full, where a data page is one up to 50 %; restated on their own, they take 0.94 to 1.05 times its coverage.
Cleaning edited drawings and texts measures every setting of main’s churn floor and of the three ripeness branches at the price of their coverage, at kladde-rs 7eb2ec4, under which the churn floor’s leaves come out about as full as its data pages.
Before the fill floor went
At kladde-rs e88fd47, the same branch before it stopped holding leaves to a fill floor, leaves stayed far emptier than data pages, and most of them sat between a fifth and a half full: the cut’s fillers took the sparsest into the room left in its last page, and the budget loop, which held the rest to a fill floor, took few of them.
The address-table pages averaged 44 to 60 % full, against 73 to 82 % for the data pages, and 40 to 67 % of them were less than half full at any time:



















































































































drawinglayouttable pagespages neededfillleaves under half fullunder a tenth fulldata pages under half fullshare of live pagestigerbase13.47.254 %51 %0 %4.3 %34 %tigerpacked6.33.860 %40 %1 %7.1 %31 %tigersmall0.80.221 %88 %44 %5.0 %5 %coat of armsbase30.515.952 %53 %0 %1.9 %31 %coat of armspacked17.09.355 %48 %0 %3.3 %32 %coat of armssmall3.41.648 %66 %4 %1.8 %7 %world mapbase183.881.444 %67 %0 %0.3 %34 %world mappacked103.050.649 %58 %0 %0.4 %28 %world mapsmall18.38.748 %65 %0 %0.3 %6 %
Were the table pages as full as each run’s own data pages, the files would have carried 2 to 15 % fewer live pages, and 8 to 15 % fewer on the coat of arms and the world map in their base and packed layouts.
Nearly empty leaves no longer stayed: on every run but the small tiger, at most 4 % of the leaves were under a tenth full, and in the base and packed layouts at most 3 % were under a fifth.
What stayed was the band between a fifth and a half full, which held 38 to 65 % of the leaves in the base and packed layouts, and holds 18 to 29 % since the fill floor went.
The world map in those layouts showed that part alone: its leaves were never nearly empty, and the new size rule raised their fill by 1 and 3 points only, where dropping the fill floor raised it by 18 and 14.
Before the newest size won
At kladde-rs 795b3b9, the same branch before it moved to the newest size rule, nearly empty leaves piled up: on the tiger and the coat of arms, 5 to 92 % of the leaves were under a tenth full, and leaves as full as the data pages would have saved 4 to 33 % of the live pages.
The same runs, then and at e88fd47:





















































































drawinglayouttable pages, thenfill, thenunder a tenth full, thenlive pages by e88fd47tigerbase15.848 %12 %−6 %tigerpacked13.132 %40 %−25 %tigersmall8.83 %92 %−32 %coat of armsbase37.246 %5 %−6 %coat of armspacked24.842 %10 %−12 %coat of armssmall9.119 %62 %−11 %world mapbase203.643 %0 %−4 %world mappacked122.446 %1 %−5 %world mapsmall24.038 %16 %−2 %
The data pages were as full then as at e88fd47, and as since, so the live pages saved are the leaves’.
The edited tiger that the variable-size evaluation, on the kladde-docs branch defrag-shifts, reports closing with 41 table pages for 2,265 statements likely showed the same effect.
On the small tiger, the leaves piled up for a dozen flushes and then vanished at once.
Its table pages climbed to 11 to 19 at the peaks of the cycle, holding between 100 and 2,800 bytes of live statements in all; almost no table page was rewritten until compaction mode turned on, and that mode then rewrote 11 to 18 of them within one or two flushes, after which the count fell to one or two and started climbing again.
At e88fd47, it held at most two leaves at any flush, and since the fill floor went, one.
Why leaves stayed empty
Three causes kept leaves nearly empty until the newest size won, and one of them, the fill floor, kept them half empty until it went too.
The budget loop held a table offer to the data pages’ fill floor
The budget loop took a page rewrite only when the restatements of its victims would fill a whole leaf to 1 − θ, 95 %, as it takes data victims only when their survivors fill a whole data page.
kladde-rs’ implementation-notes.md recorded it: “a budgeted page rewrite opens no page of its own … the budget counts it as a page all the same, and holds it to the fill floor like a data offer.”
For a data page the floor has a reason: evacuating victims into a page the flush opens for them costs that page, and a page that closes half empty is a page wasted.
For a table page it has none: a page rewrite opens no page, since what it restates joins the flush’s dirty set and the cut lays it out among everything else the flush states.
Its cost is the restatements’ bytes, which the churn floor already weighs against the page it frees.
The floor turned the cheapest victims into the hardest to take: an offer was made of whole leaves at most half live, best score first, and needed 95 % of a leaf in restatements.
A file whose leaves held less than that in all, such as the small tiger, could never pass it, however empty its leaves were.
Where the leaves held more, an offer passed only where whole leaves happened to add up to 95 % of a leaf: a leaf between two-fifths and a half full restates into 50 to 62 % of one, by the estimate of 1.25 times its coverage, so two of them did not fit together, and one alone failed the floor.
What the floor refused waited for the cut’s fillers, which take leaves only into the room left in the cut’s last page, sparsest first.
That room was 1.6 to 2.3 KB on average in these runs, enough for one leaf up to 31 to 45 % full, so the sparsest leaves went soon, and those fuller than the room allowed waited for an offer that passed, which is the band the finding showed at e88fd47.
The fillers rewrote 52 to 96 % of the leaves rewritten in each run, and the budget loop met a table offer that passed the churn floor but not the fill floor 87 to 1,283 times per run.
Held to the churn floor alone, leaves come out nearly as full as data pages, and so the floor went.
Since kladde-rs 714c602, and in Consolidation, an offer of leaves passes on the churn floor alone, and costs the budget the pages its restatements take rather than a page; a leaf reclaims its page less the room its restatements take, so that at the default churn floor it is a victim up to 40 % full.
The finding above shows the result: in the base and packed layouts, the leaves are 62 to 69 % full where they were 44 to 60 %, the files carry 4 to 10 % fewer live pages, and the flushes write 3 to 8 % more bytes per edit, restating leaves that the floor had kept waiting.
Leaves were kept alive for the size alone
Before the newest size won, much of what kept nearly empty leaves alive was statements that fixed sizes, and those could not die while anything older about their id was physically present.
On the tiger and the coat of arms at 795b3b9, 37 to 56 % of the live statements in leaves under a tenth full were Shrinks and Tombstones, and none a Grow; on the small tiger it was 95 %, and 97 % of its nearly empty leaves, counted at every flush, held nothing else live.
Under the old size rule, a Shrink stayed its id’s anchor, pinned, until a newer Shrink or Tombstone replaced it, since without it the extents of older statements still in leaves would raise the size again; and a re-allocated id’s tombstone stayed the anchor of its new incarnation.
Under the new rule, the newest statement that states the size wins, so an older one loses its pin as soon as a newer one states the size, and the cut makes every content statement that ends at its id’s size sizing, so that happens whenever the cut states the id’s tail.
A re-allocated id’s tombstone dies once the cut states the new incarnation’s size.
A leaf that held only such statements then falls to zero coverage, and the cut unlinks it without rewriting anything.
That alone, with the fillers’ check below still in place, cut the small tiger’s table pages from 8.8 to 1.9 on average, and the packed tiger’s from 13.1 to 8.5.
The cut’s fillers refused every leaf that named an id the flush touched
The leaves that the budget loop does not take are meant to go as fillers: whole table victims that fit the room of the cut’s last page, which costs nothing.
That room was ample: in 8000 edits of the small tiger, logged at every flush, it was 800 to 3,500 bytes in nearly every one, and every nearly empty leaf would have fit.
But kladde-rs took a filler only if the flush touched none of the ids the leaf names, and almost none qualified: on the small tiger, of up to 13 leaves under a quarter full, 0 were eligible in every flush, and on the coat of arms in its base layout, 0 to 2 of 2 to 14.
The check read a leaf’s ids by decoding every statement still encoded in it, dead ones included.
So a leaf with 4 to 25 bytes of live statements still named 74 to 251 ids, while each flush of the tiger touches 43 to 48 of its roughly 120 ids, and some named id was always among them.
Since kladde-rs def217a, the fillers take any leaf the flush has not rewritten already.
Neither that nor the dying size statements suffices alone: with the new size rule but the check, 3 to 17 % of the leaves of the tiger and the coat of arms in their base and packed layouts were still under a tenth full, and 66 and 47 % in their small layouts.
The check guarded against stating an id’s size twice in one epoch, which the new size rule lets the cut avoid without it; nor could the dead statements it read ever be part of a conflict.
The next two sections show both.
What the check guarded against
A filler’s victim can hold the size statement of an id the cut has already laid out statements for, and the cut must then state that id’s size again, while one epoch holds at most one size statement per id.
Content restatements cannot conflict, since a filler restates only fragments its victim still owns, which the flush has not taken.
And the size statement need not: the cut decides which of its statements states each id’s size only once the fillers are known, since the sizing bit changes no statement’s encoded length, and adds a Size to the last page only for an id none of whose content statements ends at its size.
So the cut can take any leaf as a filler, and kladde-rs dropped the check in def217a, once it had moved to these rules.
Under the old size rule, the check had a reason: the statement an id needed depended on which pages survived, a Grow if its anchor stayed and a Shrink to replace the anchor if a filler retired it, and one epoch could not hold both, so a filler chosen after the layout could change a statement laid out already.
Dead statements cannot block a rewrite
Dropping a dead statement never changes what the file resolves to; it only releases pins that newer statements hold on its account.
A statement is dead when no fragment resolves through it and it is not its id’s size statement, pins == 0, and the droppability rule is exactly that dropping such a statement leaves the resolution unchanged.
What a dead statement can still do is keep a newer statement alive, as an example shows:

At epoch 4, allocation 8 holds 40 bytes, stated by Ref*(8, 0, 40, c) in leaf L3.
At epoch 6, the application freed it: Tombstone(8), in leaf L4.

Ref*@4 is now dead, but physically present, and so it holds the tombstone: mentions(8) counts both statements, and a tombstone keeps its pin until mentions falls to 1, since without it Ref*@4 would be 8’s newest statement, and 8 would exist again with its old 40 bytes.
Dropping L3 drops Ref*@4, mentions(8) falls to 1, and the tombstone may retire: nothing resurfaces, which is the order the pins enforce, the denied statement first and its denier after.
Where the flush touched the id, a dead statement can at most make one of the flush’s own statements unnecessary.
If the flush frees an id and states its Tombstone, and a filler drops the last older statement naming the id, the new tombstone has nothing left to deny: a redundant statement of a few bytes, which the next rewrite of its page drops, never a wrong one.
If the flush allocates 8 anew, the new incarnation states its size and every byte below it, and dropping Ref*@4 changes nothing the cut has decided.
So the dead statements a leaf still encodes are no reason to keep it.
The check read them because it learned a leaf’s ids by decoding the page, which lists dead statements beside live ones, rather than by asking which of the leaf’s statements are live.
Compaction mode collected them, in bursts
Compaction mode offers the highest live page ahead of every victim, whatever its fill, and an offer holding it passes both floors.
Once free pages below the tail pass a quarter of the file, the mode works down the file’s tail, page by page; the nearly empty leaves that the other paths left behind went with it, and once the mode switched off, they piled up again.
That was the sawtooth on the small tiger, and why its file held 8.8 table pages on average for 0.2 pages’ worth of statements; with no nearly empty leaves left for the mode to collect, it held 0.8 at e88fd47, and holds 0.5 since the fill floor went.
Data pages are not hit the same way
Data pages almost never fall below half full: 0.3 to 7.1 % of them, against 40 to 88 % of the leaves at e88fd47.
They escape the fill floor: a data offer that whole victims leave short takes one more victim and cuts its survivors at the page boundary, carrying the rest into the next page, where a table offer held to the floor could take whole leaves only.
And free filling takes any whole data victim that fits the room of any data page the flush writes, where the fillers have the room of one leaf.
Their histogram’s one feature, 14 to 25 % of them between 50 and 60 % full, is the default churn floor’s own threshold, which takes victims at most half live.
But the same interleaving shapes them: a data victim is taken only if its survivors fit the room of a page being written, or fill a budgeted page to 95 % together with other victims, so which pages are cleaned depends on how their survivors pack, not only on what cleaning them is worth.
Nothing measured here shows that doing harm on data pages; the redesign below removes it on both sides alike.
The underlying error
The policy makes three decisions in one interleaved pass, which page to retire, which statements to write, and where to put them, and lets each constrain the others.

Whether a leaf was retired depended on whether its restatements filled a page, which is a question about where they go.
That was the fill floor, which no longer holds leaves.
Which leaves the cut could retire depended on the statements it had already laid out.
The fillers’ check, which enforced it, is gone.
The statements for an id were decided before the set of retired pages was final, so a later victim could contradict them.
Since the newest size wins, the cut settles which of its statements states each id’s size once the fillers are known, and content restatements never could conflict.

Each of these was locally sensible, and the later ones were added to keep the interleaving correct, but together they made the cheapest victims unreachable.
The new size rule removed the two that guarded correctness, and the third, a matter of policy alone, went once it was clear that it protected no page.
The same pattern makes the policy hard to reason about at all: the budget loop, free filling, the cut’s fillers, the rotating window, and compaction mode each choose victims under different constraints, and each constraint comes from a decision made elsewhere.
Possible solutions, from the statements up
This section ignores how consolidation and the flush after its fold work today, and starts only from what statements mean.
What a writer must guarantee
A file’s address table is the set of statements in its live table pages, each at its page’s epoch, and their resolution defines the fragment map: each id’s existence, its size, and for each byte, the statement that wins it and so its content.
Call the statements S, and the fragment map they resolve to R(S).
Statements may contradict each other across epochs, since the newest wins at every probe; within one epoch, they may not.
A flush at epoch e starts from the file’s statements S and from the map M that the application’s writes since the last flush define: R(S) updated by the fold.
It ends with a new set of live pages, whose statements S' must satisfy R(S') = M, and whose data pages hold every byte M resolves into the file.
Consolidation is the choice of which pages to give up, and what to write in their place, so that this still holds.
That is three tasks, each of which needs only the results of the ones before it.
Task 1: choose the victims
Choose a set V of pages to retire, table and data pages alike, the current header always among them, by what each costs and what it gains, and nothing else.
Retiring a data page costs the live bytes it holds, which must be written again elsewhere, and retiring a table page costs the statements that must be written because it is gone, which task 3 infers and which are usually its live statements’ worth.
Either gains a page.
Nothing about packing or layout enters the choice, since any V is feasible: task 3 can always state the resolved map again, as shown below.
So a page whose live content is nearly nothing is the best victim there is, whichever kind it is, and is taken first; a page of dead statements costs nothing at all.
How to rank the rest, by a churn floor, by ripeness, or by any other estimate of what waiting saves, is a separate question, and so is how many pages a flush may retire, which bounds its work.
Returning space to the file system belongs here too: preferring the highest pages, as compaction mode does, is a ranking, not a mechanism of its own.
Task 2: combine the victims with the fold and the header
What survives is the statements in the pages not retired, S_keep, and the data bytes in the data pages not retired; everything else that M needs must be written.

Data: every byte of M that resolves into a retired data page, or into the flush’s own new content, must be written into a new data page.
Statements: a set N of statements at epoch e must be found such that R(S_keep ∪ N) = M.
The retired header’s statements are among those that went, so whatever it stated that is still true must be inferred again like anything else.

Task 3: write the result
Writing out is two independent policies: one packs the data bytes into new data pages, and one infers N and lays it out into new table pages.
Data pages
The bytes to write are known once task 2 is done, so packing them is a bin-packing choice alone: in key order, as today, or sorted by temperature first, as the survivor-classes draft proposes, so that content that dies soon and content that waits do not share pages.
Their addresses are what N’s Ref statements then point to.
Statements, by inference
N is what a reader needs beyond S_keep to resolve to M, and it can be inferred id by id, by comparing what S_keep alone resolves to with M.
N’s epoch e is newer than everything in S_keep, so every statement in N wins over every surviving one where both match.
For each id:

Existence.
If M says the id does not exist, N needs Tombstone(id) exactly when some statement in S_keep still names the id; otherwise nothing.
If M says it exists, N needs at least one statement for it whenever S_keep’s newest statement naming it is a tombstone, or none names it; the size rule below provides one.
Content.
For every byte below the id’s size in M, the winner among S_keep’s statements, the newest that matches, either already gives M’s content, or N must cover the byte with a Ref, Inline, or Zero.
A byte whose winner sat in a retired page has no winner left among those that won it before, so it is covered again unless an older surviving statement happens to give the same content.
Size.
The size is what the id’s newest size statement states, so N needs one exactly when M’s size differs from what S_keep’s newest size statement states — because the id was resized, or that statement went with a victim, or the id is new.
It is the content statement in N that ends at the size, made sizing, or Size(id, size) if there is none.

Such an N always exists, and never breaks the rules of one epoch.
The plain solution states, for every id whose resolution under S_keep differs from M at all, Tombstone(id) if it no longer exists, and otherwise content statements covering all of [0, size), the last one sizing: it states the size, and the content statements win every probe below it.
Those are one size statement per id and content statements on disjoint ranges below the size, which is all that one epoch’s rules ask.
The inference above only leaves out of that solution what S_keep already says, so it obeys the rules too, and no choice of victims can make the vocabulary fall short.
Inferring the smallest N needs nothing beyond the fragment map and each id’s size statement.
The content half is local: the fragment map already records which statement each byte resolves through, and so which page, and a byte needs a statement in N only when that page is retired or the byte changed.
The size half is local too: each id has one size statement, and it needs stating again only when the size changed or its page is retired.
Laying N out is then a packing problem alone.
N is final when layout starts, so the header can take the hottest statements, as it does now, and the leaves the rest, in key order or sorted by temperature, every page full but the last, with nothing to revisit.
The room the last page has left is not filled by choosing more victims after the fact; if it should be used, task 1 can plan for it, since the restatements of a table victim, nearly empty or not, cost about what its live statements take.
A spec change that would make it simpler still: statements keep their epoch
Let each statement carry its own epoch, so that consolidation can move a statement to a new page without changing what it means.
Today a statement’s epoch is its page’s, so a statement moved to a new page is re-stamped as newest: it now outranks everything it used to lie beneath, and the writer must work out what else to state so that the rest still resolves the same way.
That re-stamping is why retiring a table page means deriving its restatements rather than copying them: a restated statement changes its rank, so the cut must state content as resolved truth, merged with whatever else the flush states, and state the size and the tombstone again where the victim held them.
With an epoch per statement, retiring a table page is copying its live statements, unchanged, into the flush’s pages.
They resolve exactly as before, since no two statements change their order, and the dead ones are left behind, which by the droppability rule changes nothing either.
Evacuating a data page copies its referrers the same way, each with its new address and its old epoch, since the bytes it points to are the same.
Only the flush’s own changes are stated at its epoch, so task 3’s inference is needed only for the ids the application touched, against a state the writer knows in full, and the size statements in the header stop moving every flush.
What it would cost and change:

Bytes.
A page would hold one or more runs, each of one epoch, given as a varint below the page’s own, and each sorted by (id, offset), as a page is now; a page the flush writes from its own changes alone is one run, as today, and a page of copied statements has a run per epoch it copies from.
The rule of one epoch, no conflicts within it, would speak of statements of one epoch wherever they lie; a writer keeps it by retiring the page it copies from in the same commit, so that the copy and the original never both count.
Open’s merge would merge runs instead of pages; it already relies on each run having one epoch and being sorted by key, and only the number of runs grows.
Validation would add that no statement’s epoch exceeds its page’s.
What estimates read from a page’s epoch, the age of its content, would come from its statements instead, which is finer than today.

No rule of one epoch needs relaxing for consolidation’s sake, with or without this change.
What this would remove

The cut’s fillers, since the statements are inferred once the victims are known, and nothing laid out is ever revisited.
The distinction between free filling, budgeted pages, and compaction mode as ways to choose victims: one ranking chooses every victim, and the room left in pages is a packing matter.

Open questions

Whether an epoch per run pays for itself: its bytes against the restatements and re-stamped header statements it saves, which svg-bench’s drawings could measure.
How victims are ranked once packing no longer constrains them, and how much a flush may retire, which bounds both its work and how far the file can fall behind; this is where ripeness, survivor classes, and the churn floor’s price of space come back in.
Without the fill floor on table offers, main’s churn floor fills the drawings’ live pages to about nine tenths at λ = 0.25 (the evaluation).
Whether the rotating window survives: it restates a key range for description density, which in this frame is a victim too, a range rather than a page, ranked by what its restatement saves.

drafts/cpp.title: A C++ implementation
drafts/cpp.content:
Status: the design of kladde-cpp, now built.
kladde-cpp records it as built, with the places where building it went another way, and Porting kladde to C++ and into Inkscape what building it found; the decisions below are settled, and kept for their reasoning.
It answers two questions that were open from the start — what stands in for Rust’s #[derive(Durable)], and how C++ types map to the schema’s enums — and raises a third that turned out to matter as much: how long a handle to a value may live.
The specification is not frozen, and finding out what a second language needs from it is half the point of a second implementation.
So this draft does not take the specification as given: where a change to it would make kladde-cpp simpler or its API more idiomatic, Changes to the specification proposes it, with what it costs the format and kladde-rs.
Four candidates came up, besides a few smaller points; one of them, on how an enum’s variants hold their fields, changes how C++ maps enums enough that the sections on enums assume it, and say what they would do without it.
Like every draft, it mixes what belongs in kladde-rs’s counterpart of a language section with what may turn out to be a proposal for Implementation or Specification; the open questions at the end say which parts might travel.
What drives the design
A library for many applications, with Inkscape as the first.
The first demo is a fork of Inkscape that edits a kladde file with an SVG schema and has no save button: every dragged control point and every keystroke is durable when the call that made it returns.
So the design has to suit an existing, large, object-oriented C++ code base that holds pointers to its document’s nodes for as long as it likes, and not only programs written for kladde from scratch.
C++20 as the baseline, C++26 reflection as the destination.
Inkscape builds with C++20, and the compilers of today’s long-term-support distributions (GCC 13 on Ubuntu 24.04) know nothing of reflection.
Static reflection is in C++26, and compiler support for it is arriving (GCC 16 has an implementation behind -freflection at the time of writing), so the design must work without it and get better with it, without a second API.
Idiomatic C++, not Rust transliterated.
The overview asks for this, and the differences that matter are few but deep:



































RustC++deriving code from a typeprocedural macros see the type’s tokensthe preprocessor sees tokens it cannot parse; C++26 reflection sees the typeexclusive access while mutatingenforced by the borrow checkera convention, checkable at run time in debug buildslong-lived references into a structurefight the borrow checkerordinary, and expected by existing codetrait objectsneed an enum and a dispatch attribute to be durableclass hierarchies with virtual functions are the native idiomerrorsResultexceptions, which Durability already names for C++
Everything below the typed values is the reference algorithms, ported.
The storage engine — pages, span table, rope, journal, flush, consolidation — is language-agnostic by construction, and Implementation describes it closely enough to port.
Most of the effort of kladde-cpp is there, and C++ asks almost nothing of it that Rust does not; the exceptions are a flush that does not block the caller and values detached for longer than a transaction, both of which an interactive document editor needs more than C++ does.
This draft is mostly about the part on top, where C++ and Rust part ways.
Three layers

























layerholdsformthe storethe file format, durability, journal, flush, consolidation; positions and bytes onlya compiled library with a small non-template interfacethe schemadescriptors, their canonical encoding, fingerprints, and later resolutioncompiled, plus constexpr helpers that build descriptors from typestyped valueswhich C++ types are durable, how they encode, and the handles that mutate themheader-only templates over the store’s interface
The store knows nothing about types, exactly as in the reference algorithms: it takes write, splice, move and paste at positions in the sequence, opens and ends transactions and batches, and flushes.
Keeping it free of templates keeps compile times and code size of applications down, keeps the hard part testable on its own against a plain byte vector (the differential oracle), and gives it a C ABI later almost for free, should another language want to bind it.
Why a native port rather than binding kladde-rs.
Linking the Rust store through a C ABI would be quicker to a first demo, and is a fair fallback if the port lags.
But a second, independent implementation is how the specification finds out where it is ambiguous, which is worth more at this stage than the code it saves; and a C++ library that needs a Rust toolchain to build is a hard sell to the applications it is for.
The shape of the API
#include <kladde/kladde.hpp>
 
struct Contact {
    std::string email;
    kladde::Vector<PhoneNumber> phones;
    bool starred = false;
};
KLADDE_STRUCT(Contact, email, phones, starred)
 
void example() {
    auto file = kladde::File<Contact>::create("contacts.kladde",
                                              Contact{.email = "ada@example.com"});
 
    Contact const& contact = file.get();   // reads: the plain value, no cost
    std::size_t n = contact.phones.size();
 
    auto c = file.edit();                  // kladde::Mut<Contact>
    c.starred().set(true);                 // a Write of one byte
    c.email().insert(0, "lady.");          // one Splice
    c.phones().push_back(Mobile{"555-0100"});  // one transaction
}
kladde::File<T> is the root, Rust’s Kladde<T>: it owns the value and the store behind it, and is movable but not copyable.
get() hands out T const&, so reading is plain C++: members, iterators, range-for, algorithms.
kladde::Mut<T> is the handle that mutates, the guard of kladde-rs under a name that says what it is for.
It holds a pointer to the in-memory value and the value’s region of the sequence, and every mutating method records first and changes memory second.
It dereferences to T const&, so reading through a handle works as reading the value does.
The only way to mutate a value inside a File is through a Mut, as in Rust; C++ cannot forbid const_cast, but it does not have to make it easy.
The analog of #[derive(Durable)]
What the derive gives a Rust type is five things: the encoding, the decoding, the descriptor, the fixed size, and the guard with an accessor per field.
The first four follow mechanically from the list of fields — their names, their types, and how to reach them — and the fifth needs names that the program can call.
So the question is how C++ gets at the list of fields.
The options









































optionC++how it looksverdicthand-written traitsanyspecialize kladde::Durable<T> by handalways available; the escape hatch, as in Rusta describing macro20KLADDE_STRUCT(Contact, email, phones, starred)the baselinemember enumeration without a macro20nothing, for aggregates, by the tricks of Boost.PFRtoo fragile for something that decides a file formatcode generation from a schema fileanyan IDL and a generator, as Protocol Buffers dowrong default for a code-first library; right for a later toolstatic reflection26struct [ [=kladde::durable] ] Contact { ... };the destination
Recommended: one internal description of a type, kladde::describe<T>, fed by a macro today and by reflection later.
Everything else in the library — encoding, decoding, descriptors, fixed sizes, handles — is written once against that description, so a type described by the macro and a type described by reflection behave identically and have the same fingerprint, and an application can switch per type when its compiler allows.
The macro
KLADDE_STRUCT follows the pattern that C++ libraries have converged on for exactly this job, Boost.Describe’s BOOST_DESCRIBE_STRUCT and nlohmann/json’s NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_NON_INTRUSIVE: it sits next to the type, in the type’s namespace, and lists the members to persist, in encoding order.
It expands to two things, found through argument-dependent lookup so that the user never opens namespace kladde:
// Roughly what KLADDE_STRUCT(Contact, email, phones, starred) expands to.
constexpr auto kladde_describe(kladde::type_t<Contact>) {
    return kladde::struct_description("Contact",
        kladde::field<&Contact::email>("email"),
        kladde::field<&Contact::phones>("phones"),
        kladde::field<&Contact::starred>("starred"));
}
 
template <class Self>   // mixed into kladde::Mut<Contact>
struct kladde_accessors_Contact {
    auto email()   { return static_cast<Self&>(*this).template at<&Contact::email>(); }
    auto phones()  { return static_cast<Self&>(*this).template at<&Contact::phones>(); }
    auto starred() { return static_cast<Self&>(*this).template at<&Contact::starred>(); }
};
template <class Self>
kladde_accessors_Contact<Self> kladde_accessors(kladde::type_t<Contact>, Self*);
The description is a constexpr list of member pointers and names, from which templates compute the encoding, the decoding, the descriptor and the fixed size at compile time.
The accessors give c.email() its name, which is what Rust’s email_mut() is, with completion in any editor that expands macros.
Where a field’s name collides with a method of Mut itself, such as a field named set, the member pointer reaches it instead: c.at<&Contact::set>().
auto [email, phones, starred] = c.parts(); hands out the handles of all fields at once, as Rust’s parts() does, through the tuple protocol that structured bindings use.
A second form goes inside the class, KLADDE_MEMBERS(email, phones, starred), for types whose persisted members are private: it defines the same two things as a hidden friend and a nested template, which may name private members.
What the macro buys over Rust’s derive, besides working at all:

Members it does not list are not persisted.
A cache, a handle, a pointer to a widget stay in the C++ type and out of the file, with no hand-written implementation; Rust’s derive has no attribute for this yet.
Field names on file can differ from names in C++, through a longer form, KLADDE_FIELD(member, "name").
Field names are fingerprinted and are what evolution reconciles by, so this matters for files that applications in two languages, with two naming conventions, share.
Options ride along as arguments: a field held in its fixed form, a single-field struct marked transparent, a struct marked bounded, as #[kladde(...)] attributes do in Rust.

What it costs is that the member list repeats the declaration, and nothing checks that it lists every member that should be listed.
That is the price C++20 asks of every library of this kind, and the reason to move on as soon as reflection allows.
Reflection
With C++26, the description comes from the type itself:
struct [ [=kladde::durable] ] Contact {
    std::string email;
    kladde::Vector<PhoneNumber> phones;
    [ [=kladde::fixed] ] std::uint64_t revision = 0;
    [ [=kladde::skip] ] Cache cache;   // not persisted
};
Annotations are written [ [=…] ] on these pages, which C++ accepts as readily as the usual form without the spaces, because the site would take the usual form for a link.
The annotation is the opt-in, as #[derive(Durable)] is: a file format should not change because someone added a member to an unrelated struct.
kladde::describe<T> walks the non-static data members with std::meta::nonstatic_data_members_of, takes their names from identifier_of, and their options from annotations.
Reflection cannot generate member functions, so c.email() stays the macro’s; but std::meta::define_aggregate can generate a struct with a data member per field, which gives c.parts().email with its name, and that is the form to recommend for reflected types.
Generics, and what is durable
A class template is described once, with a variant of the macro that takes its template head, and is durable wherever its parameters are.
Lifetimes have no counterpart in C++, and non-type parameters can simply be allowed, since the description is computed per instantiation.
Which C++ types are durable
Standard types are durable wherever the in-memory value needs nothing that a standard type cannot hold, and kladde’s own containers take over where it does.
Rust refuses String and Vec to make durability visible in the type; in C++ the handle, Mut<std::string>, is a type of its own whatever the value is, so the plain type costs nothing in clarity and lets existing types persist unchanged.
@Claude: the rust API has grown over many iterations with vastly different designs of kladde. An earlier design of kladde made it impossible to use String, Vec, or HashMap directly in a durable struct, which motivated the dedicated types DurableString, DurableVec, DurableHashMap, and possibly others back then. But I’m not sure if these dedicated types are still necessary in today’s design of kladde. Which of the Durable types that kladde-rs defines are still necessary and which could be replaced with their standard rust types without cost?
Claude: DurableString could be replaced by String at no cost, DurableVec<T> by Vec<T> for fixed-size T only, and DurableMap and DurableBlob are still necessary.

DurableString is a String and nothing else (struct DurableString(String)), and its guard is a type of its own anyway, so impl Durable for String in kladde-persist, where the trait lives, would give the same encoding, the same guard and the same cost.
The only argument left for it is the one the tutorial gives, that a field’s type should say it is durable, which a guard of its own already says.
DurableVec<T> is a Vec<T> plus a Fenwick tree of the elements’ sizes, and the tree is empty for a fixed-size T.
A Vec<T> has nowhere to keep the tree, so it can stand in only where no tree is needed; Rust has no specialization, so that would take a marker trait implemented by every fixed-size type (the derive can implement it where all fields are fixed-size, as it implements Bounded), and impl<T: FixedSize> Durable for Vec<T>.
For variable-size elements a Vec<T> would have to find element i by summing the sizes before it, O(m) per guard, which is what the tree exists to avoid.
DurableMap is necessary: a HashMap iterates in an order that changes when it rehashes, while the file keeps entries in one order that each entry’s position depends on, and neither HashMap nor BTreeMap can keep a Fenwick tree of entry sizes by rank.
DurableBlob is necessary as an opt-in: impl<T: Serialize> Durable for T would conflict with every other implementation, so a serde type needs a wrapper to say “persist me through serde”; it is also where the serialized bytes are cached.
Option, Box, tuples and the primitives are already the standard types, and Fixed<T> is a choice of encoding that only a type can carry.

Decision: remove DurableString; implement Durable for Vec<T> where T: Durable with a const assertion that T::FIXED_SIZE.is_some(). Update the documentation and any examples in the tutorial, if applicable. DurableVec<T> stays and should work on all T: Durable, even fixed-sized ones. For fixed-size T it should not allocate a Fenwick tree (but it still has the field for the empty Fenwick tree).
So kladde-rs could follow the C++ table: String for text, Vec<T> for fixed-size elements, and a dedicated vector for variable-size ones.

A std::vector of variable-size elements is refused at compile time with a message that names kladde::Vector, rather than accepted with a hidden linear scan: it is the one place where the plain type would quietly cost what kladde exists to avoid.
Mut<std::string>::set splices only what changed: it finds the common prefix and suffix of the old and the new text, which costs one pass over memory the application has just written, and records one splice of the middle.
Code that sets a whole string at every change, such as code that writes a path’s whole d attribute for every step of a dragged control point, then records a few bytes rather than the whole attribute, without having to be rewritten in terms of edits.
This belongs in every implementation’s text type and is worth proposing for the built-in containers.
Decision: yes, state this as a guarantee in the spec for Text and Blob. More precisely, the guarantee should be that setting them to a new whole value should result in records that edit at most the smallest subrange that contains all changes (there’s probably a more eloquent way to phrase this). Whether an implementation goes further and tries to detect if the changes are limited to multiple subranges that are far enough apart to justify more complicated optimizations is up to the implementation, but the spec should guarantee an optimization for the common case where some substring of a larger string (or Blob) has changed and the application author is simply too lazy to call the appropriate splice method and instead resets the whole string.
Claude: Agreed, with one refinement for blobs, and one question of where it goes.
The guarantee holds as you state it for Text, which has no count: one splice of the smallest range that holds every changed byte.
A blob is an Opaque without a fixed size, whose encoding starts with its length, so a blob whose length changes changes its first bytes as well, and the smallest range holding every change would then reach from the length to the last change — possibly the whole blob.
So for anything with a length prefix the guarantee should be stated per part: the length is rewritten on its own, and the payload is spliced in the smallest range that holds its changes, which is two records in one transaction.
The natural home is the specification’s guarantees an implementation must provide, beside the asymptotic complexity it already promises; I have not written it there yet, since the blob refinement is yours to accept.
@Claude: agreed, with one nit-pick: the phrasing shouldn’t make it necessary to set the length on its own. If a blob changes at its start, an implementation may decide to write the length prefix and the changed content in one go.
Enums
The schema has one kind of enum, a discriminant followed by the fields of the variant it selects, and C++ has three ways to say it.
All three map to the same descriptor kind, so which one a program uses is invisible in the file: one program may read with a std::variant what another wrote from a class hierarchy, as long as names and discriminants agree — a descriptor describes a representation, not an identity.
enum class: variants without fields
enum class Join : std::uint8_t { miter, round, bevel };
KLADDE_ENUM(Join, miter, round, bevel)
The discriminant is the enumerator’s value, the variant’s name its identifier, and the fixed form’s discriminant width the underlying type’s.
The macro exists only to supply names; with reflection, std::meta::enumerators_of does, and the annotation [ [=kladde::durable] ] is all a reflected enum needs.
std::variant: a tagged union with value semantics
struct Mobile   { std::string digits; };
struct Landline { std::string digits; };
KLADDE_STRUCT(Mobile, digits)
KLADDE_STRUCT(Landline, digits)
 
using PhoneNumber = std::variant<Mobile, Landline>;
Each alternative is a variant, named after the alternative’s described name, whose payload is the alternative — which presumes variants that hold one value, the first of the proposed changes to the specification.
With it, one rule maps every Rust enum: kladde-svg’s Node, which mixes a tuple variant holding a struct, Element(Element), a tuple variant holding text, Text(Str), and a struct variant, ProcessingInstruction { target, value }, is in C++
struct Text    { std::string content; };   // transparent: a Text is its string
struct Comment { std::string content; };
struct ProcessingInstruction { std::string target; std::string value; };
KLADDE_TRANSPARENT(Text, content)
KLADDE_TRANSPARENT(Comment, content)
KLADDE_STRUCT(ProcessingInstruction, target, value)
 
using Node = std::variant<Element, Text, Comment, ProcessingInstruction>;
with the same descriptor and the same fingerprint.
Without the change, every alternative needs a choice, and nothing in the C++ type can make it: today a Rust tuple variant Element(Element) holds one field "0" of type Element, while a struct variant ProcessingInstruction { target, value } holds two fields of its own, and the two descriptors differ although the encodings agree.
kladde-cpp would then hold each alternative as a field "0" by default, which matches tuple variants and kladde-rs’s enums in place of trait objects, and offer a flattening option per alternative for struct variants; Node would need it on ProcessingInstruction alone.
Discriminants default to the alternative’s index, which is fragile in exactly the way Rust’s implicit discriminants are: inserting an alternative renumbers the ones after it.
KLADDE_VARIANT(PhoneNumber, (Mobile, 1), (Landline, 2)) pins them, and the encoding-stability advice of kladde-rs carries over word for word.
Mut<std::variant<…>> offers set to switch alternatives, and visit, which calls a visitor with the handle of the current alternative, Mut<Mobile> or Mut<Landline>, as std::visit does with values; get_if<Mobile>() returns a handle or nothing.
Class hierarchies: a closed set of classes, held polymorphically
struct Shape {
    float x = 0, y = 0;
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
    virtual float area() const = 0;
};
struct Circle : Shape { float r = 1;    float area() const override; };
struct Rect   : Shape { float w, h;     float area() const override; };
struct Frame  : Rect  { float border;   float area() const override; };
 
KLADDE_STRUCT(Shape, x, y)
KLADDE_DERIVED(Circle, Shape, r)
KLADDE_DERIVED(Rect, Shape, w, h)
KLADDE_DERIVED(Frame, Rect, border)
KLADDE_HIERARCHY(Shape, (Circle, 1), (Rect, 2), (Frame, 3))
 
struct Drawing { kladde::Vector<kladde::Poly<Shape>> shapes; };
kladde::Poly<Base> is a non-null std::unique_ptr<Base> whose dynamic type must be one of the classes registered for Base, and it is durable as an enum with a variant per concrete class.
In memory it is exactly what object-oriented C++ code holds already, so file.get().shapes[0]->area() is a virtual call and nothing more — no enum to forward through, and nothing like kladde-rs’s #[kladde::dispatch], because C++ has the real thing.

Every concrete class is a variant, at any depth: Frame derives from Rect, and both are variants, flat, of one enum; abstract classes are not.
A variant’s payload is a struct of the members of its class and of its bases, bases first, Frame’s holding x, y, w, h, border, just as for an alternative of a std::variant.
Discriminants are explicit and belong to the hierarchy, not to a field, so a field typed Poly<Rect> is an enum of Rect and Frame with the same discriminants, 2 and 3, as in a Poly<Shape>.
Explicit, because classes are added to a hierarchy far more often than alternatives to a variant, and nothing orders them reliably.
The registry maps the dynamic type to its variant through typeid, once per encode, so the classes need no virtual function of kladde’s, and a class hierarchy that cannot be changed can still be made durable.
Decoding constructs the class, by default construction, or through a factory registered with it for classes that have none, as Inkscape’s objects do.

Mutating through a Mut<Poly<Shape>> needs no dispatch for the base’s members: every variant’s payload starts with them, right after the discriminant, so s.x().set(10) writes at the same offset whatever the shape is.
For a derived class’s members, s.as<Circle>() returns a Mut<Circle> if the shape is a circle, as dynamic_cast does for pointers, and s.set(std::make_unique<Rect>(…)) replaces the shape with another, by splicing the new encoding over the old.

All three deserve first-class support, since they serve different code rather than different tastes.
New code with a handful of small alternatives is better off with std::variant, which keeps values inline and visits them exhaustively; code that already has a hierarchy — Inkscape’s SPObject and its dozens of subclasses — needs the hierarchy, and could not reasonably be rewritten into variants.
The hierarchy is also the only form in which shared fields are written without dispatch, which a document model with many kinds of element and many common attributes uses constantly.
And for mere flags, an enum class is often still the simplest choice.
Handles: where a value lies
A handle has to know where its value starts in the sequence whenever it writes, and has to tell its ancestors when its value changes size; Values and their positions gives the algorithms, and C++ needs both of its two forms.
Short-lived handles
Mut<T> is the guard of kladde-rs: made from its parent’s handle by one lookup in the parent’s index, holding its start, and valid while nothing outside its own subtree is written.
Rust enforces that by borrowing the parent exclusively; C++ cannot, so it is a documented rule, the same kind as iterator invalidation, which C++ programmers already keep: a handle is valid until something is written through a handle that is not its descendant.
Debug builds check it, with a stack of the live handles in the store that a write pops down to the handle it went through — the discipline that Miri’s stacked borrows check for Rust — so a stale handle fails an assertion rather than writing at the wrong position.
Release builds pay nothing.
Guards made together carry over unchanged: parts() hands out handles that compute their start at every write, so that writing one field and then another works whatever the first did to its size.
Long-lived references
An application that keeps pointers into its document for as long as it likes needs handles that survive edits elsewhere, and Rust’s design deliberately has none.
Inkscape holds Inkscape::XML::Node* everywhere — in the selection, in tools, in dialogs, in the undo log — and writes through any of them at any time.
kladde::List<T> keeps its elements at stable addresses, and each element knows its parent and where it stands among its siblings.
A kladde::Ref<T> to an element is then valid until that element is removed, as an iterator of std::list is, and computes its start when it writes by climbing from the element to the root: at each level, the element’s offset among its siblings, from a Fenwick tree over the siblings’ sizes at the index the element keeps of itself, plus the offset of the list in its parent.
@Claude: is there a specific reason you chose an order-statistics tree here over a Fenwick tree? Would a Fenwick tree not work here or does it have an unfavorable trade-off concerning memory or runtime?
Claude: No good reason: a Fenwick tree works, and it is the better default, so I changed the paragraph to it.
I had reached for a tree because a Ref must find its element’s rank from the element alone, and in a tree with parent links that survives insertions before it in O(log m).
With a Fenwick tree, each element keeps its own index instead, and an insertion or removal renumbers the elements behind it and rebuilds the tree, both O(m) — the same O(m) that moving the elements’ pointers in the list’s array costs anyway, as the built-in containers argue for kladde::Vector.
In return an element costs 4 bytes of the tree and 4 of its own index instead of a tree node of 24 to 40, and finding its rank is a load rather than a climb.
An Inkscape element has tens to a few thousand siblings, for which renumbering costs microseconds; a tree would pay only for lists of hundreds of thousands that are edited in the middle, and can be an option for them, as it is for the vector.
That is O(depth · log m) per write, the cost of guards made together at every level, and a change of size updates the same path back up.
It costs a parent link, an index and a cell of the siblings’ Fenwick tree per element, about 16 bytes, which a document tree whose elements each hold a name, attributes and children affords.
So kladde::Vector and kladde::List differ the way std::vector and std::list do — compact, or stable — and an application chooses per container.
Errors, transactions and exception safety
@Claude: The statement in the specification that a C++ implementation of kladde should use exceptions was not based on any deep argument and shouldn’t be taken as a law. I haven’t been involved in any large C++ code bases for almost 20 years, so I’m not up to date about the state of exceptions in C++, neither in terms of technical changes nor in terms of community acceptance. I remember that some experts used to advise against the use of exceptions, or even against enabling exceptions in the compiler. Has the advice changed since? And is there a consensus in the community on how to do error handling in C++? What to popular code bases like chromium, llvm, react-native, llama.cpp (or others that might be more trend setting) use?
Claude: There is no consensus, and the split has barely moved in twenty years; what has changed is that the case against exceptions is now made for particular environments rather than for C++ as a whole.
So kladde-cpp should work with and without them, and should use them only for failures that end a session.
Who disables them.
Google’s style guide still says “we do not use C++ exceptions”, for the reason it always gave — its existing code is not exception-safe — and Chromium builds with -fno-exceptions.
LLVM and Clang build without exceptions and without RTTI, and report errors through llvm::Error and llvm::Expected<T>, which abort if left unchecked in builds with LLVM’s ABI-breaking checks enabled.
Firefox, most game engines (Unreal disables them by default), and most embedded code do the same.
Who uses them.
The standard library and Boost throw, and so do glibmm and gtkmm, which is why Inkscape builds with exceptions and catches Glib::Error.
LibreOffice, KDE applications, Bloomberg’s libraries and much scientific code use them, and the C++ Core Guidelines recommend them for “a function that cannot perform its assigned task”.
React Native’s C++ core (JSI, Fabric, Folly) builds with exceptions; llama.cpp’s C++ throws internally while loading a model and catches at its C API, while ggml, being C, returns codes and aborts on failed assertions.
What has changed.
C++23 standardized std::expected, so value-based error handling no longer needs a homemade type, and it has become the usual choice for failures a caller expects, such as a file that does not parse.
The cost argument has weakened: the happy path of an exception costs nothing on the common ABIs, and recent work on embedded targets (Khalil Estell’s talks at CppCon 2024) found exceptions producing smaller binaries than result types.
Herb Sutter’s proposal of cheaper, deterministic exceptions (P0709) was not adopted, so the language itself is where it was.
Widely used libraries cope with both camps by making throwing configurable — nlohmann/json and {fmt} both build without exceptions and abort or call a handler instead.
What that suggests for kladde-cpp.
Its failures come in two kinds, which deserve different mechanisms:

Opening and creating a file can fail in ordinary ways — the file is missing, damaged, or of another schema — and the caller always has to handle them, so File<T>::open returns an expected value (std::expected on C++23, a type of kladde’s own on C++20), with or without exceptions.
A mutation or a flush fails only when the disk does, and the session ends: the File is poisoned.
With exceptions, the call throws; without, it poisons the File, calls a handler the application installs (Inkscape would show a dialog), and returns as if nothing had been recorded, which is true of the value, since memory changes only after recording succeeds.
Making every set and push_back return a result that must be checked would put a branch after every edit in the application for a failure that, once it happens, makes all further edits moot.

The specification’s “in C++ by throwing” should then say only that the implementation reports the failure and refuses further work.
Decision: I agree with your suggestion for error handling in kladde-cpp.
Errors are exceptions, as the specification already says of C++: a kladde::Error hierarchy, with a failed fsync poisoning the File, so that every later call throws until it is reopened.
Applications built without exceptions are an open question.
Every mutation prepares, records, then commits, and only the first two may throw.
Rust treats a failed allocation as fatal; C++ reports it, so a push_back that recorded its splice and then failed to grow the vector in memory would leave the file and the value disagreeing.
So a mutation first does everything in memory that can fail without changing the value — reserving capacity, constructing the new element — then records, then changes memory by operations that cannot throw.
This is the strong exception guarantee, earned in the order the reference algorithms already recommend.
Transactions take a callable, which is the one form that tells success from failure without asking a destructor to do I/O:
file.transaction([] (kladde::Mut<Accounts> a) {
    a.checking().set(70);
    a.savings().set(30);
});   // appended here, as one transaction
Returning commits; an exception leaves the callable with memory already changed and no way to change it back, so it poisons the File and propagates, as a panic does in kladde-rs.
file.batch(...) has the same shape, and transactions nest inside batches as the state machine allows.
An RAII object for transactions that span functions can come later; its destructor must not do I/O, so it would need an explicit commit() and would poison if destroyed without one.
Flushing on an interactive thread
A flush ends in an fsync, and a flush can be triggered from inside any mutating call, when the journal’s budget would overflow.
In Inkscape, mutating calls run on the GUI thread, so a drag could stall for as long as the disk takes to sync — milliseconds on an SSD, more on a slow disk.
Two remedies need nothing new:


Flush when the application is idle: file.flush() from an idle callback, which an event loop offers, keeps the journal short, so the automatic flush rarely fires mid-gesture.
kladde-cpp can offer the policy, file.flush_if_journal_exceeds(fraction), and leave the scheduling to the application’s loop.
@Claude: explain: is the idea to add a method flush_if_journal_exceeds on kladde::File<T> that flushes if the journal is filled up to at least the given fraction? And does inkscape already have an idle loop where this method could be called?
Claude: Yes to both.
file.flush_if_journal_exceeds(0.5) appends a batch’s ready run if there is one and flushes if the journal pages then hold at least half of their budget, and otherwise does nothing; the check is a subtraction of two cursors, so calling it often costs nothing.
Inkscape runs GLib’s main loop, and already does its own deferred work in idle callbacks: SPDocument::requestModified connects SPDocument::idle_handler with Glib::signal_idle() after every change, to update the objects built from the XML tree.
The fork would connect a second idle callback the same way, at a priority below redrawing, so that it runs once events and frames are done — between gestures rather than during one.
An idle flush ends the journal’s epoch early, which matters for cuts that outlive their transaction as answered below, so the fraction should stay well above zero.


A generous budget, so that a gesture fits in the journal however long it lasts.


A flush on a background thread is a different matter: mutations appended while it runs would belong to the next journal, and an application crash before the flush’s header is written would lose them although their calls had returned.
That needs a change to the journal, which is proposed below, and then removes the stall altogether.
Decision: go with the flush when the application is idle. Document the flush on the background thread as a possible improvement, pending experience with the demo app.
Files and platforms
The store reads and writes through a Storage interface, as kladde-rs does: a file, and an in-memory storage for tests that can simulate power cuts by dropping any subset of the writes since the last sync.

POSIX: pread and pwrite, fsync, and posix_fallocate to grow the file, so that a full disk is reported before a flush rather than discovered at its fsync.
macOS: fsync does not ask the drive to empty its cache, so the store calls fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC); anything less breaks invariant I1 on power loss.
Windows: FlushFileBuffers, and SetFileValidData or SetEndOfFile with care for growth.
No mmap, for the reasons the reference algorithms give.

The store owns its file exclusively, and kladde-cpp locks it (flock, LockFileEx) so that a second process opening it fails cleanly rather than corrupting it.
The Inkscape demo
Inkscape funnels every change to a document through one abstract class, Inkscape::XML::Node, whose implementation is SimpleNode: setAttributeImpl, setContent, appendChild, removeChild, changeOrder, and a few more.
The objects Inkscape draws (SPObject and its subclasses) are built from that tree and updated by observing it, and its undo log records and replays changes through the same interface.
So a KladdeNode that implements Node over a durable tree makes every change durable without touching the tools, the canvas or the undo system.
The first schema should be XML’s, not SVG’s:
struct Attribute { std::string name; std::string value; };
struct Element;
using Node = std::variant<kladde::Box<Element>, Text, Comment, ProcessingInstruction>;
struct Element {
    std::string name;
    kladde::Vector<Attribute> attributes;   // in their order, as SimpleNode keeps them
    kladde::List<Node> children;            // stable, since Inkscape holds Node*
};
Every Inkscape operation is then one or two records: an attribute set is a splice of its value’s changed middle, a reorder is a Move, an insertion a splice of the new subtree’s encoding.
Two details need care: Inkscape creates nodes detached and appends them later, so a detached node is an ordinary value until it is appended, which encodes it; and a node removed and appended elsewhere in one undo step can be a cut and paste rather than a second encoding, if the step is a transaction.
A node removed in one step and inserted again in another — undoing a deletion is the common case — is encoded again, subtree and all, unless cuts outlive their transaction.
Inkscape’s undo steps (DocumentUndo::done) are natural batch boundaries.
The fork’s schema is its own, and free to follow Inkscape’s needs rather than any other program’s.
A typed SVG schema is the showcase that should follow, with Inkscape’s element classes as a hierarchy and attributes as typed fields, but it touches much more of Inkscape, and the XML schema already delivers the demo: no save button, and nothing lost to a crash.
@Claude: I’d like to have this eventually, so that I can compare file sizes, memory usage, and run times in the XML-based and the typed schema. But I agree that the XML-based schema should go first. Implement the typed SVG schema once you’re done with the XML-based schema, and implement it on a new branch typed in inkscape-kladde.
Claude: Noted: the XML schema first, then the typed schema on a branch typed of inkscape-kladde, and the comparison of file sizes, memory and run times between the two.
Changes to the specification
Four changes would make kladde-cpp simpler or its API more idiomatic, and none of them is about C++ alone: each came up because a second language, or an application of a kind kladde-rs has not met yet, looks at the format from a different side.
They are ordered by how much they would change kladde-cpp’s design, and each says what it costs.
Variants that hold one value
Proposed: an enum’s variant holds at most one value, its payload, of any type, instead of a list of fields.
A fieldless variant has no payload; a Rust tuple variant of one field, Element(Element) or Text(Str), holds that field’s value; a struct variant, ProcessingInstruction { target, value }, holds a Struct of its fields, named after the variant; and a tuple variant of several fields a Struct of positional ones.
A payload that is a Struct without fields counts as no payload, since both encode to nothing.
What it buys.
Every C++ form of an enum — an alternative of a std::variant, a class of a hierarchy, Some of a std::optional — holds exactly one value, and with this rule that value is the payload, with no choice for the programmer to make and none to get wrong.
Rust’s two spellings of “a variant that holds a struct”, Element(Element) and Element { kind, attrs, … }, get one descriptor, so the choice between them stops being a file-format decision, as a struct’s own name already is not.
And every language with tagged unions of one value — Swift’s enums with associated values, TypeScript’s discriminated unions, Python’s union types — maps the same way.
What it costs.
The canonical encoding of an Enum writes reference(payload) + 1, or 0 for none, in place of varint(field_count) and the fields; the fingerprint follows, and the vector for List changes, since Cons then holds a Struct of "0" and "1".
@Claude: I didn’t understand the last part about the vector for List. Explain in more detail.
Claude: “Vector” there meant a test vector: the second row of the table of expected fingerprints, which the proposal would change.
That row hashes this type graph:
[0] Enum "List", width 4 { 0 "Nil" {}, 1 "Cons" { "0": [1], "1": [0] } }
[1] i32

Under the proposal, Cons no longer holds two fields but one payload, a Struct of them, which becomes a descriptor of its own:
[0] Enum "List", width 4 { 0 "Nil": [2], 1 "Cons": [3] }
[1] i32
[2] Struct { }
[3] Struct { "0": [1], "1": [0] }

(Nil holds the empty Struct if variants always hold one value, as recommended below.)
The graph is a different graph, so the hash input of List changes and the row’s expected fingerprint, af12af01…, has to be recomputed; the bytes of every List value stay exactly as they were.
No value’s encoding changes, and the fixed form of an Enum is the payload’s fixed form instead of its fields’, which is the same bytes.
kladde-rs’s derive describes a struct variant as a Struct and a one-field tuple variant by its field’s type.
Files of today stop opening, which a pre-stable format allows.
@Claude: I like this proposal. One detail: I’m unsure whether variants should have at most one value or always one value (giving valueless variants a payload of type ()). Briefly discuss the trade-off.
Claude: Always one value is the better rule: it makes every variant the same shape, and it removes the one special case that at most one needed.

What always buys.
A variant is a discriminant and a payload, with no “or nothing” in the descriptors, the fingerprint, the fixed form, or any code that walks them.
And a fieldless variant, a C++ alternative that is an empty struct, std::monostate, Rust’s () and an enum class enumerator all get the same descriptor by construction — an empty Struct, whose name is not fingerprinted — where at most one needed a rule that “an empty Struct counts as no payload” to make them agree.
What it costs.
One descriptor in the table, the empty Struct, shared by every valueless variant, of three bytes; each variant then writes a reference to it, one byte, where at most one would have written a 0, also one byte.
The hash input of each valueless variant grows by a token of 17 bytes, which no one will measure.
What at most one would have bought: an enum class described without an extra descriptor, and nothing else.

Decision: adopt this change, with the always one value refinement.
Maps as a kind of their own
Proposed: a descriptor kind Map, with a key type and a value type, whose encoding is that of a Sequence of entries, each its key’s encoding and then its value’s.
Today a map is described as a Sequence of Structs of two fields, and the specification names no fields: kladde-rs calls them "key" and "value", and a C++ std::pair would call them "0" and "1", so the same map has two fingerprints until a convention is written down.
The least change is to write down kladde-rs’s names.
A kind of its own does more: every language has a native map, and a reader that knows a Sequence is a map can decode it into one — a std::map or a kladde::Map in C++, a dict in Python — and tools can render it as a JSON object rather than an array of pairs.
It costs a kind tag, of which 132 is free, and nothing in any encoding.
A flush off the caller’s thread
Proposed: a journal may end in a seal that names where the next epoch’s journal begins, so that appends continue there while a flush folds the sealed one.
A flush today blocks the mutating call that triggered it until its fsync returns, which is a stall on the GUI thread of an interactive application, mid-gesture.
