evaluation/consolidation.title: Consolidation under load
evaluation/consolidation.content:
Consolidation keeps a file at 1.5 to 1.7 times its live size under sustained overwrites, where the same file grows to 6 times without it, for about one more byte written per byte the application writes.
After three quarters of a file are freed at once, it gives the space back within 16 flushes.
Flushes that do this take 6 to 25 ms at the median.
Two of its constants do less than the design intends.
The target fill τ = 0.8 is out of reach under the churn floor λ = 1, so the budget sits at its cap and λ alone sets the fill, to within a percent of what a one-line model predicts.
And description defragmentation’s reserved page per flush merges next to nothing under appends: sixteen pages cut the statements by a third.
The benchmarks also found four defects, all fixed in the measured commit.
What was measured
Six workloads, and variants of three of them, ran on real files, each until the application had written eight times the file’s live size, with a flush after every 1000 operations.





















































workloadlive sizewhat the application doeswhat it exercisesuniform1, 8 and 64 MiBwrites of 1 to 511 bytes at random offsets of random 16 KiB allocationsevacuation and the page rewriteskewed1, 8 and 64 MiBthe same, with 90 % of the writes going to 10 % of the allocationsscoring, with hot and cold content mixed in pagesappend16 MiB512 logs, appended to in records of 16 to 240 bytes and truncated to nothing once a record would take one past 64 KiBdescription fragmentation, and mass frees when the logs rotate, nearly in stepchurn16 MiBvalues of 16 to 128 bytes, or one in five of 1 to 8 KiB, each operation replacing one with a new allocation, rewriting one whole, or patching 1 to 64 bytes of oneallocation turnover, id recycling, and Inline statementsshrink64 MiBallocations of 64 KiB, three quarters of them freed at once, then 400 flushes of 100 patches of 1 to 64 bytes eachcompaction mode and truncationtyped16 MiBa Kladde<PersistableHashMap<u64, PersistableString>> of strings of 50 to 500 bytes: 40 % of the operations replace a string, 30 % append to one, 20 % insert one, 10 % remove onethe typed layersvariants8 and 16 MiBuniform and skewed at 8 MiB with λ of 0.5 and 2, or τ of 0.6 and 0.5; append with 4 and 16 pages of defragmentation sharethe constants
The live size is the sum of the allocations’ sizes, and every ratio below is taken against it.
A workload first fills its file, which is not measured, and then records one row per flush: the file’s pages by kind and their coverage, and everything written since the fill.
The horizontal axis of most figures is the application’s bytes written since the fill, over the live size.
After the last flush, each run reopens its file and compares every byte with a model of what the application wrote.
Times include each flush’s fsync.
Journal appends are not fsynced, as the journal’s specification prescribes: an operation survives a crash of the application once its call returns, and a power cut once the next flush has returned.
The runs measured kladde-rs at commit cb34576, built with --release by Rust 1.97.1, with the default options unless a variant says otherwise, on an Intel Core i7-1165G7 with 16 GB of memory under Linux 7.0, in a development container whose files live on an overlay file system.
Identical configurations differed by up to 20 % in median flush time from one run to the next, so only differences well beyond that are worth reading into the times.
Space
Consolidation holds overwritten files at about 1.5 times their live size once they are much larger than what a few flushes write; without it, uniform overwrites grow the file sixfold.




































file size / live size, at the end1 MiB8 MiB64 MiBuniform, consolidating2.751.691.53uniform, without consolidation6.286.00—skewed, consolidating2.281.671.55skewed, without consolidation2.852.67—
Without consolidation, a data page is reused only once every byte on it has been overwritten.
Under uniform overwrites that almost never happens, and data pages end up 18 % live; under skewed ones, hot pages do empty by themselves, and the file grows more slowly.
In the 64 MiB uniform file, data pages take 1.35 times the live size, at 73 % live, address-table pages 0.15 times, at 59 % live, and reusable pages 0.03 times.
Under uniform overwrites, the data pages settle within half a live size of writes and the table pages within two.
Under skewed ones, both keep losing fill for most of the run, as they would if pages froze above the churn floor once their hot content had died, which is the problem the ripeness draft describes.

Small files pay for the quarantine: a file keeps three to four flushes’ worth of written pages free, whatever its size.
A page that a commit stops referencing can be reused only after the next commit, and the reusable pages that the next flush will write are free as well.
The 1 MiB uniform file keeps 340 pages free and writes 104 pages per flush, the 8 MiB one 430 and 130, and the 64 MiB one 490 and 138.
In the 1 MiB file, where one flush writes 40 % of the live size in pages, that is 1.33 times the live size; at 64 MiB it is 3 %.
The churn floor sets the fill, not the target
With the default constants, the budget climbs to its cap of 256 pages within 1.3 live sizes of writes and stays there in every overwrite run, but flushes open only 8 to 59 pages of it: the churn floor admits no more victims.

The fill the file reaches is then the churn floor’s.
A victim may be at most 1 / (1 + λ) live, so under uniform overwrites every data page is written full, loses its content at a steady rate, and is cleaned once it reaches that fill.
A page whose live fraction decays exponentially from 1 to 1 / (1 + λ) spends its time at an average fill of λ / ((1 + λ) · ln(1 + λ)), which matches the measurements to within about a percent:





























churn floor λdata-page fill predictedmeasured, uniformmeasured, skewed0.50.8220.8250.8191 (the default)0.7210.7330.70720.6070.6030.615
This is the opposite of the division of labour that the design intends, in which λ stays low enough never to decide the fill and the budget converges the file on τ.
At λ = 1, the 8 MiB files reach a whole-file fill of 0.63, table pages and free pages included, well short of τ = 0.8.
The controller does reach targets that the churn floor allows, but by swinging between its bounds rather than settling.
With τ = 0.6, the 8 MiB files end at whole-file fills of 0.58 (uniform) and 0.59 (skewed), and with τ = 0.5 at 0.53 and 0.51.
Under uniform overwrites, the budget meanwhile swings between one page and the cap, a swing taking one to two live sizes of writes.
Multiplying the budget by exp(4 · (τ − fill)) after every flush makes the controller an integral one, and the fill it measures, the whole file’s, answers the budget only once new writes reuse the pages cleaning frees, so it overshoots.
To trade space for writes, λ is the better knob: a lower target moves the file along a worse curve, since its budget swings.

The figure compares steady states: the file size averaged over the second half of each run, and the bytes written during that half per byte the application wrote.
Under uniform overwrites, λ = 2 writes about as much as τ = 0.5 (2.59 against 2.57 bytes per byte) and leaves a file 7 % smaller (1.96 against 2.11 times its live size).
Under skewed ones, τ = 0.6 leaves a file of 1.77 times its live size for 2.68 bytes per byte, 5 % larger than the churn floor’s curve passes at those writes.
While the swinging budget is low, the file grows, and what cleaning frees afterwards are holes, which the file keeps until new writes fill them.
Writes
Each byte the application writes costs 2.2 to 3.2 bytes written to the file: one in the journal, one in a data page, and up to one more for consolidation.

The journal takes 1.02 to 1.10 bytes per byte for the raw store, more the smaller the writes, since each record carries a header, and 1.12 through the typed layers.
Consolidation adds 0.9 bytes per byte under uniform overwrites, 0.6 to 0.8 under skewed ones, 0.7 under appends, 0.6 in the typed workload, and 0.1 under churn, whose replaced values free whole allocations.
Address-table pages add 0.02 to 0.23, headers less than 0.04.
Without consolidation, the same workloads write 1.5 to 2.2 bytes per byte: the 8 MiB uniform file 2.13, against 3.07 with it.
The uniform figure is what the churn floor predicts.
Cleaning a victim at a live fraction u writes u / (1 − u) bytes per byte it frees, 1 at u = 1/2, and under uniform overwrites nearly all garbage is freed that way, since pages seldom empty by themselves.
Mass frees
After three quarters of a 64 MiB file are freed at once, compaction mode gives the space back within 16 flushes; without it, the file never shrinks.

The file went from 4.27 to 1.14 times its live size, moving 3,221 data pages to return about 12,300, in 12 flushes in compaction mode and 12 truncations; over the remaining 385 flushes it grew by 2 %, as the patches added statements.
Consolidation without compaction mode moves nothing here: after the frees every page is either full or empty, so no page is a victim, and the holes stay holes until the application writes as much again.
The append workload’s rotations, which free most of the file within a few flushes, are absorbed the same way.
Without consolidation, the file peaks at 8.8, 6.2 and 5.5 times its live size as the logs rotate, and it has not shrunk back below 1.3 when the next rotation comes.
With it, the peaks are 2.9, 2.3 and 2.3, and the file is back below 1.3 within half a live size of appends.

The description
Description defragmentation’s reserved page per flush is too small to matter under appends; sixteen pages cut the statements by a third, for a sixth more writes.



































defragmentation share, pages per flushstatements per KiB of live datafile size / live sizebytes written per bytenone: consolidation off4.062.802.211 (the default)4.011.382.9343.721.413.06162.571.383.43
The statements and the file size are means over the second half of each run, since both swing with the rotations; the bytes written are over the whole run.
Each flush appends about 125 KiB across 512 logs, two records per log on average, which the flush states as about one statement per log.
A share of one page rewrites 4 KiB per flush, 3 % of what was appended, and that is what it did.
What merging buys here is a smaller description, which is what the fragment map in memory holds, and not a smaller file: the share leaves the file’s size where consolidation put it.

Small patches accumulate as statements of their own under every setting measured.
In the churn workload, statements grow from 1.2 to 2.7 per KiB of live data, with and without consolidation alike.
In the shrink workload’s 400 flushes of 100 patches, statements grow from 4,833 to 45,837 and address-table pages from 44 to 439: every patch stays a statement, Inline since it is at most 64 bytes.
That is the design working as intended for the writes, which cost the patch and not the page it lands in, but the description has no counterweight at this rate.
Time
A flush takes 6 to 25 ms at the median here, roughly in proportion to the pages it writes, and flushes take most of the time: the operations between them cost 1.3 to 3.2 µs each.






















































workload, consolidatingpages written per flushmean flush timeoperations per second, flushes includeduniform, 1 MiB10410.4 ms84,000uniform, 8 MiB13014.1 ms64,000uniform, 64 MiB13829.6 ms32,000skewed, 64 MiB13118.2 ms50,000append, 16 MiB6410.1 ms87,000churn, 16 MiB19210.3 ms110,000typed, 16 MiB8214.5 ms57,000
The figures are over the second half of each run.
The uniform flush doubles its time per page written between 8 and 64 MiB, from 108 to 214 µs, at about the same pages per flush.
These runs do not say why; the page-table scans a flush makes, over some 25,000 entries, are far too cheap to account for 15 ms.
The 99th-percentile flush of the 64 MiB uniform file takes 54 ms.

Throughput dips while the append workload’s logs rotate, when consolidation evacuates what the rotation left sparse.
The typed layers
Through the typed layers, a hash map of strings costs what the raw store does per byte: 1.53 times its live size in space, and 2.97 bytes written per byte.
Its journal takes 1.12 bytes per byte, the framing of its records included.
It holds 9.1 statements per KiB of live data, since each of its 137,000 strings is an allocation of its own.
A flush takes 13 ms at the median, and the map sustains 57,000 operations per second, flushes included.
Defects the benchmarks found
All four are fixed in the measured commit, and each has a test of its own.

Recycled ids resurrected old content (fixed in 58dcfa0).
A tombstone whose own page a flush dropped was released as if it had outlived its purpose, so after a reopen, older statements of a freed and recycled id could show through; the churn workload’s check caught it.
Storing a new string journaled it byte by byte (fixed in 8a2f7cb), which made the typed workload’s journal 2.8 times as large as its data.
Compaction mode stalled on a full table page at the end of the file (fixed in 4182b3f).
The restatements of a table page are estimated at 1.25 times its coverage, so a tail page more than 80 % full failed the churn floor, from which the design means the tail to be exempt: in the shrink workload, a page of Inline patches at the end of the file held compaction back for 180 flushes.
Before the fix, the file was still 3.2 times its live size after 400 flushes.
Compaction mode ran almost permanently in small files (fixed in 26dcc08), because it counted pages in quarantine as holes, although they are working space that the next flushes reuse by themselves.
In the 1 MiB uniform file it ran in 30 of 33 flushes, and the file ended 6 % larger than it does with the fix.

implementation-notes.md in kladde-rs records the first, under “Flush”; Compaction mode now states the rules the last two fixes follow.
What to change

Make the constants agree.
Either lower τ to what λ allows, which for λ = 1 is a whole-file fill of about 0.63, or lower λ to what τ needs; or replace both with a threshold per page, as the ripeness draft proposes, which Cleaning by ripeness measures.
As they stand, the controller only ever raises the budget to its cap, and the cap bounds a flush’s work only because the churn floor runs out of victims first.
Measure what the controller acts on.
Cleaning by ripeness moves a price with the same kind of controller, and its price cycled the same way while it measured the whole file; measured over the data pages and leaves, which answer within the flush, it held within a few percent.
The budget would likely settle the same way; holes are compaction mode’s to return anyway.
Scale description defragmentation with the rate at which statements accrue, rather than reserving one page per flush: appends and patches both outrun it by an order of magnitude.
Find out why flushes slow down as files grow, with a profile of the 64 MiB uniform run.
Measure small files with fewer operations per flush, since with 1000 their free space is set by the quarantine rather than by consolidation.

Reproducing
In kladde-rs, at the measured commit, run every workload and write one table per workload to a directory:
cargo run --release -p kladde-bench -- /tmp/kladde-bench
In kladde-docs, keep the tables gzipped next to this page and draw the figures from them, with matplotlib installed:
for f in /tmp/kladde-bench/*.csv; do
    gzip -9 -n -c "$f" > content/evaluation/data/consolidation/$(basename "$f").gz
done
tools/plot-evaluation.py --summary --out content/evaluation/figures/consolidation \
    main=content/evaluation/data/consolidation
--summary also prints the end state of every run as a table.
The whole benchmark takes about four minutes here.

evaluation/cpp-port.title: Porting kladde to C++ and into Inkscape
evaluation/cpp-port.content:
What a second implementation, kladde-cpp, and its first application, the Inkscape fork inkscape-kladde, found out about kladde: where the specification left a second implementer guessing, where C++ made the design harder than Rust does, and what it took to make an existing application durable.
The format held up: kladde-cpp, written from the specification and kladde-rs’s store, reads and writes files that kladde-rs reads and writes, in both directions, and the typed layers agree on fingerprints once both name an enum’s variants alike.
The obstacles were elsewhere.
The specification was silent on a dozen points where two implementers could each be right and disagree, which the port turned into rules; C++ cannot enforce the exclusive access that Rust’s handles rely on, so the C++ handles carry rules the compiler does not check; and Inkscape needed long-lived handles and a way to observe its document rather than replace it, both of which kladde-cpp now has.
The port’s findings are of kladde-rs 5d9ff9f on its branch cpp, kladde-cpp e8a3e61 and inkscape-kladde f81602b406; the measurements are of kladde-cpp c40ff8f and inkscape-kladde 6452817ae3 (branch main, the typed schema) and 04e6ea0d31 (branch untyped, attribute values as text), with kladde-rs f2f29a7 for the canonical SVG; the commands are at the end.
What was built

The schema layer, from the specification, checked against the fingerprint vectors.
The store, ported from kladde-rs’s kladde-store module by module, consolidation included, and tested as kladde-rs tests it: against a plain byte vector after every operation (the differential oracle), with simulated power cuts at every write since the last fsync, and with kladde-rs’s consolidation thresholds.
The typed layer, header-only, as the draft designed it, with the departures that kladde-cpp’s page lists.
The Inkscape demo: documents backed by a kladde file in an XML schema, with no save button.

Two implementations, one format
Files are format-compatible in both directions, but not byte-identical.
Fifty seeds of a random workload with many flushes, consolidation, cuts and pastes, and an unflushed journal, written by one implementation, read the same in the other, which then edits them and hands them back.
The bytes differ because kladde-rs iterates hash sets where the order picks consolidation’s victims, and kladde-cpp sorts there instead; the fold and consolidation are free to choose, so both files are right.
The typed layers agree on a document only once the C++ type names an enum’s variants as the Rust type does.
The cross-implementation test writes a drawing — a struct holding text, a vector of shapes, a map, an option and an integer — from each language and reads it in the other.
The shapes are a Rust enum Shape { Circle { r }, Poly(Vec<Point>), Label(String), Empty }, and the C++ type std::variant<Circle, std::vector<Point>, std::string, kladde::Unit>; thanks to variants that hold one value, the two have the same structure, descriptor for descriptor, and the encodings agree byte for byte.
But the fingerprints differed: a variant’s name is part of the fingerprint, and a std::variant names its alternatives after their types — Value, Text — where Rust names them Poly and Label.
KLADDE_VARIANT_NAMED now gives the C++ type the names the file uses, and with it each implementation opens the other’s file.
What it means for the design.
Names in the fingerprint are deliberate: evolution reconciles by names, so two types that differ only in names are different types.
The cost shows in a language whose sum type has no names of its own, which C++‘s std::variant is, and will be in Python’s unions and TypeScript’s too: a program that shares files with another must spell out the other’s names.
That is a fair price, and kladde-cpp asks it only where a program shares files across languages; within one, the names it derives are stable.
What the specification left open
Each point below is one where kladde-rs and kladde-cpp, both following the documents, could have disagreed, and most were settled while this was written.
Settled in the specification:

A schema table must be canonical to be read.
kladde-rs accepted a varint longer than it needed to be, enum variants in any order (re-sorting them, so that re-encoding changed the bytes) and two variants with one discriminant; kladde-cpp refused all three.
Canonical encoding now requires the refusal, so that a table that decodes re-encodes to its own bytes, and kladde-rs refuses them too.
An Opaque’s parameters are not containment, so a type may reach itself through one; and an enum whose every variant holds itself is legal, if useless (rules of nesting).
A Move makes no cut that a Paste could name (cuts).

Still open, for the conformance suite to decide:

whether page 1 of a file that has only ever had one header must be a header page, as the file format says “if present”, or may be zeros, as both implementations leave it at creation;
whether a header whose epoch has the wrong parity for its slot, or whose journal_pointer is below 2, makes the file invalid or is ignored, as both implementations ignore it;
whether varints in journal records and table pages may be longer than they need to be, as both implementations accept;
whether a trailer that matches its CRC but names page 0, page 1 or a page already in the journal ends the journal, as both implementations treat it, silently dropping what follows, or makes the file invalid;
whether a transaction of no records is valid, and whether a file with a format_version other than 0 is refused.

Where kladde-rs and the reference algorithms disagree, kladde-cpp followed kladde-rs, and the disagreements are now in the implementation notes: the seed of the rotating walk, what the header evicts, who takes the cut’s fillers, the order in which the budget loop applies its floors, the depth of the span table, the fold’s length check, and the bound on a Ref.
What C++ made harder
The store ported line by line; the typed layer did not.
The store is positions and bytes, and the reference algorithms describe it closely enough that a port follows kladde-rs’s structure, with one mechanical change: every fallible function returns kladde::expected<T>, and KLADDE_TRY does what Rust’s ? does.
The typed layer is where the languages part.
Handles that nothing checks
Rust’s borrow checker enforces two rules that C++ handles can only document.

A handle is valid until something is written through a handle that is not itself or made from it.
In Rust a Mut borrows its parent exclusively, so a stale one does not compile; in C++ a stale kladde::Mut writes at the wrong position.
This is the iterator-invalidation rule C++ programmers already keep, and the debug checking the draft proposed — a stack of live handles in the store — is not built yet.
A handle must not move while a handle made from it lives, since the child refers to its parent’s place.
Rust’s borrows pin the parent for free; in C++, auto [a, b] = c.parts(); is fine and returning a handle by value is fine, by guaranteed copy elision, but moving a handle into a container while its children are in use is not.
A cut is pasted at most once.
kladde-rs’s CutId is neither Copy nor Clone, so the type system enforces it; kladde-cpp’s is a plain struct, and the store’s check of it holds only while the cut’s journal lasts.

Describing types without a derive
One description per type, written by a macro today and by reflection later, drives everything else, as the draft proposed, and it works.
KLADDE_STRUCT(Contact, email, phones, starred) expands to a constexpr description found by argument-dependent lookup, and to a mixin that gives Mut<Contact> the methods email(), phones() and starred().
Two compiler problems cost time, both now in the code as comments:

a static constexpr auto member initialized through argument-dependent lookup inside a constrained partial specialization crashes GCC 13 with an internal error, the compiler that Inkscape builds with on Ubuntu 24.04; a static constexpr function avoids it;
a static member of durable<T> cannot be computed by calling durable<T>’s own functions, which are not defined until the class is complete, so the sizes and flags that follow from a struct’s fields are computed in a helper class of their own.

Recursive types need care that Rust’s lazy constant evaluation does not.
kladde::Box<T> cannot report T’s fixed size, since a recursive type reaches itself through a box and asking would instantiate the type inside itself; it reports none, which costs nothing on file and refuses only a std::vector of boxes.
Long-lived handles
Inkscape needs handles that live as long as the node they point to, and kladde-cpp’s kladde::List and kladde::Ref give them, as Values and their positions describes.
Each element of a list is an anchor that knows its list and its index; a list knows the anchor of the value that holds it, and finds its own offset inside that value by walking the value’s fields up to itself, each of which knows its encoded size in constant time.
So a write through a Ref finds its place in O(depth · log m), and its change of size climbs the same path, updating each list’s Fenwick tree.
One restriction falls out: a List may sit inside structs, variants, options, boxes and other lists, but not inside a kladde::Vector, a std::vector or a kladde::Map, whose indexes would not hear of a change made through a Ref; the compiler refuses it.
A document tree, whose children are lists all the way down, never needs it.
What Inkscape needed
inkscape-kladde observes Inkscape’s XML tree and mirrors every change into the kladde file, rather than replacing the tree’s nodes with durable ones, as the draft proposed.
The draft’s KladdeNode would have implemented Inkscape::XML::Node over the durable tree, so that the document lives in memory once.
But Inkscape’s nodes are garbage-collected objects of the class SimpleNode and its subclasses, created through the document’s factory methods and copied, compared and merged by code that assumes them; replacing them touches the XML layer’s every user.
A subtree observer on the document node, by contrast, hears every change — attributes, content, insertions, removals, reorderings and renamings — and needs nothing else of Inkscape.
What the observer costs.
The document is held twice in memory, once as Inkscape’s tree and once as kladde values, and a change is applied twice; the measurements below put a number on it.
What it does not cost: durability is the same, since each change is recorded before the call that made it returns, and the file is the same, since it holds the same schema either way.
The typed SVG schema faces the same choice, and would face it harder: Inkscape’s objects (SPObject and its subclasses) are built from the XML tree and keep their own state, so a typed schema would be a third copy, or a rewrite of the object layer.
Three details needed care:

Inkscape changes a document’s tree while building it, before anything can observe it: it adds a named view and version attributes as it creates a document from a file.
So attaching the observer first compares Inkscape’s tree with the file’s and writes the difference, and any later event for a node the file does not know rewrites the file from the tree, a fallback that the tests never reach.
Saving must not overwrite the kladde file with SVG.
A backed document’s filename is its kladde file, so the title bar names it; the commands bar and the File menu offer no Save, and Ctrl+S only flushes the file, while Save As still writes SVG wherever the user chooses, and an imported .svg is left as it was.
Only the GUI imports.
Opening an .svg in the GUI creates foo.kladde next to it, asking first if that file exists; the command line, which Inkscape uses for conversions and exports, opens files as before, so that inkscape --export-type=png foo.svg leaves no foo.kladde behind.

The idle flush fits Inkscape’s main loop: after each recorded change, a low-priority idle callback calls flush_if_journal_exceeds(0.5), at the same priority Inkscape gives its own deferred work, so that a flush, and its fsync, falls between gestures rather than in one.
The seal and the commit on a worker thread are in kladde-rs and kladde-cpp, off by default, until the demo shows whether the idle flush suffices.
Measurements
inkscape-kladde costs Inkscape about 5 µs and 19 bytes of journal per edit, and a sixth more memory; it keeps a drawing in a file of 1.2 to 2.2 times its encoding while the drawing is edited, which for the coat of arms and the world map is no larger than the drawing’s canonical SVG, and right after the import in a file of 1.03 to 1.4 times its encoding.
test_kladde-backing-bench imports three drawings of kladde-rs’s corpus — the tiger (67 KB of SVG), the coat of arms of Spain (193 KB) and the world map (1.1 MB) — and makes a drawing program’s edits through Inkscape’s XML tree: drags of twenty moves of one element (eight in ten), style changes, reorders, duplicates and deletions.
It runs the same edits on the same drawing without a backing, for what Inkscape spends on them itself, and checks that the closed file reopens as the document was.
The fork stores a drawing in a typed schema, on its branch main: each element’s attributes are one ordered list of entries, each a typed value — lengths, paints, colors with their written form, transform lists, path data with its layout, points, style declarations, decimal numbers, embedded data as its bytes — or the attribute’s text, where formatting the typed value would not reproduce Inkscape’s text byte for byte; 98.4 to 99.8% of the drawings’ attributes end up typed.
The numbers are the typed schema’s, at the journal budget sized to the file that kladde uses by default, unless they say otherwise; the XML schema of the branch untyped, which keeps every attribute value as text, serves as an ablation.
Each number is one run on a shared machine of four cores, and a range spans a run of 10,000 edits and one of 50,000; the heap is mallinfo2’s, before and after.

An edit costs about 5 µs more, and stays that cheap however long the journal grows.
The journal is appended without an fsync, and the flush that folds it, once every 400 to 500 edits, is amortized over them; the world map’s 10.5 µs came from a run of 10,000 edits whose slowest move took 23 ms, an outlier its run of 50,000 did not repeat.
An early version spent time quadratic in the journal’s length, since each append copied the journal’s list of cuts, which every attribute change extends; both implementations now append in constant time.
Saving the whole drawing as SVG, which an application without kladde does on every save, takes 1.2 to 12.7 ms here, and writes the whole file.
The second copy of the document costs a sixth of what Inkscape holds for it: 0.64 MB beside the tiger’s 4.2 MB, and 4.4 MB beside the world map’s 29 MB, since Inkscape’s tree, its objects, their styles and their rendering structures dwarf an encoding that holds each node’s name, attributes and children once.
Payload pages halve the file right after the import.
Importing is one splice of the whole encoding, whose bytes payload pages write once, into pages that the flush adopts as data pages.
Without them, the bytes went into the journal first and then into data pages, and the journal’s pages became holes below them: kladde-cpp c4ebcb2 left 100 KB, 204 KB and 1204 KB for the same three imports, where c40ff8f leaves 60 KB, 112 KB and 612 KB.
After thousands of edits the difference is gone: closed after 10,000 edits, the files were 112 KB, 200 KB and 696 KB without payload pages, since consolidation drains the import’s holes along the way.
While a drawing is edited, its file stays within 1.2 to 2.2 times its encoding, which holds the journal, the pages a flush keeps for the header before it, and those a flush frees but can reuse only after the next one; closing flushes and truncates, so a closed file is about as large as the open one was.
The drawing’s canonical SVG is the drawing as the edits leave it, saved by Inkscape and written again by kladde-svg with less whitespace, shortest decimals and shortened path data; it takes 89 / 115 KB, 212 / 286 KB and 1107 / 1192 KB after 10,000 / 50,000 edits.
Next to it, the kladde file is 1.2 to 1.3 times as large for the tiger, whose fixed overhead weighs most beside its small content, 0.9 to 1.0 times for the coat of arms, and 0.6 to 0.8 times for the world map, whose numbers and path data the typed schema stores more compactly than their text.
Opening a kladde file takes 1.3 to 2.3 times as long as parsing the SVG: 17 to 21 ms for the tiger against 11 to 12 ms to parse it, 31 to 46 ms for the coat of arms against 19 to 20 ms, and 127 to 147 ms for the world map against 93 to 99 ms.
Most of the time goes to building Inkscape’s document from the tree, as from a parsed SVG; formatting the typed values back into Inkscape’s text adds a little, since with values kept as text a file opens in 0.9 to 1.8 times the parsing time.
What the typed schema took
What the typed schema needed, beyond keeping attribute values as text, says more than its numbers:

An existing application’s formatting must be stored as data.
kladde-svg normalizes what it parses, and would have lost nearly everything Inkscape writes; reproducing it took decimal numbers rather than floats, a color’s written form, a transform’s optional arguments, and how a path’s text separates its numbers — and Inkscape’s own 10e-4 and -0 still fall back to text.
A Mut’s whole-value set records the whole encoding, where std::string’s records only the changed middle, so changing one number of a long path rewrote the path; the branch diffs the encodings itself, and kladde-cpp should offer it for every type, as the specification guarantees for Text and Opaque.
A std::variant with many alternatives of one type — x, y, width and twenty more are all lengths — cannot be reached through if_holds<A>, which needs an index-based form, and its names must be written out alike.
A std::vector of varint numbers is refused, since they are not fixed-size, so short lists that are only ever replaced whole carry a kladde::Vector’s index.
Adding a typed attribute changes the root fingerprint, so that files written before no longer open; growing a typed schema over time needs evolution, which neither implementation has yet.
Embedded data is held as its bytes: a data: URI with base64 keeps its media type and decoded bytes, three quarters of its text, and only the line breaks inside the base64 do not read back; none of the three drawings embeds data.
Under the observer, a typed copy is a third copy of the document, beside Inkscape’s XML strings and its objects; a typed schema pays off fully only where it replaces the application’s own model, which in Inkscape would mean rewriting its object layer.

The journal’s budget
kladde sizes the journal’s budget to the file, which keeps these files within 1.2 to 2.2 times their encoding at a flush of about a millisecond every 400 to 500 edits; a fixed budget of 256 pages, which almost never flushes, lets the tiger’s file grow to 16 times its encoding.
The budget is 2% of the sequence in whole pages, at least 2 and at most 10 (Options::journal_budget_pages left empty, in both implementations), which gives the tiger and the coat of arms 2 pages and the world map 3.
The runs below are the benchmark above, with KLADDE_JOURNAL_BUDGET_PAGES set for the fixed budgets; the ratios are to the encoding after the edits, and the latencies are those of each single move of a drag, which in the benchmark includes any flush the move triggers, since nothing flushes at idle there.

The world map’s slowest move of 23 ms at the budget sized to the file came from its run of 10,000 edits, whose run of 50,000 peaked at 3.0 ms.
At 256 pages, the 50,000 edits never filled the journal, which is why no move stalled for long there; the next edit would have folded a journal of a megabyte, as the ablation shows, whose larger records fill it once in 50,000 edits.
The budget trades a few long stalls for many short ones, and the short ones are the better deal for an editor.
A median move costs 3.1 µs at every budget: the move itself, recorded in the journal.
With 256 pages, a move almost never meets a flush, but the one that does folds a journal of a megabyte and stalls for 46 to 77 ms, three to five frames; with 4 pages, one move in seven hundred meets a flush of a few pages, which takes one to two milliseconds and fits within a frame.
The flushes here run inside the moves because the benchmark has no idle time; in the GUI, the idle flush moves most of them between gestures, and does so better the smaller the journal it has to fold.
The times come from a disk whose fsync is fast; on a slow disk, every flush costs more, and the small budget’s frequent flushes cost proportionally more than its few large ones save, which is the case for the commit on a worker thread.
Hence a budget that follows the file, between a floor and a ceiling, rather than a fixed one.
A budget of 1 page gains nothing in size over 2 to 4 here, and flushes two to four times as often; above a few pages, the files grow with the journal and its fallback while the flushes saved bring little, since each flush is also a chance to consolidate.
Transactions and batches gives the rule and its reasons.
Ablation: attribute values as text
Keeping every attribute value as text, as the branch untyped does, makes the encoding 1.5 to 1.8 times larger, the files 1.5 to 1.7 times larger and an edit’s journal a fifth larger; in exchange it takes two thirds of the typed schema’s memory and a third to a half of its import time, and opens a little faster.
The branch is main with the XML schema in place of the typed one, and the runs are the same.

With values as text, a kladde file is 1.1 to 2.0 times the canonical SVG, where the typed schema’s is 0.6 to 1.3 times it: both hold the drawing’s numbers, but as text they keep Inkscape’s whitespace and digits, which the canonical SVG drops and the typed schema never stores.
Per edit, the two cost the same within the noise of the machine, though a median move costs 3.1 µs typed against 2.6 µs as text, which is parsing and formatting the attribute’s value.
The journal budget behaves as with the typed schema, the world map getting 5 pages for its larger encoding: at the budget sized to the file the files stay within 1.1 to 2.1 times their encoding, at a flush every 300 to 900 edits.
At 256 pages its larger records fill the journal once in 50,000 edits, and the move that meets that flush stalls for 46 to 77 ms while it folds a megabyte of journal, where no move at the budget sized to the file took longer than 4.1 ms.
In the GUI
In the GUI, under a virtual display (inkscape-kladde f81602b406, with the XML schema), opening tiger.svg created tiger.kladde beside it and left the SVG as it was; flipping and rotating the whole drawing through Inkscape’s actions, then killing Inkscape without saving, left a file that the command line exports with the flip and the rotation in place.
The File ▸ New dialog, which asks where the new document’s file goes, was not exercised, since no test drives a file chooser.
Bugs the port found in kladde-rs
The port read kladde-rs’s store line by line, and found five things that are wrong rather than different; the implementation notes record each.

⚠️ A single write of 4 GiB or more corrupts the journal, since a record’s length is kept as a u32.
Arithmetic on values read from the file is unchecked, so a file whose CRCs match but whose numbers do not panics or wraps rather than being refused.
FileStorage takes no lock, so two processes can open one file.
A cut that escapes a transaction rolled back by Store::atomically can paste another record’s bytes.
TypeTable::fixed_size shared one memo between plain sizes and fixed forms, so a type met inside a Fixed and outside one got one size for both; fixed in d19a613.
The first version of the seal could replay a lost journal after a power cut, since the page it named was cleared without an fsync before the seal was appended; porting it found this, and both implementations and the specification now sync first.
An append copied the journal’s list of cuts, making a journal quadratic in its length, as the measurements found; fixing it took kladde-rs’s svg-bench from 136,000 to 330,000 edits a second on the tiger, and from 90,000 to 238,000 on the coat of arms.

And it confirmed one already known: ⚠️ a file whose span table outgrows the header’s references to leaves, at some two million spans, no longer opens, in kladde-rs and in kladde-cpp alike.
Reproducing
# kladde-cpp: the three test suites, under AddressSanitizer and UBSan
cmake -S kladde-cpp -B kladde-cpp/build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DKLADDE_SANITIZE=ON
cmake --build kladde-cpp/build
kladde-cpp/build/kladde-schema-tests && kladde-cpp/build/kladde-store-tests && kladde-cpp/build/kladde-typed-tests
 
# The typed cross-implementation test, in both directions
cargo run -p kladde-types --example cross_impl -- write rs.kladde
kladde-cpp/build/kladde-cross write cpp.kladde
kladde-cpp/build/kladde-cross check rs.kladde
cargo run -p kladde-types --example cross_impl -- check cpp.kladde
 
# The Inkscape demo's tests and measurements, in inkscape-kladde's build directory
ninja test_kladde-backing test_kladde-backing-bench
./bin/test_kladde-backing
# (created_KB is the file right after the import, file_KB and closed_KB the file before and after closing, edited_KB the encoding after the edits)
KLADDE_BENCH_STEPS=50000 KLADDE_SVG_CORPUS=…/kladde-rs/crates/kladde-svg/corpus/drawings ./bin/test_kladde-backing-bench
# … with a fixed budget, and keeping the edited drawings for their canonical SVG's size (kladde-rs's svg-roundtrip, column canon_bytes)
KLADDE_JOURNAL_BUDGET_PAGES=4 KLADDE_BENCH_SAVE_DIR=edited KLADDE_SVG_CORPUS=… ./bin/test_kladde-backing-bench
cargo run --release -p kladde-svg --bin svg-roundtrip -- --csv canon.csv edited

evaluation/index.title: Evaluation
evaluation/index.content:
Measurements of kladde-rs and, in the Inkscape demo, kladde-cpp under realistic workloads, and what they say about the design.
Every page but the last measured the design that the present one replaced, of allocations and an address table: “main” in them is kladde-rs’s main branch as it stood then, which holds that design and is kept as the branch address-table.
Their findings about consolidation’s policies — the churn floor, the budget, free filling, compaction mode — carry over to pages of spans, since the present design keeps those policies; their findings about statements, allocations and layouts do not.
The last page, the file as one sequence, measured, compares the present design with that main.
Each page names the commit it measured and the commands that reproduce it.
Its figures are drawn by tools/plot-evaluation.py from the tables in data/, which are kept, gzipped, so that a figure can be redrawn without rerunning the benchmark.
Benchmarks and tests describes the programs behind them, and the tests of kladde-rs: what each runs and records, how to run it, and how to read what it writes.
The numbers come from one machine.
Ratios, such as the file’s size over its live size or the bytes written per byte the application wrote, carry over to other machines far better than times do.
The evaluations

evaluation/one-sequence.title: The file as one sequence, measured
evaluation/one-sequence.content:
Executive summary
On the drawings and texts of Cleaning edited drawings and texts, under the same edits, the one-sequence branch keeps as few live pages as main’s best layout at equal writes, or fewer, and its churn floor reaches further.
kladde-rs’s branch one-sequence implements the design of one sequence, which was a proposal when this page was written, in all four of its stages, and ran svg-bench and text-bench at the six settings of the churn floor that main ran, with three bounds L of its span policy.
With its default bound, L = 64 bytes, it keeps 1 to 10 % fewer live pages than main’s small layout at equal writes on the tiger, 1 to 2 % fewer on the world map, and as many, within 1 %, on the coat of arms; 2 to 17 % fewer than the packed layout, but for the world map at λ = 1, and 35 to 61 % fewer than the base layout.
On the texts, it keeps 2 to 3 % fewer than main where their curves overlap on the 64 KiB text, and as many on the 512 KiB text, where main’s controller had cut its budget to a page.
At λ = 0.1, it keeps 1.06 to 1.11 times the drawings’ live size and 1.07 and 1.05 times the texts’, where main reached 1.08 to 1.09 in the small layout, 1.13 to 1.19 in the packed one, and 1.13 and 1.09 on the texts.
The sequence is as compact as main’s small layout, and half its base layout.
The drawings’ live size, the sequence’s bytes with the schema chain’s, is 46, 128 and 942 KiB, within 0.4 % of the small layout’s live allocation bytes, 1.3 to 2.4 % below the packed layout’s, and 0.50 to 0.70 times the base layout’s.
So the ratios of live pages to live size compare one sequence with main’s small layout byte for byte, and its live pages compare with main’s other layouts on the same drawing without a ratio.
The journal writes 14 to 27 % less, and splices restate nothing behind them.
Relative positions shorten a drawing edit’s journal bytes from 37 to 51 per edit in main’s small layout to 31 to 43, and a keystroke’s from 13.2 to 9.6, as the journal’s arithmetic expected.
On the texts, the leaves take 6 to 18 bytes of each keystroke’s writes where main’s took 15 to 30, since a splice states one to three entries rather than every statement behind it.
The span policy’s bound decides much of the writes: a merge costs the bytes it writes again, and the garbage it leaves for the cleaner.
At L = 256, the proposal’s sizing and the branch’s first default, the cleaner moves 1.6 to 2.1 times the bytes it moves at L = 64 on the drawings and texts at λ = 0.25; at L = 64, every setting of the churn floor writes 4 to 33 % less, for about as many live pages at equal writes, which made 64 the default.
At L = 64, the leaves take 8 to 26 % of the drawings’ live pages and 4 to 10 % of the texts’, against 2 to 8 % and 2 to 4 % at L = 256, since short spans keep more entries and more payloads inline; L = 32 traces nearly the same curves as 64.
Edits stay fast, flushes short, and opening fast.
At the default bound, kladde’s calls take 39,000 to 123,000 edits per second on the drawings, as many as in main’s small layout or up to 1.6 times as many, with median flushes of 2.2 to 5.0 ms, against 2.6 to 10.8; on the texts, 691,000 to 837,000 keystrokes per second, 14 to 30 % fewer than main, with flushes of 1.9 to 2.8 ms, against 6.8 to 9.2.
Reopening an edited file takes 0.8 to 7.7 ms, as on main.
Where it falls short of the proposal: the span table holds two levels only, a span costs about 90 bytes of memory rather than 32, and the cleaner, the evacuation and the walk are main’s, without the refinements the proposal names; kladde-rs’s implementation notes record every deviation.
What was measured
kladde-rs’s branch one-sequence, at b2d0649, ran the benchmarks of Cleaning edited drawings and texts unchanged but for what one sequence removes.
The branch starts from defrag-shifts at b1a7f90, as the proposal asked, and takes eight commits: seven that implement the store, the schema, persist, the derive and the facade, the containers, text-bench, and kladde-svg, and one, b2d0649, that sets the span policy’s defaults to what this page measured.
kladde-svg has one layout, since every list is a PersistableVec and every string a PersistableString, inline in its parent; text-bench splices the store’s sequence itself, as it spliced one allocation on main.
The edits are the same, edit for edit.
svg-bench ran each drawing for main’s number of edits, 31,613, 41,130 and 177,831, with the same seed, the same mix and the same focus, and every run ended with main’s canonical SVG, of 59,005, 184,541 and 1,069,891 bytes; text-bench typed main’s 100,000 keystrokes, and the texts ended at main’s 241,322 and 700,340 bytes.
The store flushed whenever the journal outgrew four pages, --journal-budget 4, and at every row, every 1000 edits or keystrokes.
Each workload ran at six settings of the churn floor, with three bounds of the span policy: 90 runs, eight at a time.

The bound is the span policy’s: two neighbouring spans whose entries leave the header for a leaf are merged if they are shorter than L together.
rewrite_below is the threshold for overwrites: where an edit cuts into a Ref span shorter than it, the flush writes the span’s bytes again, with the edit’s, rather than split it.
It applies to the span being cut, not to the parts a cut leaves, so shorter Refs still arise, from splits of longer spans and from evacuation, as do short inline spans of new bytes; the bound merges those as their entries leave the header, 0.5 to 9.3 bytes per edit at L = 64 in the span policy’s table, so the two constants matter even where they are equal.
The sweep ties them to keep its grid small, after tuning runs at λ = 1, which data/ does not keep, had varied them apart: over four workloads, rewrite_below moved the bytes written per edit by at most 7 %, and L by up to 21 %.
The span policy’s other constants kept their defaults: inline spans up to 64 bytes, 16 flushes to count as cold for the rotating walk, which looks at 256 spans per flush, and μ = 0.02.
The cleaner is main’s churn floor, with its budget controller aiming the file at a fill of 0.8, its free filling, its compaction mode and truncation, over pages of spans.
main is the churn floor’s runs of Cleaning edited drawings and texts, on defrag-shifts at 7eb2ec4, in the drawings’ base, packed and small layouts and on the texts, from the tables in data/cleaning-edits/.
The measures are main’s, with the live size taken from the sequence.
The live size is the sequence’s bytes and the schema chain’s, the column alloc_bytes of the tables; live pages are the data pages and the leaves, without the header and the journal, and the branch writes no interior pages of the span table.
Space is averaged over the second half of each run, and writes are what the store wrote during that half, per edit or keystroke: the journal’s bytes and every page written, headers included, at 4,096 bytes each.
The tables keep kladde-bench’s columns, so that tools/plot-evaluation.py reads them: statements and fragments count the spans, allocations is 0, window_restated counts every entry stated, defrag_rewrites and defrag_bytes the span policy’s merges and the bytes they wrote again, and restated_bytes the bytes of short spans written again where an edit cut into them; columns of the span policy’s own follow.
The runs were built with --release by Rust 1.97.1 and ran on the Intel Core i7-1165G7 of Cleaning edited drawings and texts, four cores and eight threads, 16 GB of memory, under Linux 7.0 in a development container.
The benchmarks are deterministic but for their times; the times come from two further passes, one run at a time, of the default bound at λ = 1, 0.25 and 0.1.
data/one-sequence/ keeps every run’s table, in a directory named <policy>-lambda<λ>-<layout>, with seq256, seq64 and seq32 for the bounds and one and text for the layouts, logs/ beside them the end of each run’s output, and timing/ and timing2/ the two timing passes’ tables and output, from which the rates, the flush times and the reopen times come.
To reproduce a run, build the benchmarks on the branch, and run them as main’s were, with the bound’s options:

target/release/svg-bench crates/kladde-svg/corpus/drawings/world-map.svg out/ \
    --edits 177831 --journal-budget 4 --churn-floor 0.25 --span-min 64 --rewrite-below 64
target/release/text-bench out/ --size 524288 --journal-budget 4 --churn-floor 0.25 \
    --span-min 64 --rewrite-below 64
The figures come from the tables of both pages, each run labelled <policy>/lambda/<λ>/<layout>:

for dir in content/evaluation/data/cleaning-edits/main-*-*/ content/evaluation/data/one-sequence/seq*-*-*/; do

The trade-off between space and writes
With the default bound, one sequence’s curve lies on or below main’s lowest on every drawing, and on or below main’s on the texts, and reaches further down.
Each curve runs through the six settings of the churn floor, from λ = 1, hollow, to λ = 0.1; main’s are dashed, one per layout.
Each drawing takes a column: above, live pages over the live size; below, the live pages in KiB, which compare the layouts on the same drawing, whatever their encodings:


Against main’s small layout, whose live size one sequence’s matches, the default bound keeps 1 to 10 % fewer live pages on the tiger, 1 to 2 % fewer on the world map, and on the coat of arms between 0.7 % fewer and 0.4 % more, at equal writes.
On the tiger the gap closes as the churn floor falls: 10 % at λ = 0.5, 1 % at λ = 0.1.
Against the packed layout, it keeps 9 to 17 % fewer live pages on the tiger, 3 to 7 % fewer on the coat of arms, and 2 to 4 % fewer on the world map at equal writes, but at λ = 1 on the world map, where the packed layout, whose writes start lowest, keeps 3 % fewer.
Against the base layout, it keeps 35 to 61 % fewer live pages in KiB, since the base layout’s live size is 1.4 to 2 times larger, and 7 to 22 % fewer relative to each layout’s own live size.
On the tiger, the base layout writes more at its least than one sequence does at its most, so the curves do not overlap.
At its lowest writes, λ = 1, an edit writes 84, 135 and 225 bytes, against 96, 142 and 215 in the small layout and 96, 121 and 164 in the packed one, and keeps 1.39, 1.39 and 1.28 times the live size, against 1.39, 1.43 and 1.34 and 1.52, 1.56 and 1.40.
The bound matters less than the churn floor: L = 32 and 64 trace nearly one curve; L = 256 writes more for the same live pages on the coat of arms and the world map, while on the tiger its curve crosses L = 64’s; at the lowest λ, it reaches furthest, 1.05 to 1.09 times the live size.

The equal-write comparisons interpolate main’s curve between its settings, at every setting of one sequence whose writes lie within it.
On the texts, a panel per text gives the live pages over the live size:


On the 64 KiB text, the default bound keeps 2.0 to 2.6 % fewer live pages than main where the curves overlap, between 38 and 48 bytes per keystroke, and writes from 30 bytes per keystroke, where main’s least is 37.
Below main’s curve, it goes on to 1.07 times the live size at 74 bytes per keystroke, where main’s λ = 0.1 kept 1.13 at 48.
On the 512 KiB text, main’s six settings lie within 2 bytes per keystroke of each other, at 1.09 to 1.10 times the live size, and one sequence’s curve passes through them: between λ = 0.5 and 0.35 it keeps 1.10 and 1.09 times the live size at 47 and 53 bytes per keystroke.
main’s controller had cut its budget to one page, since main’s file passed the target fill of 0.8 after about 11,000 keystrokes; one sequence’s file stays below it, its budget at 223 to 256 pages, so every λ cleans as its own setting says.

From L = 256 to 64, the merges at eviction write 3.5 to 11 times less, and the cleaner moves 1.6 to 2.1 times less, since every merge leaves the bytes it copied dead where they lay; the rewrites of short spans fall with rewrite_below, and the walk, which merges by temperature and μ rather than by the bound, writes about the same.

The spans stay short: 71 to 263 bytes on average on the drawings at L = 64, and 163 and 357 on the texts, against the proposal’s 128 bytes where the sequence is hot and a page where it is cold.
The rotating walk merges cold runs, 1.3 to 36.6 bytes per edit on the drawings, whatever the bound, and still the mean span stays below a page by far; this page has not traced which spans stay short, or why the walk leaves them.
Short spans move content into the leaves, and add little to the live pages: at L = 64, the leaves take 8 to 26 % of the drawings’ live pages, where they took 2 to 8 % at L = 256, and the live pages at equal writes stay within a few percent.
A bound of 64 lets spans of up to 64 bytes stay inline, in their entries, which L = 256 merged into data pages; the leaves then hold those spans’ content as well as the description.
A splice states one to three entries, and a flush folds the keystrokes at one place into one span: on the texts, a flush states 0.5 entries per keystroke at λ = 1 and splits 0.04 spans per keystroke, whatever the bound.

L = 32 writes 3 to 10 % less than 64 on the drawings, and between 14 % less and 2 % more on the texts, for about the same live pages at equal writes, with 1.1 to 1.4 times the spans; the default stays at 64, since the bound’s guarantee, a mean span in the leaves of at least L / 2, weakens as L falls, and nothing measured here asks for it.

The benchmarks’ processes peak at 3.9 to 6.1 MB of resident memory on every workload but the world map, which takes 15.7 MB, at λ = 0.25, sampled from /proc every 10 ms.
Of those peaks, 2.6 to 3.0 MB are the binary and its libraries, mapped from disk, and 1.3 to 3.0 MB anonymous memory, which holds at 1.2 to 2.7 MB over the second half of the runs.
The world map’s anonymous memory grows from 7.5 MB once the file is created to 10.4 MB, where it holds over the second half; valgrind’s massif finds 8.3 MB of heap there, at 90,000 edits, a fifth of it the store’s, and the allocator’s overhead and the freed memory it keeps make the rest:

The peak comes in svg-bench’s epilogue, which writes the edited drawing’s canonical SVG into a string of 2.1 MB and then reopens the file, decoding a second drawing: 10.6 MB of heap, which with the allocator’s overhead and the mapped binary makes the 15.7 MB.
Most of it could go, and little of it is the store’s.
A Box<Element> in kladde-svg’s Node would shrink each node from 328 bytes to 48, and vectors built at their final length would lose their spare capacity.
kladde-types’ vector spends 40 bytes on its index of sizes even where it is empty or its elements are fixed-size, 0.86 MB over the world map’s 13,385 vectors: the tree’s cached total and the count’s length need no fields, which leaves the 24 bytes of an empty Vec, or 8 with a thin one; and a Fenwick tree over blocks of 32 elements, scanning up to 31 elements’ sizes within a block, would cost an eighth of a byte per element rather than four.
The store’s journal arena should shrink to the journal’s budget after a flush, and its span table and rope could grow in smaller steps, or become a B-tree, which would bring the store’s share to about half a megabyte for this drawing; and svg-bench could drop its copy of the SVG after parsing.
main’s memory was not measured, so this page cannot say how one sequence compares with it.
Identical runs differed by more than on the cleaning page.
The two timing passes differed in the edit rate by 8 % at the median and 32 % at most, in the median flush by 5 % and 26 %, and in the reopen times by 16 % and 33 %, the largest on the 512 KiB text’s rates and on the coat of arms’ reopens, which take about two milliseconds.
The reopen times are medians of 21 opens each.
The sweep in numbers
Every setting’s steady state: the live pages over the live size, and the bytes written per edit or keystroke.
These are the points of the trade-off figures; main’s are in the cleaning page’s sweep.

evaluation/ripeness-free-filling.title: Ripeness with main's free filling
evaluation/ripeness-free-filling.content:
Executive summary
With main’s free filling, the three ripeness branches write 2 to 3 % less at the same target fill on the drawings and keep about as many live pages, which closes a third to two thirds of their gap to main’s churn floor there, and none of it on the texts.
At equal writes, the ripeness branches keep, at the median, 2.5 % more live pages than the churn floor in the drawings’ base and packed layouts, where they kept 3.7 % more without it, and 1.1 % more in the small layout, where they kept 3.0 % more; on the texts, 8.8 % more, where they kept 8.2 %.
Cleaning edited drawings and texts named the free cleaning the ripeness branches give up as the likely source of their extra writes for the same space; it accounts for a third of the gap in the base and packed layouts, two thirds in the small one, and none on the texts.
Free filling takes about one victim per flush on the drawings, as on main, where the draft’s took one in seven flushes or fewer, and the branches open fewer pages for cleaning.
At τ = 0.9, free filling takes 0.80 to 1.37 victims per flush on the drawings, where the draft’s took 0.01 to 0.15 and main’s takes 1.0 to 1.3 at λ = 1, and 0.47 to 0.73 per flush on the texts.
The branches evacuate a median 3 % more data pages whole than without it, 9 to 25 % of them free where 0 to 3 % were, and open 2 to 20 % fewer pages for cleaning, 7 % fewer at the median.
At the same setting, the drawings’ writes fall by a median 3.3 % in the base and packed layouts and 2.7 % in the small one, in 98 of 108 runs, while the live pages stay within 2.5 %; on the texts, writes fall by 0.4 % at the median, and both move in either direction, the most at τ = 0.75.
Along each branch’s curve, the drawings keep a median 1.2 % fewer live pages at equal writes in the base and packed layouts, and 1.1 % fewer in the small one, the most at τ = 0.75, up to 5.7 % fewer, and about 0.3 % fewer at τ = 0.9 and 0.95.
Single-rate ripeness gains most, and lies below the churn floor at 8 of its settings in the small layout, by up to 2.4 %; the churn floor still lies lowest nearly everywhere else, and reaches further.
At equal writes, single-rate ripeness keeps a median 1.9 % more live pages than the churn floor in the drawings’ base and packed layouts, where it kept 3.6 % more, 0.5 % fewer in the small layout, where it kept 2.3 % more, and 3.3 % more on the texts, where it kept 7.0 % more.
The static share and the Bayesian posterior move less, and on the texts by less than a point, in either direction.
The fullest any branch fills the pages moves by 0.02 times the live size at most: at λ = 0.1, the churn floor keeps 1.08 to 1.19 times the drawings’ live size, and the best setting of any branch 1.10 to 1.25.
Otherwise little changes: the ripeness branches’ pages fill as before, 80 to 88 % on the tiger and 84 to 90 % on the coat of arms at τ = 0.9, and their leaves as before, 78 to 86 % in the drawings’ base and packed layouts.
What changed
Free filling on the ripeness branches is main’s.
The room left in a page the flush writes anyway takes, in compaction mode, the tail first, then whole data victims that fit, the sparsest first, then description defragmentation’s candidates beyond its reserved share, then as many of one victim’s statements as fit, whether ripe or not.
Without it, the branches gave that room to ripe victims whose survivors take at most θ, 5 %, of a page, and then to the cursor, the least-filled data page of the previous flush, a whole statement at a time, as the ripeness draft did then; both are gone, and the draft takes main’s free filling too.
The price of space holds after a flush whose only cleaning was free filling.
The controller holds the price where moving it could change nothing: it does not lower it after a flush that cleaned nothing.
Free filling takes its victims whatever the price, in nearly every flush, so counted as cleaning, it would let the price fall in every flush while the pages are fuller than the target; its victims do not count.

The commits without main’s free filling are not those Cleaning edited drawings and texts measured.
Each branch has a commit since that fixes what its consolidator state records: the estimates the state’s own rewrite changes, after its record is written, were never recorded, and came back at a reopen as losses in the gap.
That changes only bytes the consolidator state writes, and nothing on the texts, but on the drawings it moves single runs by up to 3.1 % in live pages and 7.3 % in writes, where the ranking amplifies a small difference in what a flush writes into a different choice of victims.
So this page compares against its own runs of those commits, which the earlier page’s tables come within those bounds of, and the spread of single runs is part of every change below: a change in one run smaller than a few percent says little, while a change of one sign in most runs does.
What was measured
Everything ran as on the earlier page: the same drawings, layouts, edits, texts, keystrokes and settings, the three ripeness branches at τ = 0.75, 0.85, 0.9 and 0.95, on the same host, with text-bench from kladde-rs 7c5cdd6 added to every commit, without its --churn-floor option.
The churn floor’s numbers are the earlier page’s, from its data in data/cleaning-edits/; main’s free filling is the churn floor’s own, so its runs would not change.
This page ran 264 runs, eight at a time, 132 of each commit, and no timing passes, so it reports no times.
data/ripeness-free-filling/ keeps every run with main’s free filling, and its before/ those without, each with its table and, under logs/, the end of its output.
To reproduce a run, build as on the earlier page, on the commit with main’s free filling:
git cherry-pick --no-commit 7c5cdd6   # text-bench; drop its --churn-floor option
cargo build --release -p kladde-svg --bin svg-bench --features packed
target/release/svg-bench crates/kladde-svg/corpus/drawings/world-map.svg \
    out/ --edits 177831 --journal-budget 4 --target-fill 0.9
cargo build --release -p kladde-bench --bin text-bench
target/release/text-bench out/ --size 524288 --journal-budget 4 --target-fill 0.9
The figures come from the tables here, those without main’s free filling labelled before/…, and the churn floor’s from the earlier page’s:
D=content/evaluation/data; F=content/evaluation/figures/ripeness-free-filling
runs=()
for dir in $D/ripeness-free-filling/*-*-*/ $D/ripeness-free-filling/before/*-*-*/ \
        $D/cleaning-edits/main-*-*/; do
    IFS=- read -r p k l <<< "$(basename $dir)"; knob=${k%%[0-9]*}
    case $dir in */before/*) before=before/ ;; *) before= ;; esac
    runs+=("$before$p/$knob/${k#$knob}/$l=$dir")
done
tools/plot-evaluation.py --only svg-tradeoff,text-tradeoff --out $F "${runs[@]}"
The tables give the churn floor at λ = 0.25 for reference, and each ripeness branch at τ = 0.9, the earlier page’s regime, with its value without main’s free filling in brackets.
Free filling
Free filling takes 69 to 895 victims per run on the drawings at τ = 0.9, where the draft’s took 1 to 98, and as many as main’s at λ = 1 to within 30 %; at that target, the branches open fewer pages for cleaning in every run.
Each cell gives, over a whole run, the data victims that free filling took and the data pages opened only to take victims:

The branches evacuate about as many data pages whole as before, and more of them free.
At τ = 0.9, they evacuate between 3 % fewer and 11 % more on the drawings than without main’s free filling, 3 % more at the median, and 9 to 25 % of them by free filling, where 0 to 3 % were; on the texts, 7 to 33 % more, 24 to 33 % of them free.
So they open fewer pages for cleaning: 2 to 20 % fewer on the drawings at τ = 0.9, 7 % at the median, and 3 to 21 % on the texts.
Over every setting, as many as 38 % fewer on the drawings and 68 % on the 64 KiB text, both at τ = 0.75.
Neither count sees what the cursor cleaned without main’s free filling: it took the room that small ripe victims left, a whole statement at a time, and freed its page only once the page was empty, which counts as no victim taken.

The trade-off between space and writes
Main’s free filling moves each branch’s curve down and to the left on the drawings, the most at τ = 0.75 and by a fraction of a percent at τ = 0.9 and 0.95, and closes part of the gap to the churn floor; on the texts, it moves the curves by about as much in either direction.
Each panel shows each policy’s settings, from the one that cleans least, hollow, to the one that cleans most, and dashed and pale each ripeness branch’s curve without main’s free filling; each drawing takes a row, whose panels share their range of live pages:


At equal writes, each branch keeps between 5.7 % fewer and 0.1 % more live pages than without main’s free filling, 1.2 % fewer at the median in the base and packed layouts and 1.1 % fewer in the small one, at 42 of 44 and 22 of 22 settings whose writes the other curve spans.
At τ = 0.75, 2.4 and 2.9 % fewer at the median; at τ = 0.9 and 0.95, 0.3 % fewer.
Against the churn floor’s curve, the branches keep between 0.1 % fewer and 12 % more live pages at equal writes in the base and packed layouts, where they kept between 0.2 and 15 % more, and between 2.4 % fewer and 6.5 % more in the small layout, where they kept between 0.6 % fewer and 8.3 % more.
At the median, 2.5 % more where they kept 3.7 % more, and 1.1 % more where they kept 3.0 %.
13 of their 107 settings in range lie below the churn floor’s curve, where 3 did: 10 of single-rate ripeness’s, one of the static share’s and two of the Bayesian posterior’s, all but two in the small layout, and by 2.4 % at the most, single-rate ripeness at τ = 0.95 on the tiger; the two in the world map’s base and packed layouts lie below by 0.1 % or less.
Single-rate ripeness gains most.
At the median, it keeps 1.9 % more live pages than the churn floor at equal writes in the base and packed layouts, where it kept 3.6 % more, and 0.5 % fewer in the small layout, where it kept 2.3 % more; the static share 3.4 and 2.1 % more, where it kept 5.3 and 2.9 %, and the Bayesian posterior 2.9 and 1.8 % more, where it kept 3.6 and 4.2 %.
The furthest each branch reaches stays where it was, within 0.02 times the live size.



On the texts, the gap to the churn floor stays where it was: at equal writes, the branches keep between 2.1 and 18 % more live pages than the churn floor, where they kept between 1.9 and 22 % more, 8.8 % at the median, where they kept 8.2 %.
On the 512 KiB text, single-rate ripeness at τ = 0.75 to 0.9 keeps 1.16 times the live size, where it kept 1.17 to 1.21, for about as many writes, 49.4 to 49.5 bytes per keystroke; at τ = 0.95, it keeps 1.13 times, as before.
The static share and the Bayesian posterior keep 1 to 2 % fewer live pages at τ = 0.75 and 0.85, and within 1 % of as many at τ = 0.9 and 0.95.
On the 64 KiB text, the branches at τ = 0.75 write 4 to 5 % less, single-rate ripeness for 3 % fewer live pages and the other two for about as many; at the other targets, live pages and writes change by 2.5 % at most, in either direction.

The regime
For the space each branch kept at τ = 0.9 without main’s free filling, it writes between 9 % less and 2 % more with it, and on the drawings 0 to 9 % less.
