evaluation/ripeness.title: Cleaning by ripeness
evaluation/ripeness.content:
Updated for the draft’s clarifications, as of kladde-docs commit b33a836: the branch now measures a page’s fill relative to the fill survivors are packed at, which moved no result of 8 MiB or more by more than 1 % in file size or 2 % in writes.
The clarified draft ranks a page by h(u/u_0), with u_0 = 1 - \theta, and never cleans a page at or above u_0; the first version ranked pages by h(u), with 1 - \theta only as a cap.
The controller absorbs the difference: it settles the price of space 15 to 50 % higher, since h(u/u_0) lies below h(u) at every fill, and the trade-off curves of the two versions lie within 1 % of each other.
The branch also carries the rates that fresh content starts from across sessions now, since the clarified draft rules out estimates that start from nothing; these runs, one session each, do not exercise it.
The ablation that the clarified draft proposes, ranking without the logarithm, writes 3 to 6 % more for the same file size under skewed overwrites, and 1 to 4 % more under uniform ones: see Without the logarithm.
This update’s runs shared their host with other work, so the flush times on this page are still the first version’s; its tables are in kladde-docs commit 08febdf.
Cleaning by ripeness, as the draft proposes, keeps a file under skewed overwrites 10 to 12 % smaller than the current design for the same writes, or writes 4 to 20 % less for the same file size; under uniform overwrites the two are level, as the draft predicts.
At the default settings of each, the 8 and 64 MiB skewed files come out 5 to 6 % smaller for 10 to 11 % fewer writes.
It gains where the draft says it should: under skew, the current design’s data pages lose fill for most of a run as pages freeze above the churn floor, and ripeness’s hold at 0.76.
Where hot, cool, and never-changing cold allocations share pages at random, it gains about as much, a file 4 to 5 % smaller for 9 % fewer writes, since main’s data pages freeze there too; neither policy separates the cold content from the rest.
It took one change to the draft to work: the controller that sets the price of space must measure the fill of the data pages and leaves, not of the whole file, or the price swings over decades.
Three costs remain.
Recording every page’s estimate in the consolidator state takes 1 to 7 % of the writes.
Under churn the file comes out 19 % larger.
And after a mass free the price takes 13 to 19 flushes to climb back from where calm phases left it, so the file peaks higher.
What was measured
The same benchmark ran on the ripeness branch of kladde-rs, and on main.
Main is at commit cb34576, as on the consolidation page.
Its tables here are from a run made back to back with the first version of the branch, so that their times compare; a run of main for this update reproduced every number in them but the times, as the benchmark is deterministic but for its times.
The branch is at 362210a, which follows the draft as of kladde-docs b33a836; the first version, at f7d4eab, ranked pages by their absolute fill.
Two more runs of the branch, at the same commit, measure what the consolidator state costs, by leaving it out, and what the logarithm contributes, by ranking pages without it, as the draft’s ablation does.
The mixed workload ran later, on the branch at 799c661, and on main from the branch main-mixed at 7646408; both commits add it to kladde-bench and change nothing else.
The experiments this page cites besides, on the controller and on churn, ran on the first version, changed for the purpose, and are not part of the committed code.
The branch fills in what the draft leaves open with a forgetting rate β = 0.1 per flush, a floor R_MIN = 10⁻⁴ and a starting price κ = 0.01 (the draft’s own examples), a cursor that gives up pages older than W = 8 flushes, and a budget of 256 pages per flush, which is now a fixed cap.
Its controller aims the data pages and leaves at a fill τ = 0.75 by default, where main aims the whole file at 0.8 and never gets there.
implementation-notes.md in kladde-rs lists every departure from the draft.
Where main’s page compares policies, it uses steady states: the file size averaged over the second half of each run, and the bytes written during that half per byte the application wrote.
Both controllers take a live size or more of writes to settle, which end-of-run values would mix in.
The trade-off
Under skewed overwrites, ripeness’s curve lies below main’s everywhere they overlap; under uniform ones, the two curves cross, within 3 % of each other.










































8 MiB, steady statemainripeness, same writesripeness, same file sizeskewed, λ = 21.83 times the live size, 2.34 bytes per byte1.65 (−10 %)2.25 bytes per byte (−4 %)skewed, λ = 11.65, 2.741.46 (−12 %)2.34 (−15 %)skewed, λ = 0.51.51, 3.22below 1.422.57 (−20 %)uniform, λ = 11.69, 3.131.74 (+3 %)3.32 (+6 %)uniform, λ = 0.51.63, 3.951.61 (−2 %)3.69 (−7 %)
The ripeness columns interpolate between its runs at targets 0.65, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, and 0.85.
Skew is where ripeness gains, and for the reason the draft gives.
The churn floor cleans a page only once it is half empty; a page whose hot content has died and whose cold content stays freezes above that, and keeps its garbage.
In main’s 64 MiB skewed run, data pages lose fill for most of the run, down to 0.70; in ripeness’s, they hold at 0.76, since a frozen page, draining at the floor rate, is ripe at a fill a draining page never is.

Under uniform overwrites every page drains alike, and ripeness reduces to a single fill threshold, like the churn floor.
What remains between the curves is noise: a page’s estimate comes from its own sporadic losses, so pages that drain alike get different estimates, and a threshold that differs page by page costs a little at light cleaning.
The controller
Measuring the whole file, the price controller swung by two to three decades; measuring the data pages and leaves, it holds within about 10 %.
The draft’s controller moves κ by exp(gain · (τ − fill)) after every flush, as main’s moves its budget.
The first version’s controller measured the whole file, like main’s.
But cleaning does not shrink the file at once: the pages it frees stay free until new writes reuse them, so the whole file’s fill answers a change of price only many flushes later, and an integral controller on a lagging measure cycles.
At 8 MiB and a target of 0.5, the price swung between 2·10⁻⁴ and 0.09, a swing per one to two live sizes of writes, and at targets of 0.5 to 0.6 the files ended up 8 to 20 % larger than a fixed price gave for the same writes.
The data pages and leaves, which cleaning acts on, answer within the flush.
Measured there, the price holds within about 10 % of its median over the second half of every overwrite run of 8 MiB or more; in the first version, gains of 0.5 and 2 gave the same results, and the steady states fell on the curve that fixed prices traced.
The holes the measure leaves out are compaction mode’s to return anyway.
The consolidation page suggests the same change for main’s budget.

The price also has to hold where moving it can change nothing.
A file starts full, so without that the first flushes drove the price to its floor, and it took one to two live sizes of writes to climb back.
The branch holds the price after a flush that cleaned nothing while the fill is above target, and after one that spent its whole budget while the fill is below; the clarified draft asks for the second.
That is not enough after a mass free.
Between the append workload’s rotations, the live pages sit above target, and the price drifts down to 3·10⁻⁵ even so, since small moves by free filling count as cleaning.
When the logs rotate, the price needs 13 to 19 flushes to climb three decades, and the file peaks at 4.3, 3.5 and 2.9 times its live size, where main’s peaks at 2.9, 2.3 and 2.3.

At the default settings
Ripeness at its default target writes less than main at its default under skewed overwrites and appends, and more under uniform overwrites, where its target lies further along the same curve.





















































steady state, file size / live size and bytes written per bytemainripenesschangeuniform, 8 MiB1.69, 3.131.66, 3.44−2 %, +10 %uniform, 64 MiB1.53, 3.261.48, 3.99−4 %, +23 %skewed, 8 MiB1.65, 2.741.56, 2.44−5 %, −11 %skewed, 64 MiB1.53, 3.151.43, 2.84−6 %, −10 %append, 16 MiB1.38, 3.141.44, 2.96+4 %, −6 %churn, 16 MiB1.41, 2.181.68, 2.12+19 %, −3 %typed, 16 MiB1.53, 3.041.46, 3.81−5 %, +25 %

The 1 MiB files are dominated by the quarantine, as on the consolidation page, and their 33 flushes are too few for either controller to settle; the skewed one comes out 11 % larger with ripeness.
Under churn, ripeness’s file is 19 % larger, and neither a higher target nor more generous free filling closes the gap.
Main’s churn run keeps data pages 91 % full, taking half of its victims for free in the room of pages the flush writes anyway, and moves 14 MB of survivors against ripeness’s 4 MB.
In the first version, at a target of 0.85, ripeness’s data pages reached 0.88, but its file still kept a third of the live size in free pages, against main’s quarter, and ended 9 % larger for about the same writes.
In experiments on the first version, letting free filling take any ripe victim that fits, or any victim at all, changed nothing, or made things worse; why churn leaves ripeness with more free pages remains open.
After three quarters of a file are freed, compaction mode returns the space as fast as on main, but stops earlier.
The file reaches 1.29 times its live size within 14 flushes, where main’s reaches 1.14 within 16.
Both stop once holes fall below a quarter of the file; ripeness’s run crossed that line with 20 % holes left, main’s overshot to 11 % in its last step.

Hot, cool, and cold allocations on shared pages
When hot, cool, and cold allocations share pages at random, ripeness gains over main about as much as under skewed overwrites, a file 4 to 5 % smaller for 9 % fewer writes, but neither policy separates the cold content from the rest.
kladde-bench’s mixed workload is skewed with each allocation’s class drawn at random.
A tenth of the allocations are hot and take nine tenths of the writes; the other writes go to any allocation alike, as under skewed overwrites, except that the 45 % of allocations that are cold never change, so writes drawn for them are not made.
The allocations are 1 KiB, four to a page, so that the pages written at the start mix classes, 91 % of the live data at 8 MiB.
Skewed overwrites mix far less: their allocations of 16 KiB fill pages of their own, and their hot allocations hold the lowest ids, so a flush, which packs in key order, writes them apart from the rest.
Each row of the workload’s table records how much of the live data, and how much of the cold data, lies on pages that mix classes.























steady state, file size / live size and bytes written per bytemainripenesschangemixed, 8 MiB1.64, 2.701.56, 2.47−5 %, −9 %mixed, 64 MiB1.51, 3.151.44, 2.85−4 %, −9 %
Under skewed overwrites, ripeness gains 5 to 6 % in file size and 10 to 11 % in writes.
At 1 MiB, where the quarantine dominates, ripeness’s mixed file is 17 % larger, as its skewed one is 11 % larger.
Main’s data pages freeze here as they do under skewed overwrites.
Main’s data pages lose fill for the whole run, from about 0.85 early on to 0.71 at its end, since a page whose hot content has died keeps its cool and cold content above the churn floor; ripeness holds its data pages at 0.77.
The file’s size moves in steps, when freed pages come to lie at its end, where truncation returns them, so the space its live pages take shows the difference better: 1.39 times the live size under ripeness, against 1.47 to 1.48 under main.

Neither policy separates the cold content from the rest.
At the start, 91 % of the cold data shares a page with content that still changes.
Under ripeness, 90 % still does at the end of the 8 MiB run and 88 % at the end of the 64 MiB one, as 89 % does without any cleaning; under main, the share falls slowly, to 85 and 84 %, most likely as the cool content of frozen pages dies away and leaves some of them holding cold content alone.
Ripeness cleans the mixed pages that main leaves frozen, but packs their survivors together again: once a page’s hot content has died, what survives on it is cool content, which still dies, next to cold content, which never will, and nothing tells the two apart.
The draft’s “cold with cold” assumes that what survives has stopped dying; here it may only be slow.
Without the logarithm
Ranking pages by the myopic (1 - x)/x in place of h(x) writes 3 to 6 % more for the same file size under skewed overwrites, as the draft’s ablation predicts, and 1 to 4 % more under uniform ones, where it predicts no difference.
The ablated branch differs from the full one in nothing but the fill term of the index, and its controller aims at the same targets.
Under uniform overwrites, too, pages do not all drain at one rate: leaves drain at a rate of their own, and each page’s estimate strays from its true rate.








































8 MiB, steady stateripenessmyopic, same file sizeskewed, τ = 0.71.67, 2.322.41 (+4 %)skewed, τ = 0.751.56, 2.442.55 (+5 %)skewed, τ = 0.81.48, 2.632.78 (+6 %)uniform, τ = 0.71.75, 3.123.16 (+1 %)uniform, τ = 0.751.66, 3.443.52 (+2 %)uniform, τ = 0.81.60, 3.944.09 (+4 %)
At the default target, the 64 MiB files come out the same size either way, and the myopic rule writes 5 % more under skewed overwrites and 4.5 % more under uniform ones.
Under appends it writes 1.6 % more, under churn 1.5 % more for a file 1 % smaller, and after the mass free it compacts exactly as the full rule does.
The extra writes are survivors, and they are few because survivors are a small part of what a flush writes.
Under skew, the myopic rule moves 30 % more survivors per byte the application wrote: 0.44 bytes against 0.34 at 8 MiB, 0.59 against 0.45 at 64 MiB.
The draft’s cost table for content that drains slowly, up to seven times the optimum, applies to that share alone, and the flush’s own content, which both rules write alike, makes up most of the rest.
The myopic rule also moves cleaning from leaves to data pages.
Under skew, the leaves come out at 0.60 against 0.64 at 8 MiB, and 0.46 against 0.56 at 64 MiB, while the data pages gain a little.
That fits the draft’s warning: the myopic rule ranks slowly draining pages higher, and they take writes that would free more elsewhere.
Its controller settles the price three to five times lower, since (1 - x)/x exceeds h(x) at every fill.
What it costs
Keeping every page’s estimate in the consolidator state costs 1 to 7 % of the bytes written, and buys nothing within one session.
The draft has the state record the estimate of every page the fold drains, which at 1000 operations per flush means an entry for about every page those operations touched, and a snapshot of every page below u₀ whenever the records outgrow the last one.
Without the state, the 64 MiB runs write 7 % less under both uniform and skewed overwrites, for files 1 % smaller; append writes 3 % less, the 8 MiB runs 2 to 3 %, churn 1 %.
The estimates matter only across a reopen, which these runs do not exercise; a denser encoding, or recording only pages whose estimate moved by a margin, would cut the cost.

A flush takes time in proportion to the pages it writes, on either branch.
These times are from the first version’s run, made back to back with main’s; the pages each writes per flush have changed by 3 % at most since.
Per page written, ripeness’s flushes took between 4 % less and 16 % more time than main’s in the same session, within the spread identical runs showed before.
Where ripeness writes fewer pages, as under skew, its flushes are faster: at the median over the second half of each run, 9.7 ms against 11.6 for the 8 MiB skewed file, 16.5 against 17.7 at 64 MiB.
Where it writes more, as under uniform overwrites at its default target, they are slower: 34.9 ms against 27.0 at 64 MiB.

In memory, each page’s estimate takes 16 bytes in the page table, and each ranked page takes an entry in one of two ordered sets and one in a map from page to entry.
The ranking takes O(log P) per page that changed and per victim, where main’s bucket queues take O(1); the flush times do not show it.
What to change in the draft

Measure the fill the price acts on: the data pages and leaves, not the whole file, whose fill lags a change of price by many flushes.
Hold the price where moving it can change nothing, in both directions.
The clarified draft holds it while the budget binds; it should also hold it while the fill is above target and nothing is cleaned, and keep it from sinking in calm phases, where every page is fuller than the target: a floor well above 10⁻⁶, or holding the price whenever the budget took no ripe page, would spare the file the peaks after a mass free.
Record estimates more cheaply.
A drain record could leave out the estimate’s epoch, which is the record’s own, store the rate in a byte on a logarithmic scale, and skip pages whose estimate moved by less than a margin.
Keep the logarithm.
Without it, skewed overwrites cost 3 to 6 % more writes for the same file size, and nothing is simpler for it.
Look into churn, the one workload where ripeness loses: replaced values free whole allocations every flush, and ripeness leaves more of the file free than main does.
Do not count on survivors being cold.
On the mixed workload, survivors that still die slowly share the pages opened for them with survivors that never will, and the cold content never ends up on pages of its own.
Ordering survivors by their source page’s estimate, or by their allocation’s last_written, might separate them; this page has not tried it.
Expect noise under uniform overwrites.
Estimates from sporadic losses differ between pages that drain alike; a larger β or two rates per page, as the draft’s open questions consider, trades that noise against how soon a frozen page is recognised.

Reproducing
The runs of the branch used one checkout of kladde-rs, with main in a worktree of its own:
git worktree add ../kladde-main main
cargo build --release -p kladde-bench --manifest-path ../kladde-main/Cargo.toml
git checkout ripeness
cargo build --release -p kladde-bench
../kladde-main/target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-main
./target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-ripeness
KLADDE_BENCH_NO_STATE=1 ./target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-ripeness-no-state uniform skewed append churn
KLADDE_BENCH_MYOPIC=1 ./target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-ripeness-myopic uniform skewed append churn shrink tuning
The mixed workload ran from the branch at 799c661, with and without the consolidator state, and on main from the branch main-mixed at 7646408, which is main with the workload added:
git checkout 799c661
cargo build --release -p kladde-bench
./target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-ripeness mixed
KLADDE_BENCH_NO_STATE=1 ./target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-ripeness-no-state mixed
git checkout main-mixed
cargo build --release -p kladde-bench
./target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-main mixed
In kladde-docs, keep the tables gzipped under content/evaluation/data/ripeness/, in main/, ripeness/, ripeness-no-state/, and ripeness-myopic/, and draw the figures from them, all but the flush times, which come from the tables of commit 08febdf:
D=content/evaluation/data/ripeness
tools/plot-evaluation.py --summary --out content/evaluation/figures/ripeness \
    --only space-amplification,live-fraction,write-breakdown,budget,shrink,description,defrag-share,kappa \
    main=$D/main ripeness=$D/ripeness
tools/plot-evaluation.py --only tradeoff --out content/evaluation/figures/ripeness \
    main=$D/main ripeness=$D/ripeness myopic=$D/ripeness-myopic
tools/plot-evaluation.py --only mixed --out content/evaluation/figures/ripeness main=$D/main ripeness=$D/ripeness

evaluation/ripeness2.title: Ripeness with a static share
evaluation/ripeness2.content:
The static share makes no difference to cleaning on kladde-bench’s workloads, not even on one built for it, and costs twice as much to keep.
Without the consolidator state, the static-share branch and the single-rate branch that Cleaning by ripeness evaluates write within 0.3 % of each other in every run of 8 MiB or more, and their live pages take the same space to within 0.2 %.
With the state, the static-share branch writes 2 to 7 % more at the default target, and all of the difference is its state’s larger entries.
Few pages earn a static share, even on the mixed workload, where content that never changes makes up 45 % of the live data and nine tenths of it shares pages with content that does: 1.9 % of the live bytes count as static there at 8 MiB, and almost none at 64 MiB.
The fall that would show a static share, a page’s hot content dying, comes to a few statements of about 250 bytes, too little evidence for the test to let a static share through, and afterwards a page loses only the rare statements of its cool content, which one share draining slowly explains as well.
The other workloads give the fit less still to find: their cold content still dies, only slowly, and skewed overwrites seldom put hot and cold content on one page.
That matches what the draft’s own simulation found: the single-rate draft cleans as cheaply, and needs half the state.
What was measured
The same benchmark ran on the ripeness2 branch of kladde-rs, which implements the draft as of kladde-docs commit 7c343b7.
The branch is at 074a0df, on top of the single-rate branch at 362210a; the two differ only in how a page’s estimate is kept and fitted, and in two counters of static shares, which the benchmark records.
The benchmark is deterministic but for its times, so every number of either branch’s runs compares with the other’s: the single-rate branch’s and main’s tables are those of Cleaning by ripeness.
A second run of the static-share branch left the consolidator state out, as one of the single-rate branch did, to tell what the policy does from what its state costs.
The mixed workload ran later on both branches, with and without the state, at a856b06 here and 799c661 on the single-rate branch, which add it to kladde-bench and change nothing else.
This page compares no times, since its runs shared their host with other work.
The branch takes the draft’s constants, β = 0.1 per flush, a starting estimate worth n₀ = 10 flushes of losses, and a test that a static share must pass by c = 3 statements’ worth of log-likelihood, and the single-rate branch’s for the rest.
Its fit agrees with the tested estimator of tools/simulate-ripeness.py to within 0.1 % of the index, where the simulation fits rates on a fine grid, and reproduces the draft’s worked example.
implementation-notes.md in kladde-rs lists where it departs from the draft: both fits are solved exactly, and the test’s unit, the mean statement size, is measured separately for data pages and leaves.
How often pages earn a static share
Rarely, even where content that never changes shares pages with content that does: at most 2.6 % of the live bytes count as static, on average over the second half of any run of 8 MiB or more.























































second half of each runpages with a static sharelive bytes estimated staticuniform, 8 MiB0.15 %0.12 %uniform, 64 MiB0.16 %0.14 %skewed, 8 MiB2.6 %2.3 %skewed, 64 MiB0.57 %0.66 %mixed, 8 MiB4.3 %1.9 %mixed, 64 MiB0.06 %0.05 %append, 16 MiB2.4 %2.6 %churn, 16 MiB0.53 %0.13 %typed, 16 MiB0.70 %0.60 %
The mixed workload is built for a static share, and the fit finds almost none of it.
Its allocations, four to a page, are hot, cool, or cold at random, and the cold ones, 45 % of the live data, never change.
Nine tenths of the cold data share a page with content that still changes, 90 % at 8 MiB and 88 % at 64 MiB, on both branches alike.
Yet at most 19 of the 8 MiB file’s 2098 data pages hold a static share during the first flushes, while the hot content of the pages written at the start dies, and at most 2.4 % of the live bytes count as static at any time; at 64 MiB, never more than 0.2 %.
A page’s fall is too small to earn a static share.
A page written at the start holds four allocations of 1 KiB, usually one hot one at most, and that allocation dies within a few flushes: the whole fall, the evidence for a static share, comes to about four statements of 250 bytes, too little for the three statements’ worth of log-likelihood the test asks for.
Afterwards the page loses only its cool content, a statement every 40 flushes or so, which one share draining slowly explains as well as a draining share over a static one.
The test counts in statements, and a statement in these files states 100 to 380 bytes of data, so a data page holds 10 to 30 of them.
The draft’s simulation found the same: with statements of 32 to 256 bytes, its tested fit costs as much as the single-rate draft, and with larger ones a little less, since the test that keeps it from inventing static shares also keeps it from finding them quickly.
A leaf states some 300 statements of 10 to 14 bytes each, plenty of losses, but its content, statements that the fold supersedes, is no more static than the data they state.
The other workloads offer less to find.
Their cold content is not static, only slow: under skewed overwrites, a tenth of the writes go to all allocations alike, so a cold byte of the 8 MiB file dies at about 0.003 per flush, against a price of space of 0.025, a ratio r/κ of about 0.12, at which the draft’s threshold lies at 0.64.
The 64 MiB file’s cold content dies eight times slower, and the price settles eight times lower, at the same ratio.
And skewed overwrites seldom put hot and cold content on one page: their hot allocations hold the lowest ids, their allocations of 16 KiB fill pages of their own, and a flush packs its writes in key order, so that of the 60 or so pages of new content a flush writes at 8 MiB, one mixes hot with cold.
Cleaning
Without the consolidator state, the two branches reach the same steady states.



























































steady state, no consolidator statesingle rate: file size / live size, bytes written per bytestatic sharechangeuniform, 8 MiB1.652, 3.3421.650, 3.345−0.1 %, +0.1 %uniform, 64 MiB1.467, 3.7071.467, 3.7030.0 %, −0.1 %skewed, 8 MiB1.548, 2.3941.547, 2.397−0.1 %, +0.1 %skewed, 64 MiB1.415, 2.6481.417, 2.645+0.1 %, −0.1 %mixed, 8 MiB1.660, 2.3981.606, 2.403−3.2 %, +0.2 %mixed, 64 MiB1.412, 2.6381.412, 2.6360.0 %, −0.1 %append, 16 MiB1.420, 2.8641.424, 2.854+0.3 %, −0.3 %churn, 16 MiB1.655, 2.0881.655, 2.0930.0 %, +0.2 %
The mixed 8 MiB files differ in size only because their free pages reached the file’s end, where truncation returns them, at different times; in every run here, the live pages take the same space on both branches to within 0.2 %, 1.38 times the live size in the mixed ones.
The 1 MiB files, dominated by the quarantine and too short for the controller to settle, differ by up to 2 %.

With the state, the static-share branch writes 2 to 7 % more, and its trade-off curve lies 3 to 7 % to the right of the single-rate branch’s.

































































steady state, with the statesingle ratestatic sharechangeuniform, 8 MiB1.66, 3.441.68, 3.55+1 %, +3 %uniform, 64 MiB1.48, 3.991.49, 4.29+1 %, +7 %skewed, 8 MiB1.56, 2.441.57, 2.51+1 %, +3 %skewed, 64 MiB1.43, 2.841.45, 3.04+1 %, +7 %mixed, 8 MiB1.56, 2.471.59, 2.53+2 %, +3 %mixed, 64 MiB1.44, 2.851.44, 3.060 %, +7 %append, 16 MiB1.44, 2.961.44, 3.050 %, +3 %churn, 16 MiB1.68, 2.121.67, 2.15−1 %, +2 %typed, 16 MiB1.46, 3.811.47, 4.02+1 %, +6 %
On the mixed workload, against main, which Cleaning by ripeness compares there, the static-share branch keeps less of the single-rate branch’s gain in writes, 6 % fewer at 8 MiB and 3 % at 64 MiB, against 9 % at both; its live pages take 5 to 6 % less space than main’s, as the single-rate branch’s do.
At the targets from 0.65 to 0.85, the 8 MiB files write 3 to 6 % more under skewed overwrites and 5 to 7 % more under uniform ones for the same file size.
Main’s curve stays where Cleaning by ripeness puts it: under skew, both ripeness branches lie below it.

What it costs
The static-share branch’s consolidator state costs twice what the single-rate branch’s does: 3 to 14 % of the bytes written, against 1 to 7 %.
An entry holds the fit’s two sums, its rate, and its share, four f32s where the single-rate branch’s holds one rate, and the draft has the state record every page the fold drains.
At 64 MiB, the state takes 14 % of the writes under uniform overwrites and 13 % under skewed ones, against 7 %; at 8 MiB, 6 and 5 %, against 3 and 2 %; under appends 6 % against 3 %, and under churn 3 % against 1 %.
It also takes space: with it, the live pages hold up to 1.1 % more than without, where the single-rate branch’s adds up to 0.7 %.

In memory, a page’s estimate takes 24 bytes, against 16.
The ranking keeps its two ordered sets, and a page’s entry also holds the key of its floor, which the single-rate branch derives from its estimate.
Each flush fits every page that lost content, with two bisections of 50 steps, each step a handful of exponentials and logarithms.
The runs shared their host with other work, so this page does not say what that costs in time.
What to change in the draft

Keep one rate per page: on kladde-bench’s workloads, including one where 45 % of the data never changes and shares pages with data that does, the static share changes nothing, and doubles the state.
Expect a static share to pay only where a page’s losses are plentiful.
The evidence for one is a page’s fall, and a page of statements of 250 bytes shows a fall of a few statements at most, too little for the test; the draft’s simulation found a static share paying only on small statements, and then only without the test.
If the static share stays, record less of it.
A page’s rate and share follow from its two sums, its age, and its coverage, which an entry holds already, so they could be fitted again at open, for 8 bytes an entry less.
Say which statements the test counts in.
The draft speaks of the file’s mean statement size, but a data page loses the bytes statements state, 100 to 380 per statement in these files, and a leaf their encoding, 10 to 14.

Reproducing
The static-share branch ran from one checkout of kladde-rs, at 074a0df, and the mixed workload later, at a856b06; at a856b06, these commands run all of it:
git checkout ripeness2
cargo build --release -p kladde-bench
./target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-ripeness2
KLADDE_BENCH_NO_STATE=1 ./target/release/kladde-bench /tmp/bench-ripeness2-no-state uniform skewed mixed append churn
In kladde-docs, keep its tables gzipped under content/evaluation/data/ripeness2/, in ripeness2/ and ripeness2-no-state/, and draw the figures with those of Cleaning by ripeness:
D=content/evaluation/data
tools/plot-evaluation.py --only tradeoff --out content/evaluation/figures/ripeness2 \
    main=$D/ripeness/main single-rate=$D/ripeness/ripeness static-share=$D/ripeness2/ripeness2
tools/plot-evaluation.py --only write-breakdown --out content/evaluation/figures/ripeness2 \
    single=$D/ripeness/ripeness static=$D/ripeness2/ripeness2
tools/plot-evaluation.py --only mixed --out content/evaluation/figures/ripeness2 \
    single-rate=$D/ripeness/ripeness static-share=$D/ripeness2/ripeness2
tools/simulate-ripeness.py example prints the draft’s worked example, which the unit test the_fit_follows_the_drafts_example in kladde-rs checks the fit against.

evaluation/tools.title: Benchmarks and tests
evaluation/tools.content:
Every program that tests kladde-rs or measures it, in kladde-rs and in this repository: what each runs, what it records, how to run it, and how to read what it prints.
The results are on the other pages of Evaluation; this page has none.
It describes kladde-rs at commit 7c5cdd6 on its branch text-bench, which is the branch defrag-shifts and one more benchmark, and which holds the design of allocations and an address table that every evaluation page but the last measured; the branch address-table, kladde-rs’s main branch at the time, lacks text-bench and most of what kladde-svg measures.
kladde-rs’s main now holds the present design, and keeps less of this.
It has text-bench, and svg-bench with one layout, since every list and string is inline in one sequence, with the options --quick, --edits, --only, --seed, --variant, --focus, --focus-moves, --journal-budget, --churn-floor and --target-fill, and the span policy’s --span-min and --rewrite-below; the file as one sequence, measured describes its tables.
kladde-bench’s synthetic scenarios, which allocated, resized and freed, went with the design they measured.
Its tests are the store’s oracle, against a byte vector, its simulated power cuts and its consolidation, the containers’ randomized tests, the derive’s, and kladde-svg’s round trip.
At a glance

































































programwherewhat it doeswhat it leavescargo test --workspacekladde-rsunit, integration and documentation tests, among them a differential oracle and simulated power cutspass or failkladde-benchkladde-rs, crates/kladde-benchsix synthetic workloads on the store, and variants of the optionsone table per workloadtext-benchkladde-rs, crates/kladde-benchtyping into one long textone table, and a summarysvg-benchkladde-rs, crates/kladde-svga drawing editor’s edits on an SVG drawingone table, and a summarysvg-roundtripkladde-rs, crates/kladde-svgevery SVG file of a corpus through kladde and back, and their sizesone table, a summary, and an exit statusplot-evaluation.pykladde-docs, tools/the figures of the evaluation pages, from the tablesSVG figures, and a summary tablesimulate-ripeness.pykladde-docs, tools/a simulation of the ripeness drafts’ estimatorstables of their costscheck-examples.pykladde-docs, tools/the Rust examples of these pages, compiled and run against kladde-rspass or failmake-pdf.py --check-only, check-site-links.pykladde-docs, tools/this repository’s links and page listpass or fail
kladde-rs runs no continuous integration; this repository’s runs on every push.
Every benchmark is deterministic but for its times: the same commit, options and seed make the same operations and write the same tables.
Each one checks, at the end, that the reopened file reads what the program holds in memory, and panics otherwise, so a table from a run that finished describes a file that was right.
The tests
cargo test --workspace
The suite takes about half a minute once built, in debug mode, where the store’s debug assertions check its invariants as it goes: among others, that a page a flush retires holds no live statement.
Store::check, which the tests call after flushes, cross-checks the fragment map, the statement slab, the pins and every page’s coverage, and panics on the first disagreement.
Building with --release skips the assertions, so the tests are meant for debug builds.

































































cratetestswhat they coverkladde-storetests/oracle.rsthe differential oracle: allocations, frees, resizes, writes, splices, copies and moves, chosen at random, against a model of byte vectors; a check of every allocation’s size and bytes and of Store::check after one step in twenty, and a reopening from the storage’s bytes after one in a hundred; small and large allocations, with and without consolidation, and with a journal of one pagetests/crash.rspower cuts: MemoryStorage::with_crash_tracking fails the storage after a random number of operations, and the file as it would be with none of the writes since the last sync, all of them, or four random subsets of them, must recover onto a transaction boundary no earlier than the last completed flushtests/consolidation.rsthat consolidation keeps a file near its live size under overwrites, appends and a mass free, without changing what it readstests/churn.rs, tests/restate.rs, tests/sizes.rsid recycling, bytes that splices shift within an allocation, and the newest size rule, each checked in a reopened fileunit teststhe CRC, the fold, loading, pages, the journal, and the encoding of statementskladde-typestests/packed.rs, tests/small.rspacked vectors and small values under random edits through every mutating method they offer, against a model after every edit and a reopened file after every fewthe other tests/the whole stack through Kladde, enums’ parts(), move_element, schemas, tupleskladde-derivetests/, and compile_fail exampleswhat #[derive(Persistable)] generates, and what it must refuse to compilekladde-schema, kladde-persist, kladde-varint, kladdeunit testsdescriptors, canonical encoding and fingerprints; the serialization layer; varints; the facadekladde-svgtests/roundtrip.rsthe canonical form of SVG, what the model types, and a drawing’s trip through kladde and a reopening, byte for byteevery cratedocumentation examplesthat every public item’s example compiles and runs
The randomized tests are seeded, so a failure repeats.
They run a range of seeds each; the crash test names the failing seed in its message, and for the oracle, narrowing the range finds it.
A seed that found a defect is kept as a test of its own, as a_grow_witness_in_a_reused_page_survives keeps seed 229.
Some tests run only with a feature of kladde-svg, which the workspace’s run leaves off:
cargo test -p kladde-svg --features f64      # decimals as f64
cargo test -p kladde-svg --features packed   # and small-ids, small-attrs, small: the layouts
The tables
kladde-bench, text-bench and svg-bench write the same table: a CSV file with one row per explicit flush, which plot-evaluation.py reads whichever program wrote it.
A run first builds its file, which is not measured, then records a row after every interval of operations; the columns are the run’s identity, a snapshot of the file, the work done since the measured phase began, and two times.

















































































































columnmeaningscenariothe workload: a kladde-bench scenario, text, or svgvariantwhat distinguishes runs of one workload: on or off for consolidation, the name of a variant of the options, the text’s size, or the drawingsizethe workload’s size in bytes: its nominal live size for kladde-bench, the text’s size at the start for text-bench, and the drawing’s live bytes once stored for svg-benchflushrows so faropsoperations since the measured phase began: writes, allocations and the like for kladde-bench, keystrokes, or editsapp_bytesthe bytes the application wrote since then, by the program’s own measure (see each program)file_pagesthe file’s length, in pages of 4,096 bytesdata_pages, table_pageslive data pages, and live address-table pages without the headersfree_pagespages within the file that hold nothing live: reusable, or retired by the last commitlive_data, live_tablethe bytes of those data and table pages that current state relies onalloc_bytes, allocationsthe sizes of the live allocations, summed, and their number, without the store’s own consolidator statestatements, fragmentslive statements in the address table, and entries in the fragment mapbudgetthe consolidation budget, in pages, as the controller set itdata_written, table_written, headers_writtenpages written since the measured phase began: data pages, table pages without the headers, and headersjournal_bytesbytes appended to the journal since thenfresh_bytesbytes of the application’s content that flushes wrote into data pagesevacuated_pages, evacuated_bytesdata pages that consolidation evacuated, and the live bytes it wrote again to do sofree_filledvictims taken into pages the flush wrote anywaybudget_pagesdata pages opened only to take victimstable_rewritestable pages that a page rewrite drainedwindow_restatedfragments that the rotating window restateddefrag_rewrites, defrag_bytesrewrites by description defragmentation, and the bytes they wrotecompaction_flushes, truncationsflushes in compaction mode, and truncations of the fileflush_usthe explicit flush that ended the interval, in microseconds, its fsync includedops_usthe interval’s operations, in microseconds: for kladde-bench the whole loop, choosing the operations and keeping the model included; for text-bench and svg-bench the time in kladde’s calls alonerestated_bytes, merged_bytesbytes that splices and moves shifted within their allocation, which flushes stated at their new offsets where they lie, or wrote again to merge the fragments they lay in
Reading a table

The counters of work are cumulative: the difference between two rows is the work of the interval between them, and the last row’s is the run’s.
The bytes written are journal_bytes plus 4,096 bytes for every page in data_written, table_written and headers_written.
Over app_bytes, they are the write amplification; over ops, the bytes per operation.
The file’s size over its live size, file_pages × 4,096 over alloc_bytes, is the space amplification; the live pages, (data_pages + table_pages) × 4,096 over alloc_bytes, leave out the free pages, the headers and the journal.
A page’s fill is its live bytes over the 4,081 bytes of content it holds, so live_data over 4,081 × data_pages for the data pages, and likewise for the table.
The steady state is what the evaluation pages average over the second half of a run, after the file has settled from its fill; its first rows still show the file the fill left.
Times depend on the machine and vary between identical runs, so they compare only between runs on one machine, and best by their medians over rows; ratios such as bytes per operation carry over to other machines.
The evaluation pages name the machine and how far identical runs differed on it.

kladde-bench: synthetic workloads
cargo run --release -p kladde-bench -- <output directory> [scenario ...] [quick]
Each scenario fills a file, then writes to it until the application has written eight times its live size, flushing after every 1000 operations, and records a row per flush in <scenario>.csv.
Without a scenario, all of them run, which takes a few minutes; quick makes every one small.
The files go to files/ in the output directory and are removed when the run is done.





























































scenariolive sizewhat the application doesapp_bytes countsvariants, one run eachuniform1, 8 and 64 MiBwrites of 1 to 511 bytes at random offsets of random allocations of 16 KiBthe bytes writtenconsolidation on at each size, and off at 1 and 8 MiBskewedas abovethe same, with nine writes in ten going to a tenth of the allocationsas aboveas aboveappend16 MiB512 logs, appended to in records of 16 to 240 bytes and truncated to nothing once a record would take one past 64 KiBthe recordson, offchurn16 MiBvalues of 16 to 128 bytes, or one in five of 1 to 8 KiB, replaced by a new allocation, rewritten whole, or patched in 1 to 64 bytesthe bytes writtenon, offshrink64 MiBallocations of 64 KiB, three quarters of them freed at once, then 400 flushes of 100 patches of 1 to 64 bytesthe patcheson, no-compaction, offtyped16 MiBa Kladde<PersistableHashMap<u64, PersistableString>> of strings of 50 to 500 bytes, through the typed layers: 40 % replace a string, 30 % append to one, 20 % insert one, 10 % remove onethe strings’ bytesontuning8 and 16 MiBuniform and skewed at 8 MiB with a churn floor of 0.5 or 2, or a target fill of 0.6 or 0.5; append with 4 and 16 pages of defragmentation shareas aboveone table per workload, tuning-<workload>.csv, with the default among the variants
With quick, every live size is 1 MiB, and shrink’s 4 MiB.
The shrink scenario flushes every 100 patches rather than every 1000 operations, and its first row follows the mass free.
The branches of the cleaning policies extend it, and their evaluation pages say so where they use it: the ripeness branches add a scenario mixed, skewed overwrites of allocations that are each hot, cool or cold, and five columns after the others, kappa, the price of space their controller sets, and mixed_pages, mixed_bytes, cold_bytes and cold_mixed_bytes, how the three classes share data pages.
On those branches, KLADDE_BENCH_NO_STATE in the environment makes the stores keep no consolidator state, and KLADDE_BENCH_MYOPIC makes them rank pages by the myopic rule.
text-bench: typing into one text
cargo run --release -p kladde-bench --bin text-bench -- <output directory> \
    [--quick] [--size BYTES] [--keystrokes N] [--seed N] [--variant NAME] \
    [--focus SHARE] [--focus-moves N] \
    [--journal-budget PAGES] [--shift-decay FACTOR] [--churn-floor λ] [--target-fill τ]
A text of random words in one allocation of the store is edited keystroke by keystroke at a cursor, as a text editor would; every keystroke that changes it is a splice, which makes this the benchmark of what splices cost.
The text is 64 KiB by default, words of one to nine lowercase letters each followed by a space, and is stored below the typed layers, so that only the store is measured.
Each of the 100,000 keystrokes, 10,000 with --quick:

























sharekeystroke85 %type a letter at the cursor, which moves past it10 %delete the byte before the cursor, if there is one4.5 %move the cursor0.5 %paste 200 random letters at the cursor, which moves past them
Nine moves in ten land in a window of a tenth of the text, which jumps to a random place every 5000 keystrokes, and the tenth anywhere; --focus sets the window’s share, --focus-moves the keystrokes between its jumps, and --focus 0 sends every move anywhere.
The text grows with the typing, to about 3.7 times its size at the defaults.
Every 1000 keystrokes the store is flushed and a row goes to text-<variant>.csv, where the variant is the text’s size in KiB, as in 64k, unless --variant names it.
app_bytes counts the bytes typed and pasted; deletions count nothing.
--journal-budget sets Options::journal_budget_pages, so that the store also flushes by itself whenever a transaction would not fit in that many journal pages; --shift-decay, --churn-floor and --target-fill set the options of those names.
The summary on stderr has five lines:

the keystrokes of each kind, the text’s size before and after, and the flushes, of them those at rows;
what kladde wrote, per keystroke, split into the journal, data pages, table pages and headers;
the bytes per keystroke that splices shifted, restated where they lie and written again;
the statements, fragments, table pages and data pages the file holds at the end, and the median flush;
the closed file’s size, over the text’s, and the median of 21 reopenings.

svg-bench: a drawing editor
crates/kladde-svg/corpus/fetch.sh
cargo run --release -p kladde-svg --bin svg-bench [--features LAYOUT] -- \
    <drawing.svg> <output directory> [--quick] [--edits N] [--only KIND] [--seed N] [--variant NAME] \
    [--focus SHARE] [--focus-moves N] \
    [--journal-budget PAGES] [--shift-decay FACTOR] [--churn-floor λ] [--target-fill τ]
kladde-svg stores an SVG drawing in a model of #[derive(Persistable)] types, and svg-bench edits it with a seeded mix of what a drawing editor does.
fetch.sh downloads the corpus, pinned by SHA-256 and not committed: the Ghostscript tiger, the coat of arms of Spain and a blank world map from Wikimedia Commons, under drawings/, and resvg’s test suite at v0.48.1, under resvg/.













































shareeditwhat it does to the model30 %Dragset the translation that leads a shape’s transform list, or insert one20 %MoveNodeset the end point of a segment of a path’s data8 % / 7 %InsertNode / DeleteNodeinsert a relative line into a path’s data, or delete a segment other than the first10 %Recolorset a shape’s fill colour where it is set, in its attributes or its style, or add a fill attribute8 % / 7 %Duplicate / Deleteinsert a deep copy of a shape right above it, or delete one; each turns into the other when the drawing has grown or shrunk by a fifth5 %Restackmove a shape elsewhere among its siblings, with move_element5 %Texttype into a text, or replace it once it is long; a recolour in a drawing without text
The edits keep to one part of the drawing at a time: nine in ten pick from a window of a tenth of what they pick from, the shapes, the paths, the shapes without children or the texts, and the window jumps every 3000 edits.
--focus and --focus-moves set the window as in text-bench; --focus 0 picks every edit from the whole drawing, except that nine drags in ten move one of the first tenth of the shapes, which was the benchmark’s only mix before kladde-rs e88fd47.
--only KIND makes every edit one kind.
A run ends once the edits have stored eight times the drawing’s live size, once with --quick, or after exactly N edits with --edits, which is how runs of different layouts, branches or options make the same edits: the evaluation pages give each drawing’s number.
Every 1000 edits the drawing is flushed and a row goes to svg-<variant>.csv, where the variant is the drawing’s file name unless --variant names it.
app_bytes counts what each edit stores: the bytes of the numbers it sets, or the encoding of the value it stores, in its place, with everything that value owns; deletions count nothing.
The options of the store are set as in text-bench.
The layouts are cargo features of kladde-svg, each adding to the one before: none, the slotted layout of fixed slots; packed, lists of enums packed; small-ids, ids as small strings; small-attrs, attribute lists and strings small; small, every list small.
f64 stores decimals as f64 instead of f32.
Each layout is a build of its own, so a script that compares them builds once per feature and copies the binary aside.
The summary on stderr gives the drawing’s size in SVG and in kladde and what it holds to edit; the edits, the bytes they stored and the mix as it came out; what kladde wrote, per edit and per byte stored, and the file over its live size; what saving the whole canonical SVG every 1, 100 or 1000 edits would have written instead; the edits per second in kladde’s calls and the median flush; the closed file’s size; and the times to parse the SVG, to reopen the closed file, as the median of 21, and to write the SVG.
After the edits, the reopened drawing must write the same canonical SVG as before closing.
svg-roundtrip: a corpus through kladde
cargo run --release -p kladde-svg --bin svg-roundtrip [--features LAYOUT,render] -- \
    [--csv <table.csv>] [--render] [--journal-budget PAGES] <file or directory> ...
For every .svg file under the paths, it checks that the canonical form is stable and that kladde gives it back byte for byte, and records the sizes of the file in each form.
The canonical form is what kladde-svg writes: no whitespace between tags outside text, single spaces between attributes, and path data in the grammar’s shortcuts.
It exits with a failure if any canonical form was not idempotent or any trip through kladde differed.

The summary on stderr counts the files by status, names those that failed, and sums the sizes.
svg2kladde <in.svg> <out.kladde> and kladde2svg [--indent] <in.kladde> <out.svg>, binaries of the same crate, convert single files, for looking at one by hand.
Tools in this repository
The figures
tools/plot-evaluation.py [--only NAMES] [--summary] --out <directory> <label>=<directory> ...
Draws the evaluation pages’ figures from tables, gzipped or not, each directory a run and each label its name in the figures.
It recognizes the tables by name: kladde-bench’s by their scenario, svg-bench’s as svg-<drawing>.csv, and text-bench’s as text-<size>.csv.
--only draws the figures it names, out of space-amplification, mixed, live-fraction, write-breakdown, budget, shrink, description, flush-latency, throughput, tradeoff, defrag-share, kappa, svg, svg-tradeoff, svg-pages and text-tradeoff; a figure whose tables are missing is skipped.
svg-tradeoff and text-tradeoff also draw the runs labelled before/policy/knob/value/layout, dashed and pale, to show how a change moved each policy’s curve.
--summary prints the last row of every series as a Markdown table.
The figures are SVG, the same bytes whenever the data and matplotlib’s version are, which tools/requirements.txt pins; install it with pip into a virtual environment.
Each evaluation page keeps its tables, gzipped, in content/evaluation/data/, and lists the commands that ran them and that redraw its figures.
The ripeness simulation
tools/simulate-ripeness.py compare|sweep|example [--set drafts|bayes] [options]
Simulates pages whose statements die at the rates of the shares they belong to, cleans each page when an estimator says it is ripe, and prints how much more each estimator costs than cleaning at the true ripeness, over all pages of a scenario.
compare runs every estimator of a set, the ripeness drafts’ or with --set bayes the Bayesian draft’s; sweep varies their parameters β, n0 and c; example computes the draft’s worked example without noise.
Its module docstring lists the estimators and the options.
Checks of this repository

























commandcheckstools/check-examples.pythe Rust examples these pages mark with a kladde-example comment, compiled against a checkout of kladde-rs next to this one, and run, or refused by the compiler, where the comment says sotools/make-pdf.py --check-onlythe links and anchors between pages, and that tools/pages.py lists every pagetools/make-pdf.py --self-testthe layout passes of the diagramssite/build.sh, then tools/check-site-links.pythe links and anchors of the built site, as Quartz made them
The README describes them in full.
Continuous integration
.github/workflows/site.yml runs on every push and pull request: it builds the PDF, builds the site and checks its links, and compiles and runs the examples against kladde-rs’s main.
A broken link fails the run; a failing example does not hold up publishing.
On main, it then publishes the site and the PDF.
A measurement kept with its evaluation
The heap an open drawing takes was measured once, for the evaluation of variable-size values on this repository’s branch defrag-shifts, by content/evaluation/data/variable-size/memory.rs there.
It counts the bytes allocated through a global allocator while a drawing is parsed and while its kladde file is opened, and the median time of 21 opens, one drawing per call; it is built as the binary of a crate of its own that depends on kladde and kladde-svg, with their layout features.

impl/consolidation.title: Consolidation
impl/consolidation.content:
Reclaiming garbage: which pages to rewrite, in what order, and how much per flush.
Consolidation rewrites live content out of sparse pages so their slots become reusable, and merges short spans so the description stays small.
It is not part of the specification — an implementation that never consolidates is conforming, and merely useless — but the policy below is what makes the copy-on-write design’s space overhead bounded rather than unbounded.
The high-level picture
Consolidation fights three independent debts, and the counters that measure one are blind to the others.
Description fragmentation is a property of a region of the sequence: how many spans it takes to show its bytes.
Runs of short spans arise where edits happen, since every splice and every split leaves a boundary; they cost entries in table pages, memory in the span table and the rope, and time at open; and no page-level counter can see them, because a run of short spans whose entries sit densely in one full leaf makes that leaf look perfect.
Page fragmentation is a property of a page, Data and Table alike: how much of it current state still relies on.
It is measured by coverage against capacity; it costs file size and nothing else; and nothing that counts spans can see it, because long spans can lie thinly spread over sparse pages.
Outer fragmentation is a property of the file: reusable pages below its last live page.
It costs file size, since a file can only shrink from its end, and neither kind of counter can see it, because every page involved is either wholly reusable or wholly live.
It arises whenever the live size falls and stays down, since pages freed anywhere but at the end become holes that only future writes can fill.
The first two convert into each other, each in one direction: more spans need more table pages, and merging spans writes their bytes again, leaving the old ones as data-page garbage.
Only page fragmentation is urgent, and that asymmetry decides how each debt is scheduled.
Page fragmentation grows with write traffic and compounds, since garbage left uncleaned occupies the pages the next flush wanted to reuse — so it is attacked greedily, worst first.
Description fragmentation is bounded already by the span policy’s merges as entries leave the header, and what remains is a standing debt that does not grow while nobody writes the region — so a rotating walk pays it down eventually, without any ranking structure of its own.
Outer fragmentation is not a debt at all while the file grows, because growth fills the holes first; it becomes one only once the live size has fallen, and is then paid down in a mode of its own.
Three mechanisms

































mechanismpays downselected byreadswritesEvacuationpage fragmentation of Data pages; outer fragmentation, in compaction modethe sparsest data pages, one victim at a time — the highest first, in compaction modethe victim’s spans, through the reverse indexthe spans’ bytes, into data pages, each span restated with its new addressPage rewritepage fragmentation of Table pages; outer fragmentation, in compaction modethe sparsest table pages, one victim at a time — the highest first, in compaction modethe victim’s live entries, from the span tablethose entries, restated at the cutRotating walkdescription fragmentationa cursor that rotates through the sequencethe bytes of the runs it mergesone span per merged run, among the flush’s new bytes
All three end in the same place — fresh pages plus fresh entries — which is what lets one placement pass serve all of them.
Every one of them is simpler than it would be over allocations, because a span’s id never changes: evacuation writes a victim’s bytes elsewhere and states each span again with its new address, and nothing else changes; a page rewrite states each live span in it again under its own id, with no size to state again and no tombstone to carry; and merging a run of spans materializes no zeros, since no span has gaps.
Evacuation
Evacuating a data victim writes the bytes of its reached spans into new pages and states each span again with its new address.
The victim’s spans come from the reverse index, exactly and in O(1) each.
A span is all or nothing — its bytes move together, since a Ref shows one contiguous run — except that a span may be cut at a page boundary where packing needs it, its tail becoming a new span that leads the next page.
Neighbouring short spans in a victim can be merged in the same pass, at no extra write, since their bytes are being written anyway.
Victim selection for data pages
The classic greedy rule of log-structured file systems — lowest live fraction first — refined by age the way LFS and SSD flash translation layers refine it: prefer pages that are sparse and old.
The refinement rests on one assumption worth stating explicitly: temporal update locality — bytes written together tend to be rewritten together, and soon, or else not for a long time.
It transfers from the workload to pages mechanically: a data page’s residents are exactly the content that one flush wrote together, so if the application is still working on whatever produced them, more of its residents will be superseded shortly.
Such a “hot” page gets sparser without help, and cleaning it early wastes writes on relocating survivors that are about to die anyway; a page whose live fraction has been stable for a long time is “cold”, and its survivors are the ones worth paying to move.
It fails gracefully: under a workload with no locality at all, the age term carries no information and the policy degrades to plain greedy, which is the right fallback anyway.
Scoring a data page
Take LFS’s cost-benefit ratio unchanged, with u = coverage[p] / capacity the live fraction and age = current_epoch − page_epoch[p]:
score(p) = (1 − u) · age / (1 + u)

The numerator is what the eviction frees times how long it has been stable; the denominator is what it costs — one page read plus u of a page written back.
Evaluating it without scanning every page: the next victim is the highest-scoring of K pages sampled from the sparsest non-empty bucket, for a small constant K — eight, say.
That keeps selection O(1) and gets the age term back, and the worst outcome of a bad sample is cleaning a page slightly less old than the best one in the same bucket.
Rotating the start of the sampling window across flushes stops the same unlucky prefix from being examined forever.
Victims are pulled one at a time
A victim is taken only when all of its spans have somewhere to go in this flush, since relocating only some of a page’s spans reclaims nothing.
In free filling that means the page’s room holds all of them; on a budgeted page, one span may be cut at the boundary, its tail leading the next page — never on the budget’s last page, where the tail would have nowhere to go.
Free filling makes one exception once nothing whole fits: moving part of a victim reclaims nothing yet, but in a page that is written anyway it costs nothing either, and it leaves the victim sparser.
A marginal victim frees (1 − u_v) · C bytes and writes u_v · C: all C of the victim’s bytes come back, and u_v · C of them are spent again at once, because the survivors take up as much space in their new page as they did in the victim.
Sparsest first is exactly right, since the marginal ratio (1 − u_v) / u_v falls as u_v rises, and the churn floor then reads u_v ≤ 1 / (1 + λ).
A free sink changes the arithmetic, not the order.
A survivor landing in room that a page being written anyway would otherwise waste consumes nothing, so the victim’s net gain is the whole C: free filling takes any victim that fits, and the churn floor does not apply to it.
coverage counts bytes shown by several spans once per span, so where they are, u_v over-states both what an evacuation writes and what it reclaims.
The page rewrite
A table victim is drained by restating its live entries elsewhere: each live span in it is stated again, under its own id, at the cut, and the victim then holds nothing live.
Victims come from the table pages’ buckets — sparsest first, sampled and scored as data pages are, or the tail first in compaction mode — and a victim is taken in one of two ways: into the room of the cut’s last page, if all of its live entries fit there, which costs nothing, or under the budget, whose offers gather victims while their entries fit one leaf.
Its cost is those entries’ encoded bytes, inline payloads included, which coverage already counts; its benefit is the whole victim.
So it is priced exactly as evacuation is, (C − written) / written, and the two compete in the budget loop on equal terms, but for the fill floor, which holds evacuation’s page alone, since the page rewrite opens none.
Restated entries lie together in id order in their new leaf, so a page rewrite also repairs the delta encoding of entries that went cold far apart in the id space and were evicted together.
A victim with children — an interior page — is rewritten the same way, and its child references move with it; see unlinking.
Unlinking an emptied page
Nothing waits for a load.
With entries, inline payloads, and child references all charged per byte, a table page whose last live entry is restated elsewhere reaches zero coverage in the same flush, and the quarantine does the rest.
One step stands between zero coverage and reuse: an emptied table page is still named by its parent, so it stays reachable from the header, and I2 forbids overwriting it until a flush has also unlinked it.
When the parent is the header, the flush that emptied the page unlinks it for free, since the header is written last.
Deeper, the parent is rewritten without the child’s reference, its other children carried over, and so is its parent, up to the header — the depth − 1 path copy of a structural update.
A writer must not rely on its own shallow trees here, since another writer may shape the tree differently, so:

The page table records each table page’s parent, which the tree property makes a single page number.
A child reference is charged to its parent’s coverage, and released when the child is unlinked; without that charge, a parent whose entries had all moved elsewhere would reach zero coverage while still holding the only reference to live children, and reusing it would orphan them.
A page rewritten while it has children carries them along: into the header if its child list has room, which also flattens the tree, and otherwise into the page’s replacement.

Data pages need none of this, having no parent.
Merging spans rides the rotating walk
A rotating walk over the rope looks at a fixed number of spans per flush, and merges runs of cold spans whose entries lie in leaves where the entry bytes the merge retires pay for the bytes it writes.
The decision is per run and local: the walk visits the spans anyway, so the only question is whether a run is worth writing again as one span.

A merge pays when the entry bytes it retires exceed μ for every byte it writes.

The data terms cancel, since the bytes the merged spans showed lose their coverage exactly where they lay, so a run’s gain is the entries it retires, less the one it adds, less μ per byte.
The best runs are a maximum-subarray problem: weigh each cold span by its entry’s bytes less μ times its length, and Kadane’s algorithm, in one pass over the spans the walk is traversing anyway, finds the maximal runs of positive weight, each cut into tiles of at most a page, since a Ref shows one page at most.
A long span scores entry − μ · len, negative for any span longer than entry / μ — a few hundred bytes at μ = 0.02 — so an already-long run is left alone, which is correct, since writing it again merges nothing and only moves bytes.
A short, dense knot of tiny spans is exactly where the run of large positive weights is, so it is what Kadane returns.
Only cold spans take part, those whose bytes have gone unwritten for some number of flushes, since a run the application is still editing would be split again by its next edit, which would waste the merge; the heat of each span says how long.
And only spans whose entries lie in leaves: the header is exempt.
The walk runs before placement, so a merged run’s bytes join the flush’s own new bytes, and are packed among them.
μ is a price of the same kind as the churn floor λ — file bytes freed per byte written — and sits far lower, near 0, since what a merge chiefly buys is invisible in the file: an entry in memory per span retired, and the work of resolving it at every open.
The walk can also give a run of spans consecutive ids, so that their successors become implicit and their id deltas short, which shrinks entries without writing any data byte.
A new session resumes the walk where the last one left it, if the consolidator state says where, or else where open seeds it.
How a flush and consolidation compose
Every source changes spans as it goes, and entries come last; that gap is the whole interface between a flush and its consolidation.
The fold, the span policy’s merges, evacuation, the page rewrite and the walk all mark the spans they change as stated, and the cut derives every entry from the span table as it finally stands, so what the flush states is by construction exactly what it changed, each span once.
A relocated span is the same object as a fresh write: a run of bytes that has no place yet, differing only in whether its bytes are read from a data page or from the flush’s new bytes.
Placement cannot tell them apart, and does not need to.
Mandatory and elastic
Placement combines two streams: what the flush must write and what consolidation may add.
One stream must be written whole and the other may be cut short, and that asymmetry is the only thing the packer needs to know about where a chunk came from: a commit that omits part of what the journal produced is not a commit, while a survivor left behind costs a delay and nothing else.
The walk’s merges belong to the first stream, since they are chosen before packing, and once chosen they are writes like any other.
The elastic stream is drawn on demand: a victim is pulled into a page only at the moment that page has room its own content cannot use, and only as much of it as fits.
That is what lets consolidation fill every page the flush writes to nearly full without ever opening a page it cannot fill.
Slack is cheaper than a split — up to a point
Do not cut a chunk to make a page come out exactly full; cut only to keep a page from closing more than θ empty.
Every cut is one more span, an entry and a node in the rope, which stays until a merge removes it, whereas slack is recovered by the next consolidation that picks the page up.




















costsuntilleaving slackat most θ of a page, on every page but a flush’s last, and usually far lessthe page is next consolidatedsplitting to fill itone more entry and one more span in memorya merge writes the run again as one span
Slack has no small bound of its own, which is what θ is for.
Chunks all just over half a page are the adversarial case — no two can ever share a page, so if they were never cut, every page would close half empty, whatever the look-ahead.
So a page that would close more than θ empty is filled instead, in the order that costs least:

with whole victims, which ride for free in a page that is being written anyway;
failing that, by cutting the flush’s next chunk at the page boundary.

That makes the guarantee unconditional: every data page a flush writes, except its last, is at least 1 − θ full, at a cost of at most one cut per page.
On a page that holds content of the flush’s own, that content is what gets cut, not a victim’s survivor: the flush’s own content is what the application is working on, so its cut is the likelier to be overwritten soon and take the extra span with it.
A page opened only for consolidation has no such content, and there a survivor is cut instead, its tail leading the next page.
Packing in sequence order, with look-ahead
Pack in sequence order and fit by looking ahead, rather than first-fit over a size-sorted list.
First-fit-decreasing packs tightly and destroys locality, which costs two things worth keeping: neighbouring spans in one page, which a later evacuation moves together and can merge, and consecutive ids with implicit successors.
fn pack(mut chunks: Lookahead<Chunk>, elastic: &mut Elastic) -> Vec<Page> {
    let mut pages = Vec::new();
    if chunks.is_empty() { return pages; }       // no page is being written anyway
    let mut open = Page::new();
    loop {
        // 1. The first of the flush's own chunks that fits, in sequence order, within reach.
        if let Some(c) = chunks.take_first_fit(open.room()) { open.place(c); continue; }
        // 2. None fits: free filling, with whatever fits, in the order that pays most.
        while let Some(e) = elastic.take_fitting(open.room(), open.number()) { open.place_all(e); }
        if chunks.is_empty() { break; }          // the flush's last page: short only if nothing fits
        // 3. Still more than θ empty: cut the next chunk so the page closes full.
        if open.room() > THETA * MAX_PAGE_CONTENT {
            let (head, tail) = chunks.pop_next_to_cut().split_at(open.room());
            open.place(head);
            chunks.push_front(tail);             // shorter than the `Inline` threshold: an `Inline`
        }
        pages.push(mem::take(&mut open));
    }
    pages.push(open);
    pages
}
Chunks longer than a page never reach pack: whole pages are cut off their front first and written on their own.
Step 2 fills the room with anything that fits and costs nothing, on every page the last included: whole victims first — the tail first, in compaction mode — since each frees a page; then part of a victim too big to take whole, a whole span at a time, which frees no page yet but leaves the victim sparser.
The budget
The design has one throttle — a per-flush maintenance budget in pages written beyond the flush’s own content — and one queue of offers competing for it, ranked by bytes reclaimed / bytes written.
One further parameter, the churn floor λ, says when an offer is not worth taking at all.
Two sources compete for that budget, and they are one mechanism applied to two kinds of page: evacuation relocates a data victim’s spans and reclaims dead data bytes; the page rewrite restates a table victim’s live entries and reclaims dead entry bytes.
The rotating walk stays out of the ranking: what it retires is description, measured in entries and memory rather than in file bytes, and its price μ is its own floor.
The structures behind the ranking
Every source that starts from a page is ranked from bucket queues, which make “give me a good victim” O(1) instead of O(log P).
struct Buckets {
    lists: [Vec<PageNumber>; B],          // B is small; 16 is plenty
    at: HashMap<PageNumber, (u8, u32)>,   // which bucket, and which slot in it
}
A page’s bucket is coverage[p] * B / capacity, so moving a page is a swap-remove from its old list, a push onto the new one, and a fix of the at entry of whatever the swap moved — which matters because coverage changes on every span stated or dropped, not once per flush.
Each page kind gets its own instance, since data pages outnumber table pages by roughly the ratio of their contents; header pages belong in neither.
A page in the sparsest non-empty bucket is within 1/B of the true minimum live fraction, which is all a heuristic ranking needs.
A page whose coverage reaches zero leaves its bucket at once, since it is retired at the next commit either way.
The budget loop
A flush and its consolidation run as one straight line:
fn flush(journal: Journal, budget: Budget) {
    // 1. The fold, mapped onto spans; the header's entries chosen, and the short
    //    spans of the runs that leave it merged; the rotating walk's merges.
    let fold = fold(journal);
    map_pieces_to_spans(fold);
    choose_header_and_merge_evicted();
    rotating_walk();
 
    // 2. Data pages: the flush's own chunks in sequence order, with victims riding
    //    along wherever a page has room its own content cannot use. See `pack`.
    let mut data = pack(new_chunks(), &mut elastic);
 
    // 3. The budget, in pages written, offer by offer to whichever page kind reclaims
    //    more per byte. An offer of data victims opens a page, and only one it fills;
    //    an offer of table victims opens none, since what it restates joins the
    //    leaves step 4 lays out, and costs the budget the pages those take.
    let mut spent = 0.0;
    while spent < budget.pages {
        let left = budget.pages - spent;
        let Some(offer) = [evacuation.offer_page(left), page_rewrite.offer(left)]
                              .into_iter().flatten()
                              .max_by_key(|o| o.reclaimed / o.written) else { break };
        if !offer.holds_tail() {        // compaction mode's tail passes both floors
            if offer.reclaimed < budget.lambda * offer.written { break; }   // the churn floor
            if offer.opens_page() && offer.fill() < 1.0 - THETA { break; }  // the fill floor
        }
        spent += if offer.opens_page() { 1.0 } else { offer.written / C };
        offer.take(&mut data);
    }
 
    // 4. Table pages: the hottest entries in the header, the rest in leaves in id
    //    order, the last leaf's room to whole sparse leaves that fit.
    let table = cut();
 
    // 5. Unlink emptied pages, write, fsync, commit; then truncate a reusable tail.
    commit(data, table);
}
The two page kinds are combined, not traded off — but they do compete for the one budget, counted in the pages they write; each source’s offers decline as it takes more, so one greedy pass over the two is the right amount of machinery.
Free filling happens inside steps 2 and 4, and step 3 is the only place a page is opened for consolidation’s sake.
It opens one only for an offer of data victims, and only when the offer fills it to 1 − θ, which keeps a victim too many from costing a nearly empty page; only an offer holding compaction mode’s tail is exempt.
An offer of data victims is what the page would hold: whole victims first, by best fit, and then — if that leaves more than θ empty — one more victim with a span cut at the page boundary, exactly as pack cuts the flush’s own chunk.
An offer of table victims opens no page, so no fill floor holds it, and it costs the budget the pages its restatements take.
The restatements of a sparse leaf take a fraction of a leaf, among everything else the flush states, so there is no page a floor could keep from closing short; the churn floor already weighs their bytes against the page they free.
Held to the fill floor as well, leaves would stay half empty, since an offer would have to restate 1 − θ of a leaf, which leaves less than half full could do only three or more at a time.
The churn floor is a parameter, not an identity
The floor is a parameter λ — space freed per byte written — and its price is explicit.
Cleaning pages at live fraction u costs u / (1 − u) bytes written per byte of space freed, so a total write amplification of 1 / (1 − u): 2× at u = 1/2, 5× at 0.8, 10× at 0.9.
But λ is the wrong knob for a target file fill.
An average fill of 80–90 % does not mean cleaning pages that are 80–90 % live, and implementing it that way would buy the last few percent at five to ten times the write traffic.
It means the distribution of live fractions is bimodal enough that most pages sit near full while the garbage concentrates in a few nearly empty ones — which is what the age term is for, and the whole reason LFS’s cost-benefit cleaner beats plain greedy.
So the two knobs do different jobs, and only one of them is a floor:

λ is a churn floor. It stops the cleaner grinding when there is nothing worth cleaning, and it belongs low — near 1, i.e. near u = 1/2 — precisely so that it is not what decides the file’s fill.
The per-flush budget is the throttle, and it is what converges the file on a target fill τ: measure live_bytes / (pages · C) after each commit, over every page but the headers, and move the budget up while it sits below τ, down while above — multiplicatively, budget · exp(4 · (τ − fill)) within its bounds, is a rule that works.
Counting every page rather than only the live ones makes holes raise the budget as sparse pages do.

Ratio-greedy ranking starves costs that current ratios cannot see, and one such cost remains: description debt in a cold region, which never looks urgent, because nothing about it is changing.
It is taken out of the ranking rather than weighted inside it: the rotating walk reaches every span in turn.
The complexity this incurs

O(r · log k) in-memory work for a flush of r records over k spans, plus O(log k) per span stated, merged, or relocated under the budget;
O(1) victim selection per candidate;
page writes bounded by the flush’s new data pages plus the budget plus the tree’s depth;
