with the common small flush writing no table page beyond the header.

Two forms of consolidation

Free filling. Victims, and parts of victims too big to take whole, ride in the room of pages that are being written anyway — the flush’s own data pages, and the cut’s last leaf — so they cost no page write and compete with nothing.
It runs to exhaustion.
Budgeted cleaning. Beyond that, data pages that exist only to reclaim, offered one at a time and opened only when the offer fills them, and table victims whose restatements take leaves of their own.
These compete, under the budget and the churn floor.

Outer fragmentation
Placement decides whether holes form, truncation returns what reaches the end, and a compaction mode moves what never would.
Lowest page first
Reusable pages are handed out lowest first rather than in the order they became reusable, and the file grows only when none is left.
Lowest first keeps new content away from the end of the file, so pages that die there stay dead and the tail drains of its own accord; a first-in-first-out pool would refill the tail as readily as any hole.
The pool is an ordered set rather than a min-heap, because it is used from both ends: allocation takes the lowest page, and truncation removes the highest ones.
Lowest first gives up the contiguity that a run from the end of the file would offer a large write, but contiguity buys nothing.
Journal pages come from the same pool, so the journal, too, starts in the lowest hole rather than at the end, and so do payload pages, which become data pages where they lie.
Truncation
After a commit, the file may shrink to end right after its highest live or fallback page — the truncation rule.
It is safe for the same reason reuse is: no header that recovery could choose reaches past that point, and a power cut that loses the truncation only leaves the file longer than necessary.
The journal’s last page does not count while it is empty, since a reader treats a journal page past the end of the file as empty too.
The new end is always a page boundary, never inside the last page’s padding.
Truncating is cheap, but shrinking and regrowing the file on every flush of a workload that oscillates is not, so both reference implementations truncate only once the reusable tail exceeds a threshold, and at close and open.
An explicit full compaction would serve a file about to be exported or archived: flush, and keep flushing in compaction mode, with an unlimited budget, until no hole is left and the file ends at its last live page.
Neither the reference algorithms nor kladde-rs offer one yet; closing after a few flushes comes close.
Compaction mode
Placement and truncation return the tail only if the pages there die by themselves, and cold, full pages never do.
So while holes — pages below the highest live one that are reusable now, not in quarantine — exceed a share h of the file, the highest non-journal live page is offered to the budget loop ahead of every other victim, whatever its fill: evacuated if it is a data page, rewritten if it is a table page, with lowest-first placement landing its content in holes.
The mode needs no hysteresis, because switching in and out of it costs nothing: a tail page once moved stays moved.
An offer holding the tail passes the churn floor, and the fill floor if it opens a data page, and a table tail is taken even when its restatements need more than one leaf, so it is the budget alone that paces the mode.
The floors weigh what a page returns to the pool, and a tail victim returns more: a whole page to the file system.
The return is realised only once every page above the victim has gone too, which is why the mode works strictly from the top down; journal pages are skipped, since the next flush moves the journal to the lowest hole by itself.
The tail moves only while a page that is reusable now lies below it.
Right after a mass removal, the pages it released sit in quarantine for two commits, so content moved then would land in pages the file grows by, which become the next tail, and the same content would move again.
Holes count only reusable pages for a related reason: the pages the last commits released are working space, which the next flushes reuse by themselves.
Free filling takes part in the mode too: while it lasts, take_fitting offers the highest non-journal live page ahead of the sparsest, whenever that page is of its kind, lies above the page being filled, and its content fits the room.
Finding the highest live page needs no structure of its own: a cached index, lowered past reusable pages as the tail empties and raised when a page above it is written, is O(1) amortised.
Pacing
Each flush consumes at least one reusable page, often a few, so consolidation must reclaim at least that many on average.
The situation where no good victim exists is the situation where pages are largely full — little garbage, and the file close to its live size — so “cleaning cannot keep up” and “the file is honestly this large” coincide, which is the benign coincidence.
The one obligation this leaves is headroom, which is a requirement rather than a policy.
The bound this buys
Garbage accrues in proportion to write traffic and drains in proportion to consolidation effort, so the steady state is set by the budget: converging on a live fraction τ bounds the file at live_size / τ, at the price of the corresponding cleaning work.
The bound is controllable and, in relative terms, independent of file size; the guiding principle adds the description’s share.
Constants
kladde-rs’s defaults, of which only the span policy’s were measured:

the target fill τ, 0.8, and the budget’s start and bounds, 8 pages within 1 and 256;
the churn floor λ, 1;
the fill floor θ, 0.05, and the look-ahead, 16 chunks;
the walk’s length, 256 spans per flush, its price μ, 0.02, and the flushes after which a span counts as cold, 16;
the victims sampled per pick, 8, and 16 buckets for each page kind;
the hole share h, 0.25, and a reusable tail of 16 pages to trigger truncation.

impl/consolidator-state.title: Consolidator state
impl/consolidator-state.content:
What consolidation could carry from one session to the next in the private chain, and how it would tell whether what it finds there is still current.
Status: designed, not built.
kladde-rs writes nothing to the private chain yet: every session starts its budget from its default, its rotating walk at the sequence’s start, and its heat from the pages’ epochs.
Why it exists
Consolidation learns from many flushes, and a session that forgot what it had learned at every close would never get past the start.
The damage concentrates in workloads of many short sessions, such as a command-line tool that a script invokes over and over, each time opening a file, flushing once, and exiting:

the budget would restart from its default at every open, and never converge on its target fill;
the rotating walk would restart wherever open seeds it, rather than where the last session left off, and over many short sessions might never reach parts of the sequence;
the heat of every span would be rebuilt from the epoch of the page that holds its entry, which the header re-stamps every flush, so every span stated in the header would look freshly written at every open, and the walk and the header’s eviction would misjudge it.

What it would hold



































partwhatsizeidentificationthe implementation, and the version of this layout8 bytesup_to_datethe epoch of the flush that last brought the state up to date8 bytesthe budgetthe per-flush budget the controller had reached4 bytesthe walkthe span at which the next rotating walk begins4 bytesheatfor spans whose heat the file does not give exactly, the flush that last wrote their bytesa snapshot, plus records appended since
Everything a flush puts in the state is known before its data pages are packed, since it is written together with them.
Heat is kept only where the file gets it wrong.
A span’s entry lies in a page whose epoch can only understate how long its bytes have gone unwritten, since content is never younger than the page that holds its entry; that fallback is exact for a span written once and never restated.
So a snapshot keeps mainly the spans whose entries consolidation or the header restated since their bytes were written.
Heat records name an epoch and the span ids last written in that flush, sorted and stored as varint deltas, a byte or two per span, so a flush appends one record, one contiguous write; once the appended records outgrow the snapshot, a flush rewrites everything as a fresh snapshot, keeping only each span’s newest mention.
Writing it
Every flush brings the state up to date, together with its own writes: it appends its heat record and rewrites the fixed fields.
The state is ordinary content of the private chain, committed with the flush that wrote it, so a crash can never leave it ahead of or behind the file it describes.
A flush that finds no state it recognizes as its own replaces it, since the private chain is the only place to keep one.
Checking it
A state is used entry by entry, as far as each entry can be shown current, because a writer that kept the state without maintaining it may have changed the file since.

If up_to_date is the governing header’s epoch, everything in the state is current.
Otherwise, a span’s heat is current if no entry of the span is newer than up_to_date, since its bytes cannot change without a new entry at the epoch of the flush that changed them; one that fails the test falls back to its entry’s page epoch.
Span ids are recycled, so a span stated after up_to_date may be another span under an old id, which the same test catches.
The walk’s position and the budget are starting points either way: at worst the walk resumes elsewhere, and the controller corrects a budget that no longer fits.
A state that cannot be parsed is treated as absent, like another implementation’s.
Nothing in it can affect content, so the worst a misread state can do is mislead the heuristics.

A flush that brings a stale state up to date rewrites it as a fresh snapshot first, so that records it could not vouch for do not become current by default.

impl/flush.title: The flush
impl/flush.content:
How the journal becomes pages: what to write, where to put it, and in what order.
The protocol that commits a flush is normative; everything about what a flush chooses to write is not, and is described here.
It is a small optimizing compiler, and it should be built like one: oracle first, optimizer second.
A flush folds the journal into the new sequence, maps it onto spans, lets the span policy merge what it wants merged, places new bytes in data pages with consolidation’s victims riding along, cuts the span table into the header and leaves, and commits.
The fold
The fold keeps a piece table over the sequence, starting as one piece, the committed sequence, and the journal’s records edit it.
A piece is a run of the new sequence and where its bytes come from: the committed sequence, from some position on, as it stood after the last flush, or the journal’s byte arena, from some position on.
enum Source {
    Committed(u64),   // the committed sequence, from this position on
    Arena(u64),       // the journal buffer's arena, from this position on
}
 
struct Piece { src: Source, len: u64 }
The pieces sit in a counted tree, as the rope does over spans, so each record costs O(log p) for the p pieces the journal made, however long the sequence:

























recordeffect on the piece tableWrite(pos, bytes)take [pos, pos + len) out, as a cut; insert one Arena pieceSplice(pos, removed, bytes)take [pos, pos + removed) out, as a cut if it is not empty; insert one Arena pieceMove(from, len, to)take [from, from + len) out and insert it at toPaste(pos, removed, cut)take [pos, pos + removed) out and drop it; insert the cut’s tree
Taking a range out is two splits and a join, and returns the range as a tree of its own; inserting is a split and two joins.
A journal’s cuts are kept as those trees until the fold ends, so a paste inserts the pieces its cut removed and the flush states three to six spans for the two, however large the value, and writes none of its bytes, whichever transactions of the journal the cut and the paste lie in; replay at open does the same.
At the end, the fold lists the new sequence as pieces, merging adjacent pieces that continue each other.
A record whose range does not lie inside the sequence, or a paste of a cut its journal did not make or already pasted, makes the journal invalid.
What falls out unasked:

A splice that lands in bytes the same flush wrote costs nothing beyond them: it edits Arena pieces, and the bytes it shifts are never mentioned.
A move costs no bytes: its pieces are committed ranges, which keep the spans that show them.
Repeated writes to one place cost one write: only the last one’s bytes survive in the pieces.

Mapping pieces to spans
A committed range is shown by the spans that showed it, found through the rope; where a range begins or ends inside a span, the span is split: its left part is stated again with a shorter length, and its right part becomes a new span over the same bytes.
New bytes become new spans, inline below the threshold and placed in data pages above it, unless a payload page holds them already.
Every span is linked to the one that now follows it, and every span whose content, length or successor changed is stated, with every new one.
So a splice cuts the chain at its two ends and adds the span of its new bytes: one to three entries.
A move cuts it at three places — the start and the end of the moved run, and its destination — and splits at most one span at each; the three left parts are also exactly the spans whose successors change: the one before the run now links to what followed it, the run’s last span to what follows the destination, and the span before the destination to the run’s first span.
Where a place is the sequence’s start, the header’s first span changes instead, which costs no entry, and where a place already falls between two spans, its split goes; so a move states three to six spans, however many it moves.
Every span inside a moved run keeps its entry, since neither its bytes nor its successor change.
Spans that no chain reaches any more are dropped: their ids are free, and their entries dead.
The reach rule holds by construction, since a span becomes reached only as a new span, or as a span whose entry the flush writes anyway.
Payload pages
Bytes that a payload page of the flush’s epoch holds become a span over the page, and the page a data page of the header the flush commits, without a byte written.
The journal’s buffer records, beside its arena, which runs of the arena also lie in a payload page, and where (placing them); so the fold needs no source of its own for them, and its Arena pieces are mapped as before, except that each part of one that a placed run covers becomes a Ref over the payload page.
The page is taken into the flush as a page it fills, so that the commit makes it live with the pages it writes, its coverage the bytes its spans show; a payload page that no span shows retires with the journal’s pages.

Only payload pages of the flush’s own epoch: a flush that folds a recovered journal and, through its seal, the next one finds the next one’s pages of a higher epoch than its own, which the epoch assertion keeps out of its header’s world, so their bytes are written again, as new bytes.
Not a part shorter than rewrite_below, which a later record of the journal cut out of a run: it is written again with the bytes around it, rather than keeping a page alive for a few bytes.
The page keeps its slack, the room a payload page’s last run left, until consolidation evacuates it, since the flush writes no page it takes this way.

Overwrites: split or rewrite
An edit that cuts into a span can split it, or write it again whole with the edit’s bytes, and the flush rewrites a Ref shorter than a threshold and splits a longer one.

Splitting costs three entries the first time a place is written, and one for every later overwrite of the same bytes, which restates the middle span; it leaves the description fragmented until the span policy merges the pieces.
Rewriting costs one entry and the span’s length in data bytes, and fragments nothing; it suits short spans, and is costly for long ones.

So a drag that moves a point many times splits its span once and restates an inline span of a few bytes at every later flush.
An Inline span is always rewritten, since splitting one restates its whole payload as well, in two or three entries instead of one.
The threshold applies to the span an edit cuts into, not to the parts a cut leaves: a Ref long enough to be split leaves a left part that may be shorter than the threshold, which is stated as it is, and the span policy merges it later.
A third way, shadowing part of a span with an entry of its own, is left out of the format.
Zeros
A run of zeros among the new bytes, long enough that a Zero entry is cheaper than the bytes, becomes a Zero span: 32 bytes is a reasonable cut.
Encodings without padding hold few zeros, but Fixed values and large preallocated arrays have them.
The span policy
Two policies bound the description, and they combine: one bounds it in the leaves at a constant cost per edit, the other drives it toward nothing where the sequence has gone cold; spans whose entries sit in the header are exempt from both.

Bounded spans, the discipline of a B-tree’s leaves without the interior nodes: no two neighbouring spans whose entries lie in leaves are shorter than L together.
A flush keeps the rule after its fold has been mapped to spans and before it places anything: it writes the spans that break it again as one, among its own new bytes, which costs at most L bytes per boundary removed and never cascades, since a merged span is longer than either neighbour was.
The mean span in the leaves is then at least L / 2 long, everywhere and at all times.
Merging by temperature: a run of spans whose content has not been written for a while is written again as spans of up to a page, by the rotating walk.
Each boundary is removed once, after the edits that made it, and a cold span of a page costs about six bytes, 0.15 % of what it shows.
It needs a temperature per span, which heat gives.
The header is exempt: spans of any length may keep their entries there.
An edit site that every flush touches — typing, dragging a shape, moving a slider until a setting sounds right — splits its spans while it is hot, and merging them would write the same bytes again at every flush, only for the next edit to split them anew.
The header can afford them, since it holds the hottest entries, is written by every flush anyway, and holds at most a page of entries, so the exemption adds at most a page to the description, however large the file.

The bound takes effect where entries leave the header: when the header would overflow, the flush chooses its coldest runs of spans to evict to leaves, by heat, and merges each run’s short spans as it evicts them, so their bytes are written again once, after they have gone cold.
Since merging writes bytes, the flush makes that choice before it places anything, from entry sizes it estimates without encoding them.
The first policy gives the worst-case bound of the guiding principle, the second the low overhead of a large file that is mostly cold, and the exemption keeps the first from charging hot edits for merges that the next edit undoes.
A larger L makes the description smaller and each edit more expensive.
Neither touches the format, which allows spans of any length from one byte to a page.
The constants, as measurements chose them for kladde-rs: the bound L, 64 bytes; the length below which a Ref cut by an edit is rewritten rather than split, 64 bytes; the inline threshold, 64 bytes; the flushes after which a span counts as cold for the walk, 16; and the walk’s price μ, 0.02 entry bytes per byte written.
They were measured on a handful of drawings and texts, and remain open questions, as do what should count as cold, and how hot spans and the header should share the span table’s room.
The Inline threshold
The format fixes the ceiling at 126 bytes; the policy threshold belongs below it.
Below roughly the encoded size of a Ref, inlining is strictly better — the address would be as large as the data.
Between there and the ceiling it is a trade: inline payloads ride the header for free while hot but inflate the table pages when cold, whereas a Ref plus its data bytes is written once but occupies room in a data page and keeps that page partially live.
The accounting argues for keeping the threshold low: an inline payload is charged to the table page that holds it and is only reclaimed by rewriting that page, whereas a Ref’s bytes are charged to a data page that consolidation can clean apart from the entry.
64 bytes is a good default.
Placement
Cutting content across pages
A flush writes whole pages, and a Ref shows bytes of one page only, so new bytes are cut into spans that each fit in one page.

A run longer than a page becomes whole pages first, each one span, plus a remainder; that is the one cut that is forced rather than chosen.
The remainders are packed in sequence order with a bounded look-ahead, pulling consolidation’s victims into any page with room its own content cannot use, and cutting only to keep a page from closing more than θ empty; packing is described with consolidation, since what it has to know is consolidation’s side of the interface.
Whoever writes bytes may cut them anew: span boundaries carry no meaning beyond “these bytes lie contiguously here”, so a flush re-cuts what it writes at will, and consolidation may split or merge spans it relocates.

Free re-cutting removes the worst case of fixed-size pieces: chunks all just over half a page could otherwise never share a page.
The price of each cut is one entry, and in ordinary flushes the packer prefers slack to a split.
A flush writes every span it produces whole; the old bytes remain behind as garbage until consolidation reclaims them.
A large payload is written twice: once into the journal when its record is appended, and again into data pages when the flush places it — a pasted image, say, or a document the application built outside any handle and brought in whole.
A flush could instead state spans over the payload’s bytes where they already lie, in the journal’s pages, turning those pages into data pages, which would halve what a large paste writes; it would need journal pages that hold whole pages of a payload aligned to the data pages’ content, and the reuse rule to hold for pages that change kind, and is an open idea.
Page contiguity buys nothing
Adjacent pages need exactly as many entries as scattered ones, because a Ref shows bytes of one page only, so a bulk write of many pages is one span per page wherever those pages are.
Placement therefore does not seek runs of pages at all; it takes the lowest reusable page, which is what keeps outer fragmentation from forming.
Where the pages come from
The reusable pool is an ordered set, a list, and a watermark, because the quarantine is a rotation rather than a computation:
struct FreePages {
    ready:    BTreeSet<PageNumber>,   // reusable: neither live nor fallback
    retiring: Vec<PageNumber>,        // dropped by the last commit; not yet writable
    next_new: PageNumber,             // one past the last page of the file
}
 
// At each commit, in this order:
free.ready.extend(free.retiring.drain(..));
free.retiring = pages_this_commit_stopped_referencing();
Taking a page takes the lowest page in ready, and extends the file only when ready is empty; journal pages and payload pages come from the same pool.
Lowest-first lets pages at the end of the file stay dead once they die, so that truncation can return them.
The header as write buffer
The root of the span table is the header page, and the header page is rewritten by every flush no matter what.
That page is free real estate, so it doubles as the span table’s write buffer: every flush states the header’s entries again, and fills the header with the hottest entries before any leaf, at zero additional page writes.

The common small flush writes no table page beyond the header, and no data page when its new bytes are all inline.
An entry carried in the header is restated every flush at the new epoch, for free.

When the header overflows, the coldest entries go to leaves, ranked by heat.
What the header can hold is bounded by MAX_PAGE_CONTENT, so the ranking covers a few hundred entries however large the file is, and a sort of them on the rare flush that overflows is beneath measurement.
Evicting the coldest runs of spans contiguous in id, rather than the coldest entries wherever they sit, keeps the leaves’ ids dense, which keeps their delta encoding short, and lets the evicted run be merged to the bound as it leaves.
The shape of the tree
Table pages form a tree rooted at the header, and it is a directory, not a search structure: every lookup is served by the in-memory span table, nothing descends the tree by key, so there is no ordering invariant to maintain across pages.

While everything fits in the header: zero extra pages — the steady state of every small file.
Overflow goes to leaves referenced directly from the header, with entries continuing to share the header alongside the child references.
At one to two bytes per child reference, a header can reference two to four thousand leaves, one to two million spans.
Beyond that, one layer of interior pages reaches some million leaves; deeper is not going to be needed.

Structural updates are copy-on-write path copies, but the paths are short and the root is free: adding or removing a leaf rewrites at most depth − 1 pages besides the leaf itself.
A depth change is a single-page event: when the header’s child list outgrows its room, move the whole list into one fresh interior page and reference that instead.
The cut
The cut writes every stated span’s entry: the header’s into the header, the rest into new leaves, in id order, each leaf closed when the next entry does not fit, so that every leaf but the last is full to within one entry.
The last leaf, or the header when there is no leaf, takes fillers: whole sparse leaves whose live entries fit its room, restated there, which drains them for free (the page rewrite).
The header’s capacity is what remains after the file-header fields and its child list, and the child list depends on how many leaves the flush adds and unlinks, so the header’s share is chosen against an estimate and corrected: if the list turns out longer, the header gives up its coldest entries to the leaves.
Entries are derived from the span table as it finally stands, after everything else in the flush, so each span is stated exactly once in the flush’s epoch, as the format requires, however many sources touched it.
Correctness: the differential oracle
Build the oracle before the optimizer.
Test the store on its own against a plain byte vector: any series of Write, Splice, Move and Paste, flushes, reopens and simulated power cuts must leave the sequence holding the vector’s bytes.
Above the store, after every operation, the sequence must equal the canonical encoding of the in-memory root value, byte for byte.
Randomized operation series with shrinking.
Walk-through of an epoch
A finer-grained version of the recovery case analysis, tracking page states step by step.
This exists because two points in the argument are easy to get backwards: most pages of the older world are also in the newer one and therefore simply live, and a header slot whose write never arrived holds a valid stale header rather than garbage.
During the journaling phase of epoch E:

Header E − 2 exists and has been fsynced.
Header E − 1 was written but not fsynced yet.
Journal E is partially written, not fsynced.
All Data and Table pages of world E − 1 have been fsynced and are live — this flush must not overwrite them.
Pages of world E − 2 that are not also part of world E − 1 are fallback, and must not be overwritten either.
This includes journal E − 1, which header E − 2 names.
Pages belonging to both worlds are simply live, which is the common case rather than the exception: typically most pages of world E − 2 are in both.

Steps 1–7 of the flush protocol write data and table pages for epoch E, then fsync.
No header page is touched.
On a power cut during or after this:

If the slot written by flush E − 1 holds header E − 1 — guaranteed once fsync E completed, possible earlier — state E − 1 is recovered, the start page of journal E is found from that header, and a possibly-empty prefix of journal E is replayed.
If that slot does not hold header E − 1 — either its write tore, leaving an invalid CRC, or it never reached the disk, leaving the stale header E − 3 with a valid CRC, which is the more common sub-case — then header E − 2 has the highest epoch among valid headers and governs.
Recovery reaches state E − 2 and replays journal E − 1 in full, arriving at the same state as the other case with an empty journal-E prefix.
The lost journal-E transactions were never covered by a completed fsync, so this is within the guarantee.

Recovery is indifferent between the torn and never-arrived sub-cases, because it selects the valid header with the highest epoch rather than merely a valid one.
Step 8 overwrites header E − 2 with header E.
This turns journal E − 1 and everything reachable only from header E − 2 from fallback to reusable, and it turns everything reachable from E − 1 but not from E from live to fallback (including journal E).
On a power cut during or after:

If the slot holds header E: the flush completed; recover to state E plus whatever prefix of journal E + 1 accumulated.
If it does not: header E − 1 exists with a valid CRC, because it was fsynced in step 7, and carries the highest epoch among valid headers.
Same situation as above, except that header E − 2 may no longer exist — which is fine, since it is only consulted on the path where header E − 1 is absent.

impl/implementation-notes.title: Implementation notes
impl/implementation-notes.content:
What implementing the design in kladde-rs has shown: where kladde-rs falls short of these documents, and what it chose where they leave a question open.
This page is where kladde-rs’s findings are recorded as they come up, and proposed for the other documents from here.
Paths like spec/journal.md are relative to content/, the root of these documents.
Branches of kladde-rs that hold earlier designs, such as address-table, keep their own implementation-notes.md.
Where the implementation falls short
What the code does not do yet, or does less well than kladde-docs or its own goals ask, and what that costs.

⚠️ The span table has two levels only: the header, and the leaves it names.
A leaf that names table pages of its own is refused at open.
The header’s room for references to leaves, one or two bytes each, bounds a file to some 2,000 to 4,000 leaves, one to two million spans: a sequence of a few hundred MB in spans of the length the measurements find, and far more than any workload measured, the largest of which takes 21 to 26 leaves.
Beyond the bound, a flush fails with Error::OutOfBounds, and since opening flushes the replayed journal, a file whose journal holds such a flush no longer opens.
No workload measured comes near the bound: the world map’s sequence of 942 KiB takes 21 to 26 leaves.
The fix: write interior table pages when the leaves’ references outgrow the header, with the path copy of impl/consolidation.md#unlinking-an-emptied-page, and read them at open, which load.rs refuses today; test it with the header’s capacity settable from tests.
⚠️ A single write or splice of 4 GiB or more corrupts the journal: Records::stash keeps a record’s length as a u32, so the record states a truncated length while the store counts all of it, and one of exactly 2^32 bytes even encodes the escape.
spec/journal.md#framing bounds a transaction’s length by 2^32 − 1, so such a write must fail with Error::OutOfBounds; only the bound of 2^48 is checked today.
No application writes values of 4 GiB in one piece, but the result is a file that does not open, not an error.
Arithmetic on values read from the file is not checked: the entry decode adds deltas to page numbers, ids and ends, and the journal decode adds a move’s to_delta, without checking for overflow, so a file whose CRCs match but whose numbers do not panics in a debug build and wraps in a release build, which can accept entries out of order that the delta encoding is meant to make unrepresentable.
kladde-cpp checks each of them.
FileStorage takes no lock, where spec/file-format.md#concurrency has a second process refused cleanly, and create truncates whatever file is there; kladde-cpp locks with flock before it truncates.
A CutId that escapes a transaction rolled back by Store::atomically can match a later record that reuses its index with a cut of the same length, and a paste of it then pastes that record’s bytes without an error.
The typed layer never lets a cut out of a failed transaction, which poisons the store; only direct users of Store can meet it.
The cut never gives fillers to the header: impl/flush.md#the-cut has the last leaf take them, or the header when there is no leaf, and kladde-rs fills the last leaf only.
The budget loop filters offers by their floors before it picks the best ratio, where the pseudocode of impl/consolidation.md#the-budget-loop picks first and stops if the pick fails its floor; a table offer can then win when the data offer fails the fill floor.
The fold’s output is not checked against the tracked length, which impl/write-phase-state.md asks for as a cheap guard against a fold bug.
The decode recurses without a limit on its depth, where impl/opening.md asks for a limit or an iterative decode, so a file that nests deeply enough overflows the stack.
A container’s index panics on sizes of 4 GiB or more, where spec/span-table.md#bounds asks every limit to fail cleanly: the Fenwick tree keeps sizes in u32 cells, and converts with expect.
The load checks a reached Ref against its page’s frame, not against the page’s content_size.
It refuses a Ref into page 0 or 1, into a page that is not a Data page of the header’s world, or reaching into the framing, but not one that reaches past the content into the padding.
Nothing is kept in the private chain, where impl/consolidator-state.md designs what consolidation would carry there: every session starts its budget from Options::budget_pages, its rotating walk at the sequence’s start rather than where impl/opening.md seeds it, and each span’s heat from the epoch of the page that holds its entry.
A span costs about 90 bytes in memory, not 32.
The span table takes 48 bytes per span, since each record also holds the span’s chain, its rope node, its heat, its entry’s size and place in its table page, and its place in its data page’s reverse list, which impl/in-memory-state.md keeps beside the span table; and the rope is an implicit treap of 40 bytes per node rather than a counted B-tree of about 15 per span.
DurableVec’s index takes 40 bytes even where it is empty or the elements are fixed-size: a Vec of cells, its cached total, and the count’s varint length.
The total can live in the tree’s allocation, and the count’s length is the vector’s to pass in, which would leave 24 bytes, or 8 with a thin vector.
None of the three refinements of impl/consolidation.md is implemented: evacuation writes a victim’s spans as they are, splitting the one that crosses the end of the page it fills, and merges no neighbours; the walk merges runs of cold spans and renumbers nothing; and the churn floor, budget controller and free filling are the address-table design’s, unchanged, over pages of spans.
Compaction mode counts holes by scanning the page table once per flush.
impl/consolidation.md#compaction-mode promises O(1) amortised; kladde-rs keeps the cached index of the highest live page it describes, but counts the reusable pages below it in O(pages) at the start of every flush, which is small next to what a flush writes.
The budget loop never continues the last page of pack.
impl/consolidation.md#the-budget-loop lets that page cut a victim’s span whenever the loop opens another page, so that only the flush’s very last data page can close short; kladde-rs’s loop always opens fresh pages, so pack’s last page is filled by free filling alone, and can close short even when the loop goes on.
What rust/tutorial/durability.md says about close() was measured on the address-table design, and has not been checked since: that close truncates after the last live page only, so that a freshly created file keeps free pages below its data until a flush or two have consolidated them.
The header’s eviction ranks by heat alone, rather than evicting the coldest runs contiguous in id, and merges each evicted span with its neighbours in the sequence, extending each run while a neighbour whose entry also goes to a leaf makes a pair shorter than the bound.
A value is encoded into a buffer of its own, which the store copies into the record, a copy that a store method taking an encoding closure would save.
Cuts exist on DurableVec only: its cut, insert_cut and push_cut; impl/values.md#moving-a-value-between-containers has every method that takes a value take a cut too, but a plain Vec, the map, fields, Option and enums neither make nor take them.
split_at_mut and the count of changes are not implemented, only parts(), for derived structs and enums and for tuples.
split_at_mut was left out only because the evaluation needs it nowhere; the vector’s Fenwick tree lies in cells and answers any element’s offset, so it would serve as the two runs’ index as it is.
parts() on a temporary Mut works in a match but not in a let … else, which drops the temporary at the end of the statement.
A consuming into_parts(self) would make the let form work too; it would need a line in rust/derive-macro.md and rust/tutorial/deriving.md, and is proposed rather than built.
MemoryStorage models a power cut as any subset of the writes since the last sync, each write whole.
It does not model a write torn within a page; the page CRCs are meant to catch those, but no test exercises them yet.
Misusing the transaction and batch calls reports Error::Corrupt.
Ending a transaction that is not open is a caller’s bug rather than a damaged file, and deserves an error variant of its own; the typed layers pair the calls through Transaction, Batch and Region::transaction, so only direct users of Store can hit it.

Choices kladde-docs leaves open
Where kladde-docs leaves a question open, or allows any answer, and what the implementation chose.

The journal is replayed by folding the recovered transactions in a flush at open, before the decode, so that the decode reads the state after the last of them and needs no replay of its own; impl/opening.md#replaying-through-a-flush allows it.
The rope is an implicit treap, one arena type of under 400 lines that also serves the fold’s piece table and the journal’s cuts, since a split at a position and a join of two trees are all three need.
The span id allocator hands out the id after the predecessor’s, if it is free, and the lowest free id otherwise, which keeps the spans a flush makes one after another consecutive without looking for a run.
The flush makes a run of 32 zeros or more among new bytes a Zero span.
The span policy’s constants, chosen by the measurements of evaluation/one-sequence.md: Options::span_min, the bound L, 64 bytes; Options::rewrite_below, 64 bytes; Options::inline_threshold, 64 bytes; Options::cold_flushes, 16; Options::walk, 256 spans; and Options::mu, 0.02.
A Box<T>’s FIXED_SIZE is None whatever T’s, since a type that holds itself through a box would otherwise ask its own size of itself while rustc evaluates it, which rustc refuses as a cycle (E0391); a vector of boxes then keeps an index it could do without.
The Mut of a Fixed<T> replaces the value whole, since a Mut of one of T’s fields would have to write that field in its fixed form, which would take a second Mut for every type.
The map’s hash table is its own: open addressing over 32-bit positions, probed linearly and at most half full.
FileStorage grows the file with set_len, not with fallocate.
The new region stays unallocated until it is written, so a full disk shows up as a failed write or fsync during a flush, which poisons the store, rather than as a failed growth before the flush starts; spec/durability.md#headroom asks only that failure be clean, which poisoning provides.
The controller moves the budget multiplicatively, and measures fill against the whole file: after each commit it divides the live bytes by the capacity of every page but the headers, and multiplies the budget by exp(4 · (τ − fill)), within budget_min and budget_max.
Counting only live pages would let holes go unnoticed.
A page’s record holds what its state has, and nothing else: an enum over the page states, with a state of its own, filling, for pages a flush takes, and journal pages apart from live ones; only a live page has an epoch and a victim bucket.
The churn floor also bounds each victim, and an offer takes whole victims by score, not by best fit.
Free filling moves part of at most one victim per page, and the victim stays eligible.
impl/consolidation.md#packing-in-sequence-order-with-look-ahead lists part of a victim too big to take whole as the last filler without saying how many victims to try; one per page is enough, and excluding a victim after a partial move would starve the budget loop of exactly the sparse pages it wants.
Kladde::create_in and Kladde::open_in take any Storage and Options; Kladde::create and Kladde::open use a file and the default options, and Kladde::new is create_in with a MemoryStorage, which returns no Result, since a file in memory cannot fail to be created.

impl/in-memory-state.title: In-memory state
impl/in-memory-state.content:
The structures a loaded kladde file is held in, what each is for, and why each is the shape it is.
The store keeps a span table, a rope, the page table, a reverse index, and a span id allocator.
Together they take about 32 bytes per span, besides the resident table pages, and none of them grows with the number of values the application holds: positions of values are kept by the values’ containers, Values and their positions says how.
Integer widths below follow from the bounds the specification states, and are given because they are the same in any language.
1. The span table
An array indexed by span id, one record per span a chain reaches:
struct Span {
    content: Content,     // what the span shows
    len: u32,             // its length in bytes, never 0
    next: u32,            // the span after it in its chain, or 0
    entry_page: u32,      // the table page that holds its live entry
}
 
enum Content {
    Ref { page: u32, offset: u16 },   // bytes of a data page
    Inline { offset: u16 },           // its payload, inside its entry in `entry_page`
    Zero,                             // zeros
}
That is about 16 bytes per span.
An array, because span ids are dense integers that the allocator hands out lowest first, so every lookup is an index rather than a hash.
An id no chain reaches has an empty record, and is free.
The in-memory span table is the on-file span table resolved: it holds, for every reached span, what its newest entry says, and nothing about older entries.
Content is never copied out of the pages while they are resident: a Ref names its bytes in a data page, and an Inline names its payload inside its own entry, which lies in a resident table page.
2. The rope
The rope is a counted balanced tree over the sequence’s spans in order, each item a span id and its length, each node the total length below it.
It finds the span that holds a position, splits one, and cuts and inserts runs of spans, each in O(log k) for k spans, which is what the flush needs to map the journal’s positions to spans, and what the decode follows to read the sequence in order.
A counted B-tree with leaves of 32 entries is the recommended shape: about 11 bytes per span in its leaves at a typical fill, a few percent more in interior nodes, and 4 bytes per span in the span table for the leaf that holds it, so about 15 bytes in all; and a lookup descends three levels for any realistic file, each a scan of a node of one or two cache lines.
An implicit treap, a randomized binary tree whose nodes know their parent and the total length below them, does every operation with two primitives, a split at a position and a join of two trees, and those are exactly what the fold needs as well, so one arena type can serve the rope, the fold’s piece table and a transaction’s cuts.
It costs a node of about 40 bytes per span, and O(log k) expected steps, about 2 ln k − 3 levels on average, each likely a cache miss; that shows only once memory per span matters, 640 MB against the B-tree’s 240 for 16 million spans.
The schema’s and the private state’s chains are short and written only by flushes, so a list of span ids serves them.
3. The page table
For every page: its state, and for a live page its kind, epoch, and live-byte counter (coverage).
Coverage counts what the page holds that a reached span relies on: for a data page, the bytes reached spans show in it; for a table page, the bytes of the live entries in it, inline payloads included, and of its child references.
It is a 32-bit counter rather than a page-sized one, because a page’s live bytes exceed its capacity when several spans show the same bytes, which is legal and bounded precisely so that 32 bits suffice.
A page whose coverage reaches zero is reusable once the next commits have passed it through the reuse rule’s quarantine — a table page only once it is also unlinked from its parent (unlinking).
A page’s record holds what its state has, and nothing else: an enum over the states of the specification.
A page a flush takes is filling, which the specification counts as reusable: it has a kind and coverage but no epoch, since its epoch is the flush’s, and no place among the victims.
The commit turns every page it wrote into a live one.
Journal pages are a state of their own, although the specification counts them live, since the journal keeps what they hold.
Live pages are bucketed by live fraction — a handful of buckets suffices — which makes victim selection O(1) rather than a priority queue’s O(log P), with O(1) bucket moves as counters change.
Data and non-header Table pages are bucketed separately, and header pages in neither, since a header is rewritten every flush and so is never a victim.
An ordered set tracks reusable pages, handing out the lowest first, which keeps the file’s live pages low, where truncation can follow (where the pages come from).
4. The reverse index
For each data page, the reverse index lists the spans that show bytes in it, so that evacuation finds what a victim holds in O(1) per span.
A data page is opaque bytes with no ids in it, so decoding it tells nothing; but span ids are stable, and a span’s address changes only when the span is stated with a new one, so the list is exact and cheap to keep: a span is added to its page’s list when it is stated with a Ref there, and removed when it is restated elsewhere, merged away, or no longer reached.
Keeping each span’s place in its page’s list in its span record makes both O(1).
5. The span id allocator
The allocator hands out the lowest free id, and runs of consecutive free ids where a flush states consecutive spans, from a bitmap of free ids with a summary bit per word, which finds either in a few scans of words.
Low, consecutive ids are what keep id deltas short and successors implicit in the entry encoding.
A free list threaded through the span table’s empty records would cost no memory of its own, but would hand ids out in the order they were freed, which scatters them.
An id is free the moment its span is no longer reached, and may be handed out again in the same flush: the reach rule has the new span stated in the epoch it becomes reached, so its entry is newer than any old entry of the same id.
Liveness is one bit
An entry is live exactly while it is the span table’s entry for a span the rope, or a short chain, holds, so liveness needs no counter at all: no pins, no count of mentions, no size or tombstone to keep alive.
A dead entry survives as bytes in its page until a rewrite of that page drops it, and the page’s coverage stopped counting it the moment it died.
Heat
Each span carries its heat: the epoch of the flush that last wrote its bytes, or the number of flushes since.
The flush ranks the header’s entries by it (the header as write buffer), and the rotating walk merges only spans that have gone cold (merging spans).
It is content age, where a page’s epoch is location age: restating a span re-stamps its entry’s epoch, but not its heat.
During a flush
A flush adds transient state of its own, all dropped when it commits:

the fold’s piece table, over the sequence as the journal leaves it (the fold);
the new bytes, of new spans and of runs that have no span yet, in a scratch buffer, each with whether its entry will hold them inline;
the stated set: the spans that get a new entry in this flush, and which of them go to the header.

Coverage releases happen as the flush changes spans, so victim selection sees the state the flush will leave; charges wait for locations: at placement for bytes, and at the cut for entries.
A flush that fails must therefore unwind or poison the session.
Epochs belong to pages, not to entries
An entry inherits the epoch of the page it sits in, so restating an entry re-stamps it.
The header is rewritten every flush, so every entry in the header carries the current epoch, and two epochs can disagree about a span only between the header and a leaf, or between two leaves.
Memory for very large files
The span table and the rope take about 32 bytes per span together.
A cold gigabyte in spans of a page needs about 8 MB of them; a gigabyte edited everywhere at once, in short spans, would need far more, which is an open question, and what segments would bound.

impl/index.title: Implementation
impl/index.content:
The reference algorithms and data structures: what an implementation must maintain in memory to satisfy the specification, and how it maintains it.
Everything here is language-agnostic.
Pseudocode is written in a Rust-like notation, because enums and pattern matching make the cases concrete and easy to reason about, but nothing here depends on Rust.
For implementations in other languages, it is recommended but not required to make substantially the same choices for, e.g., integer widths or fundamental data structures like balanced trees or hash maps, both of which follow from the bounds the specification states.
What does not belong here is anything a different language would do differently: trait shapes or class hierarchies, memory layout, alignment, the mutation-capture mechanism.
Those decisions are documented in the language-specific documentations (currently kladde-rs and kladde-cpp).
The documents

















































documentcontentsIn-memory statethe structures a loaded file is held in: the span table, the rope, the page table, the reverse index, and the span id allocatorOpening a filethe steps from the headers to a decoded root valueValues and their positionsregions, what each container keeps to find its children, what a handle costs, handles that outlive edits elsewhere, the built-in containers, and moving values between containersWrite-phase statewhat is tracked between flushes, and why it is derived from the journalThe flushfolding the journal into pages: the piece table, mapping pieces to spans, the span policy, placement, and the cut of the span tableConsolidationreclaiming garbage: victim selection, evacuation, the page rewrite, merging spans, and the budgetConsolidator statewhat consolidation could carry from one session to the next in the private chainTransactions and batchesgrouping operations into transactions, and the buffering state machineRelated workwhere the design comes from, and where it parts companyImplementation noteswhere kladde-rs departs from these documents, and what it found
The shape of an implementation
A kladde file is currently read in bulk and never searched on disk.
That single decision is what keeps this design far simpler than a database engine, and it is worth stating first because almost every other choice follows from it:

On-file representations are optimized for compactness and cheap incremental edits, never for random access.
There is no on-disk search tree, no B-tree page splitting, no path copying.
The span table’s tree of child references is a directory, not a search structure: nothing ever descends it by key.
The order of the content lives in the spans’ links, which a reader walks once, at open; a tree over the spans is kept in memory only.
Epochs are consulted exactly once, during the bulk read, and never again at run time.

What this costs is that opening a file is O(entries + n) for a sequence of n bytes, and that the whole sequence is decoded into memory.
What it buys is that every read is an in-memory read of the application’s own values and every flush writes only deltas.
A future feature called segments would address the cost of bulk reads by letting application authors declare a subtree as a chain of its own, loaded lazily.
Overhead and work independent of size
The live pages exceed the sequence by three terms — the description, the garbage, and the page framing — and each can be held at a target that does not depend on the sequence’s length, at a cost per modification that does not either; the file adds to them a number of pages that depends on what a flush writes, and not on the sequence’s length either.
This is what the design is for, and the algorithms on the following pages are chosen to keep it.
Where the bytes of the file go
Let n be the length of the sequence (with the schema’s and the private chain’s, which are small), k the number of spans the chains reach, c the mean encoded size of their entries without inline payloads, and L̄ = n / k the mean length of a span.
The live pages hold:

every byte of the sequence once, in a data page or as an inline payload in a table page, and zeros nowhere: at most n;
k entries: k · c = n · c / L̄;
garbage and slack, G: bytes of data pages that no reached span shows, dead entries in table pages, and room that a writer left empty;
the page framing, 0.37 %.

So live pages come to about n · (1 + c / L̄ + G / n + 0.004).
The file holds more pages than the live ones:

the fallback pages, which the last commit stopped referencing, and which the reuse rule keeps until the next flush’s fsync;
the reusable pages that the next flush will write into, freed by the commit before the last;
the journal’s pages, at most its budget;
holes: further reusable pages below the last live page, which a fall of the live size leaves behind, and which later flushes fill, or compaction mode and truncation give back.

Each term, and what keeping it costs
The description, c / L̄, is set by the span policy.
Bounded spans keep L̄ ≥ L / 2 in the leaves, so c / L̄ ≤ 2c / L: with entries of 8 bytes and L = 256, at most 6 %, and the header’s exempt spans add at most a page.
Each modification creates a constant number of span boundaries, at most two for a splice or an overwrite and three for a move, and removing one costs at most L bytes written again and one entry, so the policy costs O(L) bytes per modification, amortized.
Merging cold regions into spans of a page lowers the term for them to about 0.15 %, once per region and cooling.
The garbage and slack, G / n, are set by the cleaner’s target.
Holding pages at a mean live fraction u leaves G ≤ (1 / u − 1) · n, 11 % at u = 0.9.
In steady state, content that the application supersedes turns into garbage, and the cleaner must win back as much room as that content took.
A cleaner that takes the emptiest page first takes one at most u full, live fraction v ≤ u; writing its survivors into pages that it fills to at least 1 − θ takes v / (1 − θ) of a page, so it wins back 1 − v / (1 − θ) of one.
Each page of room won back then costs v (1 − θ) / (1 − θ − v) pages of survivors moved, plus their spans restated, c / L̄ per byte, and the cleaner can keep up only while u < 1 − θ:




















uθ = 0θ = 0.050.855.78.10.9917
That is the classic bound for log-structured cleaning (Rosenblum and Ousterhout, “The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System”, SOSP 1991), and uniformly random overwrites are its worst case; skewed workloads clean far more cheaply, which is what age terms in victim selection try to exploit.
θ is a worst case too: packing holds every page a flush writes but its last to at least 1 − θ full and usually fills it, so the cost lies near the column for θ = 0.
The pages around the live ones are set by what one flush writes.
In steady state, a flush frees about as many pages as it writes, so with p pages written per flush, the file holds about p fallback pages and p reusable ones: 2p pages besides the live ones, plus the journal’s.
p is the flush’s new data and table pages, plus the survivors its cleaning moves: about ten pages for a flush that supersedes a page of content at u = 0.9 and θ = 0.
So a large file carries some 25 pages besides its live ones, about 100 KB, which is 0.1 % of a sequence of 100 MB and vanishes as n grows; for a file of a few pages, the same pages are most of the file.
Everything else is constant or logarithmic.
A splice, an overwrite and a move state a constant number of spans; a moved byte restates its span and nothing else, since no key changes; the rope finds and edits spans in O(log k); a handle is made from its parent’s with one lookup in the parent’s index, and a change of size updates one entry per level (what a handle costs); victims come from bucket queues in O(1), and their spans from a reverse index in O(1) each; and the table pages’ directory changes O(depth) pages per leaf added or removed, amortized over the entries a leaf holds.
So the live pages’ overhead is c / L̄ + G / n + 0.004, set by L and u, the file adds 2p pages and the journal’s, and the work per modification is O(w + L) bytes for w bytes written and O(log n) time in the store, plus the walk from the root to the modified value, which the application makes anyway.
A worked example
Arithmetic, not a measurement: a sequence of 100 MB, of which 1 MB is being edited.





















































partspansentry bytesshare of n99 MB cold, in spans of a page24,300146 KB, at 6 bytes each0.15 %1 MB hot, in spans of 128 bytes on average8,20082 KB, at 10 bytes each0.08 %garbage and slack, pages kept 90 % live11 %page framing0.4 %live pagesabout 112 %fallback and reusable pages, a flush writing 12 pages, and a journal of 40.1 %the fileabout 112 %
At u = 0.85 the garbage takes 18 %, and the cleaner moves at most 5.7 bytes per byte written instead of 9.
In either case, it is the cleaner’s target, and not the description, that decides where between 10 and 20 % the file lands.
The file as one sequence, measured shows what kladde-rs reaches on real edits.
The mirror
An implementation reads pages into its own buffers with ordinary file reads, rather than mapping the file, and reads only the pages the chains reach.
At open it reads every table page the header reaches, walks the chains, and then reads the data pages the reached spans show, in page order, into a mirror, from which the decode of the sequence reads; Opening a file gives the steps.
It might be tempting to load each data page lazily, the first time something reads from it.
Reading them eagerly turns scattered reads into one sequential pass over a set known in advance, and validates every reached page’s CRC at open rather than at first touch — which may be long after the last backup that could have helped.
And it keeps the resident set a property of the file: nothing obliges a data type to read anything, and a tool that only compacts reads no content at all.
Drop the data-page mirror once loading is done.
After the load, application reads are served by the values’ own in-memory representations and never touch the file, so a span’s bytes in a data page are read again only when a flush moves them, merges them with their neighbours, or rewrites a short span an edit cut into — all rare, and all able to afford a fresh read.
Peak memory comes at open, while the mirror and the decoded values coexist: about the sequence’s size twice over, until the decode ends and the mirror goes.
Holding the mirror for good instead, and reading values from it rather than decoding them into the host language’s vectors and strings, would halve that peak and save every in-memory copy, but it is an open idea: values would no longer be the host language’s own, reads would need the store, and the journal’s edits would have to reach the mirror too.
Table pages stay resident by default, for a reason data pages do not share: Inline payloads live inside them, and every flush that restates an inline span copies its payload.
They are also small next to the sequence.
Nothing depends on it, though: only the header must stay, being the write buffer, and dropping the leaves after load costs one read per leaf a flush rewrites or restates from.
Why not mmap.
Mapping the file would let the operating system’s page cache serve as the mirror, with pointer-dereference access and no second copy.
It is rejected for now because I/O errors arrive as SIGBUS rather than as an error value: a page that cannot be faulted in — a failing disk, or the file truncated by something else — takes the process down, and there is no portable way to catch it.
Should that trade ever be revisited, the mapping must be read-only, since kladde writes with ordinary writes and fsync, and mixing the two is only coherent by grace of the platform’s unified page cache.
Reading through a cursor.
The decode reads the sequence through a cursor that follows the rope across span boundaries and hands out slices of the mirror and of the table pages, so no byte of the sequence is copied before a value’s own decoder takes it.

impl/opening.title: Opening a file
impl/opening.content:
The steps from the two headers to a decoded root value, and what each checks.
Opening reads every live table page once, walks each chain once, reads the data pages the chains show in page order, decodes the sequence, and replays the journal: O(entries + n) for a sequence of n bytes.
There is no sweep resolving bytes across epochs, no clipping at sizes, and nothing to resolve per byte.
The steps

Read both headers and take the governing one: the CRC-valid header with the highest epoch (recovery).
fsync the file once, which makes that header durable and retires the older world at once.
Read every table page the header reaches, through its child references, checking that they form a tree, and keep, for each span id, the entry of the highest epoch in the span table.
No sorting is needed: an id’s entries are compared by their pages’ epochs as they come.
Each page’s framing is checked, and its epoch must not exceed the header’s.
Walk each chain from its head, building the rope for the sequence and lists for the short chains.
Refuse the file on an id no entry describes, a span reached twice, or a span two chains share; count each reached span’s entry, and its bytes, toward its pages’ coverage, and enter it in its data page’s reverse list.
Entries of spans no chain reaches are dead, and their ids free.
Read the data pages the reached spans show, in the order of their page numbers, into the mirror.
Each must be a Data page whose framing checks and whose epoch does not exceed the header’s, and each Ref must lie inside its content.
Reading them in the sequence’s order instead, as step 5 needs them, would jump between pages wherever the sequence was ever edited; step 3 has already found which pages are needed, so step 4 reads them in one sequential pass.
Decode the sequence through a cursor that follows the rope: the root type’s decoder reads front to back, and every container builds its index of children as it goes.
A recursive type nests as deeply as the file says, so the decode limits its depth, or does not recurse, and refuses a file beyond the limit rather than overflow its stack.
It refuses an encoding that is not canonical, and bytes left after the root value.
Then drop the mirror.
Replay the journal, applying each recovered transaction’s records to the in-memory values as well as to the store’s structures.

If the header’s root fingerprint differs from the application’s root type’s, step 5 decodes by the writer’s schema chain instead, resolving it once against the application’s types, or refuses the file if resolution is not implemented.
Replaying through a flush
An implementation may fold the recovered journal in a flush at open, before step 5, so that the decode reads the state after the last transaction and needs no replay of its own.
It has to fold a non-empty recovered journal before appending to it anyway (the start of a session), and replaying records into in-memory values would need every container to accept byte-level records it did not make.
The price is that a file whose journal was not empty costs a flush to open.
Recovery reads the payload pages the journal names, to check each reference, and keeps their bytes in the buffer with where they lie, so that the flush at open takes those of its own epoch into the file as data pages, as any flush does (payload pages); those of a later journal, reached through a seal, it writes again.
The seeds of the rotating walk and of heat
What the file does not record, open seeds:

the heat of each span, from its entry’s page epoch, which can only understate how long its bytes have gone unwritten — content is never younger than the page that holds its entry — or from the consolidator state, if one is current;
the rotating walk’s position, from the consolidator state, or else at a span chosen by the governing header’s CRC modulo the number of spans: deterministic for a given file, so tests reproduce, and spread over the sequence across sessions.

impl/related-work.title: Related work
impl/related-work.content:
Where kladde’s design comes from, and where it deliberately parts company.
No system known to these documents combines what kladde does, but each of its layers has a close precedent: kladde is an editor’s piece table kept on disk, linked rather than keyed by position, made crash-safe by shadow paging with an intent log, kept compact by a log-structured cleaner, and holding a serialization much like Avro’s.
None of the load-bearing pieces is novel, which is the point: their failure modes are understood and bounded, which is exactly what the bespoke machinery they replaced could not claim.
What is different from all of them is the premise: kladde reads in bulk and looks nothing up on disk.
Almost every divergence below is a consequence of that one fact, and every one of them cuts toward simplicity.







































































layerclosest precedentsshareddifferentthe encodingAvro’s binary encodingthe schema in the file, no tags, no padding, varints, countsedited in place; text ends in a terminator; Fixedthe sequence on fileWord’s fast save; FAT’s chainsan on-disk piece table; successors in a tablelinks instead of positions; byte-granular spansthe span tableLFS’s inode map; Bitcaska table of locations, newest wins, held in memorynothing is searched on diskthe header as write bufferLSM trees’ memtableshot entries buffered, cold ones evicted to runsone tier of unordered leaves, no levelscommit and recoveryshadow paging; LMDB; WAFL and ZFSa root written last after an fsync; a log replayed over itno tree on disk; one fsync per commitreclamationSprite LFS’s cleaner; SSD flash translation layersvictims by utilization and agepages instead of segmentsstate and durabilitysystem prevalence; Redisall state in memory, every change loggedbyte records instead of commands; incremental checkpointsmoving valuesCap’n Proto’s orphansdetach, adopt elsewhere, no copyjournaled, within a transactionpositions in memoryropes and piece treesa counted tree over pieces—order by linksYjsa linked list of items with ids, merged into runsone writer: no merging, tombstones or history
The encoding: Avro’s, nearly
Avro’s binary encoding is the closest precedent of the sequence’s encoding, and its object container files carry their schema as kladde files do.
An Avro record is its fields’ encodings concatenated, with no tags and no padding; integers are zigzag varints, a union starts with its branch’s index as a varint, and an array is its elements in blocks, each preceded by its count.
kladde’s evolution takes Avro’s model of reconciling a writer’s schema with a reader’s as well.
The differences follow from mutation: Avro data is written once and read in sequence, while kladde edits values in place, so it keeps counts in one place rather than in blocks, ends text in a terminator so that an edit of text needs one splice, and offers Fixed for values that change often.
Protocol Buffers share the varints and drop padding too, but tag every field with its number, which makes evolution possible without a stored schema at the price of bytes per field.
The sequence on file: a piece table, as Word’s fast save kept one
A piece table on disk is old: Microsoft Word’s binary .doc format kept one for its fast save, which appended the changed text to the document’s stream and wrote a new piece table over it.
Bravo, at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, introduced piece tables for editing, and Visual Studio Code’s piece tree (2018) keeps one in a balanced tree in memory, as the rope does here.
Word’s table differs from the span table in three ways that matter.
It keys each piece by its character position, so it is rewritten whole at every fast save, where links let kladde state only the spans at an edit.
It reclaims nothing until a full save rewrites the document, so deleted text stayed in fast-saved files, which leaked it to whoever received them.
And it gave no crash safety of its own.
The span table’s successors are linked allocation, as FAT keeps it, with byte-granular spans instead of clusters.
FAT file systems, and Microsoft’s compound files, keep each file or stream as a chain of fixed-size clusters, whose successors a table holds.
A chain of fixed-size clusters can take an insertion only at a cluster’s boundary; a span can be split at any byte.
And linked allocation’s classic weakness, reaching a byte by walking the chain to it, does not arise, since kladde walks each chain once, at open, and keeps a rope.
The other classic scheme is extents keyed by their offset in the file, as ext4’s and XFS’s extent trees keep them; inserting a range there, as Linux’s FALLOC_FL_INSERT_RANGE does, shifts every extent behind it — the cost that keying spans by id avoids, and that kladde’s previous design paid per allocation.
The name extent would mislead for that reason, and span is used instead; the fold’s transient runs keep the literature’s name, pieces, and a span is a piece made persistent: it has an id, links to its successor, and outlives the flush.
Storage: a log-structured file system for one file
The pages, the span table, the cleaner and the two header slots are those of a log-structured file system, with pages for segments and one file in it.
Sprite LFS (Rosenblum and Ousterhout, “The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System”, SOSP 1991, and TOCS 1992) writes everything to fresh segments, finds each file’s inode through an inode map that is itself written to the log and held in memory, tracks each segment’s live bytes in a segment usage table, cleans by moving live blocks out of segments chosen by utilization and age, and alternates between two checkpoint regions.
The span table is that inode map, coverage the segment usage table, cost-benefit scoring its cleaning policy, and the header slots the checkpoint regions.
Its cleaning unit is a large fixed segment; kladde’s is a page, and its spans can be re-cut freely because the directory keeps no order.
Bitcask (Basho, 2010) holds every key in memory, rebuilt at open from its log, lets the newest write of a key win, and merges files by writing their live values again: the span table, read at open, is a Bitcask keyed by span id.
LSM trees (LevelDB, RocksDB) resolve a key’s versions across runs by recency, as entries are resolved across epochs, and the header as write buffer is a memtable whose eviction is an L0 flush; but LSMs keep runs sorted and levelled so point lookups work without full residency, while kladde is fully resident after the bulk read and needs no sort order, no levels and no bloom filters.
The commit is shadow paging with an intent log.
System R’s shadow pages (Lorie, “Physical Integrity in a Large Segmented Database”, TODS 1977), LMDB’s two meta pages, WAFL’s consistency points with their log of requests in NVRAM (Hitz, Lau and Malcolm, USENIX Winter 1994), and ZFS’s transaction groups with their uberblocks and intent log all write a new root last, after an fsync, over pages that no older root reaches, and replay a log over the last root after a crash.
kladde’s flush is such a consistency point, its journal such an intent log, and its two header slots LMDB’s meta pages; it has no tree on disk to copy paths in, since nothing is searched on disk.
LMDB’s B-tree is sorted because readers descend it in the mapped file; kladde never descends, so it trades away the ordering along with its ~25 % slack and its rebalancing writes.
LMDB also needs two fsyncs per commit where kladde needs one, because kladde can let the header lag one write behind and lean on journal replay.
btrfs’s inline extents and ZFS’s bonus buffers store small data directly in metadata — the precedent for Inline entries.
State and durability: a memory image with incremental checkpoints
Keeping all state in memory, logging every change before it returns, and folding the log into a checkpoint is system prevalence, as Prevayler implements it and Martin Fowler describes it as a memory image; Redis does the same with its append-only file and its snapshots.
kladde differs in two ways.
Its log holds byte effects rather than commands, so replaying it needs no application code and no schema; and its checkpoints are incremental, since a flush writes what changed, where those systems write whole snapshots or rewrite their whole log.
Moving values: Cap’n Proto’s orphans
Cut and paste is Cap’n Proto’s orphans: an object disowned by its parent and adopted by another in the same message, without copying, move-only, and zeroed if nothing adopts it.
Here the cut lives in the journal’s transaction rather than in a message’s arena, and the flush turns it into a few links.
Order by links: sequence CRDTs
Yjs keeps a shared text as a linked list of items, each with an id and links to its neighbours, merges consecutive items of one writer into runs, and persists updates that it later merges into one, which is close to linked spans with ids.
Automerge keeps the history of operations, in a compressed, columnar format.
Both merge concurrent edits from many writers, and so keep tombstones and history and compact by encoding the whole document again; a single writer needs none of that.
Where the redesigns have led
Each redesign moved kladde further from object stores and closer to document storage.

The first design was a relocatable heap: allocations contiguous in the file, pointers between them, and compaction that moved whole allocations — a persistent heap, as PMDK’s libpmemobj or Boost.Interprocess’s mapped files keep one, and an object store, as ZODB’s FileStorage or Realm are.
The second kept allocations and pointers, but stored them as a log-structured file system stores files: pages written copy-on-write, an address table of extents keyed by offset, an intent log, and a cleaner.
The present design keeps the file system and drops the objects: one file whose extents are linked, a piece table, holding a serialization as Avro would write it.

So kladde has converged on known parts, put together in a way not found elsewhere: a typed document held whole in memory, durable at every change through a byte-level journal, and saved as deltas into a linked piece table on copy-on-write pages.
The nearest whole is Word’s fast save, without its rewrites of the piece table, its leaked deletions, and its lack of crash safety.
One lesson taken from the same literature rather than from a system: PostgreSQL’s transaction-id wraparound “freezing” is why epochs are 64-bit.

impl/transactions-and-batches.title: Transactions and batches
impl/transactions-and-batches.content:
How application operations are grouped into the transactions the journal records, how they wait in memory, and when they are appended to the journal pages and folded.
Status: settled apart from the open questions at the end; kladde-rs implements it as described here.
Transactions are normative — they are the unit of atomicity an application builds on.
Batches are not: they are an implementation’s mechanism for turning a long run of operations into reasonably sized transactions, and an implementation is free to offer something else or nothing at all.
Both exist only to affect how mutations are persisted; the accompanying in-memory mutations are always immediate.
From the buffer on, this page is the design of the reference implementations, not one way among several to meet the format.
kladde-rs and kladde-cpp each keep exactly one buffer of operations and the cursors into it described below, and append and flush by exactly the rules in Flush triggers.
A departure — a second buffer, copying between spans, another trigger — is a deviation: it is recorded with its reason, in the implementation notes for kladde-rs and in kladde-cpp for kladde-cpp, and proposed as a change to this page if it is better, rather than taken as a free choice.
Three mechanisms over one journal





























mechanismeffect on the journalwhat it is forwhen to usetransactionwraps a sequence of operations in a single journal transaction, appended atomically when the caller commitscorrectness: either all or none of the operations are persisted, so a crash can’t expose an invalid intermediate statewhenever intermediate state would be invalidbatchcuts a long sequence of operations into the largest pieces that fit in what is left of the journal’s page budget, respecting nested transactions, and wraps each in a transactionoptimization: fewer and fuller journal writes, while keeping the journal within its budgetwhen many operations happen at once with valid intermediate states — a large import, a pastebare operationrecorded as its own transactionsimplicity: changes persist immediatelysingle mutations, prototyping
Transactions enforce correctness.
In complex data types, one semantic operation often produces several journal records — appending to a vector splices the element in and rewrites the count — and interrupting between them leaves a sequence that does not decode.
The same happens in application code, where a transition between two valid states sometimes passes through invalid ones.
Batches are an optimization, and a necessary one.
Kladde’s promise to persist every mutation immediately carries a small unavoidable per-transaction overhead.
