That is usually worth it, but it adds up when an action triggers a large or unbounded burst — and for such bursts, per-operation durability buys little anyway.
It is tempting to wrap the burst in a transaction instead, but very large transactions perform poorly, because the whole transaction is held in memory until it ends, and the journal pages, and therefore the file, must then temporarily grow in proportion to the number and size of the operations.
A batch is the middle ground: the backend decides how to divide the sequence, respecting any explicit transaction inside it, so that each piece fills what is left of the journal’s budget as far as the transaction boundaries allow.
Recommendations

For most application code, reach for a batch or a bare operation.
Batches are cheaper for multiple operations, have no I/O overhead over a bare operation even for one, and cost a handful of instructions and no allocation.
But remember that batches delay persistence: they are only guaranteed committed when ended, so holding one open for a long time defeats the point of immediate persistence.
Use transactions when application logic requires atomicity, and keep them short.
Needing a very long transaction almost always means either that the application’s state transitions pass through too many invalid intermediate states, or that the wrong data type was chosen — a vector where a rope or an ordered tree belongs.
When atomicity is genuinely required for a large mutation, it can usually be imposed at the application level instead: build the value in memory, outside any handle, then insert it in one operation, which encodes it into one buffer and splices it in.
For a long sequence where some parts need atomicity, use a batch with a few smaller transactions inside.
This is the pattern the design is arranged around.

Nesting
Transactions and batches nest arbitrarily, so that a container’s push can open a transaction without caring whether its caller already did.
The backend flattens the nesting, because the journal only deals with a flat sequence of transactions.




















↓ outer; inner →transaction in a …batch in a …… transactiononly outer transaction survivesonly the transaction survives (shouldn’t usually occur)… batchboth surviveonly outer batch survives

Transaction in a transaction ⇒ outer. The inner one is meaningless; its atomicity is already enforced. Expected often in composable code.
Transaction in a batch ⇒ both. The inner transaction enforces atomicity, so no cutting point may lie inside it. Expected often.
Batch in a batch ⇒ outer. The inner one is meaningless; deferral is already in effect. Fine, but not useful.
Batch in a transaction ⇒ the transaction. The inner batch is meaningless, since the transaction already forces the operations to commit as one group.
A potential code smell: batches are for large or unbounded sequences, transactions should be short, so this combination implies a long chain of state transitions with only invalid intermediate states.

One buffer and three cursors
Every operation recorded since the last flush lives in one in-memory buffer ops, in the order it was recorded, whether it is already in the journal pages or not.
Between two flushes, the operations form a single stream: some prefix of it has been appended to the journal pages, the operations on top of that are a batch’s ready run, and those on top of that belong to the transaction that is still open.
So everything that happens between two flushes either appends to the buffer or moves a boundary between these spans; nothing is ever copied from one span to another.
The flush folds the operations the journal pages hold from this buffer, not from the pages, which only recovery reads back.
Recovery decodes the journal’s complete transactions into the buffer, and open folds them before it returns (see opening a file).
In kladde-rs, the buffer is a VecDeque of records, beside a byte arena, also a VecDeque, that holds their payloads.
Positions in both are counted from the start of the session rather than from the buffer’s front, so that discarding the folded prefix after a flush moves the front and nothing else: no record moves, and every position held elsewhere — a record’s payload, a pending fragment of the flush pointing into the arena — stays valid.
A journal’s cuts are positions in it too: a paste names its cut by distance among the cuts of its journal, which the records keep in order, so no cursor moves them.
Three cursors, front <= committed_cursor <= ready_cursor <= end, divide the buffer into three spans:

committed := ops[front..committed_cursor] — appended to the journal pages since the last flush: what the next flush folds;
ready := ops[committed_cursor..ready_cursor] — a batch’s operations, held back to be appended as one transaction;
transaction := ops[ready_cursor..end] — the operations of the open transaction.

Each cursor also carries the encoded size of the records before it, so that the encoded size of any span is a subtraction, and deciding whether a span fits costs constant time.
The journal’s length prefix needs a transaction’s size before its first byte is written anyway.
Moving the cursors is all that recording, appending, and flushing do:

Recording an operation appends it at end.
Appending a span to the journal pages encodes it as one transaction, writes it, and moves committed_cursor to the span’s end.
A flush folds committed and moves front to committed_cursor.
Discarding operations — a transaction that failed halfway and is rolled back, or one the application abandons — moves end back to where they began.

The backend’s state holds the depths of the open scopes and the cursors that are not implied by them:
enum TransactionState {
    Immediate,
    InBatch              { batch_depth: NonZero, committed_cursor: Cursor },
    InTransaction        { transaction_depth: NonZero, batch_depth: u32,
                           committed_cursor: Cursor },
    InTransactionInBatch { transaction_depth: NonZero, batch_depth: NonZero,
                           committed_cursor: Cursor, ready_cursor: Cursor },
}
transaction_depth and batch_depth count begins minus ends, with an implied zero in any variant where they are absent.
front and end belong to the buffer, and the table below gives the cursors each state implies.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Immediate
    Immediate --> InBatch: begin_batch
    Immediate --> InTransaction: begin_transaction
    InBatch --> Immediate: end_batch when<br> batch_depth == 1
    InBatch --> InTransactionInBatch: begin_transaction
    InTransaction --> Immediate: end_transaction when<br> transaction_depth == 1
    InTransactionInBatch --> InBatch: end_transaction when<br> transaction_depth == 1

Why four states and not three.
InTransaction carries a batch_depth that may be positive, so it overlaps with InTransactionInBatch in depth alone.
What distinguishes them is which scope was opened first.
InTransactionInBatch is batch outside, transaction inside — the useful nesting, where ending the transaction returns to InBatch and persistence stays deferred.
InTransaction { batch_depth > 0 } is transaction outside, batch inside — the code-smell nesting, where the batch is subsumed and its depth is tracked only so that its end can be matched.
Transitions in detail
The error cells are all the same mistake: ending one scope while a scope nested inside it is still open — interleaving rather than nesting.
An implementation should make that unrepresentable at the API level rather than checking for it.




































































ImmediateInBatchInTransactionInTransactionInBatchtransaction_depth0 (implicit)0 (implicit)> 0> 0batch_depth0 (implicit)> 0any> 0committed_cursorend (implicit)explicitexplicitexplicitready_cursorend (implicit)end (implicit)committed_cursor (implicit)explicitbegin_transaction()InTransaction { t: 1, b: 0 }InTransactionInBatch { t: 1, .. }transaction_depth += 1transaction_depth += 1end_transaction()errorerror−1; at 0: Immediate if batch_depth == 0, else error−1; at 0: InBatchbegin_batch()InBatch { b: 1 }batch_depth += 1batch_depth += 1batch_depth += 1end_batch()error−1; at 0: Immediatebatch_depth -= 1−1; at 0: error
The implied cursors are invariants at every operation boundary, not just labels: in Immediate, everything recorded is in the journal pages, and in InBatch, everything not yet appended is the batch’s.
Flush triggers

Keep the journal within its page budget.
A transaction that would not fit in what is left of the budget is preceded by a flush, and only a transaction too large for the budget on its own exceeds it, followed by a flush at once.

The budget is a number of journal pages, B, and a transaction fits if the journal’s stream, with the transaction appended, ends within B pages, counting each of the journal’s payload pages as one.
Each journal page holds page_size − 8 bytes of the stream, the rest being its trailer, and a transaction of n record bytes takes n plus its length prefix plus its 4-byte crc.
The writer takes the next journal page only once the stream continues past the current one, so fitting within B · (page_size − 8) stream bytes is fitting within B pages.
A transaction’s size is estimated with its bytes inline, which for large bytes is about the payload pages they will take.
A transaction that does not fit even into an empty journal is overlong.
Whenever operations close — a bare operation recorded in Immediate or InBatch, or the outermost transaction ending, InTransaction → Immediate or InTransactionInBatch → InBatch — let X be the operations that just closed, ops[ready_cursor..end], and apply:

The candidate is ops[committed_cursor..end]: X alone outside a batch, where ready is empty, and ready followed by X inside one, to be appended as one transaction.
If the candidate does not fit, the batch is cut before X: append ready as one transaction if it is not empty, which it always fits, and flush, unless the journal is empty.
The candidate is now X alone, in an empty journal.
A paste in X that names a cut of the journal just folded becomes a Splice of its value’s bytes, since that cut has ended (moving values), and X’s size is computed again.
Inside a batch, a candidate that fits stays in memory as the new ready, which the batch holds back until its next cut or its end.
Otherwise, the candidate is appended as one transaction, and if that took the journal past its budget, flush again.
Only an overlong X can do that, since step 2 left it an empty journal.

The other triggers:

The outermost batch ends, InBatch → Immediate: append ready if it is not empty.
It fits, so no flush follows.
An explicit flush(): append ready if it is not empty, then flush — on an empty journal too, since a flush also consolidates.
An open transaction stays in the buffer, past committed_cursor.
A flush when the application is idle: flush_if_journal_exceeds(fraction) appends ready and flushes if the journal pages then hold at least that fraction of the budget, and does nothing otherwise; the check is a subtraction of two cursors.
An interactive application calls it from its event loop’s idle callback, so that the automatic flush, whose fsync blocks the mutating call that triggers it, rarely fires in the middle of a gesture.
The fraction should stay well above zero: an idle flush ends the journal, and with it the cuts its records made.
Opening a file: kladde-rs folds a non-empty recovered journal before open returns, since reads see the flushed state only.
That also keeps the journal’s rule that nothing is appended to a non-empty recovered journal, and no state outlives open.

So an overlong transaction is flushed twice, once before it and once after it, the first unless the journal was empty; and a batch is always cut at the last boundary at which its run still fits, which lies between two closed transactions or operations, never inside a transaction.
The journal’s budget
B is 2% of the sequence’s length in whole pages, at least 2 and at most 10, unless the application fixes it, and the writer computes it from the length as it stands whenever it checks a transaction against it.
It is a whole number of pages, since a journal page once taken costs a page of the file however little of it is used.
A small budget keeps the file close to its content.
At a flush, the journal it folds and the previous one, still the fallback, both occupy pages, and the pages a flush frees become reusable only after the next flush; a budget of B pages thus keeps up to about 2B pages of journal beside the content.
A budget of 256 pages, a megabyte, made the files of drawings of 40 KB to 1 MB up to 16 times their content, and a budget sized to them kept them within 1.2 to 2.2 times.
Every flush is a chance to consolidate, so flushing often costs little beyond the flush’s fsync: a flush folds a journal of a few pages in one to two milliseconds, within a frame of an interactive application, where a journal of a megabyte stalled the edit that triggered it for 46 to 77 ms.
The floor of 2 pages keeps a small file from flushing at every few edits: a budget of 1 page flushed the same drawings two to four times as often as 2 to 4 pages and made their files no smaller.
The ceiling of 10 pages keeps a large file’s journal, and with it the pages it holds and the time a flush takes, bounded; a file of tens of megabytes gains from a longer journal only fewer flushes, which an application that wants them can have by fixing the budget.
Payload pages
When a transaction is appended, the bytes of each of its Writes and Splices that carries at least payload_threshold bytes, 2 KB, are written into payload pages first, and the transaction names them rather than holding them.
The decision falls at the append, not when the operation is recorded, because the records of an open transaction or a batch’s ready run may still be discarded, and the cuts that an application holds name records by their number in the buffer, which splitting a record there would change.
So the buffer keeps each record as it was recorded, its bytes in the arena, and records beside the arena which runs of it also lie in a payload page, at which page, offset and checksum; the encoder writes such a record as one record per run, and the flush maps the runs onto the pages.
Nothing above the store sees a difference: a container hands the store its bytes as before.

The bytes go into the journal’s open payload page as far as it has room, and the rest into new pages, a page’s worth at a time; a last part shorter than the threshold that would open a page stays inline in the journal, in a record of its own.
The pages a transaction touched are written whole, framed with the journal’s epoch, before the transaction is appended, and the open page is written again whenever a later transaction of the journal appends to it.
A record whose bytes are cut into runs becomes one record per run, the first removing what the record removed and the rest removing nothing at the cursor, delta 0; a Write becomes such splices too, the first removing what it overwrote, so that it still makes one cut, and a paste of the overwritten value still names one.
Payload pages come from the reusable pool, lowest first, as journal pages do, but leave its last page alone, growing the file instead: a large transaction is followed by a flush, which seals only if a reusable page is left for the next journal to begin in, and without its seal that flush could not commit on a worker, and a lost header would lose what was appended after it.
Payload pages count toward the budget, so a transaction with more payload pages than the budget is overlong: preceded by a flush if the journal is not empty, and followed by one at once, which adopts its pages and writes a header and a leaf or two.
The budget so bounds how much content waits for a flush to be durable under a power cut, as well as the journal’s share of the file.
A transaction that is abandoned after its pages were written leaves them in no world: they return to the pool, and the bytes it added to the open page are dead from the start.
A payload page that cannot be written fails the transaction and poisons the store, as a journal append that cannot get a page does.

The threshold is about half a page, and unmeasured: a payload page holding r bytes costs a page write now and leaves 4081 − r bytes of slack until an append or consolidation fills it, where inline bytes cost r in the journal and r again in a data page the flush shares with other content.
Creating a file of 4.26 MB, one splice of the whole drawing, then takes four journal pages besides its payload pages, and the file comes out at 1076 pages, within three pages of a consolidated copy, where with every byte in the journal it took 2139.
Why ready always fits
ready only becomes longer in step 3, which checked that it fits after what the journal pages already hold.
Nothing else is appended while a batch holds a ready run, since every closing operation inside the batch either joins ready or cuts the batch, and the cut appends ready first.
So what the journal pages hold does not change until ready itself is appended, and ready still fits then.
Why flush first
A flush before the append leaves no journal page behind that only the start of an overflowing transaction occupies.
Appending first and flushing once the journal is over budget would end every journal with such a page, nearly empty; and at the moment of a flush, the journal it folds and the previous one, still the fallback, are both off limits, so that it would cost two pages at a time.
It costs nothing.
The operations of X are already in the buffer, and their encoded size is known from the cursors, so deciding before the append is as cheap as deciding after it.
A flush folds only committed, so X waits in the buffer past committed_cursor and is appended to the next journal; only the order of the two steps changes.
The flush after an overlong transaction keeps a long journal from lingering: the journal is back within its budget as soon as the operation that exceeded it returns.
The budget bounds the file, not memory.
An open transaction is held in memory in full, whatever the budget, because nothing can fold an unfinished transaction; a huge transaction costs memory in proportion to its size, and journal or payload pages in proportion too once it is appended.
Consequence for write-phase state
A flush may run while operations are still in the buffer past committed_cursor: the X that step 2 holds back, or, at an explicit flush(), an open transaction.
The write-phase state — the sequence’s length and the journal’s cuts — describes them as well, so a flush leaves it as it was, and the flush folds only the records before committed_cursor, whose positions refer to the sequence as it stood before the held-back ones.
Discarding operations moves the length and the cuts back to what they were where the discarded operations began.
Checkpoint versus commit
Decided: a checkpoint never splits a commit — see the journal.
A checkpoint is a flush triggered by resource pressure, and a commit is a transaction boundary the recovered state may snap to.
The open question was whether a checkpoint could fold part of an unfinished transaction, to bound the memory the transaction holds.
It cannot: the header it committed would describe a state inside the transaction, and undoing that part on recovery would need a mechanism the format does not have.
So every flush folds complete transactions only, and the memory an open transaction holds is bounded only by keeping transactions short.
What remains is that application authors need never call flush(): the operation whose transaction would not fit in the journal’s budget flushes automatically.
Two consequences follow:
Flush needs only shared access to the backend.
The auto-checkpoint fires from inside a mutating call, which holds no exclusive reference to the whole structure.
This is safe: handles hold positions in the sequence, which a flush does not change, since it rewrites only where the sequence’s bytes lie on file.
Note that it is a reentrant call, so no write path may hold an interior borrow across a callback.
The trigger belongs at operation boundaries, not at append time.
A check on append can fire between two records of one logical mutation.
An operation is the natural atomic unit, being the smallest thing an application author perceives as one change.
A flush off the caller’s thread
An automatic flush that sealed its journal may hand its fsync and its header write to a thread of their own, and the mutating call that triggered it then returns without waiting for the disk.
Folding a journal and writing a flush’s pages take well under a millisecond for files of the sizes kladde is meant for, while the fsync takes milliseconds on an SSD and more on a slow disk, which an interactive application feels as a stall in the middle of a gesture.
So the calling thread seals, folds, places and writes the pages as before, and a worker does what remains: the fsync, then the header write.
The application goes on appending to the next journal meanwhile, which the seal makes reachable from either header, so an application crash before the header is written loses nothing that returned.
Doing it is optional; the format requires only the seal, and a flush that runs entirely on the calling thread writes the same file.
The worker shares nothing with the calling thread but the file, through a second handle to it, and one hand-over:

The next flush waits for the worker before it seals, and so do an explicit flush, before it returns, and closing the store.
One commit is in flight at a time.
The pages the commit before freed become reusable only when the worker reports, since its fsync is what retires the world that held them (the reuse rule); until then neither the next journal nor anything else may take them.
A flush that cannot seal syncs on the calling thread: without a seal, transactions appended during the fsync would belong to a journal only the unwritten header names.
A flush seals only where a reusable page can start the next journal, since a page added at the end of the file before the flush’s own pages would keep the file from being truncated to them.
A failure on the worker poisons the store when it is reported, at the next flush that waits for it, as a failure on the calling thread would at once.
Reads do not wait: the pages they read are in the file already, synced or not.
A failure reported only as the store is dropped has nobody left to tell, and is lost, which is no worse than a power cut at that moment.
A session’s first sealing flush syncs the page it seals to before appending the seal, as the specification requires; that one extra fsync per session runs on the calling thread.

An explicit flush() keeps its meaning — everything before it is durable when it returns — by waiting; only the flushes that mutations trigger run their commit off the calling thread.
kladde-rs offers this behind an option, off by default, until the Inkscape demo has shown whether the idle flush of flush triggers already keeps the stall out of gestures.
Open questions

The journal’s page budget: whether it should adapt to an application whose transactions routinely exceed it.

impl/values.title: Values and their positions
impl/values.content:
How the values an application holds find their bytes in the sequence: regions, what each container keeps to find its children, what that costs per mutation, handles that live long, the built-in containers, and moving a value from one container to another.
No value stores where it lies, and neither does the store: the store knows bytes, each container knows where its children start relative to itself, and the chain of handles from the root composes the two for as long as it lives.
A handle is what a value is mutated through, Mut in kladde-rs and kladde-cpp; a binding in another language may intercept mutation differently, but it needs the same positions, and the algorithms below are the same.
A value is a region
A data type sees only its own region of the sequence: where its value starts, resolved when its handle is made, and how long it is.
It writes and splices at offsets relative to that start, checked against its length, and it neither knows where the region lies nor can reach anything outside it.
A region offers:

write(at, bytes), which overwrites bytes in place;
splice(at, removed, bytes), which replaces bytes and shifts what follows; it records a Write wherever removed equals the number of bytes inserted, so a whole-value set calls it whether or not the size changes;
splice_value(at, removed, value), which encodes the value straight into the record, asking it for its encoded length once, since the record states the length before the bytes, and returns that length to its caller;
move_bytes(from, len, to), which reorders without writing;
paste(at, removed, cut), which inserts a cut (below);
child(at, len, index), which makes the region of one of the value’s children, together with a note that it is child number index, so that when the child changes size its region tells the value’s index of its children.

write and splice return the cut of what they remove.
Every offset is relative to the region’s start, and every method refuses one outside it.
The obligations of a data type are four: its fixed size and encoded length match what its encoder writes; its encoder and decoder are inverses; every mutation leaves its region holding the value’s encoding when its transaction ends; and its descriptor matches the bytes.
The third is checkable, which an ordering discipline over allocations was only by replay: a store in a test can keep the sequence in memory and compare a region with the value’s encoding after every method.
A push onto a vector of variable-size elements, for instance, splices the element in at the end and rewrites the count, in one transaction, and only then changes memory:
fn push(&mut self, value: T) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let n = self.vec.items.len();
    let len = self.region.transaction(|r| {
        let len = r.splice_value(r.len(), 0, &value)?;
        r.splice(0, varint_len(n), &varint(n + 1))?;
        Ok(len)
    })?;
    self.vec.sizes.push(len);     // appends to the Fenwick tree, O(log m); nothing for fixed-size `T`
    self.vec.items.push(value);
    Ok(())
}
Recording first and changing memory after means that a failed append leaves the value as it was.
In a language whose allocations can fail without ending the process, such as C++, a mutation also does everything in memory that can fail before it records — reserving capacity, constructing the new element — so that what follows the record cannot fail.
Positions belong to containers
A container hands each child a subregion and keeps, in memory, where each child starts relative to itself: by multiplication for fixed-size children, by an index otherwise.
A child that changes size reports the change to its container, which updates its index and reports its own change to its container in turn, up to the root.

A struct keeps no index at all.
Its fields up to its first variable-size field start at constants; after that, each starts at the sum of the encoded sizes of the fields before it, a number of additions fixed by the struct’s type.
A container of fixed-size elements keeps no index either: element i starts at i times the element’s size, after the count.
A container of variable-size elements keeps an index, chosen below.
Every container caches its own encoded size, so that adding up sizes never recurses.

A fixed-size type buys three things, all in memory: offsets inside it that the compiler can fold, containers of it without an index, and writes that never change its size, so nothing above it has to hear about them.
The choice is the application author’s, per field and per element type: varints and unpadded enums save bytes on file, and Fixed saves memory and time in containers that hold many values, and keeps a field that changes often, such as a counter, from changing size whenever it crosses a power of 128.
Why not a global index in the store.
One index of anchors, one for every value whose position anyone may ask for, would cost a node of an order-statistics tree per value, where a container’s index costs four bytes per variable-size element and nothing per fixed-size one, and it would teach the store about values, which nothing else requires it to know.
What a container keeps to find its children
A container of variable-size elements has five ways to keep where they start, and memory decides between them.















































indexfinding an elementa size changean insertionmemory per elementan array of startsO(1)O(m)O(m)4 bytesa Fenwick tree of sizesO(log m)O(log m)O(m)4 bytesa counted B-treeO(log m)O(log m)O(log m)about 8 bytesa tree weighted by the elements’ sizesO(1 + log(W / w)), amortizedthe samethe sameabout 16 bytesa start every 64 elementsO(64)O(m / 64)O(m)1/16 byte
m is the number of elements, W the container’s encoded size and w the element’s, and memory assumes sizes recorded in 32-bit values; a container that would outgrow them fails cleanly.
A Fenwick tree is the default: a size change of an element, typing into a string inside it, say, is the frequent case and costs O(m) in an array of starts, while an insertion costs O(m) in the array that holds the elements anyway.
The runtimes here are for lookups that happen a handful of times per mutation, when the mutation happens and not during a flush, so they matter less than memory: kladde is meant for interactive applications whose mutations follow user actions, and a Fenwick tree’s lookup or update over a million elements is about twenty steps, well under a microsecond.
For bulk operations, such as pasting large content from the clipboard, an application should build the value outside any handle and bring it in whole, which encodes it into one buffer and splices it in.
A Fenwick tree over blocks of 32 elements would keep one sum per block, an eighth of a byte per element, and find where element i starts from the tree’s sum up to i’s block plus the encoded sizes of the up to 31 elements before it in the block, which it asks of the elements themselves; for small elements such as varints that scan costs about what the tree’s own steps cost.
It is the better choice for vectors of small variable-size elements, where a full tree would double the memory.
Open: whether a Fenwick tree is the right default, what an application with millions of variable-size elements should use, and whether any data model nests deeply enough for size-weighted indexes to pay.
What a handle costs
Making a handle costs one lookup in its parent’s index, however deep its value lies, because the parent’s handle already holds where the parent starts.
Every handle holds the start of its value, which it needs anyway, since journal records name positions in the sequence.
An application reaches a value one level at a time — drawing.get_mut().shapes_mut().get_mut(7)? — and each step adds its child’s start relative to the parent to the parent’s start:

a field before its struct’s first variable-size field, or an element of a container of fixed-size elements, starts at a constant, or at i times the element’s size;
a field after it starts at the sum of the encoded sizes of the fields before it;
an element of a container of variable-size elements starts where the container’s index says.

The start a handle holds stays right for as long as the handle lives: the handle borrows its parent exclusively, so nothing before its value can change size meanwhile, and its value’s own changes of size move only what lies behind it.
A language that cannot enforce the exclusive borrow makes it a rule, the kind iterator invalidation is: a handle is valid until something is written through a handle that is not its descendant; a debug build can check it with a stack of the live handles that a write pops down to the handle it went through.
Iterating needs no index at all: a handle that steps through a container’s elements adds each element’s size to the start of the one before.
A change of size walks the same chain back up, since it changes the encoded size of every value around the one that changed: each ancestor updates its cached size and its index’s entry for the child the change came from, one update per level.
So the depth is not a cost of the design, and the logarithm per level is a choice of index.
The costs fall at three different times: making a handle costs a lookup at each level it descends, once; a write through it that keeps its value’s size costs nothing more; and a write that changes its value’s size costs an update at each level above the value.
The chain from the root is walked to make the handles anyway, so a constant per level adds nothing that grows with the file.
Handles made together
Handles made together — for every field of a struct or of an enum’s current variant at once, or for two runs of a container’s elements — ask for their start when they write instead of holding it, since a sibling before a handle can change size while the handle lives.
Such a handle holds a link to its parent’s index and its own number there, and computes its start whenever it writes, from the parent’s start and the sizes the index keeps for the children before it.
The index keeps those sizes in cells that a sibling’s report of a change of size can update while the other handles still hold shared references to it.
A write to an earlier part that changes its size, followed by a write to a later part, then works out by itself: the first write’s report updates the parent’s index, and the second write computes its start from the updated index.
Such a handle pays a lookup at every write rather than once; a count of changes kept in the index, compared with the count the handle saw last, would let it reuse its start until a sibling’s size has changed.
A field whose predecessors are all fixed-size has a constant start even then, since no sibling’s change of size can move it.
A handle made on its own below a handle made together holds its start relative to that handle, since that handle’s own start can move while it lives.
Between the two, every handle borrows the one above it exclusively, so nothing between them can change size before it, and the relative start stays right; above them, a sibling’s write can shift everything.
A write then computes its absolute start by climbing only the handles made together: at each, one lookup in the index of the parent it was made from, plus the relative starts of the handles made on their own in between, which are constants.
A write that changes its value’s size updates every level up to the root, the handles in between included, so every level keeps its cached size and its index in cells.
The test for this: in a tree, take two sibling handles of the root together, descend two levels in each on their own, take two siblings of each of those together, descend two more levels in each of the four; then write in the four remote cousins, changing their sizes, and check that each writes at the right position after the others have changed size, that the indexes at every level match the in-memory values, and that the file then holds the value’s encoding and reopens to it.
Indexes weighted by size
Indexes that weigh elements by their encoded size make the whole chain cost O(depth + log n), as one tree over every value’s position would, with no such tree.
In a tree over a container’s elements in which an element of w bytes, in a container of W, lies at depth O(1 + log(W / w)) — a biased search tree (Bent, Sleator and Tarjan, “Biased Search Trees”, SIAM Journal on Computing, 1985), or a splay tree, whose amortized cost of access is the same for any weights (Sleator and Tarjan, “Self-Adjusting Binary Search Trees”, Journal of the ACM, 1985) — the lookups from the root, of n bytes, down to a value of w bytes cost O(depth + log(n / w)) in all, since each level’s log(W / w) cancels against the next level’s.
Changes of size telescope the same way on the way back up.
That pays for deep nesting of large containers, a document tree whose nodes hold long lists of nodes, say; for shallow nesting a Fenwick tree per container is simpler, and the default.
Handles that outlive edits elsewhere
An application that keeps references into its document for as long as it likes needs handles that survive edits elsewhere, and a list whose elements know where they stand provides them.
A document editor holds references to its nodes everywhere — in the selection, in tools, in dialogs, in the undo log — and writes through any of them at any time; a handle whose start goes stale at the next write elsewhere does not serve it.
A language with a borrow checker can forbid holding such references, at the price of an API that the application must be designed around; every other language — C++, Python, Java — needs these handles for applications that were not.
A list keeps its elements at stable addresses, each element knows its parent and its own index among its siblings, and the list keeps a Fenwick tree of its elements’ sizes.
A reference to an element is then valid until the element is removed, and computes its start when it writes by climbing from the element to the root: at each level, the element’s offset among its siblings, from the Fenwick tree at the element’s index, plus the offset of the list in its parent.
That is O(depth · log m) per write, the cost of handles made together at every level, and a change of size updates the same path back up.

An insertion or a removal renumbers the elements behind it and rebuilds the Fenwick tree, O(m), which is what moving the elements’ pointers in the list’s array costs anyway; finding an element’s index is a load.
An element costs a parent link, an index and a cell of the tree, about 16 bytes, which a document tree whose elements each hold a name, attributes and children affords.
An order-statistics tree with parent links would let an element find its index by climbing, and insert in O(log m), at 24 to 40 bytes per element; it pays only for lists of hundreds of thousands of elements edited in the middle, and can be an option for them.

So a vector and a list differ the way an array and a linked list do in the host language — compact, or stable — and an application chooses per container.
The built-in containers
Their encodings are the specification’s Sequence, Map and Text; what they keep in memory is theirs.

A vector: the count, then the elements; in memory, the elements in an array, and for variable-size elements a Fenwick tree of their sizes.
A push and an insertion are a splice and a count, in one transaction; a removal likewise; a reordering a Move, which writes no element’s bytes; a size change of an element a report that updates the tree, O(log m).
A vector of fixed-size elements needs no tree, so where the host language’s own vector is durable, it serves for them.
A list: encoded as a vector is, with elements at stable addresses, above.
A string: UTF-8, then 0xFF; in memory, the host language’s string, or a rope for long text, which then needs no container of its own, since the file already takes splices in long text at constant cost.
An edit of text is one splice, since text has no count to rewrite.
Setting a whole new text compares it with the old one and splices only the range between their common prefix and their common suffix, as the specification guarantees.
A map: the count, then the entries, each its key and its value; in memory, an index map — the entries in an array, in their order on file, and a hash table of their indices, so that each key is stored once — and for variable-size entries a Fenwick tree of their sizes.
Removal swaps: the last entry moves into the removed one’s place, by a Move that writes no bytes, the removed entry is spliced out, and the count goes down, so the file stays dense, with no tombstones, and the only index that changes in memory is the moved entry’s.
An insertion appends, and a lookup is a hash and an index.
An opaque payload, such as a value serialized by a foreign library: its bytes, prefixed with their length.
Setting a new payload splices the range between the common prefix and suffix of the old and the new bytes, and rewrites the length where it changes, in one transaction; where the changed range lies near the start, it writes the length and the range as one splice.

Removing a value is one splice, whatever it held: there is nothing to free, and nothing can leak.
Moving a value between containers
Moving a value within one container is one Move record and three to six span entries, whatever its size; between containers, cutting the value out and pasting it in costs the same, as long as both happen in one journal.
Every value is its bytes, so restacking a group, reordering a list, or sorting it are Moves inside their container, and moving a subtree to another parent is the question.
Five answers were weighed, and cut and paste within a journal was adopted:

Encode it again: remove the value, and insert its encoding where it goes.
Simple, and the way to insert a value more than once; but the journal and the flush carry all of its bytes.
It stays as the fallback wherever a cut has ended.
A move at a common ancestor: a method on the container that holds both places.
A binding that forbids holding two handles at once, as Rust’s borrows do, would have the ancestor take both paths, which is awkward to type and to derive.
Cut and paste within a transaction: the bytes a record removes stay available until the transaction ends.
It serves a move within one operation, such as dropping a dragged shape into another group, but not an application that removes a value in one transaction and inserts it again in a later one, as undoing a deletion does.
Cut and paste across flushes, through a chain of cuts: the bytes of removed values kept reachable from the header until they are pasted or dropped.
Deleted content would then stay in the file until the application lets go of the values, where a user deleting it expects the file to shrink; bounding the chain would need the store to evict cuts, after which a paste must fall back to encoding anyway.
Cut and paste within a journal, which is adopted: the bytes a record removes stay available as a cut until the journal that holds the record is folded, and a later Paste in the same journal inserts them elsewhere, naming them instead of carrying them.
Nothing goes to the file that would not be there anyway, so deleted content becomes garbage at the next flush, as after any removal.

A cut is a weak promise: pasting it is cheap while its journal lasts, and encodes the value again otherwise.
A container’s cut(i) removes element i as remove(i) does, and returns a cut — the in-memory value, the cut’s number among the cuts of the journal, and the journal it belongs to.
Methods that take a value — a push, an insertion, a field’s set — take a cut too, and move the value into memory.
A cut gives no mutable access to its value, since its bytes must stay the value’s encoding until they are pasted, and it can be pasted at most once.
Dropping it unpasted does nothing more: the value was removed when it was cut.
Any method that splices a value out can return it as a cut: a field’s replacement, an option’s take, or a change of an enum’s variant, for the payload of the old variant.
And an application with references that outlive edits, above, can let a removed element remember its cut, so that inserting the same element again pastes it.
Whether a paste is a Paste or a Splice is decided when its transaction is appended, not when the application calls it.
A flush can land between a cut and its paste — triggered by the paste’s own transaction, which is preceded by a flush when it does not fit in what is left of the journal’s budget — and folding the cut’s journal ends the cut.
So the buffer holds the operation as “paste cut c, or else these bytes”, with the value’s encoding available, and the transaction’s size is computed with the Paste; if the transaction fits, it is appended with the Paste, into the journal that made the cut, and if a flush must come first, the paste is encoded as a Splice of the value’s bytes, the size is computed again, and the flush triggers continue from there.
Two cases need no fallback at all: a cut and its paste in one transaction, which no flush can separate; and the ready run of a batch, which is appended before the flush that cuts the batch.
What it costs: an implementation keeps what it needs to resolve the journal’s cuts until the journal is folded — for the fold, the trees of pieces that the cuts removed — and the length of each cut, to check pastes before they are recorded.
How long a cut lives is how long a journal lives, so an application that flushes often, when idle say, ends its cuts sooner; an undo right after a deletion pastes, and one after the next flush encodes again.
Changing a value between its cut and its paste, say to adjust a shape’s coordinates to its new group, would need records whose positions lie inside a cut rather than in the sequence; it is left out, since pasting first and changing the value then does the same.
Cap’n Proto has the same idea within one message: an orphan is an object disowned by one parent and adopted by another without copying, move-only, and zeroed if nothing adopts it.

impl/write-phase-state.title: Write-phase state
impl/write-phase-state.content:
What an implementation tracks between flushes, and why it is derived from the journal rather than kept alongside it.
The log is the sole authority

It is a totally ordered sequence of every mutation.
Everything else is derived from it and may be discarded and rebuilt.

This is the one structural rule of the write path.
The alternative — a snapshot of the changed content kept beside the log — would have to agree with the log about the order of every change, and the sequence’s positions make order decisive: a splice at position 10 followed by a write at position 20 does something else than the two in the other order, since the splice moves what the write names.
So the flush folds the log, and nothing else, into the new sequence.
Two derived structures
The sequence’s length, as every record recorded so far leaves it, so that bounds checks during the write phase are O(1): a record whose range does not lie inside the sequence is refused before it is recorded, and records nothing.
It also checks the fold: the fold’s sequence must come out exactly this long, a consistency check that costs one comparison per flush.
The cuts of the journal: for each cut, oldest first, its length, whether it was pasted, and which journal it belongs to — the epoch of the journal its record is appended to, or will be — so that a paste can be checked before it is recorded: it must name a cut that is not pasted yet, and its length gives the paste’s.
A flush drops the cuts that the records it folded made; cuts that records past the committed cursor made stay, since those records go to the next journal.
The pastes that may fall back: a paste recorded in one transaction names a cut that an earlier transaction made, and it is a Paste only if it is appended to the journal that made the cut.
So the buffer keeps, beside each such paste, what its Splice would hold — the value’s encoding, or the value to encode it from — until its transaction is appended, when the flush triggers decide which of the two it becomes (cuts).
The fold’s output — the new sequence as runs of committed bytes and new bytes — is built at flush from the log alone, consumed by the mapping onto spans, and dropped; see the fold.
After a flush, and after a rollback
An explicit flush can run while a transaction is still open, with its records buffered past the committed cursor, and an automatic one holds back the transaction that did not fit (flush triggers).
The length covers those records too, so it is right after the flush as it was before; the cuts those records made belong to the next journal, and stay.
A transaction that fails halfway and is rolled back moves the buffer’s end back to where it began, and with it the length and the list of cuts, to what they were at its start.

index.title: kladde
index.content:
Durable data structures: mutate in memory, and it’s on disk.
A cross-language file format and durability protocol with crash-safety guarantees, and libraries for building durable data types on top of it.
Founded and currently maintained by Robert Bamler.
Source on GitHub; all of these pages also as one PDF.
Kladde is becoming a system for durable data structures: containers (strings, vectors, hash maps, trees, …) and user-defined types that behave like their ordinary in-memory counterparts, but whose every mutation is durably recorded to a file as it happens, in a way that is optimized for disk I/O.
Unlike serialization formats like JSON or XML, there is no save step and no serialization pass.
Unlike sqlite, there is no SQL and no object-relational layer.
You open a kladde file containing some value (typically in some complex nested application-defined data type), you mutate some parts of the value in (almost) the same way you would mutate any other value, and each one of your changes is immediately and efficiently applied to the file.
The idea is known as orthogonal persistence: a program works with persistent data exactly as it works with transient data, and data persists by being reachable from a persistent root.
Kladde brings it to existing languages as libraries, as far as each language allows.
Reads never touch the file.
A durable data structure keeps a full, natively-typed in-memory representation, so reading a field or iterating a map costs what it costs in the host language, not what it costs in a database.
Writes go two places at once: into that in-memory representation, and into an append-only on-disk journal that is durable by the time the mutating call returns.
Whenever the journal reaches a threshold size, it is folded into the bulk part of the file, in a way that minimizes I/O and guarantees durability under application crashes and consistency even under power outages.
The bulk part holds the root value’s encoding as one byte sequence, kept on copy-on-write pages as a chain of spans that each show a run of its bytes and name the span that follows.
An edit anywhere — a keystroke in a long text, a shape moved to another group — restates the few spans where it cuts the chain and nothing behind them, so the file stays within a constant factor of its content at a constant cost per edit, however large it grows.
The name is German: a Kladde is a merchant’s rough day-book, where transactions are scribbled down in order as they happen and later transcribed into the clean Hauptbuch.
The file format has exactly that shape.
Project status
The project is still very young and under active development.
At the current stage, the main products are

a detailed file format specification and
a documentation of the reference implementations.

There are two reference implementations, kladde-rs in Rust and kladde-cpp in C++, and neither is production ready.
Their purpose at the moment is to allow rapid experimentation on new policies (non-normative decisions that an implementation may make without breaking interoperability), and to test that the specification is precise enough for two independent implementations to read each other’s files.
This is why the reference implementations are currently limited to these two languages and why they are currently fully auto-generated from the specification.
Contributions are welcome.
While this includes code contributions in principle, at the current stage, the most valuable contributions are not in the form of code but instead in the form of well-motivated opinions and proposals of what should be added or changed in the specification.
If you have a potential use case for a system like kladde and you think that something in its currently stated design would hold you back, then I want to hear your opinion.
Please feel free to describe your situation in a new issue.
The ambition
Kladde is meant to be a cross-language system, not a library for one language.
At the centre sits a language-independent specification of the file format and the schema description — everything all implementations must agree on.
Around it sit implementations for individual languages: kladde-rs first and kladde-cpp second, with kladde-python, kladde-java and others intended to follow.
The contract between them is deliberately narrow and deliberately strict:

A file written by any conforming implementation can be opened by any other conforming implementation, with no conversion step and no special treatment, as long as the opening application implements equivalent data structures.

Everything the specification does not pin down is free to vary, and implementations are expected to differ substantially beyond the normative part (e.g., how aggressively they consolidate free space).
Each language should get an API that is idiomatic for that language rather than a transliteration of the Rust one.
For example, the Rust implementation of kladde needs an explicit Mut type to intercept field assignments; by contrast, a Python implementation of kladde should intercept field assignments via property hooks so that doc.title = "..." simply persists.
Language-independent tooling
A file format that several languages can read is also a file format that tools can read, without knowing anything about the application that wrote it.
A kladde file’s content is one byte sequence, the encoding of the application’s root value with every value inline in its parent, and the file carries the descriptors of its types.
So a generic tool can measure the file’s garbage and compact it without interpreting a byte of application data, report what types the file contains, and decode its whole content from those descriptors to render it as text.
See Tooling for how far each of those goes.
The sections













































sectionwhat it holdswho it is forSpecificationthe normative, language-independent description: what a kladde file is, what invariants it must uphold, and what guarantees an implementation must provideimplementers porting kladde to a new language; tool authorsImplementationthe reference algorithms and data structures — what must be maintained in memory to satisfy the spec, and how — stated in language-agnostic pseudocodeanyone building an implementation in any languagekladde-rseverything specific to the Rust implementation: crate layout, traits, Mut handles, macros, and the Rust-specific half of the algorithmsRust users, and Rust contributorskladde-cppeverything specific to the C++ implementation: its layers, which C++ types are durable, its handles and its error handlingC++ users, and C++ contributorsEvaluationmeasurements of kladde-rs on realistic workloads, what they say about the design, and what porting it to C++ foundanyone judging the design or choosing its constantsSupersededdesigns that were worked out and then rejected, kept for the reasoninganyone tempted to re-propose one of themDraftshalf-baked ideas in progress, not yet held to the separation the other sections observethe authors
The three-way split between spec, impl, and rust is the organising idea, and the test for which one a statement belongs in is:

Could two implementations disagree about it and still read each other’s files? If no, it is spec.
Would a Python or C++ implementation make substantially the same choice? If yes, it is impl.
Otherwise it is rust.
