rust/containers.title: Containers
rust/containers.content:
How kladde-rs realises the built-in containers, and the choices that are Rust’s.
Text and vectors of fixed-size elements are the standard String and Vec<T>, durable in kladde-persist, since they need nothing in memory beyond what the standard types hold.
DurableVec<T>, DurableMap<K, V> and DurableBlob<T> live in kladde-types, since each keeps an index or a serialization of its own in memory.
All of them are hand-implemented against Durable, Mut and Region, not generated.
Everything they use is public, so a third-party library of durable types can do anything they do.
Vec<T> and DurableVec<T>
Vec<T> is durable when T is fixed-size, and DurableVec<T> for every T; DurableVec<T> is the type for elements whose size depends on their value.
Both have the same encoding and the same schema, a Sequence: the count as a varint, then the elements.
Vec<T> finds element i at i times the element’s size after the count, so the standard vector holds everything it needs.
A T whose FIXED_SIZE is None is refused at compile time by a const assertion in Vec<T>’s Durable implementation, whose message names DurableVec<T>.
Its Mut is VecMut, with set, insert, push, remove, pop, clear and get_mut; every insertion and removal is a splice of the element and a rewrite of the count, in one transaction.
DurableVec<T> keeps, in memory, a Vec<T>, and for a T whose FIXED_SIZE is None, a Fenwick tree of the elements’ encoded sizes in 32-bit cells, behind a cached total; for a fixed-size T, element i starts at i times its size after the count, and it keeps no tree.
It adds to Vec<T>’s methods those that a Vec has no room for: delete, move_element, and cuts.
The tree appends and pops in O(log m), answers where element i starts in O(log m), and is built again in O(m) after an insertion, a removal or a reordering elsewhere, beside the O(m) move of the Vec’s elements.
It lies in cells and implements Node, so the element Muts that parts-like accessors make together, or a future split_at_mut, can look their starts up through it while sharing it.

push and insert splice the element in with splice_value and rewrite the count, in one transaction.
pop, remove and delete splice it out and rewrite the count; remove and pop return the value, and delete drops it.
move_element(from, to) records one Move, which writes no element’s bytes.
get_mut(i) makes the element’s region, at the start the tree gives, and the element’s Mut; a change of the element’s size reaches the tree through the region.
set replaces the whole vector.
cut(i), insert_cut and push_cut move an element between vectors as a cut and a paste, below.

T needs only Durable — no Clone, no Serialize — since a Mut method encodes a value into the record while only borrowing it.
The vector reads through Deref<Target = [T]>, so a slice’s whole read API works on it.
The tree’s field takes 40 bytes even where it is empty or the elements are fixed-size: 24 for its Vec and 16 for its cached total and the count’s varint length, which it adds when it answers for Muts made together.
Neither number needs a field — the total can live in the tree’s allocation, and the count’s length is the vector’s to pass in — which would leave the 24 bytes of an empty Vec, or 8 with a thin one.
String
Encoding: Text: UTF-8, then 0xFF.
In memory: the String itself.
Its Mut is StringMut, whose replace_range, push_str, insert_str, truncate and set are each at most one splice, since text has no count to rewrite.
set records only what changed: one splice of the bytes between the longest prefix and the longest suffix that the old and the new text share, or nothing if they are equal.
So code that sets a whole text at every change, such as a path’s data rewritten at every step of a drag, records a few bytes rather than the whole text, at the cost of one pass over both texts.
The comparison is public as kladde_persist::splice_changed, for hand-written Muts of other values that are replaced whole.
Text is UTF-8; a byte buffer is a Vec<u8>.
DurableMap<K, V>
Encoding: a Map, a descriptor kind of its own with a key type and a value type: the count as a varint, then each entry’s key and value, in the map’s order.
In memory: an index map — the entries in a Vec<(K, V)>, in their order on file, and a hash table of their indices, its own, with open addressing over 32-bit positions, probed linearly and at most half full — and for variable-size entries a Fenwick tree of their sizes.

insert appends a new key, or splices a new value over an existing key’s, returning the old one.
remove and delete swap: the last entry moves into the removed one’s place by a Move, the removed entry is spliced out, and the count goes down, all in one transaction; only the moved entry’s index changes in memory.
get_mut hands out a Mut for a value, never for a key: keys are immutable.

Each key is stored once, in the entries, so K: Clone is not required.
DurableBlob<T>
Encoding: an Opaque without a fixed size: the serde payload, prefixed with its length.
Wraps any T: Serialize + DeserializeOwned + Default.
The escape hatch for foreign types that can get neither their own wrapper nor a derive, and deliberately the least attractive option: serialized again in full on every change, opaque to tooling, and the only thing in the workspace that needs a serialization dependency — hence the feature gate.
Its in-place edit is a closure, update(|value| ...), rather than a handle that persists when dropped, since Drop cannot report an error.
set and update record only the bytes of the serialization that changed.
The blob keeps its last serialization, compares the new one with it, and splices in the range between their common prefix and suffix with splice_changed; where the length changes, the rewritten length prefix goes in the same transaction.
Editing one nested field of a large blob then writes little, though how little depends on the serialization: postcard’s varints and length prefixes put a changed byte near the front of everything behind a value that changes size, so the one range that holds every change can reach far.
Cuts
A container’s cut(i) removes element i as remove(i) does, and returns a Cut<T, B>: the in-memory value, and the store’s handle on the removed bytes.
Cutting is an ordinary removal, recorded in a transaction of its own; it holds no transaction open.
A cut is weak: it lives as long as the journal that made it.
A paste while that journal lasts writes none of the value’s bytes, since it records a Paste; a paste after a flush has folded that journal encodes the value again, as an ordinary splice would.
Either way the sequence ends up the same, so a Cut may be held across transactions and flushes, and Cut::is_alive() tells whether a paste would still write none of its bytes.

push_cut and insert_cut take a Cut<T, B>, record the paste, and move the value into memory.
They are methods of their own, rather than push taking either a value or a cut, since one method taking either would need a conversion trait whose two impls Rust’s coherence rules make fragile.
A Cut dereferences to its value but gives no mutable access, since its bytes must stay the value’s encoding until they are pasted.
It is neither Copy nor Clone, and typed by its value’s type, so it is pasted at most once, and a Cut<Fixed<Shape>> cannot go where a Shape goes.
It borrows the store, B = &Store, not the Mut it came from, so the application can drop the source’s Mut and make the destination’s while it holds the cut.
Dropping it unpasted drops the value, which the container removed when it cut it; nothing is recorded, so a drop has no failure to report.

kladde-rs implements cuts on DurableVec only; Vec, the map, fields, Option and enums neither make nor take them yet, though any Mut method that splices a value out could return one.
What is missing
A rope, for large text with cheap lookups by position in memory.
The file already takes splices in long text at constant cost; what a String costs is the O(n) shift of its in-memory bytes.
split_at_mut on the vector, for Muts of two runs of elements at once.
The tree already lies in cells and answers any element’s start, so it would serve as the two runs’ index as it is; it was left out only because nothing measured needs it.

rust/crates.title: Crate layout
rust/crates.content:
The workspace, what depends on what, and where the language-neutral half ends.
The crates





































craterolekladde-storethe storage layer: the file, pages, the span table, the journal, the flush, and consolidation, behind the WriteBackend trait. Type-agnostic; knows nothing about serialization.kladde-persistthe serialization layer: Durable, Bounded, Mut, Region, Encoder and Decoder, the scalars, String, Vec of fixed-size elements, tuples, Option, Box and Fixed, cuts, and the schema binding.kladde-schematype descriptors, their canonical encoding, fingerprints, and the rules of nesting. Depends on nothing but kladde-varint.kladde-varintLEB128 varints and zigzag.kladde-typesthe built-in containers that keep an index or a serialization in memory: DurableVec, DurableMap, DurableBlob. The default collection, not a layer — it uses only the public API any library could.kladde-derivethe #[derive(Durable)] macro, and the #[kladde::dispatch] attribute with which a derived enum stands in for a trait object. Reached through kladde’s derive feature; applications do not depend on it directly.kladdethe application-facing entry point: creating and opening files, the root value, transactions and batches. Re-exports the derive macro and everything a Durable impl names, so an application needs this crate and nothing below it.
Two more crates sit beside them, used by the measurements and nothing else: kladde-svg, an SVG drawing held as a durable value, with svg-bench among its binaries, and kladde-bench, with text-bench; together they drive the evaluation.
A third, kladde-inspect, is a command-line tool that reports where the bytes of any kladde file go, from kladde-store’s inspect module and the file’s own schema.
The dependency direction is strictly downward, and kladde-store deliberately depends on nothing but kladde-varint — it is usable on its own as a persistent store of one byte sequence, independently of anything above it.
graph TD
  APP["<strong>application code</strong>"]
  K["<strong>kladde</strong><br/>Kladde, Transaction, Batch"]
  T["<strong>kladde-types</strong><br/>containers"]
  D["<strong>kladde-derive</strong><br/>derive macro"]
  P["<strong>kladde-persist</strong><br/>Durable, Mut, Region"]
  S["<strong>kladde-schema</strong><br/>descriptors, encoding, fingerprints"]
  V["<strong>kladde-varint</strong><br/>LEB128"]
  H["<strong>kladde-store</strong><br/>Store, journal, span table, pages,<br/>WriteBackend"]
  APP --> K
  APP -. optional but common .-> T
  K --> H
  K --> P
  K -. "derive" feature<br/>(on by default) .-> D
  T --> P
  D --> P
  P --> H
  P --> S
  S --> V
  H --> V

The parts
kladde-store — the storage layer
Owns the file.
It implements everything the implementation notes describe, and adds only what Rust needs: the Backend traits the layer above calls, the Store that implements them, and a Storage trait with two implementations, a real file and a byte vector in memory.
See The store for the Rust-specific half.
kladde-persist — the serialization layer
Where types meet bytes.
Durable and Bounded, the Mut counterpart, Region and the Node a container keeps for its children, the Encoder and Decoder, Cut, and the implementations for scalars, String, Vec of fixed-size elements, tuples, Option, Box and Fixed.
Knows about the store’s WriteBackend; knows nothing about any particular container or derived type.
kladde-schema — type descriptors
The Rust implementation of the language-independent schema model.
It depends on neither the store nor Durable, deliberately, because it must be portable and testable on its own; the binding between a Rust type and its descriptor lives one layer up, in kladde-persist.
See Schema binding.
kladde-types and kladde-derive — the type vocabulary
The built-in containers, and the macro that turns user types into backed ones.
Both build on kladde-persist, and neither depends on the other.
The macro is re-exported from kladde, not from kladde-types, so that an application can use the containers without the macro machinery and vice versa — and because generated code is rooted at ::kladde, which is where the items it names are re-exported from.
kladde — the entry point
Kladde<T> pairs a root value with a Store, and is what application code holds.
It writes the root’s descriptor table and fingerprint into the file at creation, checks the fingerprint at open, and hands out Muts, transactions, and batches.
The seam
For anyone porting kladde, one boundary matters more than the rest.
Below kladde-persist, the design is language-neutral.
The span table, the journal, the flush, the consolidation policy, the schema model, and the encoding of values all translate more or less directly; they are documented in Specification and Implementation rather than here, and so are the regions and the containers’ indexes that Values and their positions describes.
At and above kladde-persist, the design is Rust-specific and should be redone.

Durable/Mut exists because Rust cannot intercept a field assignment.
WriteBackend takes &self because sibling Muts share one backend by reborrow, which Rust’s borrow checker otherwise forbids.
FIXED_SIZE as an associated constant exists because Rust can compute field offsets at compile time.
A language without compile-time constant folding will compute them some other way — probably once per type at startup, which is fine, but it changes the shape of the code.
Bounded is a subtrait so that Fixed<T> fails to compile for a T without a fixed form; another language checks it however its type system allows.

A Python port should keep the storage layer almost verbatim and throw away the Muts entirely, intercepting assignments with property hooks.
A C++ one might use proxy objects with operator=; a Java one might use bytecode enhancement, which is what db4o did.
Cross-cutting concerns
Crash consistency is a property of the journal and the flush, and of the one rule a container must keep: every edit it makes, such as an element and its count, goes into one transaction (ordering); the Muts wrap every mutation in one.
Schema evolution touches the load path, the mutation path, and the flush, because a value read in a foreign schema must not then be written in the native one unless the file is upgraded; see the specification.
Until it exists, a file whose root fingerprint differs from the application’s is refused at open.

rust/derive-macro.title: The derive macro
rust/derive-macro.content:
What #[derive(Durable)] generates, and why.
What it generates
For a struct or enum, four things:

a Durable implementation — FIXED_SIZE, encoded_len, encode, decode, and the schema descriptor;
a Mut type, MyTypeMut, with a _mut() accessor per field, a parts() method handing out a Mut for every field at once, and a whole-value set;
a Deref implementation on the Mut, so read-only methods stay available — and no DerefMut, which would hand out a &mut whose changes no journal record describes;
with #[kladde(bounded)], a Bounded implementation: the fixed form.

#[derive(Durable)]
struct Point { x: f32, label: String, n: u32 }
generates, in essence:
impl Durable for Point {
    const FIXED_SIZE: Option<usize> = sum_sizes(&[f32::FIXED_SIZE, String::FIXED_SIZE, u32::FIXED_SIZE]);
    fn encoded_len(&self) -> usize { self.x.encoded_len() + self.label.encoded_len() + self.n.encoded_len() }
    fn encode(&self, out: &mut Encoder<'_>) { self.x.encode(out); self.label.encode(out); self.n.encode(out) }
    fn decode(input: &mut Decoder<'_>) -> Result<Self, Error> {
        Ok(Point { x: f32::decode(input)?, label: String::decode(input)?, n: u32::decode(input)? })
    }
    // ...
}
 
impl<'r, B: Backend> PointMut<'r, B> {
    fn label_mut(&mut self) -> StringMut<'_, B> {
        let offset = 4;                                  // after `x`, whose size is fixed
        let len = self.inner.label.encoded_len();
        self.inner.label.mutate(self.region.child(offset, len, None, 1))
    }
    fn n_mut(&mut self) -> SetMut<'_, u32, B> {
        let offset = 4 + self.inner.label.encoded_len(); // after a field whose size varies
        let len = self.inner.n.encoded_len();
        self.inner.n.mutate(self.region.child(offset, len, None, 2))
    }
}
A field’s accessor makes a child region at the sum of the sizes of the fields before it: a constant up to the first field whose FIXED_SIZE is None, folded by the compiler, and after that the sum of the earlier fields’ encoded sizes, which the in-memory values give in constant time.
The child region reports a change of the field’s size to the struct’s region, which passes it on up.
parts() makes every field’s Mut at once, from a FieldSizes node it fills with the fields’ sizes: a field after the first variable-size one is indexed, and looks its start up in the node at every write, so that a sibling before it may change size meanwhile (handles made together).
The aggregate records nothing of its own
A struct is its fields’ encodings back to back, so its Mut has nothing of its own to write beyond set.
Every accessor just makes a child region and the field’s own Mut, recursively.
This is why the macro is small: it computes offsets and forwards; all the actual work is in the leaf types.
Fixed forms
#[kladde(bounded)] implements Bounded, the fixed form that Fixed<T> holds: every field’s fixed form, back to back, and for an enum the discriminant at a fixed width and its variant padded with zeros to the largest.
It requires every field’s type to be Bounded, failing at the type’s definition otherwise, with the message #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented] gives, and bounds each type parameter by Bounded, so that a generic type such as Tagged<T> is Bounded where its parameter is.
The derive cannot implement Bounded unasked, exactly where the fields’ types allow it: for a type without parameters, rustc refuses an impl whose where-clause names a concrete type that lacks the trait (E0277) rather than dropping the impl, short of the unstable trivial_bounds.
So the author opts in.
Opting in marks only the types that Fixed wraps and those inside them, none in kladde-svg; opting out would mark every type that holds text, a container or itself, 6 of kladde-svg’s 15 derived types.
Primitives are Durable too
i32, bool, char and friends have implementations, specifically so the macro can treat every field uniformly rather than special-casing leaves.
Those implementations must live in the crate that defines Durable, because impl Durable for i32 is impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType from anywhere else, which the orphan rules forbid; the same reasoning forces the scalar Mut types into that crate.
The same holds for String and Vec<T>, whose Durable implementations live in kladde-persist beside the scalars’.
Enums
An enum is its discriminant as a varint, followed by the selected variant’s fields, each variant encoded like a struct in its own right.
It is fixed-size if every discriminant is below 128 and every variant takes the same fixed size.
The discriminant is Rust’s own: the explicit value where the author wrote one, otherwise one more than the previous variant’s.
In the schema, every variant holds exactly one value, as the Enum descriptor has it, so the derive picks the value’s type by the variant’s shape:

a unit variant holds (), the empty struct;
a variant with one unnamed field holds that field’s type;
any other variant holds an anonymous struct of its fields, named after the variant, its positional fields named by position — "0", "1".

So enum E { R { w: u32, h: u32 } } and enum E { R(Rect) } with struct Rect { w: u32, h: u32 } have the same fingerprint and the same bytes, and moving a variant’s fields into a struct of their own changes nothing on file.
Option’s None holds () too.
The discriminant’s width in the fixed form is as wide as its values need, unless an integer #[repr] fixes it.
#[repr(u8)], u16, u32 or u64 sets the width; without one, it is the smallest of 1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes that holds the largest discriminant value, the widths the Enum descriptor allows.
A signed or pointer-sized repr, and a negative discriminant, do not compile, since descriptors store discriminants unsigned and usize has no fixed width.
Without a repr, the width is a cliff: a 257th variant, or a discriminant of 256 or more, widens every Fixed value of the type; a repr keeps the fixed form’s size when variants are added.
The Mut’s parts() hands out the Muts of the current variant’s fields, as a generated enum {Enum}Parts with the same variants, so a field is mutated in place by matching:
match shape_mut.parts() {
    ShapeParts::Circle(mut radius) => radius.set(2)?,
    ShapeParts::Rectangle { mut width, .. } => width.set(3)?,
    ShapeParts::Origin => {}
}
Each field’s Mut is based at the field’s offset past the discriminant’s varint and writes inside its field only, so the discriminant cannot change underneath it.
And parts() borrows the enum’s Mut, so set cannot switch the variant while a field’s Mut is alive.
set is how the variant changes: it splices the new value’s encoding over the old one’s.
parts() on a temporary Mut works in a match but not in a let … else, which drops the temporary at the end of the statement; a consuming into_parts(self) would make the let form work too, and is proposed rather than built.
An enum without any fields gets no parts(), since it has nothing to mutate in place.
Trait objects, as an enum
A file can hold only values whose types it can name, so where an application would hold a Box<dyn Shape>, it holds an enum of the shapes, which implements Shape by forwarding every method to its current variant.
The trait is marked #[kladde::dispatch], and the enum #[kladde(dispatch(Shape))] beside #[derive(Durable)]; every variant holds one value, of a type that implements the trait.
The derive also implements From for every variant’s type, and for the T of a variant that holds a Box<T>, so AnyShape::from(Circle { .. }) builds the right variant.
On file the enum is an ordinary enum, with a variant per implementation, so the schema needs nothing new, and a C++ or Python implementation reads it as it reads any enum.
A variant may hold its value in a Box, to keep a large variant from making every value of the enum large in memory: a box is persisted as what it holds, its Mut is the Mut of what it holds, and it is Bounded where what it holds is, so boxing or unboxing a variant changes neither the file nor the fingerprint.
Why an enum rather than Box<dyn Trait> itself.
Rust cannot list a trait’s implementations, so the variants have to be listed somewhere, and an enum is the list Rust already checks: two variants with the same explicit discriminant fail to compile (E0081), and a variant’s type that does not implement the trait fails at the enum.
A reader has to know every variant to decode a file, so the openness of dyn would buy nothing on file; collecting implementations from several crates at link time would make the fingerprint depend on which crates a binary linked.
And Durable cannot be used through dyn — it requires Sized, has associated constants and a generic Mut, and decode returns Self — so a durable Box<dyn Shape> would need a helper trait, a table of decoders, and Muts reached by downcasting, where the enum gets parts() and an exhaustive match.
The enum is also faster, with no vtable and no allocation per value.
How the two macros meet.
A derive sees only the enum, never the trait’s methods, so #[kladde::dispatch] emits, beside the unchanged trait, a hidden macro_rules! macro, __kladde_dispatch_Shape, that knows the methods and writes the forwarding impl for an enum it is handed; it re-exports it next to the trait with pub(crate) use.
The derive invokes it by the trait’s path, with the trait’s module path and the macro’s name in place of the trait’s, so the enum may be in any module, before or after the trait.
For each variant it passes the pattern binding the held value, the value’s type, and how to reach the value by reference, by mutable reference and by value, through the box for a variant that holds one; and the impl’s where clause, with a bound of the trait on each variant’s type, spanned at that type, so that a missing implementation is reported at the enum, and a generic enum gets the bounds it needs.
This is the pattern of the ambassador crate; enum_dispatch instead passes the trait’s tokens through global state between the two macros, which depends on the order rustc expands them in.
What it forwards.
Every method of the trait, defaulted ones included, so that a variant’s own implementation wins: methods taking self, &self or &mut self, generic ones, async ones, unsafe ones, and ones with impl Trait arguments.
It refuses, at the trait, what it cannot forward: a method without a receiver, which no enum could choose a variant for; one that takes Self other than as its receiver, or returns Self or impl Trait, since each variant would bring or return a type of its own; and associated types and constants, which each variant may choose differently, and generic traits.
A variant’s type that two variants hold gets no From, nor does one that mentions a type parameter, since From<T> would overlap with every other variant’s.
Limitations.
The trait and the enum must be in one crate: a macro_rules! macro can be public only through #[macro_export], which puts it at the crate root, where a macro-expanded one may not be named by path from its own crate.
A box is recognized by its spelling, Box<T>, std::boxed::Box<T> or alloc::boxed::Box<T>, so a variant holding a box behind a type alias forwards to the box itself, which then has to implement the trait.
Generics and transparency
Type parameters are supported: each gets a Durable bound, the heuristic #[derive(Debug)] uses.
Lifetime and const parameters are rejected.
#[kladde(transparent)] on a single-field struct persists it exactly as its field — same bytes, same descriptor, same fingerprint — and gives its Mut one get_mut() returning the field’s Mut, as #[serde(transparent)] does.
Path resolution
Generated code names items by absolute path, because a macro cannot know what the user called their imports.
It roots them at ::kladde, and kladde re-exports every item generated code or a hand-written impl names, so an application depends on kladde and nothing below it.
That matters for more than convenience: if the facade did not re-export them, an author would add kladde-persist themselves, and a version that disagreed with the facade’s would produce two distinct copies of the Durable trait and an error that prints the expected and found types identically.
A library built directly on kladde-persist has no reason to pull the facade in, and redirects the macro instead, as serde’s #[serde(crate = "...")] does:
#[derive(Durable)]
#[kladde(crate = "kladde_persist")]
struct Node { /* ... */ }
What is missing
Field attributes.
There is no #[kladde(skip)] for a non-persisted field, no #[kladde(id = ...)] for rename-robust identity, and no way to declare a default for a field added later.
The last two become necessary when evolution lands.
Two more, modeled on serde’s, would serve types the derive cannot handle today:

#[kladde(with = "path")] on a field of a type that is not Durable, a foreign one or one wanting an encoding of its own, delegating its encoding, descriptor and Mut to a module of functions, so that a foreign type can be encoded inline with a real descriptor rather than wrapped in a DurableBlob.
#[kladde(bound = "...")] on the type, overriding the Durable bound the derive puts on every type parameter, for a parameter used only in PhantomData, or only inside a wrapper that needs a different bound.

Const generic parameters, which the derive rejects today.
Conveniences on Muts: set_<field>(value) on a struct’s Mut, sparing the step through the field’s accessor, and field_{i}_mut() on a tuple’s Mut, which offers only parts() and set, as tuple structs’ Muts offer it.
A tuple’s accessors cannot be generated by macro_rules! without a crate such as paste to build their names.
Testing compile failures
The macro’s compile errors are part of its contract — a field of a type that is not Durable, such as a PathBuf, must fail to compile, and that is the mechanism preventing silent data loss.
These are tested with rustdoc compile_fail doctests rather than a separate harness, which keeps the expected-failure cases next to the documentation that explains them.

rust/durable-and-mut.title: Durable and Mut
rust/durable-and-mut.content:
The central traits, why mutation needs a Mut, and why it returns a Result.
A data type encodes, decodes, and mutates its region; it never allocates, frees, or knows a position.
Durable
pub trait Durable: Sized {
    /// `Some(n)` if every value encodes to `n` bytes.
    const FIXED_SIZE: Option<usize>;
 
    fn encoded_len(&self) -> usize;
    fn encode(&self, out: &mut Encoder<'_>);
    fn decode(input: &mut Decoder<'_>) -> Result<Self, Error>;
 
    type Mut<'r, B: Backend + 'r>: Mut where Self: 'r;
    fn mutate<'r, B: Backend + 'r>(&'r mut self, region: Region<'r, B>) -> Self::Mut<'r, B>;
 
    fn describe_local(builder: &mut SchemaBuilder) -> TypeDescriptor;
}
 
/// A type with a fixed form, which `Fixed<Self>` holds.
#[diagnostic::on_unimplemented(message = "`{Self}` has no fixed form", /* ... */)]
pub trait Bounded: Durable {
    const FIXED_FORM_SIZE: usize;
    fn encode_fixed(&self, out: &mut Encoder<'_>);
    fn decode_fixed(input: &mut Decoder<'_>) -> Result<Self, Error>;
}
 
pub struct Fixed<T: Bounded>(pub T);
A Durable is a plain, in-memory value that has the right shape to be persisted, but is not itself tied to any backend.
Reading it is ordinary reading.
Besides describe_local, the trait offers to_bytes, from_bytes, describe, schema and fingerprint, with defaults.
FIXED_SIZE
Some(n) if every value encodes to n bytes, as the specification has it, and None otherwise.
A DurableVec decides by it whether to keep an index of where its elements start, a plain Vec<T> is durable only where it is Some (a const assertion refuses any other T at compile time), and the derive decides by it whether a field after another has a constant offset.
It stays an Option on Durable, rather than a subtrait, because a vector branches on it at compile time, which a subtrait could support only with specialization.
A Box<T>’s FIXED_SIZE is None whatever T’s: a type that holds itself through a box would otherwise ask its own size of itself while the compiler evaluates it, which rustc refuses as a cycle (E0391) rather than reading it as “not fixed-size”.
The derive cannot tell a recursive type from the tokens of one type, and a box is the one indirection among kladde’s types that could pass a fixed size on, so answering None there cuts every cycle; a vector of boxes then keeps an index it could do without, and nothing on file changes.
encode and decode
encode appends the value’s encoding to an Encoder, and decode reads it from a Decoder; they differ because writing goes into one buffer, while reading crosses spans.
An Encoder appends to a buffer it borrows and offers varints, zigzag, and UTF-8 with its terminator; a value is encoded once per record, into the value’s own buffer, which the store then copies into the record — a copy a store method taking an encoding closure would save.
A Decoder reads the sequence from the mirror through the rope, across span boundaries, without copying, refuses an encoding that is not canonical, and says where a decode failed.
encoded_len takes constant time for every type of the workspace: containers cache their total.
Bounded and Fixed<T>
Fixed<T> holds T’s values in their fixed form, which a subtrait, Bounded, states, so that no method panics for a type without one, and Fixed<String> fails to compile where it is written, with a message that names the fix.
The scalars, Fixed, and the Options, Boxes and tuples of Bounded types are Bounded, and a derived type is if it is marked #[kladde(bounded)] (the derive).
A Box<T> takes T’s fixed form, as it takes T’s encoding and descriptor, so boxing a field keeps Fixed of what holds it.
Its conditional impl never meets the cycle that its FIXED_SIZE cuts, since a recursive type is never Bounded; a recursive type marked #[kladde(bounded)] fails to compile, though with rustc’s cycle error (E0391) rather than kladde’s message.
A type with a fixed size and no fixed form is possible, and harmless, since nothing can wrap it in Fixed.
FIXED_FORM_SIZE is the bound on a value’s size that Fixed<T> needs, so Durable declares no other maximum: Fixed<T> stores the fixed form, every integer at its full width, rather than T’s encoding padded to its longest, in which a field would move whenever a varint before it grew.
A fixed-size type’s fixed form is its encoding byte for byte, except where an enum’s integer #[repr] sets a discriminant wider than the one byte its encoding takes: #[repr(u32)] enum Pinned { A, B } has FIXED_SIZE 1 and FIXED_FORM_SIZE 4.
The Mut of a Fixed<T> replaces the value whole, an overwrite of its fixed size, since a Mut of one of T’s fields would have to write that field in its fixed form, which would take a second Mut for every type.
That is visible to the caller: the Mut offers set(Fixed<T>) and reading, and no Mut of a field of T.
Regions
pub trait Backend: WriteBackend + Copy {}   // any `WriteBackend` that is `Copy`, such as `&Store`
pub struct Region<'r, B> { /* the backend, and where the value starts and how long it is */ }
A region is the value’s substring of the sequence, as the reference algorithms describe it: len(), write(at, bytes), splice(at, removed, bytes), splice_value(at, removed, &value), move_bytes(from, len, to), paste(at, removed, cut, bytes), transaction(f), and child(at, len, node, index).
paste takes the value’s encoding along with the cut, and writes it only if a flush has folded the journal that made the cut.
Backend is any WriteBackend that is Copy, so that a Mut hands its backend to its children and to a cut by value.
A region’s start is one of three things: the root’s, an offset from an anchor region that is constant while the region lives, or indexed — looked up in its parent’s Node at every write, for a region made together with its siblings.
When a region changes size, it tells the Node it was made from, which updates where the children behind it start, and its parent’s region, which tells its own parent in turn; lengths and indexes sit in Cells, so that regions made together, which share their parent by shared reference, can report through it.
transaction(f) poisons the store if f fails, since the regions around may have heard of a size change by then; a Mut checks what can fail before it opens one.
A child made on its own borrows its parent region mutably, so the parent cannot write while the child exists, and no sibling can move it.
Mut
pub trait Mut {
    type Durable;
    fn as_durable(&self) -> &Self::Durable;
}
A Mut borrows the value and its region for a lifetime, and stands where Rust’s &mut T would: Durable::mutate hands it out as get_mut hands out a &mut T, and Kladde::get_mut is its entry point.
It is an RAII token proving exclusive, recording access.
A Mut’s Durable need not be Self, since a Box<T> uses T’s Mut.
Every mutating method on a Mut does two things: it records the mutation through its region, and it mutates the in-memory value.
Mutating methods never return anything for the caller to separately apply.
Persistence is not optional or forgettable by construction.
Non-mutating access uses the plain value; Muts implement Deref, and not DerefMut, which would let point_mut.x = value compile and persist nothing.
Scalars, and anything whose Mut offers only a whole-value set, use the generic SetMut.
Mutations return a Result
A mutation is durable once it returns, which it can promise only because it appends to the journal before returning — and an append is I/O, which can fail.
So every mutating method returns Result<_, Error>, and the order inside it is fixed: record first, then mutate memory.
A mutation that fails leaves the in-memory value as it was, and records nothing; a mutation of several records is one transaction, appended whole or not at all.
A failed fsync ends the session, so after one the store is poisoned: every later call returns Error::Poisoned, and the application drops the Kladde and reopens the file, which then holds every mutation that returned Ok.
Muts are generated per type
Not one shared generic wrapper, and the reason is Rust’s orphan rules.
A single Mut<T, B> struct defined in the persistence crate would be a foreign type from any downstream crate’s point of view, and Rust forbids inherent impl blocks on foreign types, regardless of what their parameters are filled with.
So a library author could not write ordinary methods on their own Mut.
Per-type generation means MyTypeMut is local to the crate that declared MyType, and ordinary impl blocks just work.
Why an automatic flush cannot tear a mutation
The store flushes by itself whenever a mutation would not fit in what is left of its journal’s budget, and it does so from inside the mutating call that closed it — while a Mut is alive.
That is safe for two reasons, one per layer.
The flush touches no Durable value and moves no position.
It folds journal records into pages; it never reads or writes an in-memory value, and positions in the sequence, which Muts hold, mean the same after it.
A flush lands only on a transaction boundary.
It runs between appends, and every append is a whole transaction, so every state a flush commits is a valid sequence.
The chain, end to end
notes.get_mut()            // NotesMut  — the root's region: the whole sequence
     .lines_mut()          // DurableVecMut — a child region, after the title
     .push(value)?;        // splices the element and the count, then mutates memory
Each _mut() makes a child region from its parent’s, at the field’s offset, and reborrows the same backend.
The caller supplies a backend exactly once, at the outermost Mut.
What this costs

Verbosity. x.get_mut().field_mut().set(v)? where other languages write x.field = v.
Borrow contention. A Mut borrows the root, so nothing else can touch the structure while it lives.
Partial borrows only through parts(). Muts of two fields at once come from parts(), which looks each field’s start up at every write; there is no split_at_mut for a vector yet.

rust/index.title: kladde-rs
rust/index.content:
The Rust implementation of kladde: one of the two reference implementations of the specification, with kladde-cpp in C++.
Everything here is specific to Rust and should be expected to differ in a port.
The file format and the algorithms are shared; the trait shapes, the mutation-capture mechanism, the macros, and the memory layout are not.
Two audiences
If you want to use kladde in an application, start with the tutorial.
It assumes you know Rust and nothing about kladde, and works up from a first program to writing your own durable types.
If you want to work on kladde, or port it, read the specification and implementation notes first — they carry the parts that are not about Rust — and come back here for the rest.
What it is
A Rust workspace providing durable data structures: containers and derived types whose mutations are recorded durably as they happen.

use kladde::Kladde;
use kladde::Durable;
use kladde_types::DurableVec;
 
#[derive(Durable)]
struct Notes {
    title: String,
    lines: DurableVec<String>,
}
 
let mut notes = Kladde::new(Notes {
    title: String::from("today"),
    lines: DurableVec::new(),
});
 
notes.get_mut().lines_mut().push(String::from("wrote a doc"))?;
The push updates the in-memory vector and appends the change to the journal before it returns.
There is no save call.
Kladde::new keeps its file in memory, which suits examples and tests; Kladde::create and Kladde::open do the same on a real file.
The central problem
Rust has no way to intercept a field assignment.
Every comparable system relies on exactly such a hook: Python has __setattr__, Smalltalk has message dispatch, Swift has property wrappers.
Those systems make persistence syntactically invisible — self.foo = bar just works — because the language hands them a place to stand.
Rust hands them nothing.
So kladde-rs makes the recording point explicit and unforgeable instead: the only mutating API is the one that records, and it is reached through a Mut.
Everything idiosyncratic about this layer follows from that one constraint, and it is the single largest thing a port should expect to redesign.
A Python implementation should use property hooks and have no Muts at all.
The documents









































documentcontentsCrate layoutthe workspace, the dependency direction, and where the seam fallsDurable and Mutthe central traits, regions, Fixed, why mutation needs a Mut, and why it returns a ResultContainershow the built-in containers are encoded and indexed, and cutsThe derive macrowhat it generates, fixed forms, enums in place of trait objects, and why Muts are generated per typeTransactionsthe RAII types, and what happens on unwindSchema bindinghow a Rust type declares its descriptor, and the check at openThe storethe Rust-specific half of the storage layer: interior mutability, I/O, and the in-memory structuresTutorialfor application authors
Status
A prototype of the whole design exists; nothing is frozen.
Where the implementation departs from the reference algorithms, or found them unclear, its implementation notes say so.

rust/schema-binding.title: Schema binding
rust/schema-binding.content:
The Rust binding of the language-independent schema model, and the check it performs at open.
Two layers
The split is deliberate and worth preserving in a port.
kladde-schema — the model.
The descriptor types, the canonical encoding, the fingerprint computation, and a SHA-256 implementation.
It has no connection to the store, to Durable, or to any Rust type system machinery, which is what makes it portable and testable on its own: the conformance vectors for encoding and fingerprints exercise this layer and nothing else.
The binding — where Rust types meet the model.
A Durable type declares its own descriptor in describe_local, and the derive macro generates that declaration.
The binding
A type contributes its descriptor by describing itself into a SchemaBuilder, which interns descriptors into a table and hands back references:

Recursion terminates.
A type that refers to itself reserves its table slot, keyed by its TypeId, before describing its fields.
Descriptors are deduplicated by type, so a type used in twenty places occupies one table entry.
The table is built once, not per value.

What a type declares
A struct declares a Struct descriptor with its fields in declaration order; an enum declares an Enum with its variants canonically ordered by discriminant.
A hand-written implementation declares whatever descriptor matches the bytes it actually reads and writes — which is the rule that most often trips people up.
A hand-written implementation of a plain field-sum declares Struct, not Opaque; “hand-written” and “opaque” are different axes, see the guiding principle.
The containers declare structural descriptors, so that a tool can decode them: a Vec<T> and a DurableVec<T> alike a Sequence of the element type, a String Text, and a map a Map of its key type and its value type.
An enum’s variant holds one payload: (), the empty struct, for a unit variant, the field’s type for a variant of one unnamed field, and otherwise an anonymous struct of its fields named after the variant (the derive).
Option<T> declares an enum Option with a one-byte discriminant width, None = 0 holding () and Some = 1 holding a T; a tuple a struct TupleN with positional fields; Fixed<T> a Fixed of T’s descriptor; and Box<T> is schema-transparent, reusing T’s descriptor, as #[kladde(transparent)] types do.
Only DurableBlob declares Opaque, without a fixed size, since its serde payload is not decomposable.
At create and at open
Kladde::create encodes the root type’s descriptor table into the schema chain, which the header’s schema_head names, and writes the root’s fingerprint into the header.
Kladde::open compares the header’s fingerprint with the application’s and fails closed on a mismatch, with an error carrying both fingerprints.
It never parses the descriptor table on the matching path, which is the fast path the fingerprint exists for.
Resolution — decoding by the writer’s descriptors — does not exist yet, so a mismatch cannot be bridged; see Evolution.
Design invariants
Worth keeping in mind when changing anything here:

The fingerprint must not depend on table layout.
References are encoded structurally, so any renumbering or reordering produces the same hash; a test permutes the table and asserts equality.
A type’s own name is not fingerprinted; its fields’ and variants’ names are.
Determinism over everything.
No hash-map iteration order, no addresses, nothing incidental may reach the hash.
Encoding and fingerprinting are separate functions over the same model.
They share the canonical order but not the code, because the fingerprint deliberately omits things the encoding includes.

rust/store.title: The store
rust/store.content:
The Rust-specific half of the storage layer: interior mutability, file I/O, and the concrete types of the in-memory structures.
None of this changes what the structures mean; it is about realising them in Rust without making them awkward.
The interface
kladde-store is a persistent store of one byte sequence, usable on its own: Store implements WriteBackend, whose methods are the journal’s records — write, splice, move_range and paste — and the transaction calls, plus len.
write and splice return the cut of what they removed, an Option<CutId>, and splice records a Write wherever the lengths agree.
A cut lives as long as the journal that made it: is_alive says whether that journal is still unfolded, and paste takes the cut’s bytes along with it, which it records as a Paste while the cut lives and as an ordinary splice of those bytes after.
Store::flush, flush_if_journal_exceeds, read_all, schema and set_schema, private and set_private, and stats complete it; the schema and private chains are byte strings the next flush writes.
Interior mutability
Store keeps all of its state behind one RefCell, and borrows it for the length of one call.
WriteBackend’s methods take &self so that sibling Muts can share a backend, which forces interior mutability somewhere, and one cell is enough: no store method calls out into user code, so no borrow is ever held across a callback, and a single dynamic borrow per call costs nothing measurable next to the journal append it guards.
The one reentrant path is the automatic flush, which runs inside the mutating call whose transaction would not fit in what is left of the journal’s budget.
It runs after that call’s own borrow has ended, and takes the cell again for itself.
Store is therefore Send but not Sync, which matches the single-writer scope of the format.
Storage
The store reads and writes pages through a Storage trait with two implementations.
FileStorage is a std::fs::File driven by positional reads and writes, so no call depends on a shared file cursor, and synced with sync_data, which covers the file-size change a growth makes.
It extends the file with set_len, since the standard library offers no fallocate, and that is the ungraceful form of detecting a full disk: a disk that fills up surfaces at the flush’s fsync, which ends the session, rather than as an error the flush could return.
MemoryStorage is a byte vector, used by Kladde::new and by tests.
It also keeps the image as of the last sync apart from the writes since, so a test can simulate a power cut by discarding any subset of those writes and opening what is left — the flush-interruption test the conformance suite calls for.
The mirror
Table pages stay resident as the reference algorithms recommend, each a boxed page-sized array keyed by page number.
Data pages are read into a mirror while a file is opened, in page order, and dropped once the sequence is decoded; a flush that needs a span’s bytes again, to move, merge or rewrite it, reads them from the file through a small cache.
The in-memory structures
The span table
A Vec<Span> indexed by span id, of 48 bytes per span rather than the 16 the reference algorithms count, since each record also holds what the store keeps beside the span table in the language-agnostic design: the span’s chain, its rope node, its heat, its entry’s size and its place in its table page, and its place in its data page’s reverse list.
A bitmap of used ids beside it serves the id allocator, which hands out the id after the predecessor’s, if it is free, and the lowest free id otherwise — which keeps the spans a flush makes one after another consecutive without looking for a run.
The treap
The rope is an implicit treap, not a counted B-tree: a randomized binary tree in an arena of nodes, each knowing its parent and the total length below it, O(log k) expected steps per operation and 40 bytes per node.
It is there for ease of implementation: a split at a position and a join of two trees are all that the rope, the fold’s piece table and the journal’s cuts need, so one arena type of under 400 lines serves all three, while splitting and joining whole B-trees at a position is the intricate part of a counted B-tree.
Its priorities come from a seeded generator, so runs reproduce.
With the treap’s node, a span costs about 90 bytes in memory, against the 32 of the reference algorithms; for the files measured that is a fraction of a megabyte, and a B-tree is the better choice once memory per span matters.
Maps keyed by id or page
Sets and maps keyed by span id or page number use a multiplicative hasher rather than std’s SipHash, whose protection against HashDoS a map built from the file does not need.
The page table is a Vec of an enum over the page states, indexed by page number, since lowest-first placement keeps page numbers dense; only a live page has an epoch and a victim bucket.
The journal buffer
Every record since the last flush lives in one VecDeque<Record> beside a byte arena, also a VecDeque, that holds their payloads, with positions counted from the start of the session (one buffer and three cursors).
A record holds absolute positions in memory and is delta-encoded only when it is appended.
Where the integer widths come from
Every width below is forced by the specification’s bounds, not chosen:








































quantitywidthbecausespan idu32span ids are 32-bit, and 0 means nonespan lengthu32a Zero span may be up to 2^32 − 1 bytespage offsetu16page sizes are at most 64 KiBpage numberu32page numbers are 32-bitposition in the sequenceu64the sequence is shorter than 2^48 bytesa size in a container’s indexu32four bytes per element; a sum of 4 GiB or more panics today, where it should fail cleanly (implementation notes)

rust/transactions.title: Transactions
rust/transactions.content:
The Rust surface over the transaction and batch machinery: RAII types, and what happens when a panic unwinds through one.
RAII types
The store’s begin_transaction, end_transaction, begin_batch and end_batch are private, because they are dangerous: it is very easy to forget an end call, which prevents every subsequent mutation from ever being persisted.
The public API provides them through RAII types instead:

Kladde::transaction() returns a Transaction, and Transaction::commit(self) ends it;
Kladde::batch() returns a Batch, and Batch::end(self) ends it;
Batch::transaction() opens a transaction inside the batch — the nesting the design is arranged around.

Each offers get_mut(), so mutations go through the scope rather than around it, and commit and end return a Result, since ending a scope appends to the journal.
Because the scope object borrows the Kladde mutably and an inner scope borrows the outer one, a scope cannot be ended while a scope nested inside it is still open: the interleaving errors of the state table do not compile.
Dropping a scope without ending it ends it, and a failure to end it there — where no error can be returned — poisons the store, since the in-memory mutations have then already happened and the journal does not hold them.
There is no Transaction::cancel.
Cancelling the transaction’s effect on the file would be possible, but its effects on the in-memory representation are always immediate, and redoing them would mean reloading the entire affected value from the file.
Behaviour on unwind
Drop branches on std::thread::panicking(), because the two scopes differ:

Batch: end normally, no poisoning.
Every transaction boundary inside the batch was, by the ordering discipline, a valid state.
Committing the completed ones loses nothing, and discarding them would throw away durability the application already believes it has.
Transaction: discard the in-flight operations and poison the store.
Committing a half-built transaction would persist exactly the invalid intermediate state that transactions exist to prevent.
But not committing leaves the file and the in-memory representation disagreeing, for the same reason there is no cancel, and poisoning is what stops that divergence from being silently observable.

“Poisoned” means every subsequent store call returns an error, not panic — panicking during unwind aborts the process.
Recovery is to drop the Kladde and reopen the file, which then holds the last completed transaction.
So a panic loses the in-flight transaction, a crash loses the in-flight transaction, and both leave the file at the last valid state.
Open questions

Is a long-lived batch a footgun?
Batches delay persistence until they are ended, so holding one across a long computation quietly defeats kladde’s main feature.
Whether the API makes that tempting in common usage patterns is worth checking before it is frozen.

rust/tutorial/comparison-to-serde.title: Compared to serde
rust/tutorial/comparison-to-serde.content:
The most common question about kladde is how it relates to serde.
The short answer: they solve different problems and compose badly, and if you are choosing between them you are probably choosing between “exchange” and “storage.”
The core difference
Serde serializes a value.
You call to_vec(&value), you get bytes, you write them somewhere.
The cost is proportional to the size of the whole value, every time.
Kladde stores a structure and records changes to it.
You mutate it, and the cost is proportional to the size of the change.
For a 100 MB structure with a one-field edit:






























serdekladdecost of one small editrewrite 100 MBappend tens of bytescost of a readfree (already in memory)free (already in memory)cost of openingparse 100 MBread the compact form, replay the journalcrash mid-editlose everything since the last writelose nothing acknowledged
The interesting column is the first one, and it is the whole reason kladde exists.
What serde does better
Interchange.
Serde targets many formats — JSON, MessagePack, CBOR, YAML — and other systems can read them.
A kladde file is a heap with an embedded schema.
Another kladde implementation can read it; nothing else can.
Type coverage.
Serde works on essentially any Rust type, including String, Vec<T>, HashMap, and third-party types with derives.
Kladde takes String and a Vec of fixed-size elements as they are, but needs its own container types for maps and for vectors of anything else.
Maturity.
Serde is one of the most-used crates in the ecosystem.
Kladde is early.
Zero setup.
#[derive(Serialize)] and you are done.
Kladde asks you to restructure your types around durable containers.
What kladde does better
Incremental durability.
The one thing serde structurally cannot do.
There is no serde-based design where a small edit to a large structure costs less than rewriting the structure, short of building an incremental format yourself — which is what kladde is.
Crash safety with no explicit save.
With serde you choose when to write, and everything since the last write is at risk.
With kladde, a mutation that has returned is durable.
In-place mutation of stored data.
A kladde file is randomly addressable and mutable.
A serde document is a byte stream you rewrite.
Language-independent tooling.
A kladde file carries its own schema, so a generic tool can inspect and even compact it.
A postcard blob is opaque without the writing program.
They are not exclusive
DurableBlob<T> wraps any serde type as an opaque payload inside a kladde structure.
This is the right escape hatch for a foreign type you cannot change, and the wrong default for anything else: a blob is serialized again in full on every change, so each edit costs time in proportion to the blob’s size, the very cost you came to kladde to avoid, even though only the bytes that changed reach the file.
Use it at the leaves, for things that change rarely.
Choosing
Use serde when the data leaves your process: config files people edit, API payloads, anything another program reads.
Use kladde when the data is your application’s state: it lives across runs, it is large relative to each change, and losing it to a crash is unacceptable.
Use both when your state is mostly kladde-shaped but contains a few foreign leaves.
An honest caveat
Serde is a safe default and kladde is not yet.
If your structure is small enough that rewriting it is cheap — under a few megabytes, say, edited a few times a second — serde is simpler, better tested, and fast enough.
Kladde starts winning when rewriting starts hurting.

rust/tutorial/containers.title: The built-in containers
rust/tutorial/containers.content:
Kladde has durable text, two vectors, a map and a blob.
Text and vectors of fixed-size elements are the standard String and Vec<T>, durable as they are, since they need nothing beyond what the standard types hold.
kladde-types provides the other three, DurableVec<T>, DurableMap<K, V> and DurableBlob<T>, since each keeps an index or a serialization of its own in memory.
Every container’s content lies inline in the file’s one sequence of bytes, wherever its value lies, so a short list costs no more on file than its elements and its count.
A default library, not a privileged one
kladde-types is not part of the machinery, and nothing depends on it.
It is a collection of types most applications turn out to want, offered so that you do not have to write them yourself.
Everything in it is built on the same public Durable/Mut surface available to any crate.
There is no internal kladde magic here that a third-party library — or your own application — could not use equally well, and third-party libraries of general-purpose durable types are welcome.
String
Growable text.

let mut owner = journal_mut.owner_mut();
owner.set("ada")?;
owner.push_str(" lovelace")?;
On file, the text’s UTF-8 bytes and then the byte 0xFF, which UTF-8 never contains; in memory, the String itself.
Text states no count, so every edit — push_str, insert_str, replace_range, truncate — is one splice of the file’s sequence, wherever it lands and however long the text is.
set records only what changed: it compares the new text with the old one and splices in the bytes between their common prefix and suffix, or nothing if they are equal.
So you may set a whole text at every change — a path’s data rewritten at every step of a drag, say — and the file records a few bytes rather than the whole text.
Text is UTF-8; for a byte buffer, use a Vec<u8>.
Vec<T> and DurableVec<T>
A growable sequence, in two types with the same encoding: Vec<T> for elements of a fixed size, and DurableVec<T> for any.
A Vec<T> is durable when every value of T encodes to the same number of bytes — u8, f32, a tuple or struct of them, or Fixed<T> — since then it finds element i by multiplication.
For any other T, such as String, using a Vec<T> as a durable value fails to compile, and the message names DurableVec<T>:

#[derive(Durable)]
struct Journal {
    entries: Vec<String>,  // a `Vec<T>` is durable only for a fixed-size `T`
}
DurableVec<T> takes any Durable T, and nothing more — no Clone, no Serialize — and adds cutting and reordering:

let mut journal_mut = journal.get_mut();
let mut v = journal_mut.entries_mut();
v.push(String::from("a"))?;
v.insert(0, String::from("b"))?;
v.get_mut(1).unwrap().push_str("c")?;  // the `Mut` of one element
let first = v.remove(0)?;   // yours now, as a plain value
v.push(first)?;             // encoded again, at the end
let moved = v.cut(0)?;      // removed, its bytes kept for a paste
v.push_cut(moved)?;         // pasted at the end, without writing its bytes again
v.move_element(0, 1)?;      // reordered, without writing an element's bytes
v.delete(0)?;               // removed and dropped
A Vec<T>’s Mut offers the methods they share: set, insert, push, remove, pop, clear and get_mut.
Reading needs no Mut: both dereference to [T], so len, indexing and iter work on the in-memory elements.
Encoding. The number of elements as a varint, then the elements, back to back; a Vec<T> and a DurableVec<T> of the same elements have the same bytes and the same schema.
In memory, a DurableVec<T> of elements whose size depends on their value keeps a Fenwick tree of their sizes beside its Vec<T>, four bytes per element, so that the Mut of element i finds where it starts in O(log m); for fixed-size elements it keeps no tree.
Cost. A push, an insertion and a removal are each a splice of the element plus a rewrite of the count, in one transaction; a change of an element’s size is a splice inside it; and move_element writes no element’s bytes at all.
None of them rewrites the elements behind it: the file records where its bytes lie as linked runs, so bytes that shift are not restated.
Moving. remove and pop hand the element back as a plain value; pushing it elsewhere encodes it again.
cut removes it too, but keeps its bytes as a cut, which push_cut or insert_cut pastes into any DurableVec of the same element type without writing them again: the move costs a few entries in the file however large the element is.
A cut lives as long as the journal that made it: you may hold it across transactions, and a paste after the next flush still works, but encodes the element again, as push would.
Cut::is_alive() tells you whether a paste would still write none of its bytes; dropping a cut unpasted drops the element.
delete and clear remove and drop.
DurableMap<K, V>
A key-value map that keeps its entries in insertion order.
K: Eq + Hash + Durable, V: Durable.

let mut contacts = book_mut.contacts_mut();
let ada = String::from("ada");
contacts.insert(String::from("ada"), contact)?;
contacts.get_mut(&ada).unwrap().email_mut().set("ada@example.com")?;
contacts.delete(&ada)?;     // removes and drops; `remove` hands the value back
Reading — get, contains_key, iter, len — needs no Mut.
Inserting under a key that is already present replaces its value and returns the old one, as HashMap::insert does.
Encoding. The number of entries, then each entry’s key and value, in the map’s order; the schema describes it as a map of its key and value types, so a tool can show it as one.
The file does not support key lookup at all — that is what the in-memory map is for — so it needs no hashing structure on file.
In memory, the entries sit in a vector, in their order on file, beside a hash table of their indices, so each key is stored exactly once and K: Clone is not required.
Removal swaps: the last entry moves into the removed one’s place, without writing its bytes, so the file stays dense, and an insertion appends.
Keys are immutable.
No Mut is ever handed out for a key; Durable on K governs only how its bytes are encoded.
DurableBlob<T>
An escape hatch for foreign types.

#[derive(Durable)]
struct Config {
    window: DurableBlob<WindowGeometry>,  // a foreign serde type
}
Wraps any T: Serialize + DeserializeOwned + Default as an opaque, serialized payload, prefixed with its length.
Use it when a type is not yours to change and cannot get its own Durable implementation.
It is deliberately the worst option.
A blob is serialized again in full on every change, which costs time in proportion to its size, though only the bytes of the serialization that changed are recorded; it is opaque to tooling; and it drags in a serialization dependency.
Prefer a derived type or a hand-written implementation whenever you can.
It is gated behind kladde-types’ serde feature — the only thing in the workspace that needs serde at all.
What is missing
A rope, for large text with efficient middle-insertion, is designed but not built.
Tuples of up to twelve components are durable, encoded like a tuple struct, and their Mut’s parts() hands out a Mut per component.
Option<T> is durable as an enum, and its Mut offers set, take and as_mut; Box<T> is persisted as the T it holds, which is how a recursive type gets a size in Rust.
Choosing

















































you haveusea sequence of fixed-size valuesVec<T>a sequence of anything else, or one you cut and paste fromDurableVec<T>textStringbytesVec<u8>a lookup tableDurableMap<K, V>a value that changes often and should keep its sizeFixed<T>a few values that belong togethera tuple, or a derived structyour own struct or enum#[derive(Durable)]a foreign type you cannot changeDurableBlob<T>, reluctantlya foreign type whose layout you knowa hand-written impl

rust/tutorial/index.title: Tutorial
rust/tutorial/index.content:
For people who want to use kladde in a Rust application.
Assumes ordinary Rust knowledge and no prior exposure to kladde.

Getting started — your first durable value, and the mental model.
The built-in containers — vector, map, string, blob.
Deriving your own types — structs, enums, and enums in place of trait objects.
Compared to serde — when you want kladde and when you want serde, and why they are not competitors.
Durability and flushing — what is guaranteed when, what a crash costs you, and transactions.
Implementing Durable by hand (advanced) — opaque types, and implementing the trait by hand.

Is kladde the right tool?
Kladde is a good fit when all of these hold:

you have a long-lived, mutable data structure that must survive a crash;
you read it far more often than you write it, and you want reads to cost what in-memory reads cost;
your mutations are small and frequent relative to the size of the whole structure;
one process owns the file.

It is a poor fit when:

you want to exchange data with other systems — that is serde’s job, and kladde’s format is a heap, not a document;
you need concurrent writers, or readers in other processes;
your data is append-only and never mutated in place — a log file is simpler and faster;
your working set does not fit in memory.
Kladde keeps the whole structure resident by design.

The comparison that most often matters in practice is with “just serialize the whole thing on every change,” which is what most applications do.
That is O(total size) per mutation.
Kladde is O(size of the change), at the cost of a more constrained type vocabulary.
Status warning
Kladde is early: the file format is a draft, and a file written today may not open with a later version.

spec/conformance.title: Conformance
spec/conformance.content:
What an implementation must do to claim it implements kladde, and how that claim is meant to be checked.
Status: intent only.
No conformance suite exists.
This document describes what one should contain.
What conformance means
An implementation is conforming if:

every file it writes can be opened by every other conforming implementation, and
it can open every file that any other conforming implementation writes,

subject to the compatibility contract — the opening application must implement equivalent data structures for the types the file contains.
Note what this does not require.
It does not require that two implementations produce the same file for the same sequence of operations.
Placement, compaction, and fold timing are all free, so two implementations will routinely produce byte-different files with identical contents, and that is correct.
Must

Header. Write and validate the magic, format version, and minimum reader version.
Refuse to open a file whose minimum reader version exceeds the implementation’s own.
Fail closed. Never interpret a file whose root fingerprint differs from the expected one unless resolution actually succeeded.
Silent misinterpretation is a conformance failure, not a quality-of-implementation issue.
Content. Keep the sequence the canonical encoding of one root value at every transaction boundary, and refuse a file whose sequence is not.
The reuse rule. Write only to reusable pages, or extend the file (I2).
One fsync before the header. Issue a header only after an fsync that covered everything it references and the previous header (I1); treat a failed fsync as fatal for the session.
Page framing. Write the kind, content_size, epoch and crc on every non-header page, and ignore any page whose CRC does not validate.
Journal encoding. Encode records, transactions, and journal pages as specified, and recover a torn tail by keeping the longest valid prefix — without skipping a hole.
The start of a session. Fold a non-empty recovered journal before appending to it, and write the journal page that a session’s first flush names (the start of a session).
Transaction atomicity. Replay every transaction completely or not at all.
Valid transaction boundaries. Group records so that every transaction takes a sequence that decodes to one that decodes (ordering).
Cuts. Paste only cuts of the same journal, each at most once, and refuse a journal that does otherwise (cuts).
Bounds. Support the stated bounds, and fail cleanly rather than wrap when an application exceeds them.
Entries. Keep the rules for writers — one entry per span id and epoch, and the reach rule — and refuse a file that resolution finds invalid: a chain that names an id no entry describes, reaches a span twice, or shares a span with another chain, or a reached Ref outside a data page’s content.
Descriptor encoding. Produce byte-identical output to the canonical encoding for the same type graph.
Fingerprints. Produce bit-identical output to the fingerprint computation, including on recursive types.
Crash consistency. Ensure that a crash at any instant leaves a file that opens.

May

Choose any placement policy — which reusable page a flush writes to, how content is cut across pages, and how it is cut into spans.
Consolidate, or not consolidate, by any strategy.
Group application operations into transactions however it likes, including not at all.
Fold at any time, and optimize the fold arbitrarily, so long as the resulting sequence is the one an in-order replay produces.
Assign, reuse, and recycle span ids however it likes, within the reach rule.
Expose any API shape at all.
Nothing above the storage layer is constrained.
Keep the sequence in any in-memory form, or decode none of it: a tool that only compacts reads no content at all, so what a file keeps resident must follow from the file, never from which types happened to look.
Keep state of its own in the private chain, and keep, replace, or clear a state it finds there.
Give a reusable page’s blocks back to the file system (deallocating reusable pages).

Must not

Change the content of any chain during consolidation.
Overwrite or deallocate a page that is not reusable, or truncate the file below one or to anything but a page boundary (the truncation rule).
This rule is relaxed for the last journal page, which may be appended to, and if it is empty (i.e., if its prefix of CRC-valid transactions is empty) then the file may be truncated below it.
Continue a session after a failed fsync.
Depend on the descriptor table’s index assignment for any semantic purpose.
Make a page’s residency, or any storage-layer decision, depend on whether a data type read from it.
Emit a fingerprint that depends on table layout, traversal order, or any runtime-incidental state.
Let the private chain affect the sequence or the schema, or rely on a state found there without first checking that it is its own and still current (the private chain).

The suite
The conformance suite should have four parts.
Vector tests — pure functions, checkable without any file I/O.

A set of type graphs with their expected canonical encodings, byte for byte.
The same graphs with their expected fingerprints, including recursive and mutually recursive cases, and cases that differ only by table permutation (which must produce equal fingerprints) or only by variant declaration order (likewise).
Descriptor decoding, including rejection of malformed input.

File tests — a corpus of files, each with a manifest describing its expected level-2 and level-3 interpretation.
Every implementation must reproduce the manifest from the file.
Files written by each implementation are added to the corpus, so that the suite grows to cover the cross product.
Crash tests — two kinds, checking different things.

Journal prefix. For each of a set of mutation sequences, truncate the resulting journal at every byte offset, open it, and assert that it opens successfully and that its sequence decodes to the state after some prefix of the transactions.
This is the mechanical check on the ordering rule: that every container groups the records of one edit into one transaction.
Payload pages. For each of a set of mutation sequences with external bytes, drop every subset of the payload page writes since the last fsync, and assert that the file opens on the state after some prefix of the transactions, losing none that every write of its payload pages reached.
Flush interruption. For each of a set of flushes, simulate a power cut after every individual page write — including reordering the writes, since write-back is not ordered — and assert that the file opens and lands on either the previous committed state or the new one, never in between.
This is the mechanical check on I1 and I2.

Differential tests — an implementation checks itself against a model.

The store against a byte vector. Any series of Write, Splice, Move and Paste, flushes, reopens and simulated power cuts must leave the sequence holding the vector’s bytes.
The values against their encoding. After every operation, the sequence must equal the canonical encoding of the in-memory root value, byte for byte.

No leak detector is needed: nothing in a file can be unreachable from the header.
Open questions

Should conformance be versioned — an implementation claiming “conforms to spec version N” — and can a level of partial conformance (say, read-only) be meaningful?
How are reserved features handled?
An implementation that encounters a reserved primitive code, an unassigned kind tag, or an undefined escape in the journal must reject it rather than guess, but should that be a conformance requirement or a recommendation?
Should the suite mandate a minimum level of tooling support, so that every implementation ships something that can dump a file?

spec/durability.title: Durability
spec/durability.content:
Which pages a write may touch, the protocol that commits a flush, and exactly what survives a crash.
This is the layer that makes durability a guarantee by prevention rather than a detection scheme: committed state is never overwritten, so there is nothing to detect.
What is guaranteed
Under an application crash — the process dies, the operating system survives — every mutation whose call returned successfully survives.
The journal’s pages, and the payload pages its transactions name, remain in the OS page cache and are written back on the OS’s own schedule, which an application crash does not interrupt.
Under a reported error the same holds, for a simpler reason: the process is still running.
An implementation that cannot complete an operation reports the failure, by whatever means its language makes idiomatic, and refuses further work — and every mutation that returned successfully before that is in the journal exactly as if nothing had gone wrong.
The exception is a failed fsync, after which the page cache may have discarded writes the kernel had already reported as clean; that is why a failed fsync ends the session instead of being reported as an ordinary error.
Under a power cut, recovery reaches the state of some transaction boundary, including at least every transaction folded by the last completed flush().
Transactions issued after that flush survive up to a valid journal prefix, minus whatever the operating system never wrote out.
That last clause is the one worth reading twice.
Journal appends are not fsynced individually, so they sit in the page cache until write-back; a power cut freezes whichever subset of journal pages the OS happened to have written.
Write-back is not ordered, so a later journal page can be on disk while an earlier one is not.
The chained, epoch-salted transaction CRCs deliberately refuse to skip such a hole: what recovery keeps is the longest valid prefix ending at a transaction boundary, which can be shorter than the raw journal bytes that survived.
Never guaranteed: that a partial transaction is visible, or that a flush is partially applied.
Both are excluded by construction rather than by cleanup.
Page states
Page states are derived, not stored.
Define the world of a header as everything reachable from it: its span-table pages, the data pages that reached spans show bytes of, every page of the next epoch’s journal, of which the header names only the first page, the rest reached from it, and every payload page that a complete transaction of that journal names.
At any moment the two on-disk header slots define at most two worlds that can (and typically do) overlap, and every page is in exactly one of three states:

live — in the world of the newer on-disk header;
fallback — in the world of the older on-disk header but not in the world of the newer on-disk header, and the newer header hasn’t been fsynced yet;
reusable — in neither on-disk header’s world, or only in the older header’s world after the newer header has been fsynced.

stateDiagram-v2
  %% Bottom-up, starting from `live`, and in this order: anything else crosses arrows in mermaid or in make-pdf.py.
  direction BT
  live --> fallback: header E+k written, whose<br>world no longer contains<br>the page
  fallback --> reusable: header E+k is fsynced<br>(at latest in flush E+k+1)
  live --> nonexistent: file shrinks past the<br>journal's empty last page
  nonexistent --> reusable: file grows, bringing page<br>into existence
  reusable --> live: (a) written during flush E<br>and in header E's world<br>or (b) appended to journal,<br>or named by it as payload
  reusable --> nonexistent: file shrinks once every<br>higher page is reusable<br>or the journal's empty<br>last page
  live --> live: append transaction<br>(journal and payload<br>pages only)

The reuse rule

A flush may write only to reusable pages, or extend the file.

The writes between flushes keep to the same rule: the journal and its payload pages take reusable pages or extend the file, and write again only pages of the journal being appended to.
The whole durability argument rests on this.
