Keeping parts of a file in different versions of their schema, and upgrading each part on its own, is what capsules were sketched for, and one sequence makes them cheap.
Three ideas made them up:

a Capsule<T> is a schema boundary: a subtree that records which version of T’s schema it is written in, as an index into a table of the versions the file holds, each stored once and resolved once per session, however many capsules use it;
fingerprints computed outside a capsule erase its inner type, so the root fingerprint does not change when T does, and a stale capsule is found by comparing the table’s fingerprints with the reader’s, once per version;
each capsule upgrades on its own, at first touch, or keeps its version for as long as nothing writes it.

In one sequence a value’s size concerns nothing but positions in memory, so a capsule is inline: its version’s index as a varint, then T’s encoding in that version.
Upgrading one at first touch is a splice of its region, with the new index, in the same transaction as the write that touched it; the capsule’s handle, or whatever a binding has in its place, is where that happens.
The schema chain would hold the table of versions in use: a session whose types are missing from it adds them in the flush at open, before any capsule names them, and a count of capsules per version, built at open, says when a flush may drop a version.
Nothing in the span format or the journal would change: capsules are a matter of the schema and of one wrapper type, and can come later.
They would let a large file whose element type changed upgrade a part at a time rather than every element at the first open.
How much semantic-migration machinery to expose.
Structural resolution handles add, remove, reorder, and rename-with-annotation.
It cannot handle a change that is semantic rather than structural — splitting one field into two, changing units.
Whether kladde offers registered from-fingerprint/to-fingerprint hooks, or leaves such changes entirely to the application, is undecided.
Rename robustness.
Name-based identity is ergonomic but not rename-robust.
An optional explicit ordinal annotation, used when present and falling back to the name otherwise, would cover both; whether to specify one is undecided.
Defaults for added fields.
A reader whose type gained a field needs a value for it when reading an older file.
Whether the default is declared in the schema, supplied by the language binding, or required to be the type’s zero value is undecided.
Relationship to application-level versioning.
A file-level semantic version for the application — as opposed to the format or the schema — has a natural home in the same header slot.
These should be one mechanism, not two parallel ones.
What was considered and declined
A fingerprint alone, with no descriptor table.
Compact and a fine integrity check, but a hash can only report that something differs.
It cannot say what differs, so it cannot implement levels (b) or (c).
It also conflates “I changed” with “something I contain changed,” and is unusable for generic types, where Container<A_v1> and Container<A_v2> hash differently with nothing shared.
The fingerprint is kept, but as a fast path on top of the descriptors rather than as a replacement.
Per-value vtables, in the FlatBuffers style, giving true in-place forward compatibility.
Declined: it taxes the steady state of every value to solve a problem kladde only has at load.
Revisit only if level (d) with preservation becomes a hard requirement for files concurrently shared between application versions.
Prior art
The model borrowed here is Avro’s: the writer’s schema travels with the data, the reader has its own, and resolution reconciles them at read time.
The fingerprint plays the role of Avro’s schema-registry key.
Kladde’s encoding is close to Avro’s binary encoding too — no tags, no padding, zigzag varints, a union’s branch as a varint, counts before sequences — and differs where mutation asks it to: Avro writes data once and reads it in sequence, while kladde edits values in place, so it keeps a sequence’s count in one place rather than in blocks, ends text in a terminator so that an edit of text is one splice, and offers Fixed for values that change often.

spec/schema/fingerprints.title: Fingerprints
spec/schema/fingerprints.content:
A fixed-size, reproducible hash identifying a type’s representation.
Status: settled and implemented.
This document is normative: two conforming implementations must produce bit-identical fingerprints for the same type graph.
The value
A fingerprint is a 128-bit (16-byte) hash.
Two fingerprints are equal iff all 128 bits are equal.
It carries no flags and no reserved bits — every bit is hash output.
Hash function
SHA-256, truncated to its leading 128 bits — the first 16 bytes of the digest, byte 0 first.
SHA-256 is chosen for exact cross-language reproducibility.
It has universal test vectors, it is in the standard library of most languages and a few hundred lines of code in those without one, such as C and C++, and “compute SHA-256, keep the first 16 bytes” is trivial to reimplement identically.
128 bits gives a negligible accidental-collision probability for any realistic number of distinct schemas.
Cryptographic strength is deliberately not relied upon.
A fingerprint is an integrity and identity check against accident, not against an adversary.
An attacker who can write to a file can do far worse than collide a schema hash, so the format does not attempt to defend against one here.
A future format revision may substitute another hash or width; the choice is a format-version property.
What is and is not fingerprinted
The fingerprint of a type is computed from the type graph reachable from that type.
Included — everything that affects the representation or the identities used to reconcile it:

the kind of each descriptor;
primitive codes;
discriminant widths and discriminant values;
field names and variant names;
field order and canonical variant order;
an Array’s length, and an Opaque’s library name, type name and size mode.

Excluded:

the name of Struct and Enum descriptors.
A type’s own name does not affect its byte layout, so renaming a type must not change its fingerprint.
table indices, entirely.
References are encoded structurally, so the fingerprint is invariant under any renumbering or reordering of the descriptor table.

Reduced: an Opaque’s version contributes only its compatibility component — the stability flag plus the leading nonzero component.
Patch releases, and minor releases above 0.x, therefore do not churn the fingerprints of every type that transitively contains them.
Cycles
The type graph may contain cycles, so a naive post-order fold does not terminate.
The traversal is a white/grey/black depth-first search with memoization.
A node currently on the stack (grey) that is encountered again is a back edge, and is encoded as a relative reference — “the k-th enclosing type currently being hashed” — rather than by recursing.
This makes the hash a pure function of graph structure, and it is the standard technique for hashing mutually recursive definitions.
Memoization on black nodes keeps the traversal linear in the number of distinct reachable descriptors.
The same cycle-awareness is needed for descriptor equality on recursive types, so this is shared machinery rather than fingerprint-specific work.
The computation, exactly
Every descriptor starts white.
visit(node, depth) colours node grey, records its depth, feeds a fresh SHA-256 the node’s hash input, colours it black, remembers the first 16 bytes of the digest as its fingerprint, and returns them.
The file’s root fingerprint is visit(0, 0).
A node’s hash input is its canonical encoding, with three changes:

a Struct’s and an Enum’s string(name) is left out;
an Opaque’s varint(major) varint(minor) varint(patch) becomes byte(stable) varint(leading), with stable 1 if major > 0 and 0 otherwise, and leading the major version if major > 0 and the minor version otherwise;
every reference(child) becomes a token, emitted in the order the encoding emits references, variants in ascending discriminant order:

if child is white, byte(0) followed by the 16 bytes of visit(child, depth + 1);
if child is black, byte(0) followed by its remembered 16 bytes;
if child is grey, which makes the edge a back edge, byte(1) followed by varint(depth − depth[child]).



So the token for a child is computed in the middle of its parent’s input, which is why the hash state of every node on the stack stays open until its own input is complete.
A memoized fingerprint is reused wherever its node is met again; for a node inside a cycle that depends on where the traversal first met it, so it is not that node’s identity as a root, and only root fingerprints are compared.
Vectors

























type graph, root firstfingerprint[0] Struct "Point" { x: [1], y: [1] }, [1] i320d91791f5827efadfa8150af9812fad6[0] Enum "List", width 4, { 0 "Nil": [2], 1 "Cons": [3] }, [1] i32, [2] Struct "Unit" {}, [3] Struct "Cons" { "0": [1], "1": [0] }abdbb8e6f2b104819c9b608dd77aaedf[0] Opaque "lib" "T", version 1.2.3, fixed size 8, no parameters81a2a3d8b939f4f216a344cf10758953[0] Map { key: [1], value: [2] }, [1] Text, [2] u326a33dc4a1e560e465f7a50543f62c492
Hex, byte 0 first.
The Point’s hash input, for instance, is 80 02 01 78 00 <16 bytes of i32's fingerprint> 01 79 00 <the same 16 bytes>, and i32’s is the single byte 06.
Determinism
The fingerprint must be a pure function of the type graph.
Two implementations that agree on the graph must agree on the hash, with no dependence on:

table layout, index assignment, or descriptor ordering;
traversal order beyond what the canonical order fixes;
hash-map iteration order, allocation addresses, or any other incidental runtime state.

An implementation that cannot demonstrate this on the conformance vectors is not conforming.
As a fast path
The file header stores the root type’s fingerprint.
This makes the overwhelmingly common case — an application opening a file it wrote itself, with an unchanged schema — a single 16-byte comparison.
If it matches, the reader knows its own types encode exactly as the writer’s did, and decodes the sequence natively without parsing the descriptor table at all.
Only when it differs does the reader parse the writer’s descriptors and attempt resolution.
So the fast path costs one comparison and the slow path costs one graph reconciliation per open — never per value.
This is the standard arrangement: the fingerprint is a registry key, the schema is the source of truth.
A fingerprint alone can detect a difference; it cannot bridge one, which is why it complements the descriptor table rather than replacing it.

spec/schema/index.title: Schema
spec/schema/index.content:
How a kladde file describes the types it contains.
This is the most fully specified part of kladde: it is pinned down precisely enough that any conforming implementation, in any language, produces byte-identical descriptor serializations and bit-identical fingerprints.
Why a file carries its schema
Two reasons, one defensive and one enabling.
Defensive. Without a schema, opening a file written by a different version of an application is undefined behaviour dressed as a successful read: a field is decoded as the field next to it, and the corruption is silent.
An embedded schema turns that into a detectable error.
Enabling. A schema that describes encoding, not merely identity, carries enough information to actually bridge a difference rather than just report one.
A reader whose struct gained a field can decode the writer’s values by the writer’s descriptors, and read the fields it does share correctly.
That is what makes evolution possible at all.
The cost model is what makes this affordable.
The schema is stored once per file, not per value — unlike a tagged format such as JSON or Protobuf, where every instance pays.
For a file holding millions of instances of a type, the schema blob is negligible; for a small settings file it may be a noticeable fraction, which is the honest trade.
The documents

























documentcontentsType descriptorsthe model: what kinds of type exist, what each carries, and how its values are encoded in the sequenceCanonical encodingthe byte serialization of a descriptor tableFingerprintsthe reproducible 128-bit hash identifying a type’s representationEvolutionhow a reader reconciles its own types against a writer’s — largely TBD
The guiding principle

A descriptor describes a representation, not an identity.

A descriptor says how bytes are laid out and interpreted.
It does not say which source-language type produced them.
Two types with byte-identical representations have identical descriptors and identical fingerprints, and this is intentional.
It is also harmless, because a value is always reconstructed top-down from a known root type.
A reader never asks “what type is this anonymous blob?” — the parent field’s declared type already determines which loader to call.
The descriptor exists only to answer “does the writer’s encoding for this field match what my decoder expects, and if not, how do I bridge it?”
This principle resolves several questions that otherwise look hard.
A type with a hand-written implementation that happens to write exactly the bytes of a plain struct has that struct’s descriptor — the presence of non-persisted fields in the author’s source type is invisible and irrelevant.
A type is Opaque not because its implementation is hand-written but because its representation is genuinely not decomposable.
Scope
These documents define how every value is encoded, and how descriptors are modeled, serialized, and fingerprinted.
The descriptor table sits in the file’s schema chain, and the root fingerprint in the header.
How a reader resolves a mismatch — the compatibility policy — is Evolution, and is the least settled part of the specification.

spec/schema/type-descriptors.title: Type descriptors
spec/schema/type-descriptors.content:
The language-neutral model of how a value type encodes into the sequence, and what its bytes mean.
Status: settled and implemented.
This document is normative.
Terminology

Type descriptor (descriptor): a node describing one value type’s encoding.
Descriptor table: an ordered array of descriptors.
A descriptor refers to another by its index in this table — a table-local, otherwise arbitrary integer.
Indices are an artifact of one serialization; a type’s fingerprint does not depend on them.
Type graph: the directed graph whose vertices are descriptors and whose edges are the references one descriptor makes to others.
It may contain cycles — recursive and mutually recursive types are legal, within the rules of nesting.

The kinds
A descriptor is one of nine kinds: Primitive, Struct, Enum, Array, Sequence, Map, Text, Opaque, and Fixed.
Every type has one encoding, which a reader decodes front to back from the type’s descriptor, below.
Primitive
A scalar, identified by a primitive code.



















































































codetypeencodingfixed form0u8one bytethe same byte1u16unsigned LEB1282 bytes, little-endian2u32unsigned LEB1284 bytes, little-endian3u64unsigned LEB1288 bytes, little-endian4i8one byte, two’s complementthe same byte5i16zigzag, then LEB1282 bytes, little-endian two’s complement6i32zigzag, then LEB1284 bytes, little-endian two’s complement7i64zigzag, then LEB1288 bytes, little-endian two’s complement8f324 bytes, little-endian IEEE-754the same bytes9f648 bytes, little-endian IEEE-754the same bytes10boolone byte, 0x00 false, 0x01 truethe same byte11charUTF-8, 1 to 4 bytesthe Unicode scalar value, 4 bytes, little-endian
Zigzag maps 0, −1, 1, −2, … to 0, 1, 2, 3, …, so that a number of small magnitude takes one byte whatever its sign.
The fixed form is what the type’s values take inside a Fixed value.
The primitive code doubles as the descriptor’s kind tag: codes 0..=127 are reserved for primitives, so a Primitive descriptor is a single byte with no further content.
Reserved primitive codes
Fixed here so later additions cannot conflict.
An implementation need not accept them until a corresponding type exists and can be tested, and must refuse a table that uses one it does not implement.

































codetype12u12813i12814f16, IEEE-754 binary1615bf16, bfloat1616–19u24, u40, u48, u5620–23i24, i40, i48, i56
Struct
An ordered, fixed set of named fields, encoded back to back — no discriminant, no header.
Carries:

name: UTF-8, diagnostics only; a struct’s own name is not fingerprinted.
fields: an ordered list of (field_name, type_reference).

Field order is significant: it is the order of the encodings.
Each field name is significant.
A positional (tuple) field’s name is the decimal rendering of its position — "0", "1", … — so the model stays uniform.
Enum
A discriminated union: a discriminant, followed by the value that the variant it selects holds, its payload.
Carries:

name: UTF-8, diagnostics only.
discriminant_width: the bytes the discriminant takes in the fixed form — 1, 2, 4, or 8; every discriminant value must fit in it.
The encoding itself writes the discriminant as a varint.
variants: each (discriminant_value, variant_name, payload), canonically ordered by ascending discriminant_value; discriminant values are distinct, and payload is a reference.

Each discriminant value, each variant name, and each variant’s payload type is significant.
Variant declaration order is not: a value’s encoding is selected by the stored discriminant, not by a variant’s position, so reordering variants in the source without changing their discriminants changes neither the encoding nor the fingerprint.
Every variant holds exactly one value.
A variant that holds nothing holds the empty Struct, which encodes to no bytes; a variant that holds several fields holds a Struct of them; and a variant that holds one value of any type holds that type directly.
So in Rust, a unit variant Nil holds the empty Struct, a tuple variant Element(Element) or Text(String) holds its field’s type, a struct variant Point { x: f32, y: f32 } holds a Struct of its fields named after the variant, and a tuple variant of several fields Pair(u8, u8) a Struct of positional fields.
Why one value, always.
Languages disagree about what a variant holds: Rust has unit, tuple and struct variants, while a C++ std::variant, a C++ class hierarchy, Swift’s enums with associated values and TypeScript’s discriminated unions all hold exactly one value per alternative.
Describing a variant by one payload lets every one of them map to the same descriptor with no choice left to the programmer: Rust’s Element(Element) and a struct variant with Element’s fields describe the same bytes and get the same fingerprint, as a struct’s own name already does not matter.
And holding always one value, rather than at most one, keeps every variant the same shape: a valueless variant, a C++ alternative that is an empty struct and Rust’s () all hold the empty Struct, and need no rule to say they agree.
An Option<T> is an enum, None with discriminant 0 holding the empty Struct, and Some with discriminant 1 holding a T.
Array
len values of one element type, back to back, with no count.
Carries element (a reference) and len.
An Array is deliberately not interchangeable with a Struct of len identically-typed positional fields: the encodings coincide, but the kind tags differ and therefore so do the fingerprints.
The kind exists to avoid spelling out a large len as that many fields.
Sequence
Any number of values of one element type: their count, then the values.
Carries element (a reference).
A vector is a Sequence; a map is a Map.
Map
Any number of entries, each a key and a value: their count, then each entry’s key and value.
Carries key and value (references).
The entries are in the order the writing library keeps them; the format neither sorts them nor checks that keys are distinct, which is the library’s business, as is how it finds a key in memory.
Why a kind of its own.
A Map encodes exactly as a Sequence of two-field Structs would, but every language has a native map that a reader can decode one into, and a tool can render one as a JSON object rather than as an array of pairs.
It also leaves nothing to agree on: a Sequence of Structs would need every implementation to name the two fields alike, or the same map would get two fingerprints.
Text
UTF-8 text, ended by the byte 0xFF.
Carries nothing.
Why a terminator rather than a count.
UTF-8 never contains 0xFF, so no byte of text needs escaping, and an edit of text is then one splice, where a count would add a second record — and a second place where the chain of spans is cut — to every keystroke.
A decoder finds the end by scanning for the terminator, which it does while it checks the UTF-8 anyway; text below 128 bytes takes the byte a count would have taken, and longer text saves the count’s further bytes.
Only text can have a terminator, since a terminator must be a byte the content cannot hold, so bytes and sequences of any other type keep their count.
Opaque
A type whose internal structure the format does not decompose — a black box identified nominally.
Used for types with hand-written encodings that no structural descriptor fits: externally serialized payloads, say.
Carries:

library_name: the package, module, or crate defining the type.
Language-neutral: not necessarily a Rust crate.
type_name: UTF-8.
version: a (major, minor, patch) triple.
fixed_size: the number of bytes every value takes, or none, in which case each value is prefixed with its length.
parameters: an ordered list of type references, for generic parameters.

Only the compatibility component of version is fingerprinted, and it has two parts, both of which are necessary:

a stability flag — true when major > 0, false when major == 0;
the leading nonzero component — major if major > 0, otherwise minor.

Without the stability flag, 0.1.z and 1.y.z would both reduce to 1 and collide, even though crossing 0.x → 1.x is a breaking change.
Patch-level changes, and minor-level changes above 0.x, are thereby treated as encoding-compatible.
This tuple is the same identity that semantic versioning already relies on, and it carries the same risk: it trusts the author to bump the major version whenever the encoding changes.
A structural descriptor needs no such trust, which is a standing argument for preferring structural descriptors wherever a type admits one, and reserving Opaque for encodings that genuinely are not decomposable.
Whether a fixed size or a length prefix per type is enough, or whether some opaque types want both modes, is open.
Fixed
The values of a wrapped type, each encoded at the same size: its fixed form.
Carries target (a reference).
Fixed(T) is a type of its own, with the values of T: it lays out everything inside T at its largest, so every field lies at a constant offset whatever the value, and a container of them finds its ith element by multiplication.
It applies to all of T and not to what wraps it: Fixed(Option<u32>) takes five bytes for every value, while Option<Fixed<u32>> takes one for None and five for Some.
Encodings













































kindencodingPrimitiveas its code givesStructits fields’ encodings, concatenated, in declaration orderEnumthe discriminant as unsigned LEB128, then the selected variant’s payload’s encodingArraylen element encodingsSequencethe number of elements as unsigned LEB128, then the element encodingsMapthe number of entries as unsigned LEB128, then each entry’s key’s encoding and its value’sTextthe UTF-8 bytes, then 0xFFOpaquefixed_size bytes, or, without a fixed size, the number of bytes as unsigned LEB128 and then the bytesFixedthe target’s fixed form, below
The fixed form of a type is:

































kindfixed formPrimitivethe fixed form of its codeStructits fields’ fixed forms, concatenatedEnumthe discriminant in discriminant_width bytes, little-endian, then the variant’s payload’s fixed form, then zeros up to the size of the largest payload’sArraylen element fixed formsOpaqueits encoding, if it has a fixed sizeFixedthe target’s fixed form
Sequence, Map, Text, and an Opaque without a fixed size have no fixed form, and neither has any type that holds one of them, or itself.
The canonical encoding is the only one a writer may produce, and a reader refuses any other: varints are minimal, text is valid UTF-8, discriminants name variants, integers lie in range of their type — a u16’s varint at most 2^16 − 1, an i16’s zigzag likewise — bools are 0 or 1, a char’s fixed form is a Unicode scalar value, and an enum’s padding in the fixed form is zeros.
So a value has exactly one encoding, and the sequence is a function of the root value.
A worked example
With struct Point { x: f32, label: Text, n: u32 }, the point (1.5, "ab", 300) encodes as
00 00 C0 3F      x: 1.5
61 62 FF         label: "ab", and its terminator
AC 02            n: 300 as LEB128

and Fixed(Option<u32>) holding Some(300) as 01 2C 01 00 00: the discriminant in one byte, then 300 in four, little-endian; None is 00 00 00 00 00.
Fixed-size types
A type whose every value encodes to the same number of bytes is fixed-size, and the descriptors say which types are, so a reader computes it as a writer does:

u8, i8, bool, f32 and f64 are, with sizes 1, 1, 1, 4 and 8; the other primitives are varints or UTF-8, and are not;
a Struct is if all its fields are, with the sum of their sizes;
an Enum is if every discriminant is below 128, so that its varint takes one byte, and every variant’s payload is fixed-size with the same size: its size is 1 plus that size;
an Array is if its element is, with len times the element’s size;
an Opaque is if it declares a fixed size;
a Fixed always is, with the size of its target’s fixed form;
Sequence, Map and Text never are, nor is a type that holds itself.

A fixed-size type’s fixed form is its encoding byte for byte, except where an enum’s discriminant_width exceeds the one byte its encoding spends on the discriminant: a writer may set a wider width so that the fixed form keeps its size when variants are added.
Rules of nesting
A table must keep two rules, which a reader checks when it decodes one:

A Fixed holds a type that has a fixed form.
A type reaches itself only through an Enum, a Sequence or a Map, whose discriminant or count can end the recursion, and never through Structs, Arrays and Fixed alone, whose values would be infinite.
A tree whose nodes hold their children inline is a Struct holding a Sequence of itself; a list is an Enum one of whose variants holds itself.
An Opaque’s parameters are not containment: an Opaque says nothing of how its value holds them, so a type may reach itself through one.
The rule asks only that recursion can end; an Enum whose every variant holds itself has no finite value, and is legal but useless.

A decoder of a recursive type nests as deeply as the file says, so it limits its depth, or does not recurse, and refuses a file beyond its limit rather than overflow its stack.
References and the root
A reference is an index into the descriptor table.
Every field type, payload, element, key, value, target, and parameter is a reference.
By convention the descriptor at index 0 is the root — the type actually stored in the file.
Why the model is enough for evolution.
Every encoding is decodable from the descriptors alone, so a reader can skip, or read, a writer’s values by the writer’s graph, even when its own types differ.
See Evolution.

spec/sequence.title: The sequence
spec/sequence.content:
What a kladde file’s content is: one byte sequence holding the root value’s encoding, beside the schema and the implementation’s private state, each a chain of spans.
Three chains
The header names three chains, and each holds a byte string:





























chainheader fieldholdschanged bythe sequencesequence_headthe root value’s encoding, by the root type’s descriptorthe journal, and flushesthe schemaschema_headthe descriptor table of the root type, root firstflushes onlythe private chainprivate_headwhatever the writing implementation keeps from one session to the next (rules)flushes only
The journal edits only the sequence, so no journal record needs to say which chain it edits, and every position in the journal is a position in the sequence, counted in bytes from the root value’s first byte.
The schema changes only when a flush writes it: when a file is created, or upgraded to a new schema before the application gets it.
A file whose root fingerprint matches the reader’s never needs to decode its schema chain (the fast path).
Why chains of their own rather than a prefix.
The schema could be a prefix of the sequence, which would work as well; but it would offset every position by the schema’s length, and a reader would decode the schema to find where the root begins.
Chains cost nothing extra in the span format.
One sequence, holding the root value’s encoding
The sequence is the encoding of the root value, with every value inline in its parent; there is no allocation and no pointer.
A container states how many elements it holds, text ends in a byte that UTF-8 never contains, no value states its own encoded size, and every value decodes front to back from its type’s descriptor.
For example, with these types,
struct Drawing { title: Text, shapes: Sequence<Shape> }
enum Shape { Circle { r: f32 }, Path { points: Sequence<(f32, f32)> } }
a drawing titled “Map” with a circle of radius 1 and a path from (0, 0) to (1, 1) is this sequence of 28 bytes:
4D 61 70 FF                  title: "Map", and the end of the text
02                           shapes: 2 elements
00 00 00 80 3F               Circle (variant 0), r = 1.0
01 02                        Path (variant 1), 2 points
00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00        (0.0, 0.0)
00 00 80 3F 00 00 80 3F        (1.0, 1.0)

Nothing in it is a pointer, a size of an allocation, or a byte of padding.
Renaming the drawing to “World map” is one journal record, Splice(0, 3, "World map"), and every byte behind it moves by 6 without being mentioned; on file it is two span entries, wherever in the sequence the splice lands.
Why one sequence.

The description stops depending on the data model.
When every value lives in an allocation of its own, every value costs a pointer in its parent, a description naming its allocation, and a size, so the description grows with the number of values, and short strings and short lists dominate that number.
With one sequence, the description depends only on how a writer cuts the sequence into spans, which it chooses and the data model never sees.
The unit of description and the unit of the data model stop pulling against each other.
A cheap description wants few allocations, so values move inline into long ones; a cheap splice wants short allocations, since content keyed by its offset in an allocation makes a splice restate everything behind it.
Separating the two removes the trade-off rather than choosing a point on it.
Everything that exists because of allocations goes with them: ownership, freeing, publishing a pointer before freeing what it replaced, tombstones, id recycling, and leaks.
Removing a value is one splice, whatever it held, and nothing can leak, since nothing can be unreachable.
The file is its own serialization.
A tool decodes the whole content from the schema, with no pointer graph to follow and no opaque container to stop at.

It gives up reaching a value on file without decoding what lies before it, which kladde never does, since it reads in bulk.
And positions change whenever something before them changes size, so an implementation tracks them in memory: each container knows where its children start, relative to itself (the reference algorithms).
Allocations and the address table records the design this replaced.
What a valid sequence is
At every transaction boundary, the sequence is the canonical encoding of exactly one value of the root type: it decodes by the root descriptor to the end, with no byte left over, and every encoding in it is canonical — minimal varints, valid UTF-8, discriminants that name variants, integers in range of their type, and zeros wherever a Fixed value pads.
A reader refuses a file whose sequence, after the journal is replayed, is not.
Inside a transaction, anything goes: the states between its records are never observed.
This is the journal’s one ordering rule, and it is all that is left of the ordering discipline allocations needed: nothing can dangle and nothing can leak, so nothing has to be published before something else is freed.
A canonical encoding makes the sequence a function of the root value, so two implementations that hold the same value hold the same bytes, and a test can compare a file’s sequence with the canonical encoding of the value in memory, byte for byte.
Free space
Free space is not represented on disk, and neither is liveness.
A page is live if it is reachable from a committed header; bytes within a data page are live if a span a chain reaches shows them.
Both are derived, and neither is recorded; see page states.
An implementation’s in-memory accounting of how much of each page is still relied upon — what drives its consolidation — is its own business, and nothing about it is persisted.
Reclamation is not part of this specification
Whether an implementation reclaims garbage, when it does so, and which pages it chooses are unconstrained.
A consolidation step writes live content into fresh pages and states the spans that show it again, producing a file indistinguishable from one that happened to be laid out that way from the start.
Two implementations with different policies therefore produce files that are equally valid and mutually readable.
An implementation that never consolidates is conforming; it will simply accumulate garbage until it runs out of space, which is a quality-of-implementation failure rather than a correctness one.
The one thing that is required is that reclamation be externally invisible: it must not change the content of any chain.
How the content is cut into spans, and which span ids it uses, are not content: a writer may split, merge, renumber and restate spans freely.
Partial loading, later
Loading part of a file means skipping a subtree without decoding it and without reading its spans, and one sequence offers neither.
A segment would therefore be a chain of its own, named from the sequence by a reference: one coarse kind of pointer, reintroduced deliberately, for exactly the subtrees an application declares.
The format already has three chains, so a fourth kind changes the header’s fields and a descriptor kind, not the span machinery; whether references to segments may move, and how their transactions relate to the sequence’s, is open.

spec/span-table.title: Span table
spec/span-table.content:
The span table describes the file’s content as chains of spans: each span shows a run of bytes and names the span that follows it.
It is the only structure in a kladde file that is interpreted rather than merely pointed at, and it is what makes a flush write a small delta rather than rewriting the world.
The idea
The file’s content is three byte strings, each kept as a chain of spans: a span shows a run of bytes — bytes in a data page, bytes in its entry itself, or zeros — and names the span after it.
The header names the first span of each chain: the sequence, which is the root value’s encoding, the schema, and the implementation’s private state.
An entry in a table page describes one span, and the entries of all live table pages together are the span table.
This is a piece table, the structure in which text editors have kept documents under editing since Xerox’s Bravo: a document is a list of pieces, each a run of some buffer, and an edit changes the list but never a buffer.
Here the buffers are data pages and entries, the pieces are spans, and the list is kept in the file, as the spans’ successor links.
A span is known by an id, not by a position, so an edit restates only the spans at the places where it cuts the chain.
A span’s id stays the same when bytes before it come or go, and the order of the content is recorded nowhere but in the links, so an edit changes what the spans at its cuts show and where they link, and nothing behind them.
A splice states one to three entries, counting the span of its new bytes, and a move three to six, wherever it lands and however long the content around it is.
Why links rather than positions.
Keying each piece by its position, as an extent tree keys extents by their offset in a file, would make an insertion change the key of every piece behind it, and each of those would have to be written again.
Links cost a reader nothing it does not pay anyway: kladde reads the file whole, so it walks each chain once, at open, and keeps a tree over the spans in memory.
A tree of spans on file would let a reader find a position without reading what lies before it, which kladde never does, and keeping the lengths in its interior nodes current would restate a path to the root at every edit.
Logical level
Entries
One kind of entry, in three forms:





















formshowsRef(id, length, address, next)length bytes of the file at address, inside the content of one Data pageInline(id, payload, next)its payload, 1 to 126 bytesZero(id, length, next)length zeros
id is the span’s id, and next the id of the span after it in its chain, or none at the end of the chain.
No span is empty.
Writing a span’s entry is called stating the span, and writing it again restating it.
Why Inline.
Below the encoded size of a Ref, a few bytes, the address would be as large as the data, and a short span that a page rewrite moves would cost a data page’s bytes as well as an entry.
Inline spans ride in the table pages, which the header rewrites every flush anyway; how short a span must be to be kept inline is a writer’s choice, below the format’s ceiling.
Why Zero.
Encodings without padding hold few zeros, but Fixed values and large preallocated arrays have runs of them, and a Zero states any length of them in a few bytes.
Resolution

A span id’s entry in the table page of highest epoch is its description.
An epoch holds at most one entry per id, so the winner is unique.
Only pages the header reaches through child references are consulted.
Each chain runs from the span its header field names, following next, and holds its spans’ content in that order.
A header field of 0 names an empty chain.
A file is invalid if a chain names an id that no entry describes, reaches a span twice, or shares a span with another chain.
A reader must check that no span is reached twice, which would otherwise trap the walk in an endless loop at open.
A file is invalid if a reached Ref shows bytes outside the content of a Data page, or in a page whose epoch exceeds the governing header’s (the epoch assertion).

A reader refuses an invalid file rather than return content from it.
Liveness follows: an entry is live if it is the newest of a span that some chain reaches.
There are no fragments, no sizes stated apart from content, no tombstones and no counts of mentions, and dropping any other entry can never change what the file holds.
A page rewrite states each live span in it again, under the span’s own id, and no entry elsewhere changes its meaning.
Rules for writers

At most one entry per span id and epoch.
The reach rule: a span that a chain reaches at the end of an epoch, but that no chain reached at the end of the epoch before, is stated in that epoch.
No two reached spans show the same byte of a data page.
This is a writer invariant that readers do not depend on; it keeps a data page’s live bytes a plain sum, see design directions.

Why the reach rule.
Entries of older epochs stay in their pages until those pages are rewritten, so without it a writer could link in a span id whose newest entry a page rewrite had dropped as dead, and an older entry of the same id, still in a page nobody rewrote, would show its stale bytes.
With it, a span id can be handed out again as soon as its span is no longer reached, since the new span’s entry is newer than any old one.
Readers cannot check the rule, since checking it would need the chains of the epoch before.
Physical format
Span-table pages follow the general page framing with kind == Table (0x01), and encode their payload in the content field.
The header page is always a table page.
Every table page contains zero or more references to other table pages followed by zero or more entries.
References between table pages form a tree rooted at the header page: every page reachable from the header other than the header itself is named by exactly one child_ref among the pages reachable from the header, and no child_ref names a header slot, page 0 or page 1.
; `content` field of a table page:
table_page := child_ref* 0:byte entry*
child_ref  := page_number_delta:varint
entry      := id_delta:varint tag:byte body next?
; bit 0 of tag: 1 if the next span is id + 1, and no `next` field follows;
;               0 if a `next` field follows the body
; tag >> 1 = 0:        Ref     body := length:varint address_delta:varint
; tag >> 1 = 1:        Zero    body := length:varint
; tag >> 1 = 2..127:   Inline  body := payload:byte{(tag >> 1) - 1}
next       := varint   ; 0: the chain ends here; else zigzag(next - id)

zigzag maps a signed integer to an unsigned one, 0, −1, 1, −2, … to 0, 1, 2, 3, …, as Protocol Buffers’ sint types do: zigzag(v) = (v << 1) ^ (v >> 63) on 64-bit two’s complement.
Delta encoding
A reader decodes a page in order, with a page_cursor, an id_cursor and an end_cursor, all starting at 0.

For each child_ref, page_cursor grows by page_number_delta, and is then the referenced page’s number.
Child references end at the delimiter byte 0, which cannot be a page_number_delta: the first child’s number is at least 2, since no child_ref names a header slot, and each later one exceeds its predecessor, since child references are sorted and the tree names each page once.
For each entry, id_cursor grows by id_delta, and is then the entry’s id.
Entries are sorted by id, so id_delta is at least 1; a delta of 0 makes the page invalid.
A Ref’s address is end_cursor + unzigzag(address_delta), after which end_cursor is that address plus the Ref’s length, where that Ref ended.
Zero and Inline entries leave end_cursor alone.
Entries continue to the end of content, which content_size gives.

next never names the span itself, which would be a cycle, so 0 is free to end the chain.
A next that would name the span itself, id 0, or an id outside the bounds makes the page invalid.
Delta encoding makes a wrong order unrepresentable: entries out of id order would need a negative id_delta, which a varint cannot hold.
A span written together with its neighbours — by a merge, by evacuation, or when its content was new — gets the next id, and its data follows theirs in the page, so its entry takes about five bytes: one each for the id delta, the tag and the address delta, and two for the length.
A worked example
A drawing whose sequence was one span, #1, showing 28 bytes at address 8203 (page 2, right after its framing), is renamed by a splice of 9 bytes over its first 3.
Afterwards, #2 holds the 9 new bytes inline and links to #1, and #1 is restated to show the last 25 bytes, at address 8206; the header’s sequence_head becomes 2.
If both entries go in the header, its content is:
00                                  no child references
01 00 19 9C 80 01 00                #1: id 0 + 1; Ref, next follows; length 25;
                                        address 0 + unzigzag(16412) = 8206; next: end of chain
01 14 57 6F 72 6C 64 20 6D 61 70 01 #2: id 1 + 1; Inline of 20 >> 1 − 1 = 9 bytes, next follows;
                                        "World map"; next = 2 + unzigzag(1) = 1

Had the splice landed in the middle of a sequence of a million spans, the same two entries, and one more for the span its start cut in two, would have described it: every span behind it keeps its entry although its bytes moved.
Notes on the physical format

The root table page is the current header slot, so before its content it carries the file-header fields, all covered by the header CRC.
A child_ref stores only a page number and no epoch.
The child’s own framing carries its epoch, and invariant I1 guarantees that a page referenced by a valid header is present and intact.
Nothing in the format constrains which page an entry lives in or how the tree is shaped; those are writer policies.
The tree is a directory, not a search structure: nothing descends it by key.
A reader should verify that the child_refs form a tree, so that cyclic references, or a page named twice in a graph that is not a tree, cannot trap it in a loop or have it decode a page twice.

Bounds
An implementation must support these, and must fail cleanly rather than silently wrap when an application exceeds them.

Span ids are 32-bit, and range from 1 to 2^32 − 2: 0 means “none” in the header and in next, and the largest id is left out so that id + 1, which an implicit successor names, is always a valid id.
So a file holds at most 2^32 − 2 spans per moment, and a varint-encoded id takes at most 5 bytes.
Page sizes are uniform throughout a file and given by the header’s log2_page_size, currently 4 KiB with 8, 16, 32, and 64 KiB reserved, so an offset within a page fits in 16 bits.
A Ref’s length is at most MAX_PAGE_CONTENT, the page size minus the 15 bytes of page framing: at most 2^12 − 15 bytes with 4 KiB pages, and 2^16 − 15 with 64 KiB ones; its varint takes at most 3 bytes.
An Inline payload is 1 to 126 bytes, and a Zero’s length 1 to 2^32 − 1.
Page numbers are 32-bit, so addresses fit in 48 bits (49 to point at the end of the file), an address_delta takes at most 7 bytes, and the largest file is 2^(32+12) bytes, about 17.6 TB, with 4 KiB pages.
Each chain’s content is shorter than 2^48 bytes, so a position in the sequence takes at most 7 bytes as a varint.
An entry’s framing — its encoded length without an Inline payload — is at most 21 bytes: a Ref with 5 bytes of id_delta, a tag byte, 3 bytes of length, 7 of address_delta and 5 of next.
The live Refs showing bytes of one Data page have lengths summing to at most 2^32 − 1, so that a reader can track a page’s live bytes in a 32-bit counter.
The writer invariant holds that sum below one page’s worth; the bound binds only files that let several reached spans show the same byte, which is legal and which a reader must therefore survive.
An encoded transaction, without framing, takes at most 2^32 − 1 bytes, so that its length prefix fits in 32 bits.
An external reference names 1 to MAX_PAGE_CONTENT bytes inside one page’s content, as a Ref does, so its length takes at most 3 bytes and its address at most 7.
Trying to encode a larger transaction must fail rather than silently cut it in parts.

Design directions
The byte-referenced-once invariant.
Not required for read correctness; keeping it makes data-page coverage a plain counter and consolidation locally decidable.
Relaxing it would enable copy-on-write clones and deduplication, at the price of refcounted coverage and clone-aware consolidation.
Since it is a writer invariant invisible to readers, choosing the strict form now costs nothing later.
Copy-on-write clones are not pursued: they add complexity and open a zip-bomb-like attack vector, and duplicating a value writes its encoding instead.
Per-page epochs versus per-entry epochs.
Per page is cheaper and imposes exactly one discipline — a rewrite states the newest entries — which consolidation requires anyway.
Overwrites inside a span: split or rewrite, not shadow.
An overwrite of bytes inside a span either splits the span in three around the written bytes, or writes the whole span again with the new bytes; which one is a writer’s choice (the flush).
A third form, an entry that overwrites part of a span by offset, would cost one entry and write no other byte, but it would bring back per-byte resolution, fragments inside spans, and liveness that counts them: most of what one entry per span removes.
It is the option to revisit if overwrites inside long, cold spans turn out to dominate a workload.
A smaller first step would be entries that only shrink or relink a span stated by an Inline entry of an earlier epoch, sparing a restatement of its payload of up to 126 bytes.
They would be restricted to spans that a chain reached at the end of the epoch before, by the reach rule; they would keep the Inline entry alive with a dead part of its payload; “newest wins” would then apply separately to an inline span’s payload, size and successor, so a span could have two live entries; and a page rewrite that writes the Inline entry again would have to state the span’s current size and successor with it.
Neither is adopted until measurements motivate it.
The Inline threshold.
The encoding fixes the ceiling at 126 bytes; the policy threshold belongs below it, and is an implementation choice rather than a format one.
See the implementation notes.

spec/tooling.title: Tooling
spec/tooling.content:
What a generic tool may assume about a kladde file it did not write, and how far it can get without knowing the application’s data structures.
Status: design intent.
kladde-rs’s kladde-inspect reports on any kladde file at all three levels below, without consolidating or exporting it; kladde-cpp’s kladde-store-dump prints a file’s sequence, fingerprint and schema.
The premise
A kladde file is self-describing in two independent ways.
It describes its storage: the span table is reachable from the header and describes every span of every chain, so the file’s structure is recoverable without any application knowledge at all — and without a scan, since everything is rooted.
And it describes its types: the schema chain says how every value in the sequence is encoded.
Together these mean a tool can be useful at three levels, each requiring strictly more than the last.
Level 1 — storage analysis
Requires: the page, span-table and sequence layers.
Requires no schema and no application knowledge.
A tool at this level can:

list every chain, its length, and its spans with the pages they show bytes of;
compute the live bytes, the description’s share, the file’s length, and therefore garbage;
report the per-page live fraction, and how much of the file is superseded pages awaiting reuse;
report the journal’s length, the payload pages it names, and how far the committed state lags behind it;
consolidate the file into a tight new one, and truncate it.

Rewriting a file from an external tool is safe for exactly the reason it is safe internally: it changes the content of no chain, so it is invisible to any reader.
This makes a standalone kladde compact genuinely implementable, which is unusual for a format of this kind.
What it cannot do is tell you what any of it means.
Level 2 — schema inspection
Requires: additionally the descriptor table.
Still requires no application knowledge.
A tool at this level can:

list every type in the file, with its kind, fields, variants, and whether it is fixed-size;
compute and display each type’s fingerprint;
identify the root type;
report which types are Opaque, and their declaring library and version — which is exactly the list of things a reader would need an implementation of;
diff two files’ schemas, or a file’s schema against an application’s.

This is what makes “why won’t my application open this file?” a diagnosable question rather than a guess.
Level 3 — structural export
Requires: additionally decoding the sequence by the descriptors.
Requires no application knowledge.
A tool at this level can render the whole content as text by decoding the sequence from the root descriptor, front to back: primitives decode by their code, structs by their fields, enums by their discriminant, sequences and maps by their count, text up to its terminator.
Every container is described structurally, there is no pointer graph to follow, and nothing can be unreachable, so the export is complete.
It stops only at Opaque types, whose content is by definition not decomposable: a tool can report their identity and version, and dump their bytes, which the encoding delimits, but not interpret them.
A canonical textual representation
The specification should eventually define a canonical textual representation of kladde files, and canonical conversions to and from common human-readable formats such as JSON.
These representations would cover the schema and the sequence: not the private chain, which any writer may keep, replace or clear without changing what the file holds, and not how either is cut into spans.
Two files with the same schema and sequence would then have the same text, whatever implementation wrote them and however often they were consolidated.
Cross-implementation testing
Tools are also the natural vehicle for testing the cross-language contract.
A conformance suite would consist of files written by each implementation, plus the expected level-2 and level-3 output for each, so that every implementation can be checked against every other’s output without either needing to link the other.
See Conformance.

superseded/allocations.title: Allocations and the address table
superseded/allocations.content:
Superseded. Replaced by the sequence and the span table.
The design between the relocatable heap and the present one: the file’s content as allocations that pointed at each other, described on copy-on-write pages by an address table of statements keyed by an allocation’s id and an offset in it.
Implemented in full by kladde-rs, whose branch address-table holds it as it stood, measured in most of the evaluation pages, and specified in detail; kladde-docs’ history holds every document of it, up to commit bf13c73.
What follows is its outline, and why it was replaced.
What it was
Allocations.
An allocation was an untyped byte range with a stable 32-bit id, a size, and content; ids were never zero, which left zero for a null pointer.
A value lived in an inline slot of a fixed INLINE_SIZE inside some allocation, and a value with content of variable length — a string, a vector, a map — owned allocations of its own, reached through a pointer serialized as the target’s id.
Every allocation had exactly one owning pointer, so the value graph was a tree of ownership; dropping or overwriting an owning value freed what it owned, recursively, in the same transaction and after the write that superseded the pointer.
The address table was a list of statements in table pages, each inheriting its page’s epoch: Ref(id, offset, size, address), Zero(id, offset, size), and Inline(id, offset, size, payload) stated content, each with a sizing variant that also said the allocation ended where the content ended; Size(id, n) stated a size alone, and Tombstone(id) ended an allocation’s existence.
Statements of different epochs were resolved per byte, the newest winning wherever it applied, and an allocation’s size was its newest size statement’s.
A writer had to keep the coverage rule — every byte that became part of an allocation was stated in that epoch — or truncated content could reappear.
The journal recorded effects on allocations: Free, Resize, Write, Splice, Copy and Move, each but Free bringing its allocation into existence.
Every mutation decomposed as prepare new, unreachable state → one publishing write → clean up what it replaced, an ordering discipline no type system enforced.
In memory, a loaded file was a fragment map from (id, offset) to the resolved content, a statement slab counting each live statement’s pins — the fragments, sizes and tombstones that kept it alive — an allocation map of sizes, fragment counts and mentions, and the page table.
A flush folded the journal into a piece table per allocation, took the fragments it changed, and derived every statement from one dirty set at the cut; consolidation added a fourth mechanism, description defragmentation, which rewrote stippled ranges of an allocation as one statement, materializing the zeros between them.
Values came in slotted and packed places, small values kept short content inline, and the Rust binding had Location, UniquePointer, store, load and free, with one hole through which load could mint a second owner.
Why it was replaced
The description was paid per allocation and a splice per allocation’s tail, so keeping either small made the other grow.
A small description wanted values inline in few allocations, and then each allocation was long, and a splice into one restated or rewrote everything behind it, since statements were keyed by their offset in the allocation: on kladde-svg’s small layout of the world map, flushes were measured to restate 24 bytes of statements per edit that had lain in leaves and to write 16 bytes of data again, growing with the length of the lists.
Cheap splices wanted short allocations, and then each value paid its pointer and statements, a cost that grew with the number of values rather than with their bytes.
No policy escaped that, because the format tied the unit of description to the unit of the data model.
The one-sequence design untied them: the description depends only on how a writer cuts one sequence into spans, and spans are keyed by id, so a splice restates the spans at its cuts and nothing behind them.
The file as one sequence, measured compares the two on the same drawings and texts.
Compared with the present design

What the present design pays for it: containers keep positions in memory, four bytes per variable-size element; offsets after a value whose size depends on its value are computed at run time; making a guard costs a lookup in its parent’s index and a change of size an update per level; an overwrite inside a long span splits it; every insertion into a sequence takes two records, the element and the count; moving a value between containers holds a transaction open; and partial loading needs segments, which need a pointer of their own.
The vocabulary that went with it
